en: Abhidharma-prakaraṇa-pāda-śāstra, Fascicle One.
Composed by the Venerable Vasumitra;
translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang by imperial decree.
Chapter One: An Exposition of the Five Categories. There are five dharmas:
first, form; second, mind; [third, mental factors; fourth, conditioned phenomena dissociated from mind; fifth, unconditioned phenomena].
3. Mental factors (caitta-dharma);
4. Formations dissociated from mind (citta-viprayukta-saṃskāra);
5. Unconditioned phenomena (asaṃskṛta).
What is form?
It refers to all that is form: all the four great elements and the form derived from the four great elements.
The four great elements are the earth element, the water element, the fire element, and the wind element.

Derived matter refers to the eye faculty, ear faculty, nose faculty, tongue faculty, body faculty; visible form, sound, odor, taste, and a portion of the tangible; as well as unmanifest form (*avijñapti-rūpa*).
What is mind? It refers to mind, thought, and consciousness.
What, moreover, is this?
That is to say, the six groups of consciousness: namely, eye-consciousness, ear-consciousness, nose-consciousness, tongue-consciousness, body-consciousness, and mind-consciousness.
What are the mental factors (caitta-dharma)?
It refers to those phenomena that are associated with the mind.
What, furthermore, are these? They are:

feeling, perception, volition, contact, attention, desire, resolve, mindfulness, concentration, wisdom, faith, diligence, applied thought, sustained thought, negligence, non-negligence, the roots of the wholesome, the roots of the unwholesome, the roots of the indeterminate; all fetters, bonds, latent tendencies, secondary afflictions, and envelopments; and all forms of knowledge, all views, and all clear realizations.
Furthermore, whatever other dharmas of this kind are associated with the mind are collectively termed mental factors (*caitasika-dharma*).
What are the formations dissociated from the mind (*citta-viprayukta-saṃskāra*)? They are those dharmas that are not associated with the mind.

What, then, are these? They are: acquisition (*prāpti*), the attainment of non-perception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*), the attainment of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*), the state of non-perception (*asaṃjñika*), the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*), the commonality of group (*nikāya-sabhāga*), acquisition of support (*āśraya-prāpti*), acquisition of entity (*vastu-prāpti*), acquisition of location (*sthāna-prāpti*), birth (*jāti*), aging (*jarā*), duration (*sthiti*), impermanence (*anityatā*), the body of names (*nāma-kāya*), the body of phrases (*pada-kāya*), and the body of phonemes (*vyañjana-kāya*). Furthermore, all other such factors that are dissociated from the mind are collectively termed formations dissociated from the mind (*citta-viprayukta-saṃskāra*).
What is the unconditioned?
It refers to the three unconditioned phenomena:
first, space; [second, analytical cessation; third, non-analytical cessation].
2. Cessation not through deliberation (apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha);
3. Cessation through deliberation (pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha).
What is the earth element?
That is to say, the nature of solidity.
What is the water element?
It is the nature of moisture.
What is the fire element?
It is the nature of heat.
What is the wind element?
It refers to the nature of lightness and mobility.
What is the eye faculty?
It refers to the translucent matter that serves as the basis for visual consciousness.
What is the ear faculty?
It is the translucent matter that serves as the basis for auditory consciousness.
What is the nose faculty?
It refers to the translucent matter that serves as the basis for olfactory consciousness.
What is the tongue faculty?
It refers to the translucent matter that serves as the basis for gustatory consciousness.
What is the body-faculty (*kāyendriya*)?
It is the translucent matter (*rūpaprasāda*) that serves as the basis for body-consciousness (*kāyavijñāna*).
What is matter (*rūpa*)?
That is to say, all forms whatsoever—whether of beautiful color, of ugly color, or those intermediate between the two—which appear as the locus of color:
such forms are cognized by two consciousnesses, namely, eye-consciousness and mental consciousness.
In this regard, one class [of teachers] maintains that the eye-consciousness cognizes first, and having been experienced by the eye-consciousness, the mental consciousness subsequently cognizes it.
What of sound?
There are two types: sound caused by appropriated primary elements (*mahābhūta*) and sound caused by non-appropriated primary elements.
Thus, these various sounds are cognized by two consciousnesses, namely, the ear-consciousness (*śrotra-vijñāna*) and the mental consciousness (*mano-vijñāna*).
Among these, one class [of sounds] is first cognized by the ear-consciousness; once the ear-consciousness has apprehended them, the mental consciousness subsequently cognizes them.
What is odor?
It refers to all odors whatsoever—whether pleasant, unpleasant, or neutral—that are smelled by the nose.
Such odors are cognized by two consciousnesses: namely, olfactory consciousness and mental consciousness.

In this context, one class [of consciousness] first cognizes by means of olfactory consciousness; once the olfactory consciousness has experienced it, the mental consciousness subsequently cognizes it.
What is taste?
It refers to all tastes whatsoever—whether agreeable, disagreeable, or conducive to equanimity—that are tasted by the tongue.
These various tastes are cognized by two consciousnesses, namely, the tongue-consciousness and the mental consciousness.
In this regard, one class [of beings] first cognizes them with the tongue-consciousness; once the tongue-consciousness has experienced them, the mental consciousness subsequently cognizes them.
What is the "one part of the tangible"?
It refers to smoothness, roughness, lightness, heaviness, cold, hunger, and thirst—these are what the body touches.
These various tangibles, together with the four great elements, are cognized by two types of consciousness: namely, body-consciousness (*kāyavijñāna*) and mental-consciousness (*manovijñāna*).
In this regard, for one type [of person], the body-consciousness cognizes first; once the body-consciousness has experienced it, the mental consciousness subsequently cognizes it.
What is non-informative matter (*avijñapti-rūpa*)?
It is matter included within the sphere of mental objects (*dharmāyatana-saṃgṛhīta-rūpa*).
These, together with the five material sense-faculties, are at all times cognized by a single consciousness, namely, the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*).
What is visual consciousness?
It is that which, depending on the visual faculty, individually discerns visible forms.
What is auditory consciousness?
It is the distinct discernment of sounds based upon the ear-faculty.
What is olfactory consciousness?
That is to say, it is the distinct discernment of odors based on the olfactory faculty.
What is tongue-consciousness?
It is the distinct discernment of tastes based on the gustatory faculty.
What is body-consciousness?
It is the distinct discernment of tactile objects based on the body-faculty.
What is mind-consciousness?
This refers to the discernment of all phenomena based on the mental faculty (*manas*).
What is feeling (*vedanā*)?
It is the nature of experiencing.
This is of three kinds: namely, pleasant feeling, painful feeling, and neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling.
What is perception?
It is the nature of grasping mental images.
This is of three kinds: namely, small perception, great perception, and immeasurable perception.
What is volition?
It is the nature of mental formation, which is precisely mental action (manas-karman).
This is of three kinds: namely, wholesome volition, unwholesome volition, and neutral volition.
What is contact?
It is the nature of the conjunction of the three.
This is of three kinds: namely, contact conducive to pleasant feeling, contact conducive to painful feeling, and contact conducive to neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling.
What is attention?
It is the nature of mental alertness.
This is of three kinds: namely, the attention of one in training (*śaikṣa*), the attention of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), and the attention of one who is neither in training nor beyond training.
What is desire? It is the nature of delighting in activity.
What is resolve (adhimokṣa)?
It refers to the nature of the mind that is currently resolving, has resolved, or will resolve.
What is mindfulness (smṛti)?
It refers to the nature of the mind’s clear recollection.
What is concentration?
It refers to one-pointedness of mind.
What is wisdom (prajñā)?
It is the nature of the mind that discerns phenomena (dharmapravicaya).
What is faith (śraddhā)?
What is mental clarity? It is the nature of the mind’s lucidity.
What is diligence?
It is the nature of the mind’s fortitude.
What is vitarka?
It is the nature of coarse mental movement.
What is vicāra?
It refers to the nature of subtle mental fluctuation.
What is heedlessness?
It refers to the nature of not cultivating wholesome dharmas.
What is non-negligence?
It is the nature of cultivating wholesome dharmas.
What are the roots of goodness?
These are the three roots of goodness: namely, the root of goodness of non-attachment, the root of goodness of non-hatred, and the root of goodness of non-delusion.
What are the unwholesome roots?
They are the three unwholesome roots: namely, the unwholesome root of attachment, the unwholesome root of hatred, and the unwholesome root of delusion.
What are the indeterminate roots?
They are the four indeterminate roots, namely: indeterminate craving, indeterminate views, indeterminate pride, and indeterminate ignorance.

There are nine kinds of fetters, namely: the fetter of craving, the fetter of aversion, the fetter of pride, the fetter of ignorance, the fetter of views, the fetter of grasping, the fetter of doubt, the fetter of envy, and the fetter of stinginess.
What is the fetter of attachment (*anunaya-saṃyojana*)?
It refers to greed for the three realms.
What is the fetter of aversion (*pratigha-saṃyojana*)?
That is to say, it is that which can cause harm to sentient beings.
What is the fetter of pride (*māna-saṃyojana*)?

It refers to the seven types of pride: namely, pride (*māna*), excessive pride (*atimāna*), pride beyond pride (*mānātimāna*), the pride of self (*asmimāna*), overweening pride (*adhimāna*), inferiority pride (*ūnamāna*), and false pride (*mithyāmāna*).

Pride (*māna*) is the state of considering oneself superior to those who are inferior, or equal to those who are one's equals; by means of this, one is currently proud, has been proud, or will become proud, such that the mind is uplifted and the mind is haughty and contemptuous.

Excessive pride (*atimāna*) consists in regarding oneself as superior to those who are equal, or regarding oneself as equal to those who are superior; by means of this, one has been proud, is now proud, or will become proud, such that the mind is uplifted and the mind relies upon itself with contempt.

*Abhimāna* (conceit beyond conceit) is to claim superiority over those who are superior; by means of this, one is currently conceited, has been conceited, or will be conceited, with the mind uplifted and the mind characterized by arrogance and disdain.

*Māna* (self-conceit) is to regard the five aggregates of clinging as "I" or "mine" through such observation; by means of this, one is currently conceited, has been conceited, or will be conceited, with the mind uplifted and the mind characterized by arrogance and disdain.

One who possesses overweening pride (*adhimāna*) claims, regarding superior and sublime dharmas of realization not yet attained, "I have already attained them"; regarding superior and sublime states of realization not yet reached, "I have already reached them"; regarding superior and sublime dharmas of realization not yet touched, "I have already touched them"; and regarding superior and sublime dharmas of realization not yet realized, "I have already realized them. Due to this correct pride—having been proud, being proud, or about to be proud—the mind becomes uplifted and the mind becomes conceited and disdainful.

Inferiority pride (*ūnamāna*) consists in regarding oneself as slightly inferior when one is actually much superior to others; by means of this, through present, past, or future conceit, the mind becomes uplifted and the mind becomes arrogant and disdainful.

Pride of error (*mithyāmāna*) is when one claims to possess virtues that one actually lacks; by means of this, through present, past, or future pride, the mind becomes uplifted and the mind becomes arrogant and contemptuous.
What is the fetter of ignorance?
It refers to the lack of wisdom regarding the three realms.
What is the fetter of views?
This refers to three views: namely, the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), the view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*), and false view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*).

Regarding the view of a self-identity: it consists of observing and grasping at the five aggregates of clinging (*pañcopādānaskandha*) and so forth as "self" or "mine," and from this, giving rise to acceptance, pleasure, wisdom, contemplation, and vision.

The view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*) consists of observing the five aggregates of clinging (*pañcopādānaskandha*) and so forth, and adhering to them as either annihilated or eternal; from this, one gives rise to acceptance, pleasure, wisdom, contemplation, and vision.

Wrong view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*) consists of slandering the cause, slandering the result, slandering functional efficacy, or denying real entities; from this, one gives rise to acceptance, pleasure, wisdom, contemplation, and vision.
What is the fetter of clinging?
It refers to the two types of clinging: namely, clinging to views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*) and clinging to precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*).

As for clinging to views, it is the persistent observation and grasping of the five aggregates of clinging as being supreme, excellent, superior, or ultimate; based upon this, one gives rise to acceptance, pleasure, wisdom, contemplation, and view.

The clinging to precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*) consists in regarding the five aggregates of clinging as capable of purification, capable of liberation, or capable of deliverance, and thereby giving rise to acceptance, pleasure, wisdom, contemplation, and views.
What is the fetter of doubt?
It is hesitation regarding the Truths.
What is the fetter of envy?
This refers to a mind of envy and jealousy.
What is the fetter of stinginess?
It refers to a mind of meanness and parsimony.
What are the bonds?
The fetters (*saṃyojana*) are also called bonds.
Furthermore, there are three bonds: the bond of greed (*rāga-bandhana*), the bond of hatred (*dveṣa-bandhana*), and the bond of delusion (*moha-bandhana*).

There are seven types of latent dispositions (*anuśaya*): namely, the latent disposition of sensual desire, the latent disposition of aversion, the latent disposition of attachment to existence, the latent disposition of pride, the latent disposition of ignorance, the latent disposition of views, and the latent disposition of doubt.

The latent tendency of sensual desire (*kāmarāgānuśaya*) is of five kinds: namely, the greed abandoned through the vision of suffering, origin, cessation, and the path, as well as that abandoned through cultivation, all pertaining to the desire realm.

The latent tendency of aversion (*pratighānuśaya*) is of five kinds: namely, the aversion abandoned through the vision of suffering, origin, cessation, and the path, as well as that abandoned through cultivation.
There are ten types of the latent tendency of attachment (*rāgānuśaya*): namely, five pertaining to the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*) and five pertaining to the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*).

The five pertaining to the realm of form refer to the attachment abandoned through the vision of suffering, origin, cessation, and the path, as well as that abandoned through cultivation, all of which pertain to the realm of form.
The five [latent dispositions] bound to the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) are likewise.

There are fifteen types of the latent disposition of pride (*mānānuśaya*): namely, five bound to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), five bound to the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), and five bound to the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*).

The five [types of pride] bound to the desire realm refer to the pride to be abandoned through the vision of suffering, origin, cessation, and the path, as well as that to be abandoned through cultivation, all bound to the desire realm.
The same applies to those bound to the form and formless realms, each having five.

The latent tendencies of ignorance (*avidyā-anuśaya*) are of fifteen kinds: namely, five bound to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*), five bound to the form realm (*rūpadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*), and five bound to the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*).

The five bound to the desire realm refer to the ignorance associated with the desire realm that is to be abandoned through the vision of suffering, origin, cessation, and the path, as well as that to be abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*).
The same applies to the five types each belonging to the form realm and the formless realm.

There are thirty-six kinds of latent tendencies of views (*dṛṣṭyanuśaya*): namely, twelve belonging to the desire realm, twelve belonging to the form realm, and twelve belonging to the formless realm.

The twelve [factors] bound to the desire realm refer to: the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and the view of extreme adherence (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*) bound to the desire realm; wrong view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*), the esteeming of views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*), and the esteeming of precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*) to be abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkha*) and the path (*mārga*); and wrong view and the esteeming of views to be abandoned through the vision of origination (*samudaya*) and cessation (*nirodha*).
The twelve types [of latent dispositions] bound to the form and formless realms are likewise.
There are twelve kinds of doubt-latent dispositions (*vicikitsā-anuśaya*): namely, four bound to the desire realm, four bound to the form realm, and four bound to the formless realm.
The four [types of] doubt bound to the desire realm refer to the doubts to be abandoned through the vision of suffering, origin, cessation, and the path within the desire realm.
The same applies to the four for each of those bound to the form and formless realms.
What are the secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*)?
This means that all latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) are also called secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*).

However, there are secondary afflictions that are not called latent dispositions; these refer to all other defiled mental factors (*caitasika*) within the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*), excluding the latent dispositions themselves.

There are eight kinds of fetters (*paryavasthāna*), namely: torpor (*styāna*), restlessness (*auddhatya*), sleep (*middha*), regret (*kaukṛtya*), envy (*īrṣyā*), avarice (*mātsarya*), lack of shame (*āhrīkya*), and lack of dread (*anapatrāpya*).

All that exists as knowledge consists of ten knowledges (*jñāna*), namely: dharma-knowledge (*dharmajñāna*), subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*), knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*), conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*), knowledge of suffering (*duḥkhajñāna*), knowledge of origin (*samudayajñāna*), knowledge of cessation (*nirodhajñāna*), knowledge of the path (*mārgajñāna*), knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*), and knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*).
What is the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*)?

It refers to the untainted knowledge (*anāsravajñāna*) that takes as its object the conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) bound to the desire realm, the causes of those phenomena, the cessation of those phenomena, and the path capable of abandoning them.
Furthermore, the untainted knowledge that takes as its object this knowledge of phenomena and the stages of the knowledge of phenomena is also called the knowledge of phenomena.
What is subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*)?

It refers to all untainted knowledge (*anāsrava-jñāna*) that takes as its object the conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) pertaining to the form and formless realms, the causes of those conditioned phenomena, the cessation of those conditioned phenomena, and the path capable of abandoning those conditioned phenomena.
Furthermore, the untainted knowledges (*anāsrava-jñāna*) pertaining to the subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*) and its stage are also termed subsequent knowledge.
What is the knowledge of others' minds (*paracitta-jñāna*)?

It refers to any knowledge that is produced through cultivation (*bhāvanā-maya*), which is the fruit of cultivation and its support, and which is attained and not lost once cultivated; it consists of the mental states and mental factors (*citta-caitta*) of others belonging to the desire and form realms when they are conjoined and manifest, as well as a portion of the untainted mental states and mental factors of others—all these are termed the knowledge of others' minds.
What is conventional knowledge?
It refers to all contaminated wisdom (*sāsravaprajñā*).
What is the knowledge of suffering (*duḥkhajñāna*)?
It refers to the untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-jñāna*) that arises from contemplating the five aggregates of clinging (*pañca-upādānaskandha*) as impermanent, suffering, empty, and non-self.
What is the knowledge of origin (*samudaya-jñāna*)?
It refers to the untainted wisdom that arises from contemplating the causes of tainted phenomena (*sāsrava-hetu*) as cause, origin, production, and condition.
What is the knowledge of cessation (*nirodha-jñāna*)?

It refers to the untainted knowledge (*anāsrava-jñāna*) that arises from contemplating cessation, tranquility, excellence, and renunciation with respect to analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).
What is the knowledge of the path (*mārga-jñāna*)?
It refers to the untainted knowledge (*anāsrava-jñāna*) that arises from contemplating the Noble Path as the path, as suchness, as practice, and as deliverance.
What is the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣaya-jñāna*)?

It is the self-awareness: "I have known suffering, I have abandoned its origin, I have realized its cessation, and I have cultivated the path. The wisdom, vision, clarity, awakening, understanding, insight, light, and contemplation that arise from this are all termed the knowledge of exhaustion.

What is the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpāda-jñāna*)? It refers to one’s own thorough realization: "I have already known suffering and shall not need to know it again; I have already abandoned the origin and shall not need to abandon it again; I have already realized cessation and shall not need to realize it again; I have already cultivated the path and shall not need to cultivate it again. From this, there arise knowledge, vision, clarity, awakening, understanding, wisdom, light, and contemplation—all of which are termed the knowledge of non-arising.
Regarding all that is called "view" (*dṛṣṭi*), it should be understood that while all forms of knowledge (*jñāna*) are also called views, there are views that are not knowledge;
namely, the eight types of patience (*kṣānti*) at the conclusion of the clear realizations (*abhisamaya*).
The first is the patience regarding the dharma-knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-dharma-jñāna-kṣānti*).
2. The patience regarding the subsequent knowledge of suffering;
3. The patience regarding the dharma-knowledge of origin;
4. The patience regarding the subsequent knowledge of origin;
Five: the receptivity to the knowledge of the dharma regarding cessation;
six: the receptivity to the subsequent knowledge regarding cessation;
seven: the receptivity to the knowledge of the dharma regarding the path.

Regarding the eight types of patience associated with the subsequent knowledge of the path (*mārga-anvaya-jñāna-kṣānti*): whatever constitutes realization (*abhisamaya*), whether it be wisdom (*jñāna*) or vision (*darśana*), is collectively termed "realization.
What is its acquisition (*prāpti*)?
This refers to the attainment of the various dharmas.
What is the state of non-ideation (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*)?

It is the cessation of mind and mental factors preceded by the mental attention of the perception of renunciation, occurring when one has already abandoned the defilements of the Sphere of Universal Purity (*śubhakṛtsna*) but has not yet abandoned the defilements of the higher spheres.
What is the attainment of cessation?

It refers to the cessation of mind and mental factors, preceded by the mental attention that brings about the stilling of perceptions, for one who has already become detached from the defilements of the sphere of nothingness.
What is the state of non-perception?
This refers to the cessation of the mind and mental factors upon being born among the non-percipient beings (*asaṃjñisattva*) in the heavens.
What is the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*)?
It is the lifespan (*āyus*) of the three realms.
What is the homogeneous character of beings (*nikāya-sabhāga*)?
It refers to the commonality among sentient beings.
What is acquisition (*prāpti*) based upon?
This refers to the acquisition of the basis.
What is the acquisition of the entities that constitute the bases?
It refers to the acquisition of the aggregates (*skandha*).
What is acquisition (*prāpti*)?
It refers to the acquisition of the internal and external sense bases (*āyatana*).
What is birth (*jāti*)?
This means causing the aggregates to arise.
What is aging?
It means causing the aggregates to mature.
What is stability?
It is that which prevents already arisen conditioned phenomena from decaying.
What is impermanence?
That which causes already arisen conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) to cease and perish is called "destruction.
What is the "body" (*kāya*)?
It is the "designation" (*adhivacana*).
What is the body of phrases (*padakāya*)?
It refers to the completion of syllables (*vyañjana*).
What is the body of phonemes (*vyañjanakāya*)?
This refers to the collection of syllables. What is space?
It is that which is empty and void in essence, vast and unobstructed, not hindering the movement of matter.
What is non-analytical cessation?
It is cessation that is not dissociation [from defilements].
What is analytical cessation?
That is to say, cessation is disjunction.
Chapter Two, Part One: Exposition of the Various Knowledges (*Jñāna-nirdeśa*) from the *Abhidharmaprakaraṇapāda-śāstra*. There are ten knowledges, as previously explained.
What is the object of dharma-knowledge?
It takes as its object all conditioned phenomena (saṃskāra) bound to the desire realm, as well as a portion of untainted (anāsrava) phenomena.
What is the object of subsequent knowledge (anvaya-jñāna)?
That is to say, it takes as its object the conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) associated with the form and formless realms, as well as a portion of untainted (*anāsrava*) phenomena.
What is the object of the knowledge of others' minds?

It takes as its object the minds and mental factors of others that are associated with the desire and form realms and are present and manifest, as well as a portion of the minds and mental factors of others that are untainted.
What is the object of conventional knowledge?
It takes all phenomena as its object.
What is the object of the knowledge of suffering?
That is to say, it takes the five aggregates of grasping as its object.
What is the object of the knowledge of origination?
It takes the causes of that which is with outflows as its object.
What is the object of the knowledge of cessation?
It is the analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).
What is the object of the knowledge of the path (*mārgajñāna*)?
That is to say, it takes the dharmas of those in training (śaikṣa) and those beyond training (aśaikṣa) as its object.
What is the object of the knowledge of exhaustion (kṣayajñāna)?
It takes all conditioned dharmas (saṃskṛtadharma) and analytical cessation (pratisaṃkhyānirodha) as its object.
What is the object of the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*)?
It takes as its object all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*) and analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyānirodha*).

For what reason does the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*) take as its object the formations (*saṃskāra*) bound to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*) and a portion of the untainted phenomena (*anāsravadharma*)?
Answer:

Because dharma-knowledge (dharma-jñāna) knows the conditioned phenomena (saṃskāra) bound to the desire realm, the causes of those phenomena, the cessation of those phenomena, and the path capable of abandoning them.
For what reason does subsequent knowledge (anvaya-jñāna) take as its object the conditioned phenomena bound to the form and formless realms, as well as a portion of the untainted (anāsrava) dharmas?
Answer:

Because subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*) knows the formations (*saṃskāra*) associated with the form and formless realms, the causes of those formations, the cessation of those formations, and the path capable of abandoning them.

For what reason does the knowledge of others' minds (*paracitta-jñāna*) take as its object the combined and manifest minds and mental factors of others associated with the desire and form realms, as well as a portion of the uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) minds and mental factors of others?
Answer:

Because the knowledge of others' minds cognizes the minds and mental factors of others that are bound to the desire and form realms and are currently manifesting in combination, as well as a portion of the uncontaminated (anāsrava) minds and mental factors of others.
Why, then, does conventional knowledge (saṃvṛtijñāna) take all phenomena as its object?
Answer:

Conventional knowledge knows all phenomena, because they are either produced by reasoning in accordance with reality, produced by reasoning not in accordance with reality, or produced by neither reasoning in accordance with reality nor reasoning not in accordance with reality.
Why does the knowledge of suffering take the five aggregates of clinging as its object?
Answer:
Because the knowledge of suffering knows that the five aggregates of clinging are impermanent, suffering, empty, and non-self.
Why does the knowledge of origination (samudaya-jñāna) take contaminated causes as its object?
Answer:
Because the knowledge of origination knows that contaminated causes are the cause, the origination, the production, and the condition [of suffering].
Why does the knowledge of cessation take analytical cessation as its object?
Answer:
Because the knowledge of cessation knows analytical cessation as cessation, tranquility, excellence, and renunciation.
Why does the knowledge of the path (mārgajñāna) take the dharmas of those in training (śaikṣa) and those beyond training (aśaikṣa) as its object?
Answer:
Because the knowledge of the path knows the path, the suchness, the progression, and the emergence of the dharmas of those in training and those beyond training.
Why does the knowledge of exhaustion (kṣayajñāna) take all conditioned phenomena (saṃskṛtadharma) and analytical cessation (pratisaṃkhyānirodha) as its objects?
Answer:
Because the knowledge of exhaustion fully cognizes for itself: "I have known suffering; I have abandoned the origin; I have realized cessation; I have cultivated the path."
Why does the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*) take all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*) and analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyānirodha*) as its objects?

Answer: Because the knowledge of non-arising thoroughly cognizes for itself: "I have already known suffering; it need not be known again. I have already abandoned the origin; it need not be abandoned again. I have already realized cessation; it need not be realized again. I have already cultivated the path; it need not be cultivated again. Thus [it takes these as its objects].
How many knowledges (*jñāna*) does the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*) consist of in its entirety, and how many knowledges does it consist of in part?
Answer:

The knowledge of phenomena consists of the knowledge of phenomena in its entirety, and seven knowledges in part; namely, the knowledge of others' minds, the knowledge of suffering, the knowledge of origin, the knowledge of cessation, the knowledge of the path, the knowledge of exhaustion, and the knowledge of non-arising.
How many knowledges (*jñāna*) does subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*) comprise in their entirety, and how many does it comprise as partial portions?
Answer:

Subsequent knowledge comprises subsequent knowledge in its entirety, and seven knowledges as partial portions, namely: the knowledge of others' minds (*paracitta-jñāna*), the knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-jñāna*), the knowledge of origin (*samudaya-jñāna*), the knowledge of cessation (*nirodha-jñāna*), the knowledge of the path (*mārga-jñāna*), the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣaya-jñāna*), and the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpāda-jñāna*).
How many knowledges (*jñāna*) are the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*) in its entirety, and how many are it in part?
Answer:

The knowledge of others' minds is the knowledge of others' minds in its entirety; it is also a partial portion of four knowledges, namely: the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*), subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*), conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*), and the knowledge of the path (*mārgajñāna*).
How many knowledges (*jñāna*) does conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*) comprise in their entirety, and how many does it comprise as partial portions?
Answer:
Conventional knowledge comprises conventional knowledge in its entirety, and one knowledge as a partial portion, namely, the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*).
How many knowledges (*jñāna*) is the knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-jñāna*) in its entirety, and how many are it in part?
Answer:

The knowledge of suffering is the knowledge of suffering in its entirety; it is also a partial portion of four knowledges, namely: the knowledge of phenomena (*dharma-jñāna*), subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*), the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣaya-jñāna*), and the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpāda-jñāna*).
It should be understood that the same applies to the knowledge of origination (*samudaya-jñāna*) and the knowledge of cessation (*nirodha-jñāna*).
As for the knowledge of the path (*mārga-jñāna*), how many knowledges does it comprise in their entirety, and how many knowledges does it comprise in part?
Answer:

The knowledge of the path (*mārgajñāna*) is the entirety of the knowledge of the path and a partial portion of five knowledges, namely: the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*), subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*), knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*), knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*), and knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*).
How many knowledges (*jñāna*) is the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) complete in its entirety, and how many knowledges does it comprise as partial portions?
Answer:

The knowledge of exhaustion is complete in its entirety as the knowledge of exhaustion; it comprises partial portions of six knowledges, namely: the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*), subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*), the knowledge of suffering (*duḥkhajñāna*), the knowledge of origin (*samudayajñāna*), the knowledge of cessation (*nirodhajñāna*), and the knowledge of the path (*mārgajñāna*).
The same applies to the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*).
Why is the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*) considered the entirety of the knowledge of phenomena?
Answer:
Because dharma-knowledge knows the formations (saṃskāra) bound to the desire realm, the causes of those formations, the cessation of those formations, and the path capable of abandoning them.
For what reason is dharma-knowledge a partial aspect of the knowledge of others' minds?
Answer:
Because dharma-knowledge (dharma-jñāna) cognizes the uncontaminated minds and mental factors of others within the path that severs the conditioned phenomena (saṃskāra) bound to the desire realm.
For what reason is dharma-knowledge a portion of the knowledge of suffering (duḥkha-jñāna)?
Answer:
Because dharma-knowledge cognizes the five aggregates of clinging bound to the desire realm as impermanent, suffering, empty, and non-self.
For what reason is dharma-knowledge a partial aspect of the knowledge of origin?
Answer:
Because dharma-knowledge knows the causes, origins, productions, and conditions of all conditioned phenomena (saṃskāra) bound to the desire realm.
For what reason is dharma-knowledge a partial aspect of the knowledge of cessation?
Answer:
Because dharma-knowledge knows the cessation of all conditioned phenomena (saṃskāra) bound to the desire realm as cessation, peace, excellence, and renunciation.
For what reason is dharma-knowledge a partial aspect of path-knowledge?
Answer:

Because dharma-knowledge (dharma-jñāna) knows the path that severs the conditioned phenomena (saṃskāra) bound to the desire realm, as well as its path-characteristic (mārga), truth-characteristic (nyāya), practice-characteristic (pratipatti), and deliverance-characteristic (nairyāṇika).
For what reason is dharma-knowledge a portion of the knowledge of exhaustion (kṣaya-jñāna)?

Answer: Dharma-knowledge itself fully cognizes: "I have already known that all conditioned phenomena (saṃskāra) bound to the desire realm are suffering; I have already abandoned the origin of all conditioned phenomena bound to the desire realm; I have already realized the cessation of all conditioned phenomena bound to the desire realm; and I have already cultivated the path capable of abandoning all conditioned phenomena bound to the desire realm."
Why is dharma-knowledge (dharma-jñāna) a portion of the knowledge of non-arising (anutpāda-jñāna)?

Answer: Because through dharma-knowledge one fully cognizes for oneself: "I have already known the suffering associated with the desire realm; it need not be known again. I have already abandoned the origin associated with the desire realm; it need not be abandoned again. I have already realized the cessation associated with the desire realm; it need not be realized again. I have already cultivated the path that abandons the [suffering] associated with the desire realm; it need not be cultivated again. Thus, dharma-knowledge is a portion of the knowledge of non-arising.
Why is subsequent knowledge (anvaya-jñāna) considered to be subsequent knowledge in its entirety?
Answer:

Because subsequent knowledge cognizes all conditioned phenomena (saṃskāra) pertaining to the form and formless realms, the causes of those conditioned phenomena, the cessation of those conditioned phenomena, and the path capable of abandoning them.
Why is subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*) a portion of the knowledge of others' minds (*para-citta-jñāna*)?
Answer:

Because subsequent knowledge knows the uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) minds and mental factors of others within the paths capable of abandoning the conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) associated with the form and formless realms.
Why is subsequent knowledge (anvaya-jñāna) a portion of the knowledge of suffering (duḥkha-jñāna)?
Answer:
Because subsequent knowledge knows that the five aggregates of grasping (pañca-upādāna-skandha) bound to the form and formless realms are impermanent, suffering, empty, and non-self.
Why is subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*) a portion of the knowledge of origin (*samudaya-jñāna*)?
Answer:
Because subsequent knowledge knows the causes, origins, productions, and conditions of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) bound to the form and formless realms.
Why is subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*) a partial aspect of the knowledge of cessation (*nirodha-jñāna*)?
Answer:
Because subsequent knowledge knows the cessation of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) bound to the realms of form and formlessness as cessation, tranquility, excellence, and renunciation.
Why is subsequent knowledge (anvaya-jñāna) a portion of the knowledge of the path (mārga-jñāna)?
Answer:

Because subsequent knowledge knows the paths that can sever the conditioned phenomena (saṃskāra) associated with the form and formless realms as being the path, the truth, the practice, and the escape.
Why is subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*) a portion of the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣaya-jñāna*)?

Answer: Because subsequent knowledge itself fully cognizes: "I have known that all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) associated with the form and formless realms are suffering; I have abandoned the origin of all conditioned phenomena associated with the form and formless realms; I have realized the cessation of all conditioned phenomena associated with the form and formless realms; and I have cultivated the path that leads to the abandonment of all conditioned phenomena associated with the form and formless realms."
Why is subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*) a portion of the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpāda-jñāna*)? Answer: Because subsequent knowledge itself fully comprehends:

"I have already known the suffering of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) associated with the form and formless realms; it need not be known again. I have already abandoned the origin of all conditioned phenomena associated with the form and formless realms; it need not be abandoned again. I have already realized the cessation of all conditioned phenomena associated with the form and formless realms; it need not be realized again. I have already cultivated the path that leads to the abandonment of all conditioned phenomena associated with the form and formless realms; it need not be cultivated again. Therefore, it is so.
Why is the knowledge of others' minds considered the entirety of the knowledge of others' minds?
Answer:

Because the knowledge of others' minds cognizes the minds and mental factors of others that are bound to the desire and form realms when they are conjoined and manifest, as well as a portion of the uncontaminated (anāsrava) minds and mental factors of others.
Why is the knowledge of others' minds a portion of the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*)?
Answer:
Because the knowledge of others' minds cognizes the uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) minds and mental factors of others within the path that severs those formations (*saṃskāra*) bound to the desire realm.
Why is the knowledge of others' minds (paracittajñāna) a portion of subsequent knowledge (anvayajñāna)?
Answer:

Because the knowledge of others' minds cognizes the uncontaminated (anāsrava) minds and mental factors of others within the paths capable of abandoning the conditioned phenomena (saṃskāra) associated with the realms of form and formlessness.
Why is the knowledge of others' minds (paracittajñāna) a portion of conventional knowledge (saṃvṛtijñāna)?
Answer:
Because the knowledge of others' minds cognizes the other's contaminated (sāsrava) minds and mental factors (citta-caitta).
Why is the knowledge of others' minds (paracittajñāna) a portion of the knowledge of the path (mārgajñāna)?
Answer:
Because the knowledge of others' minds cognizes the other's uncontaminated (anāsrava) minds and mental factors within the noble path.
Why is conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*) the entirety of conventional knowledge?
Answer:

Because conventional knowledge cognizes all phenomena—whether they are induced by correct reasoning (*yoniśomanasikāra*), induced by incorrect reasoning (*ayoniśomanasikāra*), or induced by neither correct nor incorrect reasoning.
Why is conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*) a portion of the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*)?
Answer:
Because conventional knowledge cognizes the contaminated (*sāsrava*) minds and mental factors of others.
Why is the knowledge of suffering (duḥkha-jñāna) the entirety of the knowledge of suffering?
Answer:
Because the knowledge of suffering knows the five aggregates of clinging (pañca-upādānaskandhāḥ) as impermanent (anitya), suffering (duḥkha), empty (śūnya), and non-self (anātman).
Why is the knowledge of suffering (duḥkha-jñāna) a portion of the knowledge of phenomena (dharma-jñāna)?
Answer:
Because the knowledge of suffering cognizes the five aggregates of clinging (pañca-upādāna-skandha) bound to the desire realm as impermanent, suffering, empty, and non-self.
Why is the knowledge of suffering (duḥkha-jñāna) a portion of subsequent knowledge (anvaya-jñāna)?
Answer:
Because the knowledge of suffering cognizes the five aggregates of clinging (pañca-upādānaskandha) bound to the realms of form and formlessness as impermanent, suffering, empty, and non-self.
Why is the knowledge of suffering (duḥkha-jñāna) a portion of the knowledge of exhaustion (kṣaya-jñāna)?
Answer:
Because through the knowledge of suffering, one personally and fully realizes, "I have already known suffering."
Why is the knowledge of suffering (duḥkha-jñāna) a portion of the knowledge of non-arising (anutpāda-jñāna)?
Answer:
Because through the knowledge of suffering, one thoroughly knows for oneself: "I have already known suffering; there is nothing further to be known."
Why is the knowledge of origination (samudaya-jñāna) the entirety of the knowledge of origination?
Answer:
Because the knowledge of origination knows the cause of the outflows (āsrava) as cause, origination, production, and condition.
Why is the knowledge of origination (samudaya-jñāna) a portion of the knowledge of phenomena (dharma-jñāna)?
Answer:
Because the knowledge of origination knows the causes, origins, productions, and conditions of all conditioned phenomena (saṃskāra) bound to the desire realm.
Why is the knowledge of origination (samudaya-jñāna) a portion of subsequent knowledge (anvaya-jñāna)?
Answer: Because the knowledge of origination knows the causes, origins, productions, and conditions of all conditioned phenomena (saṃskāra) bound to the realms of form and formlessness.
Why is the knowledge of origination (samudaya-jñāna) a portion of the knowledge of exhaustion (kṣaya-jñāna)?
Answer:
Because the knowledge of origination itself fully realizes, "I have already abandoned origination."
Why is the knowledge of origination (*samudaya-jñāna*) a portion of the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpāda-jñāna*)?
Answer:
Because through the knowledge of origination, one fully realizes for oneself: "I have already abandoned origination; it shall not be abandoned again."
Why is the knowledge of cessation considered the complete knowledge of cessation?
Answer:
Because the knowledge of cessation knows that analytical cessation is cessation, tranquility, excellence, and renunciation.
Why is the knowledge of cessation (*nirodha-jñāna*) a portion of the knowledge of phenomena (*dharma-jñāna*)?
Answer:
Because the knowledge of cessation knows the cessation of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) bound to the desire realm as cessation, tranquility, excellence, and renunciation.
Why is the knowledge of cessation (nirodha-jñāna) a portion of the subsequent knowledge (anvaya-jñāna)?
Answer:
Because the knowledge of cessation knows the cessation of all conditioned phenomena (saṃskāra) of the form and formless realms as cessation, tranquility, excellence, and renunciation.
Why is the knowledge of cessation (*nirodha-jñāna*) a portion of the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣaya-jñāna*)?
Answer:
Because the knowledge of cessation itself fully cognizes, "I have realized cessation."
Why is the knowledge of cessation (*nirodha-jñāna*) a portion of the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpāda-jñāna*)?
Answer:
Because the knowledge of cessation fully cognizes for itself, "I have already realized cessation; it need not be realized again."
