Those that increase both by way of the object and by way of association refer to all other latent dispositions (anuśaya) associated with outflows (sāsrava) and having the cessation of suffering as their object, which are abandoned through the vision of the cessation of suffering, excluding the ignorance (avidyā) associated with outflows that has the cessation of suffering as its object.

Those that increase neither by way of the object (*ālambana*) nor by way of association (*samprayoga*) are: the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) associated with the uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) objects abandoned through the vision of cessation (*nirodha-darśana-prahātavya*), those non-universal (*asarvatraga*) dispositions abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkha*) and origin (*samudaya*), and all [dispositions] abandoned through the vision of the path (*mārga*) and through cultivation (*bhāvanā*).

Regarding those associated factors (*saṃprayukta-dharma*), those that increase by way of the object (*ālambana*) but not by way of association (*saṃprayoga*) are the universal underlying tendencies (*sarvatraga-anuśaya*).

Those that increase by way of association but not by way of the object are the remaining underlying tendencies abandoned through the vision of cessation (*nirodha-darśana-prahātavya*) that take the untainted (*anāsrava*) as their object, excluding wrong view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*), doubt (*vicikitsā*), and the ignorance (*avidyā*) associated with them that are abandoned through the vision of cessation.

Those that increase by way of the object (*ālambana*) and also by way of association (*samprayoga*) are the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) with outflow-objects (*sāsrava-ālambana*) to be abandoned by the vision of cessation (*nirodha-darśana-prahātavya*).

Those that do not increase by way of the object nor by way of association are: the false view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*), doubt (*vicikitsā*), and the ignorance (*avidyā*) associated with them, which are to be abandoned by the vision of cessation; as well as all non-universal (*asarvatraga*) latent tendencies to be abandoned by the vision of suffering (*duḥkha*) and origin (*samudaya*), and all latent tendencies to be abandoned by the path (*mārga*) and through cultivation (*bhāvanā*).

Regarding those formations dissociated from mind that arise therein, the outflow-tainted objects and universal underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) to be abandoned by the vision of cessation increase [in strength] through being their object, but not through association;
as for all other underlying tendencies, they do not increase therein either through being their object or through association.
The same applies to those abandoned by the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*).
As with those that are not bound to a specific realm, so it is for those bound to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), and the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*).

Regarding the various latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) that have outflow-objects (*sāsrava-ālambana*): because those latent dispositions are associated with their objects (*ālambana-samprayukta*), do they increase [in strength] through them?
Answer:
If a latent tendency (anuśaya) increases by way of both its object (ālambana) and its association (samprayoga), that latent tendency has a contaminated object (sāsravālambana).

There are also latent tendencies with a contaminated object that do not increase by way of their object or association; these are the universal latent tendencies (sarvatragānuśaya) that take objects belonging to different realms (dhātu) or levels (bhūmi).
Furthermore, what are these? They are:

those underlying tendencies (anuśaya) bound to the desire realm that take objects bound to the form realm; those underlying tendencies bound to the desire realm that take objects bound to the formless realm; those underlying tendencies bound to the form realm that take objects bound to the formless realm; and those underlying tendencies bound to the desire realm that take objects bound to both the form and formless realms.
The same applies to those with objects in different stages (*bhūmi*).
Regarding those latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) that have the untainted (*anāsrava*) as their object: do they increase by way of association with those latent dispositions?
Answer: If a latent disposition has the untainted as its object, it increases by way of association with those latent dispositions.

Because they are associated with latent dispositions (*anuśaya*), those latent dispositions increase accordingly; however, they do not have the untainted (*anāsrava*) as their object. This refers to the universal latent dispositions (*sarvatraga-anuśaya*) that take other realms and stages as their objects. What, then, are these?

That is to say: those latent dispositions (anuśaya) bound to the desire realm that take as their object the form realm; or those latent dispositions bound to the desire realm that take as their object the formless realm; or those latent dispositions bound to the form realm that take as their object the formless realm; or those latent dispositions bound to the desire realm that take as their object both the form and formless realms.
The same applies to objects belonging to different stages (*bhūmi*).

Chapter Six: On Comprehension and the Like, Part One of the *Abhidharmaprakaraṇapāda-śāstra*. There are dharmas that are objects of knowledge (*jñeya*), dharmas that are objects of cognition (*vijñeya*), dharmas that are objects of thorough penetration (*parijñeya*), dharmas that are objects of focus (*ālambana*), and dharmas that are predominant (*adhipati*).
There are material phenomena and immaterial phenomena; visible phenomena and invisible phenomena; resistant phenomena and non-resistant phenomena;
tainted phenomena and untainted phenomena; conditioned phenomena and unconditioned phenomena;
contentious phenomena and non-contentious phenomena; mundane phenomena and supramundane phenomena; and phenomena that fall within the realms.
...phenomena that do not fall into the realms; phenomena associated with attachment and phenomena not associated with attachment;
phenomena based on indulgence and phenomena based on renunciation; mental phenomena and non-mental phenomena; mental factors and non-mental factors;
phenomena associated with the mind and phenomena dissociated from the mind; phenomena coexistent with the mind and [phenomena] not coexistent with the mind...
Co-existent dharmas; dharmas that follow the mind and dharmas that do not follow the mind; dharmas that have the mind as their cause and dharmas that do not have the mind as their cause;
dharmas that are the equal-and-immediate condition of the mind and dharmas that are not the equal-and-immediate condition of the mind;
dharmas that are the object-condition of the mind and dharmas that are not the object-condition of the mind; dharmas that are the dominant condition of the mind...
Dharmas that do not have mind as their predominant condition; dharmas that are results of mind and dharmas that are not results of mind;
dharmas that are the maturation of mind and dharmas that are not the maturation of mind; dharmas that are karma and dharmas that are not karma;
dharmas associated with karma and dharmas dissociated from karma; dharmas coexistent with karma and dharmas not coexistent with karma; and dharmas that follow the turning of karma.
...dharmas not following the transformation of karma; dharmas having karma as their cause and dharmas not having karma as their cause;

dharmas having karma as their equal-and-immediate condition and dharmas not having karma as their equal-and-immediate condition; dharmas having karma as their object-condition and dharmas not having karma as their object-condition;
dharmas having karma as their predominant condition and dharmas not having karma as their predominant condition; karma...
Phenomena that are results, phenomena that are not results of karma; phenomena that are karmic maturation, phenomena that are not karmic maturation;
existent phenomena, non-existent phenomena; phenomena associated with existence, phenomena dissociated from existence;
phenomena coexistent with existence, phenomena not coexistent with existence; phenomena that follow the movement of existence, phenomena that do not follow the movement of existence; existence...

Dharmas that are causes of conditioned phenomena and dharmas that are not causes of conditioned phenomena; dharmas that are the equal-and-immediate conditions of conditioned phenomena and dharmas that are not the equal-and-immediate conditions of conditioned phenomena;
dharmas that are the objects of conditioned phenomena and dharmas that are not the objects of conditioned phenomena;

dharmas that are the predominant conditions of conditioned phenomena and dharmas that are not the predominant conditions of conditioned phenomena; dharmas that possess results and dharmas that do not possess results.
There are dharmas with maturation and dharmas without maturation; dharmas to be fully known and dharmas not to be fully known;
dharmas to be abandoned and dharmas not to be abandoned; dharmas to be cultivated and dharmas not to be cultivated;
dharmas to be realized and dharmas not to be realized; dharmas to be practiced...
Dharmas not to be practiced; dharmas with fault and dharmas without fault; black dharmas and white dharmas; obscured dharmas and unobscured dharmas;
dharmas conducive to decline and dharmas not conducive to decline; determinate dharmas and indeterminate dharmas;
already arisen dharmas and not yet arisen dharmas; dharmas currently arising and not currently arising...
Arising phenomena and ceased phenomena; non-ceased phenomena; presently ceasing phenomena and non-presently ceasing phenomena;
dependently originated phenomena and non-dependently originated phenomena; dependently arisen phenomena and non-dependently arisen phenomena;
causal phenomena and non-causal phenomena; phenomena with causes and phenomena without causes; and phenomena arisen from causes.
Dharmas that have arisen from causes and those that have not; dharmas associated with causes and those dissociated from causes;
fetters and non-fetters; dharmas conducive to fetters and those not conducive to fetters;
grasping and non-grasping; appropriated dharmas and unappropriated dharmas; dharmas conducive to grasping and those not conducive to grasping.
Afflictive phenomena and non-afflictive phenomena; defiled phenomena and undefiled phenomena; phenomena that are thoroughly afflicted and phenomena that are not thoroughly afflicted;
phenomena that are fetters and phenomena that are not fetters; phenomena that are bound by fetters and phenomena that are not bound by fetters;
phenomena conducive to fetters and phenomena not conducive to fetters; phenomena with an object and phenomena without an object...
Conditioned phenomena; phenomena with vitarka and without vitarka; phenomena with vicāra and without vicāra; phenomena with prīti and without prīti;
phenomena with ābhoga and without ābhoga; phenomena with an object and without an object;
phenomena with an objective support and without an objective support; superior phenomena and unsurpassed phenomena.
Distant phenomena and proximate phenomena; finite phenomena and infinite phenomena; phenomena that are views and phenomena that are not views;
phenomena that are bases for views and phenomena that are not bases for views; phenomena associated with views and phenomena dissociated from views;
phenomena pertaining to ordinary beings and phenomena not pertaining to ordinary beings; phenomena shared with ordinary beings and phenomena not shared with ordinary beings.
Dharmas of ordinary beings; determinate dharmas and indeterminate dharmas; dharmas conducive to feverish affliction and dharmas not conducive to feverish affliction;
root dharmas and non-root dharmas; dharmas subsumed under the Noble Truths and dharmas not subsumed under the Noble Truths;
coexistent dharmas and non-coexistent dharmas; associated dharmas and dissociated dharmas.
Fruit-dharmas and non-fruit-dharmas; dharmas with fruit and dharmas without fruit;
ripening-dharmas and non-ripening-dharmas; dharmas with ripening and dharmas without ripening; causal-condition-dharmas and non-causal-condition-dharmas;
dharmas with causal conditions and dharmas without causal conditions; detached-dharmas and non-detached-dharmas.
There are phenomena that involve detachment and phenomena that do not involve detachment; phenomena that are continuous and phenomena that are not continuous;
there are phenomena that possess continuity and phenomena that lack continuity.
There are three types of phenomena, namely: wholesome phenomena, unwholesome phenomena, and indeterminate phenomena.
Dharmas of those in training (*śaikṣa*), dharmas of those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), and dharmas of neither training nor beyond training (*naivaśaikṣanāśaikṣa*).
Dharmas to be abandoned by vision (*darśana-prahātavya*), dharmas to be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-prahātavya*), and dharmas not to be abandoned (*aprahātavya*).
Dharmas having as their cause those to be abandoned by vision, dharmas having as their cause those to be abandoned by cultivation, and dharmas having as their cause those not to be abandoned.
There are phenomena that are visible and impinging, phenomena that are invisible and impinging, and phenomena that are invisible and non-impinging.
There are phenomena that are results of maturation, phenomena that are productive of maturation, and phenomena that are neither results of maturation nor productive of maturation.
Inferior phenomena, middling phenomena, and sublime phenomena;
small phenomena, great phenomena, and immeasurable phenomena;
agreeable phenomena, disagreeable phenomena, and neither-agreeable-nor-disagreeable phenomena.
Dharmas associated with pleasure, dharmas associated with suffering, and dharmas associated with neither-suffering-nor-pleasure;
dharmas that arise together, dharmas that abide together, and dharmas that cease together.
They are not dharmas that arise together, do not abide together, and do not cease together.
They are dharmas that arise together with the mind, abide together with the mind, and cease together with the mind.
They are not dharmas that arise together with the mind, not dharmas that abide together with the mind, and not dharmas that cease together with the mind.
There are three realms, namely: the realm of desire, the realm of ill-will, and the realm of harmfulness.
Furthermore, there are three realms: the realm of renunciation, the realm of non-ill will, and the realm of non-harming.
Furthermore, there are three realms: the realm of desire, the realm of form, and the formless realm.
Furthermore, there are three realms, namely: the realm of form, the formless realm, and the realm of cessation.
There are three types of existence, namely: existence in the desire realm, existence in the form realm, and existence in the formless realm.
There are three outflows (āsrava), namely: the outflow of sensual desire (kāmāsrava), the outflow of existence (bhavāsrava), and the outflow of ignorance (avidyāsrava).
There are three time periods (adhvan), namely: the past, the future, and the present.
There are three bases for speech: namely, the past basis for speech, the future basis for speech, and the present basis for speech.

There are three natures of suffering: namely, the nature of suffering as suffering (*duḥkhaduḥkhatā*), the nature of suffering as change (*vipariṇāmaduḥkhatā*), and the nature of suffering as conditioned formations (*saṃskāraduḥkhatā*).
There are three types of phenomena: namely, phenomena with vitarka and vicāra, phenomena without vitarka and with only vicāra, and phenomena without both vitarka and vicāra.
There are three stages: namely, the stage with vitarka and vicāra, the stage without vitarka and with only vicāra, and the stage without both vitarka and vicāra.
There are three types of karma, namely: bodily karma, vocal karma, and mental karma.
Furthermore, there are three types of karma, namely: wholesome karma, unwholesome karma, and indeterminate karma.

Furthermore, there are three types of karma: the karma of those in training (*śaikṣa*), the karma of those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), and the karma of those who are neither in training nor beyond training.

Furthermore, there are three types of karma: karma to be abandoned by vision (*darśana-prahātavya*), karma to be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-prahātavya*), and karma that is not to be abandoned (*aprahātavya*).
Furthermore, there are three types of karma: namely, karma to be experienced in the present life, karma to be experienced in the next birth, and karma to be experienced in subsequent births.
Furthermore, there are three types of karma: namely, karma conducive to pleasant experience, karma conducive to painful experience, and karma conducive to neither-painful-nor-pleasant experience.

There are four foundations of mindfulness: namely, the foundation of mindfulness of the body, the foundation of mindfulness of feelings, the foundation of mindfulness of the mind, and the foundation of mindfulness of phenomena.

There are four right endeavors: namely, the right endeavor practiced with diligence to bring about the permanent abandonment of evil, unwholesome states that have already arisen; the right endeavor practiced with diligence to ensure that evil, unwholesome states that have not yet arisen never arise; the right endeavor practiced with diligence to cause wholesome states that have not yet arisen to arise; and the right endeavor practiced with diligence to cause wholesome states that have already arisen to remain firm, to be not forgotten, to be cultivated to fulfillment, to increase further and further, and to be realized through wisdom.

There are four bases of spiritual power (*ṛddhipāda*), namely: the basis of spiritual power consisting in the accomplishment of concentration of desire through the exercise of abandonment; the basis of spiritual power consisting in the accomplishment of concentration of energy through the exercise of abandonment; the basis of spiritual power consisting in the accomplishment of concentration of mind through the exercise of abandonment; and the basis of spiritual power consisting in the accomplishment of concentration of investigation through the exercise of abandonment.
There are four dhyānas, namely: the first dhyāna, the second dhyāna, the third dhyāna, and the fourth dhyāna.
There are four noble truths, namely: the noble truth of suffering, the noble truth of the origin [of suffering], the noble truth of cessation, and the noble truth of the path.
There are four immeasurables, namely: the immeasurable of loving-kindness, the immeasurable of compassion, the immeasurable of sympathetic joy, and the immeasurable of equanimity.
There are four formless attainments, namely: the sphere of infinite space, the sphere of infinite consciousness, the sphere of nothingness, and the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.

There are four noble lineages (āryavaṃśa): namely, the noble lineage of contentment with whatever robes one obtains, the noble lineage of contentment with whatever food one obtains, the noble lineage of contentment with whatever bedding and seating one obtains, and the noble lineage of delighting in renunciation and delighting in cultivation.
There are four fruits of śramaṇaship, namely: the fruit of stream-entry, the fruit of once-returning, the fruit of non-returning, and the fruit of arhatship.
There are four types of knowledge, namely: dharma-knowledge, subsequent knowledge, knowledge of others' minds, and conventional knowledge.
Furthermore, there are four knowledges, namely: the knowledge of suffering, the knowledge of the origin, the knowledge of cessation, and the knowledge of the path.

There are four analytical insights (pratisaṃvid), namely: the analytical insight into phenomena, the analytical insight into meaning, the analytical insight into language, and the analytical insight into eloquence.

There are four conditions: namely, the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*), the immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*), the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*), and the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*).

There are four nutriments: namely, substantial nutriment, whether coarse or subtle; the nutriment of contact (*sparśa-āhāra*); the nutriment of mental volition (*manaḥsaṃcetanā-āhāra*); and the nutriment of consciousness (*vijñāna-āhāra*).
There are four floods (*ogha*): namely, the flood of desire, the flood of existence, the flood of views, and the flood of ignorance.
There are four yokes (*yoga*): namely, the yoke of desire, the yoke of existence, the yoke of views, and the yoke of ignorance.
There are four types of clinging: namely, clinging to sensual pleasures, clinging to views, clinging to rules and observances, and clinging to the doctrine of self.
There are four categories of phenomena: namely, past phenomena, future phenomena, present phenomena, and phenomena that are neither past, nor future, nor present.

Furthermore, there are four categories of phenomena: those bound to the desire realm, those bound to the form realm, those bound to the formless realm, and those that are unbound. Furthermore, there are four categories of phenomena:

those having the wholesome as their cause, those having the unwholesome as their cause, those having the indeterminate as their cause, and those having neither the wholesome, nor the unwholesome, nor the indeterminate as their cause.

Furthermore, there are four types of dharmas: those that take an object as their condition, those that do not take an object as their condition, those that take both an object and the absence of an object as their condition, and those that neither take an object nor the absence of an object as their condition.
There are five aggregates (skandhas), namely: the aggregate of form, the aggregate of feeling, the aggregate of perception, the aggregate of mental formations, and the aggregate of consciousness.

There are five aggregates of clinging (upādānaskandhas), namely: the aggregate of clinging to form, the aggregate of clinging to feeling, the aggregate of clinging to perception, the aggregate of clinging to mental formations, and the aggregate of clinging to consciousness.
There are five destinies, namely: the destiny of hell-beings, the destiny of animals, the destiny of hungry ghosts, the destiny of humans, and the destiny of gods.

There are five classes of afflictions, namely: the class of afflictions to be abandoned through the vision of suffering, the class of afflictions to be abandoned through the vision of the origin [of suffering], the class of afflictions to be abandoned through the vision of cessation, the class of afflictions to be abandoned through the vision of the path, and the class of afflictions to be abandoned through cultivation.
There are five categories of phenomena: namely, form-phenomena, mind-phenomena, mental concomitants, formations dissociated from mind, and unconditioned phenomena.
There are six elements: namely, the earth element, the water element, the fire element, the wind element, the space element, and the consciousness element.

There are six categories of phenomena: those to be abandoned by seeing suffering, those to be abandoned by seeing the origin, those to be abandoned by seeing cessation, those to be abandoned by seeing the path, those to be abandoned by cultivation, and those not to be abandoned.

There are seven underlying tendencies (anuśaya), namely: the underlying tendency of sensual desire, the underlying tendency of aversion, the underlying tendency of attachment to existence, the underlying tendency of pride, the underlying tendency of ignorance, the underlying tendency of views, and the underlying tendency of doubt.

There are seven stations of consciousness (*vijñānasthiti*). First, there are sentient beings possessing form, with diversity of body and diversity of perception, such as humans and certain classes of gods; this is the first station of consciousness.

Second, there are sentient beings possessing form, with diversity of body and unity of perception, such as the gods of the Brahma-realm at the beginning of an eon; this is the second station of consciousness.
There are sentient beings with form who have a single body but diverse perceptions, such as the gods of the Ābhāsvara Heaven; this is the third station of consciousness.
There are sentient beings with form who have a single body and a single perception, such as the gods of the Śubhakṛtsna Heaven; this is the fourth station of consciousness.

Formless sentient beings, transcending all perceptions of form, extinguishing perceptions of sensory resistance, and not attending to perceptions of diversity, enter and dwell fully in the sphere of infinite space, just like the devas of the Sphere of Infinite Space; this is the fifth station of consciousness.

Formless sentient beings, having transcended the sphere of infinite space, enter the sphere of infinite consciousness and dwell fully therein; like the gods of the Sphere of Infinite Consciousness, this is the sixth station of consciousness.

Formless sentient beings who, transcending the sphere of infinite consciousness, enter the sphere of nothingness and dwell fully established therein—like the gods of the sphere of nothingness—this is the seventh abode of consciousness.

There are seven factors of enlightenment: namely, the enlightenment factor of mindfulness, the enlightenment factor of investigation of phenomena, the enlightenment factor of energy, the enlightenment factor of joy, the enlightenment factor of tranquility, the enlightenment factor of concentration, and the enlightenment factor of equanimity.
There are eight liberations: perceiving forms while possessing the perception of form is the first liberation;
having no internal perception of form, one perceives external forms is the second liberation.
The third liberation is the attainment and dwelling in the purity of liberation through bodily realization.

The fourth liberation is the transcendence of all perceptions of form, the cessation of perceptions of sensory resistance, and the non-attention to perceptions of diversity; entering the sphere of infinite space, one attains and dwells in the sphere of infinite space.
Transcending the sphere of infinite space, one enters the sphere of infinite consciousness and dwells, having fully attained it; this is the fifth liberation.
Transcending the sphere of infinite consciousness, one enters the sphere of nothingness and dwells, having fully attained it; this is the sixth liberation.
Transcending the sphere of nothingness, one enters and dwells in the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception; this is the seventh liberation.

Transcending the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, one enters the cessation of perception and feeling, realizes it through the body, and dwells in its fulfillment; this is the eighth liberation.

There are eight bases of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*). That is to say: possessing the perception of internal forms, one contemplates external forms that are few in number, whether they be beautiful colors or ugly colors; having mastery over those forms and seeing them with mastery, while possessing such a perception—this is the first base of mastery.

Having the perception of internal forms, one observes external forms that are manifold, whether beautiful in color or ugly in color; having superior knowledge and superior vision regarding those forms, possessing such a perception—this is the second base of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*).

Having no perception of internal forms, one perceives external forms as limited, whether they be beautiful in color or ugly in color; having superior knowledge and superior vision regarding those forms, possessing such a perception is the third base of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*).

Having no perception of internal forms, one perceives external forms that are manifold, whether they be beautiful in color or ugly in color; having superior knowledge and superior vision regarding those forms, possessing such a perception—this is the fourth sphere of mastery (abhibhvāyatana).

Without the perception of internal forms, one perceives external forms that are blue, blue in appearance, blue in manifestation, and blue in radiance—just like the umakā flower, or like deep-dyed blue cloth from Vārāṇasī, blue, blue in appearance, blue in manifestation, and blue in radiance.

Without internal perception of form, one perceives external forms that are blue, appearing blue, manifesting as blue, and emitting blue light; likewise, having superior knowledge and vision regarding those forms, possessing such a perception is the fifth sphere of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*).

Without the perception of internal forms, one perceives external forms that are yellow, manifest as yellow, appear as yellow, and emit yellow light—just like a *karnikāra* flower, or like a deep yellow robe from Vārāṇasī, which is yellow, manifest as yellow, appears as yellow, and emits yellow light.

Having no perception of internal forms, one perceives external forms that are yellow, yellow in appearance, yellow in manifestation, and yellow in luster; this is likewise. Having superior knowledge and superior vision regarding those forms, possessing such a perception, this is the sixth sphere of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*).

Without the perception of internal forms, one perceives external forms that are red, appearing red, manifesting as red, and emitting a red luster—just like a *pāṇḍu-tīvra-karṇikāra* flower, or like a deep crimson robe from Vārāṇasī, which is red, appears red, manifests as red, and emits a red luster.

With no perception of internal forms, one perceives external forms that are red, appearing red, manifesting as red, and emitting red light; this too is likewise. Having superior knowledge and superior vision regarding those forms, possessing such a perception, is the seventh sphere of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*).

Having no perception of internal forms, one perceives external forms that are white, white in appearance, white in manifestation, and emitting white light—just like the star Ursa Major (Uśanas), or like a very fresh white cloth from Vārāṇasī, which is white, white in appearance, white in manifestation, and emitting white light.

Having no perception of internal forms, one perceives external forms that are white, white in appearance, white in manifestation, and emitting white light; likewise, having superior knowledge and vision regarding those forms, and possessing such a perception, this is the eighth sphere of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*).
There are eight factors of the noble path, namely: right view, right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration.
*Abhidharmaprakaraṇapādaśāstra*, Fascicle Five.

composed by the Venerable Vasumitra.
