Chapter Six, Part Two: On the Compendium of the Fetters. There are nine fetters (*saṃyojana*), namely: the fetter of attachment (*anunaya-saṃyojana*), the fetter of aversion (*pratigha-saṃyojana*), the fetter of pride (*māna-saṃyojana*), the fetter of ignorance (*avidyā-saṃyojana*), the fetter of views (*dṛṣṭi-saṃyojana*), the fetter of grasping (*parāmarśa-saṃyojana*), the fetter of doubt (*vicikitsā-saṃyojana*), the fetter of envy (*īrṣyā-saṃyojana*), and the fetter of avarice (*mātsarya-saṃyojana*).

There are nine abodes of sentient beings: namely, those sentient beings who possess form, with diverse bodies and diverse perceptions, such as human beings and certain classes of devas; this is the first abode of sentient beings.
There are beings with form who have diverse bodies but a single perception, such as the gods of the Brahma-group at the beginning of the kalpa; this is the second abode of sentient beings.
There are beings with form who have a single body but diverse perceptions, such as the gods of the Ābhāsvara Heaven; this is the third abode of sentient beings.
There are beings with form who are uniform in body and uniform in perception, such as the gods of the Universal Purity Heaven; this is the fourth abode of sentient beings.
There are beings with form who are without perception and without differentiated perception, such as the gods of Non-percipient Beings; this is the fifth abode of sentient beings.

Formless sentient beings, having transcended all perceptions of form and extinguished perceptions of sensory resistance, no longer attending to perceptions of diversity, enter the sphere of infinite space and dwell fully established therein, like the gods of the Sphere of Infinite Space; this is the sixth abode of sentient beings.

Formless sentient beings, having transcended the sphere of infinite space, enter the sphere of infinite consciousness and dwell fully established therein; like the gods of the sphere of infinite consciousness, this is the seventh abode of sentient beings.

There are formless sentient beings who, transcending the sphere of infinite consciousness, enter the sphere of nothingness and dwell fully established therein; like the gods of the sphere of nothingness, this is the eighth abode of sentient beings.

Formless sentient beings, having transcended the sphere of nothingness, enter and dwell fully in the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, just like the gods of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception; this is the ninth abode of sentient beings.

There are ten universal bases (*kṛtsnāyatana*). That is to say, the uniform perception of the earth as all-pervading, extending upward, downward, and across, without duality and immeasurable—this is the first universal base.
The uniform perception of water as all-pervading, extending upward, downward, and across, without duality and immeasurable—this is the second universal base.
The third *kṛtsnāyatana* (base of totality) is the uniform perception of fire pervading everywhere—above, below, and across—as non-dual and immeasurable.
The fourth *kṛtsnāyatana* is the uniform perception of wind pervading everywhere—above, below, and across—as non-dual and immeasurable.
The fifth base of totality (*kṛtsnāyatana*) is the unified perception of blue pervading everywhere—above, below, and across—as non-dual and immeasurable.
The sixth base of totality is the unified perception of yellow pervading everywhere—above, below, and across—as non-dual and immeasurable.
The uniform perception of a pervasive red, extending above, below, and across, without duality and immeasurable, is the seventh base of totality (*kṛtsnāyatana*).
The uniform perception of a pervasive white, extending above, below, and across, without duality and immeasurable, is the eighth base of totality.
The ninth base of totality (*kṛtsnāyatana*) is the uniform perception of space as all-pervading, extending above, below, and across, undivided and immeasurable.
The tenth base of totality is the uniform perception of consciousness as all-pervading, extending above, below, and across, undivided and immeasurable.

There are ten dharmas of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), namely: the right view, right thought, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, right concentration, right resolve, and right knowledge of one beyond training.

There are eleven dharmas, namely: contaminated form, uncontaminated form; contaminated feeling, uncontaminated feeling; contaminated perception, uncontaminated perception; contaminated formations, uncontaminated formations; contaminated consciousness, uncontaminated consciousness; and unconditioned phenomena.

There are twelve bases (āyatana), namely: the eye-base and the form-base; the ear-base and the sound-base; the nose-base and the odor-base; the tongue-base and the taste-base; the body-base and the tangible-base; and the mind-base and the mental-object-base.

There are eighteen elements (dhātus), namely: the eye element, the form element, and the eye-consciousness element; the ear element, the sound element, and the ear-consciousness element; the nose element, the odor element, and the nose-consciousness element; the tongue element, the taste element, and the tongue-consciousness element; the body element, the tangible element, and the body-consciousness element; and the mind element, the mental-object element, and the mind-consciousness element.

There are twenty-two faculties (indriya), namely: the eye faculty, the ear faculty, the nose faculty, the tongue faculty, the body faculty, the female faculty, the male faculty, the life faculty, the mind faculty, the faculty of pleasure, the faculty of pain, the faculty of joy, the faculty of grief, the faculty of equanimity, the faculty of faith, the faculty of vigor, the faculty of mindfulness, the faculty of concentration, the faculty of wisdom, the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown," the faculty of "knowing," and the faculty of "one who has known."

There are ninety-eight latent dispositions (*anuśaya*): namely, thirty-six bound to the desire realm, thirty-one bound to the form realm, and thirty-one bound to the formless realm, as previously explained.
What are the phenomena that are objects of knowledge?
They are all phenomena known by wisdom, according to their respective natures.
Furthermore, what are these?
That is to say, the knowledge of suffering knows suffering; the knowledge of origin knows origin; the knowledge of cessation knows cessation; and the knowledge of the path knows the path.

Furthermore, there is wholesome conventional knowledge that knows suffering, origin, cessation, and the path, as well as space and non-analytical cessation. Therefore, it is said that all phenomena are objects known by knowledge according to their respective natures; these are called "knowable phenomena" (*jñeya-dharma*).
What are the phenomena that are cognized?
It refers to all phenomena being cognized by consciousness, according to their respective objects.
Furthermore, what does this mean?

That is to say: eye-consciousness cognizes forms, ear-consciousness cognizes sounds, nose-consciousness cognizes odors, tongue-consciousness cognizes tastes, body-consciousness cognizes tangibles, and mind-consciousness cognizes mental objects. There are the eye and form with eye-consciousness, the ear and sound with ear-consciousness, the nose and odor with nose-consciousness, the tongue and taste with tongue-consciousness, the body and tangible with body-consciousness, and the mind and mental object with mind-consciousness. Therefore, it is said that all phenomena are what is cognized by consciousness according to their respective cases; these are called the phenomena that are cognized.
What is the dharma that is thoroughly penetrated?
"Thorough penetration" refers to excellent wisdom (*sādhumati*); this takes all dharmas as its object of thorough penetration, according to their respective natures.
Furthermore, what is this?

This refers to the penetration of suffering through the patience regarding suffering (*duḥkha-kṣānti*) and the knowledge regarding suffering (*duḥkha-jñāna*); the penetration of origination through the patience regarding origination (*samudaya-kṣānti*) and the knowledge regarding origination (*samudaya-jñāna*); the penetration of cessation through the patience regarding cessation (*nirodha-kṣānti*) and the knowledge regarding cessation (*nirodha-jñāna*); and the penetration of the path through the patience regarding the path (*mārga-kṣānti*) and the knowledge regarding the path (*mārga-jñāna*).

Furthermore, there is wholesome, out-flowing wisdom (*sāsrava-prajñā*) that penetrates suffering, origination, cessation, and the path, as well as space (*ākāśa*) and non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*); therefore, it is said that "penetration" refers to wholesome wisdom. This takes all phenomena as its objects of penetration; according to their respective natures, these are called the "phenomena to be penetrated."
What are the phenomena that serve as objects of perception (*ālambana*)?
It refers to all phenomena being the objects of mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta*), according to their respective natures.
Furthermore, what does this mean?

That is to say: visual consciousness and its associated mental factors take form as their object; auditory consciousness and its associated mental factors take sound as their object; olfactory consciousness and its associated mental factors take fragrance as their object; gustatory consciousness and its associated mental factors take flavor as their object; tactile consciousness and its associated mental factors take tangibles as their object; and mental consciousness and its associated mental factors take phenomena as their object.

The eye and forms, the eye-consciousness; the ear and sounds, the ear-consciousness; the nose and odors, the nose-consciousness; the tongue and tastes, the tongue-consciousness; the body and tangibles, the body-consciousness; the mind and mental phenomena, the mind-consciousness—therefore it is said that all phenomena are the objects of the mind and mental factors. According to their respective functions, these are called the "objects of cognition" (*ālambana-dharma*).
What are the predominant phenomena (*adhipati-dharma*)?

They refer to all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*) acting as predominant conditions for one another, as well as unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*) acting as predominant conditions for conditioned phenomena; these are called predominant phenomena.
What are material phenomena?
They are the ten bases and a portion of one base.
What are immaterial phenomena?
That is to say, a portion of one location.
What is the dharma that is visible?
It is one location.
What are the phenomena that are non-visible?
They are the eleven bases.
What are the phenomena that are resistant?
That is to say, the ten bases.
What are the non-resistant dharmas?
That is to say, the two bases.
What are the contaminated phenomena (*sāsravadharma*)?
They are the ten bases (*āyatana*) and a portion of the two bases.
What are the uncontaminated phenomena (*anāsravadharma*)?
This refers to a portion of two bases.
What are conditioned phenomena?
They refer to eleven bases and a portion of one base.
What are unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛtadharma*)?
They are a portion of one base (*dhātu*).
What are phenomena associated with contention (*saraṇadharma*)?
This refers to ten bases (*āyatana*) and a portion of two bases.
What is the dharma of non-contention (*araṇa*)?
It refers to a portion of two bases.

The same applies to mundane and supramundane phenomena, phenomena that fall within the realm and those that do not, phenomena with attachment and those without attachment, and phenomena based on indulgence and those based on renunciation.
What are mental phenomena?
They are one base.
What are non-mental phenomena?
That is to say, the eleven bases.
What are the mental factors (caitta-dharma)?
They are those phenomena that are associated with the mind (citta-samprayukta).
What, furthermore, are these?
They are the aggregate of feeling, the aggregate of perception, and the aggregate of formations associated with the mind.
What are the factors that are not mental concomitants (*citta-saṃprayukta*)?
That is to say, those phenomena that are dissociated from the mind.
Furthermore, what are these?
They are: form, mind, and formations dissociated from the mind.
What are the unconditioned factors associated with the mind?
They are the mental concomitants (*caitta-dharma*). What, again, are these?
This refers to the aggregate of feeling, the aggregate of perception, and the associated aggregate of formations.
What are the factors dissociated from mind?
They are those factors that are not mental concomitants.
What, then, are these? They are matter (rūpa), mind (citta), formations dissociated from mind (citta-viprayukta-saṃskāra), and the unconditioned (asaṃskṛta).
What are the factors that coexist with the mind (cittasahabhū-dharma)?
This refers to a portion of eleven bases coexistent with the mind, excluding the mind base (*manāyatana*).
What are the phenomena not coexistent with the mind?
This refers to the mind base, as well as a portion of the eleven bases not coexistent with the mind.
What are the phenomena that arise concomitantly with the mind?
They are those phenomena which, together with the mind, arise, abide, and cease as one.
Furthermore, what does this mean?

This refers to all mental factors (caitta-dharma), as well as the concentration co-existent with the Path (mārga-sahabhū-samādhi) and the morality co-existent with it (sahabhū-śīla), along with the arising, aging, duration, and impermanence of that mind or those factors; these are called the dharmas that follow the mind in their transformation (cittānuvartin).
What are the phenomena that do not follow the mind?
They are those phenomena that do not arise, abide, or cease simultaneously with the mind.
Furthermore, what are these?
This refers to all other material phenomena (*rūpadharma*) excluding those bodily and vocal actions that follow the mind;

and all other formations dissociated from the mind (*cittaviprayuktasaṃskāra*) as well as the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), excluding those formations dissociated from the mind that follow the mind. These are called phenomena that do not follow the mind.
What are phenomena that have the mind as their cause?
This refers to all minds other than the first untainted mind of a person who has already entered the state of rightness and departure from birth;
and all minds other than the future first untainted mind of those ordinary persons who are certain to enter the state of rightness and departure from birth.
Furthermore, the eleven bases (*āyatana*) in part that have mind as their cause are called phenomena with mind as their cause (*cittahetuka-dharma*).
What are phenomena not with mind as their cause?

They refer to the first untainted mind (*anāsrava-citta*) of a person (*pudgala*) who has already entered the state of rightness and departure from birth (*samyaktva-niyāma*), as well as the future first untainted minds of other ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) who are certain to enter the state of rightness and departure from birth, together with the eleven bases in part that have mind as their cause; these are called phenomena not with mind as their cause.
What is meant by "the mind as a condition of equal immediacy" (*samanantara-pratyaya*)?

It refers to those mental states and mental factors (*citta-caitta-dharma*), whether already arisen or currently arising, that have the mind as their condition of equal immediacy; as well as the attainment of non-perception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*) and the attainment of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*), whether already arisen or currently arising. This is called the mind as a condition of equal immediacy.
What are those phenomena that have non-mind as their equal and immediate antecedent (*samanantara-pratyaya*)?

This refers to all other mind and mental factors, excluding those mind and mental factors for which mind serves as the equal and immediate antecedent; and all other formations dissociated from mind, excluding those formations dissociated from mind for which mind serves as the equal and immediate antecedent; as well as matter and the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*). These are called phenomena that have non-mind as their equal and immediate antecedent.
What are the phenomena that have mind as their object?
This refers to the mental consciousness and its associated mental factors that take mind as their object; these are called the phenomena that have mind as their object.
What are phenomena that do not have mind as their object?

This refers to all other mental consciousnesses and their associated factors, excluding those mental consciousnesses and their associated factors that have mind as their object; as well as the five groups of sensory consciousnesses and their associated factors, and all material phenomena, unconditioned phenomena, and formations dissociated from mind. These are called phenomena that do not have mind as their object.
What are phenomena that have the mind as their predominant condition?
It refers to conditioned phenomena for which the mind is the predominant condition; these are called phenomena that have the mind as their predominant condition.
What are phenomena that do not have the mind as their predominant condition?
That is to say, unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*).
What are the phenomena that are fruits of the mind?
They are all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*) as well as analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).
What are the dharmas that are not the fruit of mind?
They are space and non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).
What are the dharmas that are the maturation of mind (*citta-vipāka*)?
The mind’s maturation consists of a portion of eleven bases, excluding the sound base.
What are the phenomena that are not the mind’s maturation?
They are the sound base and a portion of the eleven bases that are not the mind’s maturation.
What are the dharmas that are action?
They are bodily and vocal actions, as well as volition.
What are the dharmas that are not action?

This refers to all other forms (*rūpa*) excluding bodily and vocal actions; all other formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) excluding volition (*cetanā*), as well as the three remaining aggregates (*skandha*) in their entirety, together with unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*).
What are the factors associated with action (*karma-saṃprayukta-dharma*)?
It refers to those phenomena that are associated with volition (*cetanā*). What, then, are these?
They are all mental states and mental factors (*citta-caitta-dharma*), excluding volition itself.
What are the factors dissociated from karma?
They are those factors that are dissociated from volition (*cetanā*).
Furthermore, what are these?
This refers to form (*rūpa*), volition (*cetanā*), formations dissociated from mind (*citta-viprayukta-saṃskāra*), and the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
What are the factors co-existent with karma?
They refer to the sphere of mind (*manāyatana*) and a portion of eleven spheres co-existent with karma, excluding volition.
What are the phenomena that do not coexist with karma?
They are volition (*cetanā*) and a portion of the eleven bases (*āyatana*) that do not coexist with karma, excluding the mind base (*manāyatana*).
What are the phenomena that follow the transformation of karma?
This refers to those phenomena that arise, abide, and cease simultaneously with volition (*cetanā*).

What, then, are these? They are all mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta-dharma*), excluding volition itself, the concentration co-existent with the Path (*mārga-sahagata-samādhi*), and the morality co-existent [with it] (*sahabhū-śīla*), as well as the arising, aging, duration, and impermanence of volition and those aforementioned phenomena. These are called the phenomena that follow the transformation of karma (*karmānuvartaka-dharma*).
What are phenomena that do not follow the transformation of karma?
They are those phenomena that do not arise, abide, or cease simultaneously with volition (*cetanā*).
Furthermore, what are these?

This refers to all other forms of bodily and vocal action apart from those that follow the transformation of karma; all other formations dissociated from mind apart from those that follow the transformation of karma; volition (*cetanā*); and unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*). These are called the factors that do not follow the transformation of karma.
What are phenomena that have karma as their cause?

They refer to all volitions (*cetanā*) other than the first untainted volition of a person who has already entered the state of rightness and departure from birth (*samyaktva-niyāma*); and all volitions other than the future first untainted volition of those ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*) who are certain to enter the state of rightness and departure from birth; and the sphere of mind (*manāyatana*), along with a portion of the eleven spheres that have karma as their cause. These are called phenomena that have karma as their cause.
What are phenomena that do not have karma as their cause? They are:

the first untainted volition (*anāsrava-cetanā*) of a person who has entered the state of rightness and departure from birth (*samyaktva-niyāma*); the future first untainted volitions of other ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*) who are certain to enter the state of rightness and departure from birth; and a portion of eleven bases (*āyatana*), excluding the mind base (*manāyatana*), which do not have karma as their cause. These are called phenomena that do not have karma as their cause.
What is a dharma that has karma as its equal-and-immediate condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*)?
It refers to those dharmas for which the mind is the equal-and-immediate condition.
What is a dharma that does not have karma as its equal-and-immediate condition?
What are those phenomena that do not have mind as their equal-and-immediate antecedent, yet have karma as their object?
They are the three groups of consciousness and their associated mental factors, which take karma as their object; these are called phenomena that have karma as their object.
What are the phenomena that have non-karma as their object?

This refers to all other phenomena—namely, these three groups of consciousness and their associated mental factors, as well as other three groups of consciousness and their associated mental factors, along with form, unconditioned phenomena, and formations dissociated from mind—excluding those three groups of consciousness and their associated mental factors that have karma as their object. These are called the phenomena that have non-karma as their object.
What are the phenomena for which karma is the predominant condition?
They are the conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*), for which karma is the predominant condition.
What are the phenomena for which karma is not the predominant condition?
These refer to unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*).
What are the phenomena that are the fruits of karma?
They refer to all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*) and analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).
What are the phenomena that are not the fruit of karma?
They are space and non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).
What are the phenomena that are the maturation of karma (*karmavipāka*)?
This refers to a portion of eleven bases (*āyatana*) that are the maturation of karma (*karmavipāka*), excluding the sound base (*śabdāyatana*).
What are the phenomena that are not the maturation of karma?
They refer to the sound base and a portion of the eleven bases that are not the maturation of karma.
What are existent phenomena?
They are the contaminated phenomena (*sāsravadharma*).
What are non-existent phenomena?
That is, untainted phenomena (*anāsrava-dharma*).
What are associated phenomena (*saṃprayukta-dharma*)?
They are tainted mental states and mental factors (*sāsrava-citta-caitta-dharma*).
What are the dissociated phenomena (*viprayukta-dharma*)?

They are the untainted mind and mental factors (*anāsrava-citta-caitta*), as well as form (*rūpa*), the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), and the formations dissociated from mind (*citta-viprayukta-saṃskāra*).
What are the co-existent phenomena (*sahabhū-dharma*)?
This refers to contaminated phenomena (*sāsrava-dharma*) and those uncontaminated phenomena (*anāsrava-dharma*) that arise simultaneously with them.
What are the non-coexistent phenomena?

They are all other uncontaminated phenomena, excluding those uncontaminated phenomena that arise simultaneously with contaminated ones, as well as all phenomena that follow the existence [of others] (*anuvartaka*).
What are the conditioned phenomena that serve as causes?
They are the contaminated phenomena (*sāsrava-dharma*) that do not follow the movement of existence (*na bhavapravartin*).
And what are the phenomena that do not serve as causes for the conditioned?
This refers to untainted (*anāsrava*) phenomena.
What are conditioned phenomena that are equal-and-immediate (*samanantara*)?

They are all other tainted or untainted mind and mental states (*citta-caitta*)—whether already arisen or currently arising—that follow immediately after tainted mind and mental states; as well as the attainment of non-perception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*) and the attainment of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*), whether already arisen or currently arising. These are called conditioned equal-and-immediate phenomena.
What are the dharmas that are not "immediately antecedent conditions" (*samanantara-pratyaya*) for conditioned phenomena?

This refers to all other mind and mental factors (citta-caitta) excluding those mind and mental factors that serve as immediately antecedent conditions for conditioned phenomena; and all other formations dissociated from mind (citta-viprayukta-saṃskāra) excluding those formations dissociated from mind that serve as immediately antecedent conditions for conditioned phenomena; as well as matter (*rūpa*) and unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*). These are called the dharmas that are not immediately antecedent conditions for conditioned phenomena.
What are phenomena that have conditioned things as their object?

They refer to the five groups of consciousness together with their associated mental factors, as well as the mental consciousness together with its associated mental factors, which take conditioned things as their objects; these are called phenomena that have conditioned things as their object.
What are phenomena that have non-conditioned things as their objects?

This refers to all other mental consciousnesses and their associated mental factors, excluding those mental consciousnesses and their associated factors that have conditioned things as their objects, as well as form, unconditioned phenomena, and formations dissociated from mind; these are called phenomena that have non-conditioned things as their objects.
What is the conditioned predominant dharma?
It refers to conditioned dharmas.
What is the non-conditioned predominant dharma?
That is to say, unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛtadharma*).
What are phenomena that possess results (*saphaladharma*)?
They are contaminated phenomena (*sāsravadharma*), as well as the abandonment of fetters (*saṃyojanaprahāṇa*) realized through the mundane path (*laukikamārga*).
What are phenomena that do not have results?
They are all other untainted phenomena (*anāsrava-dharma*), excluding those untainted phenomena that possess results.
What are phenomena that have maturation (*vipāka*)?
This refers to a portion of eleven bases (āyatana) that possess maturation (savipāka), excluding the sound base (śabdāyatana).
What are the phenomena that do not possess maturation?
They are the sound base and a portion of the eleven bases that do not possess maturation.
What are the phenomena to be fully known?
There are two types of full knowledge:
first, full knowledge through wisdom; second, full knowledge through abandonment.
What are the phenomena that are to be fully known by wisdom?
It refers to all phenomena, because they are all that which ought to be known through the full knowledge of wisdom.
What are the phenomena that are not to be fully known by wisdom?
This means that such phenomena cannot be found when sought, because there is no phenomenon that is not to be known by wisdom.
Those phenomena which are to be fully understood through the thorough knowledge of abandonment are precisely those phenomena that ought to be abandoned.
What, then, is this? It refers to contaminated phenomena (*sāsravadharma*).
Those phenomena which are not to be fully known through the thorough knowledge of abandonment (*prahāṇaparijñā*) are precisely those that are not to be abandoned.
What, then, is this? It refers to untainted phenomena (*anāsravadharma*).
What are the phenomena that ought to be cultivated?
It refers to wholesome conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*).
What are the phenomena that are not to be cultivated?
They are unwholesome (*akuśala*) and indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) phenomena, as well as analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).
What are the dharmas to be realized?
There are two kinds of realization:
first, realization through knowledge; second, realization through attainment.
What are the phenomena that are to be realized through the realization of wisdom?
They are all phenomena, because they are all to be realized through the realization of wisdom.
What are the phenomena that are not to be realized through the realization of wisdom?
This means that such phenomena cannot be found through seeking, for there is no phenomenon that is not to be realized by wisdom.
What are the phenomena that should be realized through attainment?
They are all wholesome phenomena, as well as the unobscured-neutral divine eye and divine ear realized through meditative concentration.
What are the dharmas that are not to be realized through attainment?

They are all other neutral (*avyākṛta*) dharmas, as well as all unwholesome (*akuśala*) dharmas, with the exception of the unobscured-neutral divine eye and divine ear realized by relying on meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
What are the dharmas that should be practiced?
They are the conditioned wholesome dharmas.
What are the dharmas that should not be practiced?
This refers to unwholesome (*akuśala*) and indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) phenomena, as well as analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).
What are blameworthy (*sāvadya*) phenomena?
They are unwholesome and obscured-indeterminate (*nivṛtāvyākṛta*) phenomena.
What are the faultless dharmas?
They are the wholesome dharmas and the non-obscured neutral dharmas.
The same applies to black and white dharmas, obscured and non-obscured dharmas, and dharmas conducive to decline and dharmas not conducive to decline.
What are determinate dharmas?
They are wholesome and unwholesome dharmas.
What are indeterminate dharmas?
This refers to all other phenomena (dharma) excluding those that are wholesome or unwholesome.
What are phenomena that have already arisen?
They are past and present phenomena.
What are non-arisen dharmas?
They are future dharmas and unconditioned (asaṃskṛta) dharmas.
What are dharmas currently arising?
That is to say, those dharmas that are yet to come and are currently arising before one.
What are the dharmas that are not currently arising?
They are all other future, past, and present dharmas, as well as unconditioned (asaṃskṛta) dharmas, excluding those dharmas that are yet to come and are currently arising before one.
What are phenomena that have already ceased?
They are past phenomena.
What are phenomena that have not yet ceased?
This refers to future, present, and unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) dharmas.
What is a dharma that is currently ceasing?
It refers to any dharma that is present, manifest, and in the very process of ceasing.
What are the phenomena that are not currently ceasing?

They are all other present phenomena, as well as past and future phenomena, together with unconditioned phenomena, excluding those present phenomena that are currently manifesting and in the process of ceasing.
What is the dharma of dependent origination?
It refers to conditioned dharmas.
What is the dharma that is not of dependent origination?
That is to say: unconditioned phenomena;

conditioned phenomena that have arisen from conditions and those that have not arisen from conditions; causal phenomena and non-causal phenomena; phenomena that possess causes and phenomena that do not possess causes; and likewise, phenomena that have arisen from causes and phenomena that have not arisen from causes.
What are the factors associated with causes?
They are all mind and mental factors.
What are the factors dissociated from causes?
These refer to form, the unconditioned, and formations dissociated from mind.
What are the phenomena that constitute fetters? They are the nine fetters.
What are the non-fetters (asaṃyojana-dharma)?
They are all other dharmas, excluding the nine fetters.
What are the dharmas conducive to fetters (saṃyojanānukūla-dharma)?
That is to say, all contaminated (*sāsrava*) phenomena.
What are the phenomena that do not accord with the fetters?
That is to say, all uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) phenomena.
What are the phenomena of grasping?
They are the four types of grasping.
What are the phenomena that are not grasping?
This refers to all other phenomena (dharmas) excluding the four types of clinging (*upādāna*).
What are the phenomena that are appropriated (*upātta*)?
They consist of a portion of nine bases (*āyatana*), excluding the bases of sound, mind (*manas*), and mental objects (*dharma*).
What are the non-appropriated phenomena (*anupātta-dharma*)?
They are the sense bases of sound, mind, and mental objects, as well as a portion of the nine [other] sense bases that are non-appropriated.
What are the phenomena conducive to grasping (*upādānīya-dharma*)?
That is to say, all contaminated (*sāsrava*) phenomena.
What are the phenomena that do not conform to grasping (*anupādāniya*)?
That is to say, all uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) phenomena.
What are the phenomena that are afflictions (*kleśa*)?
They are those phenomena which are entanglements (*paryavasthāna*).
What are the phenomena that are not afflictions?
That is to say, those factors which are not *paryavasthāna* (obsessions).
What are the defiled (*kliṣṭa*) factors?
They are the unwholesome (*akuśala*) factors and the obscured-unneutral (*nivṛtāvyākṛta*) factors.
What are non-defiled phenomena?
They are wholesome phenomena and non-obscured neutral phenomena.
What are defiled phenomena?
That is to say, they are contaminated phenomena (*sāsrava-dharma*). What are non-defiled phenomena?
That is to say, they are uncontaminated phenomena (*anāsrava-dharma*).
What are the phenomena that are envelopments (*paryavasthāna*)?
They are those phenomena which are afflictions (*kleśa*).
What are the phenomena that are not envelopments?
That is to say, what are those phenomena that are not enveloped by afflictions?
They are the defiled mind and mental factors.
What are the factors not associated with entanglement (*paryavasthāna*)?
They are undefiled minds and mental factors (*citta-caitta-dharma*), as well as matter (*rūpa*), the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), and formations dissociated from mind (*citta-viprayukta-saṃskāra*).
What are the factors conducive to entanglement?
This refers to contaminated phenomena (*sāsrava-dharma*).
What are phenomena that do not accord with the fetters (*paryavasthāna*)?
This refers to uncontaminated phenomena (*anāsrava-dharma*).
What are phenomena with an object of cognition?
They are all minds and mental factors.
What are phenomena without an object of cognition?
That is to say: form, the unconditioned, and formations dissociated from mind.
What are the factors associated with vitarka?
They are those factors associated with vitarka.
What are phenomena without vitarka?
They are those phenomena that are dissociated from vitarka.
What are phenomena with vicāra?
This refers to phenomena associated with vicāra.
What are phenomena without vicāra?
They are phenomena dissociated from vicāra.
What are phenomena associated with joy?
They are phenomena associated with the faculty of joy (*saumanasyendriya*).
What are phenomena dissociated from joy?
This refers to those factors dissociated from the faculty of joy (*saumanasyendriya*).
What are the factors characterized by alertness?
They are the factors associated with attention (*manasikāra*).
What are phenomena that lack alertness?
They are those phenomena dissociated from attention (*manasikāra*).
What are phenomena that possess a basis and an object?
That is to say, conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*).
What are phenomena that have no objective basis (*anālambana*) and no object (*anālambana*)?
That is to say, unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛtadharma*).
What are the dharmas with superior [states]?
They are all conditioned dharmas (*saṃskṛtadharma*), as well as space (*ākāśa*) and cessation not through deliberation (*apratisaṃkhyānirodha*).
What are the unsurpassed dharmas?
This refers to analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*). What are distant phenomena?
They are past and future phenomena.
What are proximate phenomena?
They are present phenomena and unconditioned phenomena.
What are limited phenomena?
That is to say, if a phenomenon has both its fruit and its maturation (vipāka) as limited,
what is it for a phenomenon to have both its fruit and its maturation as immeasurable? It is when a phenomenon has both its fruit and its maturation as immeasurable.
What are the phenomena that are views (*dṛṣṭi*)?
They are the five defiled views of the eye-faculty, mundane right view, the view of one in training (*śaikṣa*), and the view of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*).
What are the phenomena that are not views?

That is to say: with the exception of the eye-faculty, all remaining aggregates of form; with the exception of the other eight views, all remaining aggregates of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) and the entirety of the other three aggregates, together with unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*).
What are the phenomena that are the bases of views (*dṛṣṭi-sthāna*)?
That is to say, they are the contaminated phenomena (*sāsrava-dharma*). What are the phenomena that are not the locus of views (*adṛṣṭisthāna-dharma*)?
That is to say, they are the uncontaminated phenomena (*anāsrava-dharma*).
What are the phenomena associated with views?
They are the eight phenomena associated with views.
What are the phenomena dissociated from views?
This refers to the eight types of factors dissociated from views.
What are the factors of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana-dharmas*)?

They are the aggregates, elements, and bases of sentient beings in the hells, the animal realm, the realm of hungry ghosts, humans of Uttarakuru, and the non-percipient gods, as well as the karma that leads to birth therein; these are called the factors of ordinary beings.
What are the phenomena that are not the qualities of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*)?

They are: the four paths of practice (*pratipad*), the four analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*), the four fruits of asceticism (*śrāmaṇyaphala*), the knowledge of non-contention (*araṇājñāna*), the knowledge resulting from resolve (*praṇidhijñāna*), the ultimate meditative absorption (*prāntakoṭika-dhyāna*), the great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*), the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*), emptiness-of-emptiness (*śūnyatā-śūnyatā*), wishlessness-of-wishlessness (*apraṇihitā-apraṇihita*), signlessness-of-signlessness (*animittā-animitta*), the mundane knowledge at the limit of clear realization (*abhisamayāntika-saṃvṛtijñāna*) resulting from the mixed cultivation of dhyānas, and the aggregates, elements, and sense bases of the Śuddhāvāsa deities along with the karma for rebirth there. These are called the phenomena that are not the qualities of ordinary beings.
What are the dharmas shared with ordinary beings?
They are the meditative attainments shared [with them] and the births shared [with them].
What, furthermore, are these?
That is to say, such meditative absorptions and such births may both occur for ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*) and noble ones (*ārya*); these are called qualities shared with ordinary worldlings.
What are the qualities not shared with ordinary worldlings?

These are: the four paths of practice, the four analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*), the four fruits of the ascetic life (*śrāmaṇyaphala*), the knowledge of non-contention (*araṇājñāna*) and the knowledge resulting from aspiration (*praṇidhijñāna*), the meditative absorption of the limit (*prāntakoṭika-dhyāna*), the great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*) and the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*), the emptiness-of-emptiness (*śūnyatā-śūnyatā*), the wishlessness-of-wishlessness (*apraṇihitā-apraṇihita*), and the signlessness-of-signlessness (*animittā-animitta*); the mixed cultivation of the dhyānas, the conventional knowledge at the edge of clear realization (*abhisamayāntika-saṃvṛtijñāna*), and the aggregates, elements, and sense-bases of the Śuddhāvāsa deities along with the karma for rebirth there—these are called the qualities not shared with ordinary beings (*asaṃdhāraṇa-pṛthagjana-dharma*).
What are the fixed dharmas?
They are the five deeds of immediate retribution and the dharmas of those in training and those beyond training.
What are the non-fixed dharmas?
This refers to all other contaminated (*sāsrava*) phenomena and unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) phenomena, excluding the five deeds of immediate retribution (*ānantarya-karma*).
What are the phenomena conducive to feverish affliction (*paridāha-dharma*)?
They are the unwholesome (*akuśala*) and obscured-unneutral (*nivṛtāvyākṛta*) phenomena.
What are the phenomena that do not accord with the affliction of heat?
They are wholesome phenomena and non-obscured neutral phenomena.
What are the phenomena that are faculties?
This refers to the six internal bases (*āyatana*) and those root-factors (*indriya-dharma*) subsumed under the base of mental objects (*dharmāyatana*).
What are non-root factors?
They refer to the five external bases and those non-root factors subsumed under the base of mental objects.
What are the phenomena subsumed under the Noble Truths?
They are all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*) and analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyānirodha*).
What are the phenomena not subsumed under the Noble Truths?
That is to say, space and cessation not through deliberation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).
What are co-existent phenomena (*sahabhū-dharma*)?
They are all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*).
What are non-coexistent dharmas?
They are unconditioned dharmas (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*).
What are associated dharmas (*saṃprayukta-dharma*)?
This refers to all minds and mental factors.
What are the non-associated phenomena?
They are matter, the unconditioned, and the formations dissociated from mind.
What are the dharmas that are results?
They are all conditioned dharmas (*saṃskṛtadharma*) and analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyānirodha*).
What are the dharmas that are not results?
That is to say: space and non-analytical cessation.
What are dharmas that possess results?
They are all conditioned dharmas.
What is the dharma that has no fruit?
It refers to unconditioned dharmas (*asaṃskṛtadharma*).
What is the dharma that is maturation (*vipāka*)?
This refers to a portion of eleven bases (*āyatana*) that are of the nature of maturation (*vipāka*), excluding the sound base (*śabdāyatana*).
What are the non-maturation phenomena?
They refer to the sound base and a portion of those same eleven bases that are not of the nature of maturation.
What are dharmas with maturation?
They are unwholesome dharmas and wholesome impure dharmas.
What are dharmas without maturation?
This refers to indeterminate and untainted dharmas.
What are causal-condition dharmas?
They refer to all dharmas.
What is the dharma that is not produced by causes and conditions?
It refers to such dharmas that cannot be found when sought, because all dharmas are produced by causes and conditions.
What is the dharma that is produced by causes and conditions?
That is to say, all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*).
What are phenomena that lack causes and conditions?
That is to say, unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛtadharma*).
What is the state of being dissociated from phenomena (*visamyoga*)?

It refers to the wholesome discipline (*śīla*) bound to the desire realm; the wholesome meditative absorption (*samādhi*) arising from renunciation and seclusion bound to the form and formless realms; as well as the dharmas of those in training (*śaikṣa*) and those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), together with analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).
What is that which is not dissociated from phenomena?

It refers to all other phenomena associated with the desire realm, excluding the wholesome precepts bound to the desire realm; all other phenomena associated with the form and formless realms, excluding the wholesome meditative concentrations arising from renunciation and seclusion bound to the form and formless realms; as well as space and non-analytical cessation.
What are the phenomena that involve separation?
They are all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*).
What are the phenomena that do not involve separation?
This refers to unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*).
What are continuous phenomena (*saṃtati-dharma*)?
They are those phenomena that have extinction as their precursor, or which have already arisen, or are currently arising.

What, then, is this? It refers to phenomena of the past, present, and future that are currently arising; when such subsequent phenomena continue in succession with preceding phenomena, this is called "successive phenomena" (*saṃtati-dharma*).
What are non-continuous phenomena?
They refer to all other future phenomena, as well as unconditioned phenomena, excluding those future phenomena that are currently arising and manifesting; these are called non-continuous phenomena.
What is the dharma of continuity?
It refers to those dharmas that have arisen having been preceded by a dharma that has ceased.
Furthermore, what is this?

This refers to all other past and present phenomena, excluding the five aggregates at the moment of death of an Arhat in the past or present; such preceding phenomena having subsequent continuous phenomena is called "having continuous phenomena."
What are phenomena that lack continuity?
They are the five aggregates at the time of death of an Arhat in the past or present, as well as future [phenomena] and unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*).
What are wholesome phenomena (*kuśala-dharma*)?
This refers to the five aggregates of wholesome phenomena and analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).
What are unwholesome phenomena?
They refer to the five aggregates of unwholesome phenomena.
What are the indeterminate dharmas?
They are the five indeterminate aggregates, as well as space and non-analytical cessation.
What are the dharmas of those in training (śaikṣa)?
That is to say, the five aggregates of one in training.
What are the dharmas of one beyond training?
That is to say, the five aggregates of one beyond training.
What are the dharmas that are neither-learner-nor-non-learner?
They are the five contaminated aggregates (pañca-skandhāḥ sāsravāḥ) and unconditioned dharmas (asaṃskṛta-dharmāḥ).
What are the dharmas to be abandoned by vision (darśana-prahātavya-dharmāḥ)?

This refers to those phenomena abandoned by the patiences at the limit of clear realization (abhisamaya) for those who practice in accordance with faith or in accordance with the Dharma. What, then, are these?

They are the eighty-eight latent dispositions (anuśaya) to be abandoned through seeing, along with their associated phenomena and the non-associated formations (citta-viprayukta-saṃskāra) that arise together with them.
What are the phenomena to be abandoned through cultivation?
They are those phenomena which, for one who has seen the path (the śaikṣa), are to be abandoned through cultivation.
Furthermore, what are these?

This refers to the ten latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) abandoned through cultivation and their associated dharmas, as well as the bodily and vocal actions they give rise to, the formations dissociated from mind that they give rise to, and all non-defiled outflowing (*sāsrava*) dharmas.
What are the dharmas not to be abandoned?
They are the untainted (anāsrava) dharmas.
What are the dharmas that have as their cause those to be abandoned by insight (darśana-prahātavya)?
What are the factors that have all defiled phenomena (*kliṣṭadharma*) and the maturation (*vipāka*) of phenomena abandoned through insight (*darśana-prahātavya*) as their cause?
They are exclusively all phenomena abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-prahātavya*).
What are the phenomena that have non-abandonable factors as their cause?
They are the conditioned uncontaminated phenomena (*anāsrava-saṃskṛta-dharma*).
What are the phenomena that are visible and resistant (*sanidarśana-sapratigha*)?
That is to say, one base.
What are the dharmas that are invisible and impinging?
That is to say, nine bases.
What is the dharma that is non-visible and non-obstructive?
It refers to two bases.
What is the dharma that is a result of maturation (*vipāka*)?
This refers to a portion of eleven bases (*āyatana*), excluding the sound base (*śabdāyatana*).
What are the resultant (*vipāka*) dharmas?
They are the unwholesome (*akuśala*) and wholesome-with-outflows (*sāsrava-kuśala*) dharmas.
What is that which is neither maturation nor a dharma subject to maturation?
It refers to all remaining indeterminate dharmas, as well as wholesome and untainted dharmas, excluding those indeterminate dharmas that are maturations.
What are inferior dharmas?
They are unwholesome dharmas and obscured-unspecified dharmas.
What are intermediate dharmas?
This refers to wholesome contaminated phenomena (*sāsrava*) and non-obscured neutral phenomena (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*).
What are sublime phenomena (*sadharma*)?
They refer to uncontaminated conditioned phenomena (*anāsrava-saṃskṛta-dharma*) and cessation through deliberation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).
What are the minor dharmas?

They refer to minor faith, minor aspiration, and minor resolute conviction, along with their associated dharmas and co-existent dharmas; as well as all material dharmas that are slight, minute, subtle, not many, and not extensive—these are called minor dharmas.
What are the great dharmas?

They refer to great faith, great aspiration, and great resolve, along with their associated dharmas and co-existent dharmas. Even though various material dharmas may be numerous and extensive, they are not infinite, boundless, or immeasurable; likewise, space and non-analytical cessation are called great dharmas.
What are immeasurable phenomena (*apramāṇa-dharma*)?
They are immeasurable faith, immeasurable aspiration, immeasurable resolve, and their associated factors;

as well as those co-existent factors, whether they be material phenomena that are manifold, vast, boundless, limitless, and immeasurable, or analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*). These are called immeasurable phenomena.
What are agreeable phenomena?
They are those phenomena that are pleasing to the mind.
What are disagreeable phenomena? They are those phenomena that are not pleasing to the mind.
That is to say, those phenomena which are not pleasing to the mind.
What are phenomena that are neither agreeable nor disagreeable?
They are those phenomena that accord with equanimity.
What are phenomena associated with pleasure?
They are those phenomena that are associated with pleasant feeling (*sukha-vedanā*).
What are phenomena associated with suffering?
That is to say, if a phenomenon is associated with painful feeling (*duḥkhā vedanā*),
what is a phenomenon that occurs together with neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling (*aduḥkhāsukhā vedanā*)?
It refers to any phenomenon associated with neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling.
What are co-nascent phenomena?
They are conditioned phenomena, because they possess the characteristic of arising.
What are co-abiding phenomena?
This means that conditioned phenomena possess the characteristic of duration.
What are phenomena that perish together?
This means that conditioned phenomena possess the characteristic of cessation.
What are non-simultaneously-arisen phenomena?
They are unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*), because they lack the characteristic of arising.
What are non-simultaneously-abiding phenomena?
This refers to unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*), because they lack the characteristic of abiding.
What are non-simultaneously-ceasing phenomena?
This refers to unconditioned phenomena, because they lack the characteristic of cessation.
What are the phenomena that arise together with the mind (*citta-sahaja-dharma*)?
They are a portion of the eleven bases (*āyatana*) that arise together with the mind, excluding the mind-base (*manāyatana*).
What are the phenomena that abide together with the mind (*citta-saha-sthita-dharma*)?
This refers to the factors that follow the mind (*cittānuvartin*).
What are the factors that perish together with the mind (*sahanaśvara*)?
They refer to a portion of ten bases (*āyatana*), excluding the sound base (*śabdāyatana*) and the mind base (*manāyatana*).
What are phenomena that do not arise simultaneously with the mind?
They are the sense-base of the mind (*manāyatana*) and a portion of the eleven sense-bases that do not arise simultaneously with the mind.
What are phenomena that do not abide simultaneously with the mind?
What are the phenomena that do not follow the mind and do not perish simultaneously with the mind? They are the sphere of sound (*śabdāyatana*),
the sphere of the mind (*manāyatana*), and a portion of the ten spheres that do not perish simultaneously with the mind.
What is the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*)?

It refers to sensual craving and the feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness associated with that sensual craving; as well as the bodily and vocal actions arising from them, and the formations dissociated from mind arising from them—this is called the desire realm.
What is the element of ill-will (*vyāpādadhātu*)?

It refers to hatred and the feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness associated with hatred; as well as the bodily and vocal actions arising from them, and the formations dissociated from mind arising from them—this is called the element of ill-will.
What is the element of harm?

It refers to harm itself, as well as the feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness associated with it; furthermore, it includes the bodily and vocal actions arising from them, and the formations dissociated from mind arising from them—this is called the element of harm.
What is the element of renunciation (*niḥsaraṇadhātu*)?

It refers to renunciation itself, as well as the feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness associated with renunciation; furthermore, it includes the bodily and vocal actions arising from those, the formations dissociated from mind arising from those, and analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyānirodha*). This is called the element of renunciation.
What is the element of non-ill will?

It refers to non-hatred and the feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness associated with non-hatred; as well as the bodily and vocal actions arising from them, and the formations dissociated from mind arising from them—this is called the element of non-ill will.
What is the element of non-harming?

It refers to non-harming and the feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness associated with non-harming; as well as the bodily and vocal actions arising from them, and the formations dissociated from mind arising from them—this is called the element of non-harming.
What is the desire realm?
It refers to those phenomena in which sensual craving increases.
What is the form realm?
That is to say, those phenomena in which attachment to form increases.
What about the formless realm?
It refers to those phenomena in which attachment to the formless increases.
What is the form realm (*rūpadhātu*)?
It refers to the desire realm and the form realm collectively termed the "form realm.
What is the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*)?
That is to say, the four formless [attainments].
What is the element of cessation?
It refers to analytical cessation and non-analytical cessation.
Furthermore, all material phenomena (*rūpadharma*) are collectively termed the form realm (*rūpadhātu*).

With the exception of analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyānirodha*) and non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyānirodha*), all other non-material phenomena are collectively termed the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*).
Cessation through deliberation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) and cessation not through deliberation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) are collectively termed the element of cessation (*nirodha-dhātu*).
What is sensual existence (*kāma-bhava*)?

It refers to that karma bound to the desire realm which, taking grasping as its condition, is capable of producing the maturation (*vipāka*) of that karma in the future; this is called sensual existence.
What is form-existence (*rūpabhava*)?
It refers to that karma bound to the realm of form which, taking grasping as its condition, is capable of producing the maturation of that karma in the future; this is called form-existence.
What is formless existence?
It refers to that karma bound to the formless realm which, taking grasping as its condition, is capable of producing its maturation in the future; this is called formless existence.
What is the outflow of desire (*kāma-āsrava*)?

It refers to all other fetters (*saṃyojana*), bonds (*bandhana*), latent tendencies (*anuśaya*), secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*), and envelopments (*paryavasthāna*) bound to the desire realm, excluding the ignorance (*avidyā*) bound to the desire realm; these are called the outflow of desire.
What are the outflows (āsrava)?

They refer to all other fetters (saṃyojana), bonds (bandhana), latent tendencies (anuśaya), secondary afflictions (upakleśa), and envelopments (paryavasthāna) associated with the form and formless realms, excluding ignorance (avidyā) associated with the form and formless realms; these are called the outflows.
What is the outflow of ignorance?
It refers to the lack of wisdom regarding the three realms.
What is the past life?

That is to say, if conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) have already arisen and fully arisen, already been born and fully born, already occurred and fully manifested, already accumulated and fully appeared, and have already passed away, ceased, been extinguished, departed, and become decayed; being past, fallen into the past, categorized as the past, and subsumed within the past time—this is called the "past world."

What is the future time? It refers to those conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) that have not yet arisen, have not yet fully arisen; have not yet been born, have not yet fully been born; have not yet occurred, have not yet manifested; have not yet accumulated, have not yet appeared; have not yet come together, have not yet become present. These belong to the future, fall within the future portion, are of the future category, and are subsumed under the future time; this is called the future time.
What is the present time?

It refers to those conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) that have already arisen and fully arisen, already been born and fully born, already manifested and fully manifested, already accumulated and fully appeared; which are currently abiding and have not yet deteriorated, being conjoined and present before one—these belong to the present, fall within the category of the present, are of the nature of the present, and are subsumed under the present time. This is called the present time.
What is the objective basis for discourse concerning the past?
It refers to formations comprised within the past.
What is the objective basis for discourse concerning the future?
That is to say, formations comprised within the future.
What is the basis for the expression "present"?
It refers to formations comprised within the present.
What is the nature of suffering as suffering (*duḥkha-duḥkhatā*)?
It refers to the fact that the desire realm is suffering by virtue of suffering as suffering.
What is the nature of suffering as change (*vipariṇāma-duḥkhatā*)?

This means that the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*) is suffering by virtue of the suffering of change (*vipariṇāmaduḥkha*). What is the nature of the suffering of conditioned existence (*saṃskāraduḥkhatā*)?
It means that the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) is suffering by virtue of the suffering of conditioned existence.

Furthermore, disagreeable conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are suffering by virtue of the suffering of suffering (*duḥkha-duḥkhatā*); agreeable conditioned phenomena are suffering by virtue of the suffering of change (*vipariṇāma-duḥkhatā*); and conditioned phenomena that are neither agreeable nor disagreeable are suffering by virtue of the suffering inherent in conditioned existence itself (*saṃskāra-duḥkhatā*).

Furthermore, painful feeling is suffering by way of the suffering of suffering (*duḥkhaduḥkhatā*); pleasant feeling is suffering by way of the suffering of change (*vipariṇāmaduḥkhatā*); and neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling is suffering by way of the suffering of conditioned formations (*saṃskāraduḥkhatā*).
What are the phenomena associated with vitarka and vicāra?
This refers to phenomena associated with both vitarka (applied thought) and vicāra (sustained thought).
What are phenomena without vitarka and with only vicāra?
This refers to phenomena that are not associated with vitarka but are associated with vicāra.
What are phenomena without vitarka and without vicāra?
They are those phenomena that are dissociated from vitarka and vicāra.
What is the stage with vitarka and vicāra?
This refers to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), the Brahma-world (*brahmaloka*), and a portion of untainted phenomena (*anāsravadharma*).
What is the stage characterized by the absence of vitarka and the presence of vicāra alone?
It refers to the attainment of the intermediate dhyāna (*dhyānāntara*), the [lower] Brahmās, the Mahābrahmās, and a portion of untainted phenomena.
What is the stage without vitarka and vicāra?
It refers to all the Ābhāsvara [heaven], all the Śubhakṛtsna [heaven], all the Bṛhatphala [heaven], all the formless realms, and a portion of the untainted (anāsrava) dharmas.
*Abhidharmaprakaraṇapādaśāstra*, Fascicle Six.
*Abhidharmaprakaraṇapādaśāstra*, Fascicle Seven.
Composed by the Venerable Vasumitra.
