Chapter Six, Part Three: On the Compendium of Categories. What is bodily action?
It refers to bodily intimation and non-intimation.
What is vocal action?
It refers to vocal intimation and non-intimation.
What is mental action?
It refers to volition (*cetanā*).
What is wholesome karma?
It refers to wholesome bodily and vocal actions, as well as wholesome volition.
What is unwholesome karma?
It refers to unwholesome bodily and vocal actions, as well as unwholesome volition.
What is neutral karma?
This refers to indeterminate bodily and vocal actions, as well as indeterminate volition (*cetanā*).
What are the actions of one in training (*śaikṣa*)?
They are the bodily and vocal actions of one in training, as well as the volition of one in training.
What is the karma of one beyond training (aśaikṣa)?
It refers to the bodily and vocal karma of one beyond training, as well as the volition (cetanā) of one beyond training.
What is the karma that is neither of one in training nor of one beyond training?
This refers to contaminated bodily and vocal actions, as well as contaminated volition (*cetanā*).
What is action to be abandoned by insight (*darśana-prahātavya*)?

It refers to those actions that are abandoned by the patiences (*kṣānti*) at the edge of clear realization (*abhisamaya-anta*) for those who follow by faith (*śraddhānusārin*) or follow by dharma (*dharmānusārin*).
What, then, is this? It refers to the volition associated with the eighty-eight proclivities (*anuśaya*) to be abandoned through seeing (*darśana-prahātavya*).
What is karma to be abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-prahātavya*)?
This refers to karma that is abandoned through cultivation by one who has seen the tracks and is still in training.
Furthermore, what is this?
It refers to the volition associated with the ten proclivities abandoned through cultivation, as well as the bodily and vocal actions arising therefrom, and non-defiled impure karma.
What is karma that is not to be abandoned?
It refers to untainted (anāsrava) bodily and vocal actions, as well as untainted volition (cetanā).
What is karma to be experienced in the present life (dṛṣṭadharmavedanīya)?

That is to say, if karma is performed and accumulated in this very life, and that karma ripens as its maturation in this very life and not in another life, it is called karma to be experienced in the present life (*dṛṣṭadharmavedanīya-karman*).
What is karma to be experienced in the next life?
It refers to karma that is performed and accumulated in this life, the maturation of which is experienced in the second life and no other; this is called karma to be experienced in the next life.
What is karma to be experienced in subsequent lives?

It refers to karma that is performed and accumulated in this life, the maturation of which is experienced in the third life, or the fourth life, or even beyond that, but not in any other life; this is called karma to be experienced in subsequent lives.
What is karma conducive to pleasant feeling?
It refers to wholesome karma bound to the desire realm, as well as wholesome karma bound to the form realm up to the level of the third dhyāna.
What is karma conducive to painful feeling?
This refers to unwholesome karma.
What is karma that accords with neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling?
It refers to wholesome karma bound to the level of the fourth dhyāna, as well as wholesome karma bound to the formless realm.
What is the application of mindfulness to the body?
It refers to the ten bases of form and the form included within the sphere of mental objects (*dharmāyatana*).
What is the application of mindfulness to sensation?
This refers to the six groups of feeling, namely: feeling born of eye-contact, up to feeling born of mind-contact.
What is the application of mindfulness to the mind?
It refers to the six groups of consciousness, namely: eye-consciousness, up to mind-consciousness.
What is the application of mindfulness to phenomena (*dharmasmṛtyupasthāna*)?
It refers to the sphere of non-material phenomena (*arūpadharmāyatana*) not included within feeling (*vedanā*).

Furthermore, the wholesome paths—both with and without outflows (*sāsrava-anāsrava-mārga*)—arising through the predominance of the body are called the application of mindfulness to the body (*kāyasmṛtyupasthāna*).
The wholesome, contaminated, and uncontaminated paths arising through the predominance of sensation are called the application of mindfulness to sensation (*vedanā-smṛtyupasthāna*).
The wholesome, contaminated, and uncontaminated paths arising through the predominance of mind are called the application of mindfulness to mind (*citta-smṛtyupasthāna*).
The wholesome, contaminated, and uncontaminated paths arising through the predominance of the Dharma are called the mindfulness-establishment of phenomena (*dharmasmṛtyupasthāna*).
Furthermore, the wholesome, contaminated, and uncontaminated wisdom arising by taking the body as its object is called the mindfulness-establishment of the body (*kāyasmṛtyupasthāna*).
The wholesome, outflow-tainted (*sāsrava*), and outflow-free (*anāsrava*) wisdom that arises conditioned by feeling is called the mindfulness-establishment of feeling (*vedanā-smṛtyupasthāna*).
The wholesome, outflow-tainted, and outflow-free wisdom that arises conditioned by the mind is called the mindfulness-establishment of mind (*citta-smṛtyupasthāna*).
The wholesome, outflow-tainted (*sāsrava*) and outflow-free (*anāsrava*) wisdom that arises conditioned by phenomena is called the application of mindfulness to phenomena (*dharmasmṛtyupasthāna*).
What is the right effort (*samyakprahāṇa*) practiced with diligence for the sake of the permanent abandonment of evil, unwholesome states that have already arisen?
It refers to the wholesome, contaminated, and uncontaminated paths that arise through predominant effort in order to permanently abandon evil and unwholesome states that have already arisen.
What is the right effort (*samyakprahāṇa*) applied with diligence in order that evil and unwholesome states not yet arisen may never arise?
It refers to the predominant wholesome, outflow-tainted (*sāsrava*) and outflow-free (*anāsrava*) paths that are undertaken so that unarisen evil and unwholesome states do not arise.
What is the right effort (*samyakprahāṇa*) applied with diligence so that unarisen wholesome states may arise?

What are the right efforts (*samyakprahāṇa*) applied with diligence for the sake of causing unarisen wholesome dharmas to arise, and for the sake of causing already arisen wholesome dharmas to remain firm, not be forgotten, be cultivated to fulfillment, increase further, expand, and be realized through wisdom? They are the superior paths, both contaminated (*sāsrava*) and uncontaminated (*anāsrava*), that are brought forth. What are they? [They are: the effort to prevent the arising of unarisen unwholesome dharmas; the effort to abandon unwholesome dharmas that have already arisen; the effort to cause the arising of unarisen wholesome dharmas; and the effort to maintain, not forget, cultivate to fulfillment, increase, expand, and realize through wisdom those wholesome dharmas that have already arisen. These are called the four right efforts. What is the basis for these four right efforts? It is the four foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*). What are the four foundations of mindfulness? They are: the foundation of mindfulness of the body, the foundation of mindfulness of feelings, the foundation of mindfulness of the mind, and the foundation of mindfulness of phenomena. What is the foundation of mindfulness of the body? It is the contemplation of the body as the body, internally, externally, and both internally and externally. What is the foundation of mindfulness of feelings? It is the contemplation of feelings as feelings, internally, externally, and both internally and externally. What is the foundation of mindfulness of the mind? It is the contemplation of the mind as the mind, internally, externally, and both internally and externally. What is the foundation of mindfulness of phenomena? It is the contemplation of phenomena as phenomena, internally, externally, and both internally and externally. What is the contemplation of the body as the body internally? It is when a bhikṣu dwells observing the body as the body in relation to his own internal body, possessing application of mindfulness (*smṛti-samprajanya*), clearly comprehending (*samprajānan*), and mindful (*smṛtimān*), having removed covetousness and dejection regarding the world. What is the contemplation of the body as the body externally? It is when a bhikṣu dwells observing the body as the body in relation to the external body of others, possessing application of mindfulness, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and dejection regarding the world. What is the contemplation of the body as the body both internally and externally? It is when a bhikṣu dwells observing the body as the body in relation to both his own internal body and the external bodies of others, possessing application of mindfulness, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and dejection regarding the world. Furthermore, what is the contemplation of the body as the body internally? It is when a bhikṣu dwells observing the body as the body in relation to his own internal body, from the soles of the feet upward and from the hair of the head downward, bounded by skin and filled with various impurities. That is to say: "In this body there are head-hairs, body-hairs, nails, teeth, skin, flesh, sinews, bones, bone-marrow, kidneys, heart, liver, pleura, spleen, lungs, small intestines, large intestines, stomach, feces, brain, bile, phlegm, pus, blood, sweat, fat, tears, grease, saliva, nasal mucus, synovial fluid, and urine. Just as one might look at a bag full of various grains such as rice, barley, millet, wheat, and beans, and distinguish them: "This is rice, this is barley, this is millet, this is wheat, and these are beans," so too does a bhikṣu dwell observing the body as the body internally, from the soles of the feet upward and from the hair of the head downward, bounded by skin and filled with various impurities. This is called the contemplation of the body as the body internally. What is the contemplation of the body as the body externally? It is when a bhikṣu dwells observing the body as the body in relation to the external body of others, from the soles of the feet upward and from the hair of the head downward, bounded by skin and filled with various impurities. That is to say: "In this body there are head-hairs, body-hairs, nails, teeth, skin, flesh, sinews, bones, bone-marrow, kidneys, heart, liver, pleura, spleen, lungs, small intestines, large intestines, stomach, feces, brain, bile, phlegm, pus, blood, sweat, fat, tears, grease, saliva, nasal mucus, synovial fluid, and urine. Just as one might look at a corpse discarded in a charnel ground—one day dead, two days dead, or up to seven days dead—swollen, discolored, and festering, a bhikṣu compares it to his own body: "This body, too, is of the same nature, will become like this, and cannot escape this fate. This is called the contemplation of the body as the body externally. What is the contemplation of the body as the body both internally and externally? It is when a bhikṣu dwells observing the body as the body in relation to both his own internal body and the external bodies of others, from the soles of the feet upward and from the hair of the head downward, bounded by skin and filled with various impurities. That is to say: "In this body there are head-hairs, body-hairs, nails, teeth, skin, flesh, sinews, bones, bone-marrow, kidneys, heart, liver, pleura, spleen, lungs, small intestines, large intestines, stomach, feces, brain, bile, phlegm, pus, blood, sweat, fat, tears, grease, saliva, nasal mucus, synovial fluid, and urine. Just as one might look at a bag full of various grains such as rice, barley, millet, wheat, and beans, and distinguish them: "This is rice, this is barley, this is millet, this is wheat, and these are beans," so too does a bhikṣu dwell observing the body as the body both internally and externally, from the soles of the feet upward and from the hair of the head downward, bounded by skin and filled with various impurities. This is called the contemplation of the body as the body both internally and externally. Furthermore, what is the contemplation of the body as the body internally? It is when a bhikṣu dwells observing the body as the body in relation to his own internal body, contemplating its origination, its passing away, and both its origination and passing away. That is to say: "Such is the body, such is the origination of the body, such is the passing away of the body. This is called the contemplation of the body as the body internally. What is the contemplation of the body as the body externally? It is when a bhikṣu dwells observing the body as the body in relation to the external body of others, contemplating its origination, its passing away, and both its origination and passing away. That is to say: "Such is the body, such is the origination of the body, such is the passing away of the body. This is called the contemplation of the body as the body externally. What is the contemplation of the body as the body both internally and externally? It is when a bhikṣu dwells observing the body as the body in relation to both his own internal body and the external bodies of others, contemplating its origination, its passing away, and both its origination and passing away. That is to say: "Such is the body, such is the origination of the body, such is the passing away of the body. This is called the contemplation of the body as the body both internally and externally. Furthermore, what is the contemplation of the body as the body internally? It is when a bhikṣu dwells observing the body as the body in relation to his own internal body, removing desire and lust for the body. This is called the contemplation of the body as the body internally. What is the contemplation of the body as the body externally? It is when a bhikṣu dwells observing the body as the body in relation to the external body of others, removing desire and lust for the body. This is called the contemplation of the body as the body externally. What is the contemplation of the body as the body both internally and externally? It is when a bhikṣu dwells observing the body as the body in relation to both his own internal body and the external bodies of others, removing desire and lust for the body. This is called the contemplation of the body as the body both internally and externally. Furthermore, what is the contemplation of the body as the body internally? It is when a bhikṣu dwells observing the body as the body in relation to his own internal body, contemplating the body according to its elements. That is to say: "In this body there are the earth element, the water element, the fire element, and the air element. Just as a skilled butcher or a butcher’s apprentice, having slaughtered a cow and divided it into

It refers to the wholesome, contaminated (*sāsrava*) and uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) paths that arise through superior effort, in order to cause already arisen wholesome dharmas to remain firm, not be forgotten, be cultivated to fulfillment, and increase further until they are realized through wisdom.
What is the basis of psychic power consisting of concentration of desire and the accomplishment of the formations of abandonment?
It refers to the wholesome, contaminated, and uncontaminated paths arising through the predominance of desire.
What is the basis of psychic power consisting of concentration of energy and the accomplishment of the formations of abandonment?
This refers to the wholesome, contaminated, and uncontaminated paths arising through the predominance of diligence.
What is the basis of psychic power consisting in the accomplishment of concentration of mind through the formative forces of abandonment?
It refers to the wholesome, contaminated, and uncontaminated paths arising through the predominance of the mind.
What is the basis for psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*) consisting in the accomplishment of the formative forces of abandonment through the concentration of contemplation?
It refers to the wholesome, both contaminated and uncontaminated, paths arising from the predominance of contemplation.
What is the first dhyāna?
This refers to the five aggregates of wholesome states subsumed under the first dhyāna.
What is the second dhyāna?
It refers to the five aggregates of wholesome states subsumed under the second dhyāna.
What is the third dhyāna?
It refers to the wholesome five aggregates (pañca-skandha) subsumed under the third dhyāna.
What is the fourth dhyāna?
It refers to the five aggregates of wholesome phenomena subsumed under the fourth dhyāna.
What is the Noble Truth of Suffering?
It refers to the five aggregates of clinging.
What is the noble truth of origination?
It refers to the cause of outflows (*sāsrava*).
What is the noble truth of cessation?
What is the noble truth of the path? It refers to the dharmas of those in training (śaikṣa) and those beyond training (aśaikṣa).
What is the immeasurable state of loving-kindness (*maitrī-apramāṇa*)?

It refers to loving-kindness itself, as well as the feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness associated with it; furthermore, it includes the bodily and vocal actions arising from those, and the formations dissociated from mind arising from them. This is called the immeasurable state of loving-kindness.
What is the immeasurable of compassion (*karuṇā-apramāṇa*)?

It refers to compassion itself, as well as the feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), formations (*saṃskāra*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*) associated with it; furthermore, it includes the bodily and vocal actions (*kāya-vāk-karman*) arising from those, and the formations dissociated from mind (*citta-viprayukta-saṃskāra*) arising from them. This is called the immeasurable of compassion.
What is the immeasurable state of sympathetic joy (*muditā*)?

It refers to joy and the associated aggregates of feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness; as well as the bodily and vocal actions arising from them, and the formations dissociated from mind arising from them—this is called the immeasurable state of sympathetic joy.
What is the immeasurable of equanimity (*upekṣā-apramāṇa*)?

It refers to equanimity and the feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness associated with it; as well as the bodily and vocal actions arising from them, and the formations dissociated from mind arising from them—this is called the immeasurable of equanimity.
What is the sphere of infinite space?
It is of two kinds:
first, meditative absorption; second, rebirth. All feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness contained therein are called the sphere of infinite space.
What is the sphere of infinite consciousness (*vijñānānantyāyatana*)? It is of two kinds:

first, meditative absorption (*samādhi*), and second, rebirth (*upapatti*). All feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness present therein are called the sphere of infinite consciousness.
What is the sphere of nothingness?
It is of two kinds:
first, meditative absorption; second, rebirth. All feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness contained therein are called the sphere of nothingness.
What is the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception?
This is of two kinds:
first, meditative absorption; second, rebirth. The feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness bound to this [sphere] are called the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
What is the noble lineage of contentment with whatever robes one obtains?

It refers to the wholesome, out-flowing (*sāsrava*) and non-out-flowing (*anāsrava*) paths arising from the predominance of contentment with whatever robes one obtains; this is called the noble lineage of contentment with whatever robes one obtains.
What is the noble lineage of contentment with whatever food one obtains?

It refers to the wholesome, contaminated, and uncontaminated paths arising from the predominance of contentment with whatever food one obtains; this is called the noble lineage of contentment with whatever food one obtains.
What is the noble lineage of contentment with whatever bedding and seats one obtains?

It refers to the wholesome, contaminated, and uncontaminated paths arising from the predominance of contentment with whatever bedding and seats one obtains; this is called the noble lineage of contentment with whatever bedding and seats one obtains.
What is the noble lineage of delighting in abandonment and delighting in cultivation?

It refers to the wholesome, contaminated, and uncontaminated paths arising from the predominance of delighting in abandonment and delighting in cultivation; this is called the noble lineage of delighting in abandonment and delighting in cultivation.
What is the fruit of stream-entry?
It is of two kinds:
first, the conditioned; second, the unconditioned.
What is the conditioned fruit of stream-entry?
It refers to all the dharmas of training (śaikṣadharma) pertaining to the realization of the fruit of stream-entry that have been, are being, or will be attained.
What is the unconditioned fruit of stream-entry?
The abandonment of all fetters that is realized upon attaining the fruit of stream-entry— whether already attained, currently being attained,
or yet to be attained— is called the fruit of stream-entry.
What is the fruit of once-returning?
This is of two kinds:
first, conditioned; second, unconditioned.
What is the conditioned fruit of once-returning?
This refers to all the qualities of training (*śaikṣadharma*) realized by one who has attained the fruit of once-returning (*sakṛdāgāmiphala*), which have been, are being, or will be acquired.
What is the unconditioned fruit of once-returning?
It refers to the abandonment of all fetters (*saṃyojana*) realized by one who has attained the fruit of once-returning, which have been, are being, or will be acquired.
This is called the fruit of once-returning.
What is the fruit of non-returning?
This is of two kinds:
There are two: the conditioned and the unconditioned.
What is the conditioned fruit of non-returning?
It refers to all the dharmas of training (śaikṣadharma) pertaining to the realization of the fruit of non-returning that have been, are being, or will be attained.
What is the unconditioned fruit of non-returning?
It refers to the abandonment of all fetters attained through the realization of the fruit of non-returning—whether already attained, currently being attained, or yet to be attained.
This is called the fruit of non-returning.
What is the fruit of arhatship?
It is of two kinds:
first, the conditioned; second, the unconditioned.
What is the conditioned fruit of arhatship?
It refers to all the dharmas of no-more-learning (aśaikṣadharma) pertaining to the realization of the fruit of arhatship that have been, are being, or will be attained.
What is the unconditioned fruit of arhatship?
The abandonment of all fetters (saṃyojana) realized through the attainment of the fruit of arhatship— whether already attained, currently being attained, or yet to be attained—
is called the fruit of arhatship. The two sets of four knowledges,
such as the knowledge of phenomena (dharmajñāna) and the knowledge of suffering (duḥkhajñāna), should be understood as previously explained.
What is the analytical knowledge of phenomena (*dharma-pratisaṃvid*)?
It is the non-retrogressive wisdom regarding all sets of names, phrases, and syllables.
What is the analytical knowledge of meaning (*artha-pratisaṃvid*)?
That is to say, it is the non-retrogressive knowledge regarding the ultimate truth.
What is the analytical knowledge of language?
It is the non-retrogressive knowledge regarding linguistic expression.
What is the analytical knowledge of eloquence (*pratibhāna-pratisaṃvid*)?
It refers to the non-retrogressive knowledge that manifests unimpeded, reasoned speech and mastery over meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
What is its causal condition?
This refers to all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*).
What is the equal-and-immediate condition (*samanantarapratyaya*)?
It refers to all other past and present minds and mental factors (*cittacaitta*), excluding those minds and mental factors at the moment of the final death of an Arhat in the past or present.
What are the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*) and the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*)?
They are all phenomena (*dharmas*).
What is edible food (*kavaḍīkāra-āhāra*)?

That which, by taking edible food as its object, nourishes the sense faculties, increases the primary elements, and provides support, further support, satisfaction, further satisfaction, protection, further protection, transformation, further transformation, and benefit, further benefit—this is called edible food (*kavaḍīkāra-āhāra*).
What is the nutriment of contact?

It refers to that which, conditioned by tainted contact, nourishes the sense faculties, increases the primary elements, and provides assistance, further assistance; satisfaction, further satisfaction; protection, further protection; transformation, further transformation; and benefit, further benefit. This is called the nutriment of contact.
What is the nutriment of mental volition (*manaḥsaṃcetanāhāra*)?

It refers to that which, conditioned by contaminated volition (*sāsravacetanā*), nourishes the sense faculties, increases the primary elements (*mahābhūta*), and provides assistance, further assistance; satisfaction, further satisfaction; protection, further protection; transformation, further transformation; and benefit, further benefit. This is called the nutriment of mental volition.
What is the nutriment of consciousness?

It refers to the nourishment of the sense faculties and the augmentation of the primary elements based upon tainted consciousness; that which assists, provides further assistance, satisfies, provides further satisfaction, protects, provides further protection, transforms, provides further transformation, and benefits, provides further benefit—this is called the nutriment of consciousness.
What is the flood of desire (*kāma-ogha*)?

It refers to all other fetters (*saṃyojana*), bonds (*bandhana*), latent tendencies (*anuśaya*), secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*), and envelopments (*paryavasthāna*) bound to the desire realm, excluding the views and ignorance associated with the desire realm; these are called the flood of desire.
What is the flood of existence (*bhava-ogha*)?

It refers to all other fetters (*saṃyojana*), bonds (*bandhana*), latent tendencies (*anuśaya*), secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*), and envelopments (*paryavasthāna*) bound to the realms of form and formlessness, excluding the views and ignorance associated with those realms; this is called the flood of existence.
What is the flood of views (*dṛṣṭi-ogha*)?

It refers to the five views of the three realms, namely: the view of a self-entity (*satkāya-dṛṣṭi*), the view of extremes (*antagrāha-dṛṣṭi*), false view (*mithyā-dṛṣṭi*), the esteeming of views (*dṛṣṭi-parāmarśa*), and the esteeming of precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*). These are called the flood of views.
What is the flood of ignorance?
It refers to the lack of wisdom regarding the three realms.
The four yokes are likewise.
What is the grasping of sensual desire (*kāma-upādāna*)?

It refers to all other fetters (*saṃyojana*), bonds (*bandhana*), latent tendencies (*anuśaya*), secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*), and obsessions (*paryavasthāna*) bound to the realm of sensual desire (*kāmadhātu*), excluding the five views (*dṛṣṭi*) bound to the realm of sensual desire; this is called the grasping of sensual desire.
What is the grasping at views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*)?

It refers to the four views, namely: the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), the view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*), false view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*), and the grasping at views; these are called the grasping at views.
What is the grasping at precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*)?

That is to say, there is one who clings to precepts, saying that precepts can purify, can liberate, can lead to transcendence, and can surpass suffering and pleasure to reach the state beyond suffering and pleasure;
or who clings to prohibitions, saying that prohibitions can purify, can liberate, can lead to transcendence, and can surpass suffering and pleasure to reach the state beyond suffering and pleasure;

or who clings to both precepts and prohibitions, saying that precepts and prohibitions together can purify, can liberate, can lead to transcendence, and can surpass suffering and pleasure to reach the state beyond suffering and pleasure.
This is called the clinging to rules and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*).
What is the clinging to the doctrine of self (*ātmavādopādāna*)?

It refers to all other fetters (*saṃyojana*), bonds (*bandhana*), latent tendencies (*anuśaya*), secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*), and outbursts (*paryavasthāna*) bound to the realms of form and formlessness, excluding the five views bound to those realms; this is called the clinging to the doctrine of self.
What are past phenomena?
They are the five aggregates of the past.
What are future phenomena?
That is to say, the five aggregates of the future.
What are present phenomena?
That is to say, the five aggregates of the present.
What are phenomena that are neither past, nor future, nor present?
They are unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛtadharma*).
What are phenomena bound to the desire realm (*kāmadhātupratisaṃyuktadharma*)?
This refers to the five aggregates bound to the desire realm.
What are the phenomena bound to the form realm?
This refers to the five aggregates bound to the form realm.
What are the phenomena associated with the formless realm?
They are the four aggregates of the formless realm.
What are the unassociated phenomena?
This refers to all untainted (anāsrava) dharmas.
What are dharmas that have wholesome (kuśala) as their cause?
They are wholesome conditioned (saṃskṛta) dharmas and the maturation (vipāka) of wholesome dharmas.
What are the phenomena that have the unwholesome as their cause?
They are the defiled and unwholesome phenomena pertaining to the desire realm, as well as the maturation [of those].
What are the phenomena that have the indeterminate as their cause?
That is to say, the indeterminate conditioned factors and the unwholesome factors.
What are the factors that do not have wholesome factors as their cause, nor unwholesome factors as their cause, nor indeterminate factors as their cause?
They are the unconditioned factors.
What is the dharma that has an object of perception?
It refers to the mind, mental factors, mental consciousness, and their associated dharmas.
What is the dharma that lacks an object of perception?

This refers to the five groups of consciousness and their associated mental factors, as well as those conditioned phenomena that take form, the unconditioned, formations dissociated from mind, and mental consciousness along with their associated mental factors as their objects.
What are the phenomena that take objects as their conditions and those that do not take objects as their conditions?
That is to say: [it takes as its objects] mind, mental factors, form, the unconditioned, formations dissociated from mind, the mental consciousness, and associated dharmas.
What is that which does not take as its object dharmas with an object, nor take as its object dharmas without an object?
These are matter, the unconditioned, and formations dissociated from mind.
The five aggregates and the five aggregates of clinging are as previously explained.
What is the destiny of hell-beings?

It refers to those sentient beings belonging to the hells who share the same nature, the same category, and the same homogeneous class (*nikāya-sabhāga*); based on their acquisition of [existence], acquisition of [objects], and acquisition of [place], they give rise to non-obscured, neutral (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*) form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness—this is called the hellish destiny (*naraka-gati*).
What is the realm of animals?

It refers to those classes of sentient beings who are animals, sharing the same nature, the same category, and the same homogeneous group (*nikāya-sabhāga*); through the acquisition of their basis, their objects, and their location, they are born as those sentient beings with unobscured-neutral form, feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness—this is called the realm of animals.
What is the realm of hungry ghosts (*preta-gati*)?

It refers to those classes of sentient beings who are hungry ghosts, sharing the same nature, the same category, and the same homogeneous class (*nikāya-sabhāga*), and who, through their acquisition of basis, acquisition of things, and acquisition of location, give rise to unobscured-unspecified (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*) form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness; this is called the realm of hungry ghosts.
What is the human realm?

It refers to those sentient beings who are humans—sharing the same nature, the same category, and the same homogeneous group (nikāya-sabhāga)—who, through the acquisition of their basis, the acquisition of their entities, and the acquisition of their location, give rise to unobscured-unspecified (anivṛtāvyākṛta) form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness; this is called the human realm.
What is the celestial realm (*devagati*)?

It refers to the various classes of sentient beings who are gods, sharing the same nature, the same category, and the same homogeneous group (*nikāyasabhāga*), and who, through the acquisition of their basis, the acquisition of their entities, and the acquisition of their location, give rise to unobscured-unspecified (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*) form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness; this is called the celestial realm.
What is the category of afflictions abandoned through the vision of suffering?

It refers to those categories of afflictions that are abandoned by the patiences at the limit of the clear realization of suffering for those who practice in accordance with faith or in accordance with the Dharma.
Furthermore, what are these?
This refers to the twenty-eight underlying tendencies (anuśaya) abandoned through the vision of suffering, as well as the collection of various afflictions associated with them.
What are the categories of afflictions abandoned through the vision of the origin [of suffering]?

This refers to the categories of afflictions abandoned by the forbearances at the limit of the clear observation of the origin (samudaya-satya), which follow either faith or the Dharma. What, then, are these?
They are the nineteen underlying tendencies (anuśaya) abandoned through the vision of the origin, along with the collection of various afflictions associated with them.
What is the category of afflictions abandoned through the vision of cessation?

It refers to those categories of afflictions that are abandoned by the patiences at the limit of the clear realization of cessation for those who practice in accordance with faith or in accordance with the Dharma.
Furthermore, what are these?
This refers to the nineteen underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) abandoned through the vision of cessation, as well as the collection of afflictions associated with them.
What is the category of afflictions abandoned through the vision of the path?

It refers to that category of afflictions abandoned by the patiences (*kṣānti*) at the limit of clear realization (*abhisamaya*) for those who practice the paths of following faith or following dharma.
What, then, are these? They are the twenty-two underlying tendencies (anuśaya) abandoned through the path of seeing (darśana-mārga), as well as the various groups of afflictions associated with them.
What is the category of afflictions abandoned through the path of cultivation (bhāvanā-mārga)?
This refers to the category of afflictions belonging to those in training who have seen the path and are to be abandoned through cultivation. What, then, is this?
It refers to the ten latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) to be abandoned through cultivation, as well as the collection of afflictions associated with them.
The five dharmas, such as form (*rūpa*), are as previously explained.
The six elements (*dhātu*), such as earth (*pṛthivī*), are as previously explained.
What are the dharmas to be abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya*)?

This refers to those phenomena (*dharma*) abandoned by the patience (*kṣānti*) at the limit of the clear observation of suffering (*duḥkha-abhisamaya-anta*) for those who practice in accordance with faith (*śraddhānusārin*) or in accordance with the Dharma (*dharmānusārin*). What, then, are these?

They are the twenty-eight underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) abandoned through the vision of suffering, along with their associated phenomena (*saṃprayukta-dharma*) and the non-associated formations (*citta-viprayukta-saṃskāra*) arising together with them; these are called the phenomena abandoned through the vision of suffering.
What are the phenomena to be abandoned through the vision of the origin (*samudaya-darśana-prahātavya*)?

They are those phenomena which are abandoned by the patiences (*kṣānti*) at the limit of the clear realization of the origin (*samudaya-abhisamaya-anta-kṣānti*) for those who practice in accordance with faith (*śraddhānusārin*) or in accordance with the Dharma (*dharmānusārin*).
Furthermore, what are these?

This refers to the nineteen underlying tendencies abandoned through the vision of the origin [of suffering], along with their associated phenomena and the mind-dissociated formations arising together with them; these are called the phenomena abandoned through the vision of the origin.
What are the phenomena to be abandoned through the vision of cessation?
They are those phenomena abandoned by the patiences at the limit of the clear realization of cessation for those who practice in accordance with faith or in accordance with the Dharma.
What, furthermore, are these?

This refers to the nineteen underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) abandoned through the vision of cessation, along with their associated factors and the mind-dissociated formations (*citta-viprayukta-saṃskāra*) arising together with them; these are called the factors abandoned through the vision of cessation.
What are the phenomena to be abandoned by the path of seeing?
They are those phenomena abandoned by the patiences at the limit of clear realization (*abhisamaya*) through the paths of following faith or following dharma.
Furthermore, what are these?

This refers to the twenty-two underlying tendencies (anuśaya) abandoned through the path of seeing, along with their associated dharmas and the non-associated formations (citta-viprayukta-saṃskāra) arising together with them; these are called the dharmas abandoned through the path of seeing.
What are the phenomena to be abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*)?
They are those phenomena which are to be abandoned through cultivation by one who has entered the path of vision (*dṛṣṭi-pada*).
Furthermore, what are these?

The ten latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) to be abandoned by cultivation, along with their associated factors; the bodily and vocal actions arising from them; the formations dissociated from mind arising from them; and all non-defiled contaminated phenomena—these are called the factors to be abandoned by cultivation.
What are the dharmas not to be abandoned?
They are all untainted (anāsrava) dharmas.
What is the latent tendency of sensual desire (kāmarāgānuśaya)?
This refers to desire for various sensual objects, as well as craving and intense craving; it involves grasping and hoarding, guarding and protecting, and being addicted to and delighting in them.
What is the latent tendency of aversion (*pratighānuśaya*)?

It refers to harboring resentment and malice toward sentient beings, desiring to cause them harm; it is the root of obstruction, characterized by hatred, anger, and perversity, as well as being fierce, violent, and cruel. Whether past, present, or future, it constitutes aversion that causes sentient beings to oppose and injure one another.
What is the latent tendency of attachment (*rāgānuśaya*)?
It refers to various forms of attachment and pervasive attachment toward the realms of form and formlessness, characterized by grasping, concealing, guarding, indulgence, and craving.
What is the latent tendency of pride (*mānānuśaya*)?
This refers to pride, past pride, and future pride; it is the loftiness of mind and the haughty disdain of mind.
What is the latent tendency of ignorance?
It is the lack of wisdom regarding the three realms.
What is the latent tendency of views?
It refers to the five defiled views.
What is the latent tendency of doubt?
It refers to doubt regarding the truths.
What is the first station of consciousness?
It refers to sentient beings possessing form who differ in body and differ in perception, such as humans and some classes of devas; this is the first station of consciousness.
Regarding this, "the first" refers to that which stands at the very beginning according to the sequence of calculation, the gradual progression, and the continuous order of succession.
The various forms, feelings, perceptions, formations, and consciousnesses bound to that [first stage] are collectively termed "abodes of consciousness."
What is the second station of consciousness?

It refers to sentient beings possessing form who differ in body but are uniform in perception, such as the gods of the Brahma-group at the beginning of the kalpa; this is the second station of consciousness.
Regarding "the second among these," it refers to being the second in accordance with the gradual, sequential, continuous, and successive order of calculation.
Those various forms, feelings, perceptions, formations, and consciousnesses bound thereto are collectively termed "abodes of consciousness" (*vijñānasthiti*).
What is the third station of consciousness?
It refers to sentient beings possessing form who are uniform in body but diverse in perception, such as the gods of the Ābhāsvara Heaven; this is the third station of consciousness.
Regarding the third among these, it refers to that which occupies the third position according to the gradual, sequential, continuous, and successive order of calculation.
Those various aggregates of form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness bound therein are collectively termed "abodes of consciousness" (vijñānasthiti).
What is the fourth station of consciousness?

It refers to sentient beings possessing form who are uniform in body and uniform in perception, such as the gods of the Universal Purity (Śubhakṛtsna) heaven; this is the fourth station of consciousness.
Regarding the term "fourth" herein, it means that according to the gradual, sequential, continuous, and orderly progression of enumeration, this occupies the fourth position.
The form, feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness bound therein are collectively termed the stations of consciousness (*vijñānasthiti*).
What is the fifth station of consciousness?

It refers to those sentient beings of the formless realm who, transcending all perceptions of form and extinguishing perceptions of sensory resistance, no longer attend to manifold perceptions and enter the sphere of infinite space; they dwell fully endowed with the sphere of infinite space, like the gods of the Sphere of Infinite Space. This is the fifth station of consciousness.
Regarding "the fifth among these": it refers to the position as the fifth according to the gradual, sequential, continuous, and orderly progression of enumeration.
Those fetters consisting of feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness are collectively termed the "abodes of consciousness" (*vijñānasthiti*).
What is the sixth station of consciousness?

It refers to formless sentient beings who, transcending the entire sphere of infinite space, enter the sphere of infinite consciousness and dwell fully therein; like the devas of the sphere of infinite consciousness, this is the sixth station of consciousness.

Regarding "the sixth among these": this refers to its position as the sixth according to the progressive enumeration, the sequential order, and the continuous succession; it is the sixth in this series.
Those aggregates of feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness that are bound to it are collectively termed "abodes of consciousness" (*vijñānasthiti*).
What is the seventh station of consciousness?

It refers to formless sentient beings who, transcending the sphere of infinite consciousness, enter the sphere of nothingness and dwell fully therein; like the gods of the sphere of nothingness, this is the seventh station of consciousness.
Regarding "the seventh here," it refers to the seventh position according to the progressive, sequential, continuous, and successive order of enumeration.
Those [factors] bound to which feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness are collectively termed the stations of consciousness (*vijñānasthiti*).
What is the enlightenment factor of mindfulness (*smṛti-saṃbodhyaṅga*)?

It refers to when noble disciples contemplate suffering as suffering, the origin as the origin, cessation as cessation, and the path as the path; associated with untainted attention (*anāsrava-manasikāra*), it consists of mindfulness, recollection, distinct mindfulness, and memory—being without forgetfulness, without loss, without omission, and without leakage; it is the nature of not forgetting the dharma-nature and the nature of the mind’s clear recording. This is called the enlightenment factor of mindfulness.

What is the factor of enlightenment of discrimination of phenomena (*dharmapravicaya-saṃbodhyaṅga*)? It refers to noble disciples who, regarding suffering, contemplate it as suffering; regarding its origin, contemplate it as its origin; regarding its cessation, contemplate it as its cessation; and regarding the path, contemplate it as the path. In association with untainted attention (*anāsrava-manasikāra*), they discriminate, thoroughly discriminate, and most thoroughly discriminate phenomena; they understand, comprehend, fully comprehend, and closely comprehend them. With keen intelligence, penetration, investigation, sagacity, awakening, clarity, wisdom, and practice—namely, *vipaśyanā*—they resolve the nature of phenomena. This is called the factor of enlightenment of discrimination of phenomena.

What is the enlightenment factor of energy (*vīrya-sambodhyaṅga*)? It refers to the noble disciples who, regarding suffering, contemplate it as suffering; regarding its origin, contemplate it as its origin; regarding its cessation, contemplate it as its cessation; and regarding the path, contemplate it as the path. Associated with untainted mental attention (*anāsrava-manasikāra*), it consists of all diligent effort, valorous vigor, fierce intensity, invincibility, and unremitting exertion of the will—the nature of mental fortitude. This is called the enlightenment factor of energy.
What is the enlightenment factor of joy (*prītisaṃbodhyaṅga*)?

It refers to when noble disciples contemplate suffering as suffering, the origin as the origin, cessation as cessation, and the path as the path; being associated with untainted mental attention (*anāsravamanasikāra*), their minds experience gladness, intense gladness, and manifest extreme gladness; it is the nature of gladness and the class of gladness, what is agreeable and pleasing, the nature of joy and the class of joy, the union of bliss and non-separation, exultation and delight, a state of fitness, a state of leaping up and exultation, and a state of jubilation and rejoicing—this is called the enlightenment factor of joy.
What is the factor of enlightenment of pliancy (*praśrabdhi-saṃbodhyaṅga*)?

It refers to noble disciples who, contemplating suffering as suffering, contemplating the origin as the origin, contemplating cessation as cessation, and contemplating the path as the path, possess a state associated with untainted attention (*anāsrava-manasikāra*), consisting of physical pliancy, mental pliancy, that which has already become pliant, and the category of pliancy; this is called the factor of enlightenment of pliancy.
What is the enlightenment factor of concentration?

It refers to the noble disciples who, regarding suffering, contemplate suffering; regarding its origin, contemplate its origin; regarding its cessation, contemplate its cessation; and regarding the path, contemplate the path—with attention associated with the untainted (*anāsrava*). All those states that cause the mind to abide, abide evenly, abide securely, abide closely, abide firmly, and which are non-distraction, non-dispersion, gathering, tranquility, meditative absorption (*samādhi*), and one-pointedness of mind—this is called the enlightenment factor of concentration.
What is the factor of enlightenment of equanimity (*upekṣā-saṃbodhyaṅga*)?

It refers to the noble disciples who, regarding suffering, contemplate it as suffering; regarding its origin, contemplate it as its origin; regarding its cessation, contemplate it as its cessation; and regarding the path, contemplate it as the path. Being associated with untainted mental attention (*anāsrava-manasikāra*), it is the state of mental evenness, the state of mental rectitude, and the state of mental abiding in tranquility free from agitation; this is called the factor of enlightenment of equanimity.
What is the first liberation?
It is the contemplation of forms while possessing form; this is the first liberation.
Herein, "first" refers to its position at the very beginning according to the progressive, sequential, continuous, and orderly succession of enumeration.
Furthermore, following the gradual, sequential, continuous, and orderly progression of entering meditative absorption, this [state] is foremost at the beginning.
All wholesome form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness present within such concentration are called liberation.
What is the second liberation?
It is the perception of external forms while internally having no perception of form; this is the second liberation.
Herein, "second" refers to its position as the second according to the progressive, sequential, continuous, and orderly succession of enumeration.
Furthermore, according to the gradual, sequential, continuous, and orderly progression of entering meditative absorption, this constitutes the second stage.
Thus, all wholesome form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness within such concentration are called "liberation."
What is the third liberation?
It is the liberation of the beautiful, which one realizes with the body and dwells in, having fully attained it; this is the third liberation.
Herein, "third" refers to its position as the third according to the progressive enumeration, the sequential order, and the continuous succession of the stages.
Furthermore, following the gradual, sequential, continuous, and orderly progression of entering meditative absorption, this constitutes the third stage.
Thus, all wholesome form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness within such concentration are called "liberation."
What is the fourth liberation?

It is the transcendence of all perceptions of form, the cessation of perceptions of sensory resistance, and the non-attention to perceptions of diversity, whereby one enters and dwells, having fully attained, in the sphere of infinite space; this is the fourth liberation.
Regarding "the fourth among these": it refers to being the fourth according to the gradual, sequential, continuous, and orderly progression of counting;
furthermore, it is the fourth according to the gradual, sequential, continuous, and orderly progression of entering meditative absorption.
In this way, all wholesome feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness within meditative concentration are called liberation.
What is the fifth liberation?

It is said that by transcending the sphere of infinite space, one enters the sphere of infinite consciousness and dwells fully possessed of the sphere of infinite consciousness; this is the fifth liberation.
Regarding "the fifth herein": it refers to being the fifth in the sequence of calculation, the sequence of progression, the sequence of continuity, and the sequence of order;
furthermore, it is the fifth in the sequence of entering meditative absorption, the sequence of progression, the sequence of continuity, and the sequence of order.
In this way, all wholesome feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness within meditative concentration are called liberation.
What is the sixth liberation?
It refers to transcending the sphere of infinite consciousness and entering the sphere of nothingness; dwelling fully perfected in the sphere of nothingness—this is the sixth liberation.
Regarding "the sixth" herein: it refers to the sixth position according to the gradual, sequential, and continuous order of counting;
furthermore, it refers to the sixth position according to the gradual, sequential, and continuous order of entering meditative absorption.
In this way, all wholesome feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness within meditative concentration are called liberation.
What is the seventh liberation?
It refers to transcending the sphere of nothingness and entering the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, where one dwells in its full possession; this is the seventh liberation.
Regarding "the seventh herein": it refers to its position as the seventh according to the gradual, sequential, continuous, and successive order of calculation;
furthermore, it refers to its position as the seventh according to the gradual, sequential, continuous, and successive order of entering meditative absorption.
All wholesome feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness within such concentration are called liberation.
What is the eighth liberation?

It refers to transcending the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, entering the cessation of perception and feeling, realizing it through bodily witness, and dwelling in its full perfection; this is the eighth liberation.
Regarding "the eighth herein," this refers to its position as the eighth according to the gradual, sequential, continuous, and orderly progression of counting;
furthermore, it refers to its position as the eighth according to the gradual, sequential, continuous, and orderly progression of entering meditative absorption.
In this meditative concentration, there are various liberations, superior liberations, and distinct, ultimate liberations.

Furthermore, if a phenomenon has subtle ideation as its cause and subtle ideation as its immediately preceding condition, it is in the sense of not being simultaneous with ideation, rather than in the sense of not being accomplished; this is called liberation.
What is the first sphere of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*)?

It refers to one who possesses the perception of internal forms and observes external forms that are few in number, whether they be beautiful in color or ugly in color; having mastery over those forms, one knows them and sees them with excellence, possessing such a perception—this is the first sphere of mastery.
Regarding this, "the first" refers to that which stands at the very beginning according to the gradual, sequential, continuous, and orderly progression of counting;
it also stands at the very beginning according to the gradual, sequential, continuous, and orderly progression of entering meditative absorption.
Thus, all wholesome form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness within this meditative concentration are called the bases of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*).
What is the second base of mastery?

It refers to having the perception of internal forms while observing external forms that are manifold—whether of beautiful color or ugly color—and having superior knowledge and superior vision regarding those forms, possessing such a perception; this is the second base of mastery.
Regarding "the second" herein: it is the second in the sequence of calculation, the gradual order, the regular order, and the continuous succession;
furthermore, it is the second in the sequence of entering meditative absorption, the gradual order, the regular order, and the continuous succession.
All wholesome form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness present within such concentration are called "bases of mastery" (*abhibhvāyatana*).
What is the third base of mastery?

It refers to one who, being internally without the perception of form, contemplates external forms that are few—whether they be beautiful in color or ugly in color—and having surpassed those forms, knows them and sees them; possessing such a perception, this is the third base of mastery.
Regarding "the third" herein: it refers to the third position according to the sequence of calculation, the gradual order, the regular succession, and the serial progression;
furthermore, it is the third position according to the sequence of entering meditative absorption, the gradual order, the regular succession, and the serial progression.
All wholesome form, feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness present within such concentration are called "bases of mastery" (*abhibhvāyatana*).
What is the fourth base of mastery?

It refers to one who, internally perceiving no form, contemplates external forms that are manifold—whether of beautiful color or ugly color—and who, with respect to those forms, possesses superior knowledge and superior vision, maintaining such a perception; this is the fourth base of mastery.
Regarding "the fourth among these": it refers to being the fourth according to the gradual, sequential, continuous, and orderly progression of counting;
furthermore, it is the fourth according to the gradual, sequential, continuous, and orderly progression of entering meditative absorption.
In this way, all wholesome form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness within meditative concentration are called "bases of mastery" (*abhibhvāyatana*).
What is the fifth base of mastery?

It refers to one who, being internally without the perception of form, perceives external forms that are blue, blue in appearance, blue in manifestation, and blue in radiance—just like the *umakā* flower, or like deep-dyed blue robes from Vārāṇasī, which are blue, blue in appearance, blue in manifestation, and blue in radiance.
Without the perception of internal forms, one perceives external forms that are blue—blue in color, blue in appearance, and blue in luster—and it is likewise so.
Having superior knowledge and superior vision regarding those forms, and possessing this specific perception, this is the fifth sphere of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*).
Regarding "the fifth herein," it refers to being the fifth according to the gradual, sequential, continuous, and successive order of counting;
furthermore, it is the fifth according to the gradual, sequential, continuous, and successive order of entering meditative absorption.
Thus, all wholesome form, feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness within this meditative concentration are called "bases of mastery" (*abhibhvāyatana*).
What is the sixth base of mastery?

It refers to one who, having no perception of internal form, perceives external forms that are yellow—yellow in appearance, yellow in manifestation, and yellow in luster—just like a *karṇikāra* flower, or like a deep yellow robe from Vārāṇasī, yellow in appearance, yellow in manifestation, and yellow in luster.
Having no perception of internal forms, one perceives external forms that are yellow, appearing yellow, manifesting as yellow, and emitting yellow light; it is also like this.
Having superior knowledge and superior vision regarding those forms, and being fully possessed of such a perception, this is the sixth sphere of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*).
Regarding "the sixth" herein: it refers to the sixth position according to the gradual, sequential, continuous, and successive order of counting;
furthermore, it refers to the sixth position according to the gradual, sequential, continuous, and successive order of entering meditative absorption.
All wholesome form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness within such meditative concentration are called "bases of mastery" (abhibhvāyatana).
What is the seventh base of mastery?

It is when, having no perception of internal form, one perceives external forms that are red, reddish in appearance, manifesting as red, and emitting a red luster—just like the *pāṇḍu-tīvra-karṇikāra* flower, or like a deep crimson robe from Vārāṇasī, which is red, reddish in appearance, manifesting as red, and emitting a red luster.
Without the perception of internal forms, one contemplates external forms that are red, appearing red, manifesting as red, and emitting a red luster; it is also like this.
Having superior knowledge and superior vision regarding those forms, and possessing such a perception, this is the seventh base of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*).
Regarding the seventh among these: it is the seventh according to the gradual, sequential, continuous, and orderly progression of counting;
furthermore, it is the seventh according to the gradual, sequential, continuous, and orderly progression of entering meditative absorption.
In this way, all wholesome form, feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness within meditative concentration are called "bases of mastery" (*abhibhvāyatana*).
What is the eighth base of mastery?

It refers to one who, being internally percipient of no-form, perceives external forms that are white—white in color, white in appearance, white in manifestation, and emitting white light—just like the star Uśanas, or like a very fresh white cloth from Vārāṇasī, which is white in color, white in appearance, white in manifestation, and emits white light.
With the internal perception of formlessness, one contemplates external forms that are white, appearing white, manifesting as white, and emitting white light; it is also like this.
Having superior knowledge and superior vision regarding those forms, and possessing such a perception, this is the eighth base of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*).
Regarding the eighth among these, it is so called because it occupies the eighth position according to the gradual, sequential, continuous, and orderly progression of calculation;
furthermore, it occupies the eighth position according to the gradual, sequential, continuous, and orderly progression of entering meditative absorption.
In this way, all wholesome form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness within meditative concentration are called "bases of mastery" (*abhibhvāyatana*).
