Chapter Six, Part Four: "Discrimination of the Compendia," etc. What is right view?

It refers to the noble disciples and others who, regarding suffering, contemplate it as suffering; regarding its origin, contemplate it as its origin; regarding its cessation, contemplate it as its cessation; and regarding the path, contemplate it as the path. Being associated with untainted mental attention (*anāsrava-manasikāra*) toward phenomena, they exercise discernment, thorough discernment, and supreme discernment; they understand, comprehend equally, understand universally, and understand closely. Possessing keen intelligence, penetration, investigation, sagacity, awakening, clarity, and the practice of wisdom (*prajñā*), this is called right view (*samyagdṛṣṭi*).

What is right intention (*samyak-saṃkalpa*)? It refers to when noble disciples, regarding suffering, contemplate it as suffering; regarding its origin, contemplate it as its origin; regarding its cessation, contemplate it as its cessation; and regarding the path, contemplate it as the path. It consists of all minds associated with untainted attention (*anāsrava-manasikāra*), which involve seeking and thoroughly seeking, deliberating and thoroughly deliberating, and immediate deliberation; investigating and pursuing, thoroughly contemplating, and the nature of contemplation itself—this is called right intention.
What is right speech?

It refers to when noble disciples contemplate suffering as suffering, the origin as the origin, cessation as cessation, and the path as the path; setting aside the four types of unwholesome verbal conduct that lead to wrong livelihood, they—by the power of discernment—achieve untainted detachment, cessation, individual detachment, tranquility, and restraint regarding other unwholesome verbal conduct. They do not perform, do not create, do not practice, and do not transgress; they do not destroy the boundaries, embankments, bridges, or rafts [of virtue]. Abandoning improper conduct, they abide without violating or overstepping, remaining without transgression. This is called right speech.

What is right action? It refers to when noble disciples contemplate suffering as suffering, the origin as the origin, cessation as cessation, and the path as the path; having abandoned the three types of bodily misconduct that lead to wrong livelihood, they—by the power of discernment—achieve the untainted (anāsrava) renunciation, cessation, and distinct seclusion regarding other bodily misconduct. This consists of tranquility and restraint: not doing, not creating, not practicing, and not transgressing; not violating the boundaries, embankments, bridges, or rafts; and by abandoning improper conduct, dwelling without contravening or overstepping, and remaining without transgression. This is called right action.
What is right livelihood?

It refers to the noble disciples who contemplate suffering as suffering, the origin as the origin, cessation as cessation, and the path as the path; who, through the power of discernment, achieve the untainted (*anāsrava*) distancing, cessation, and individual seclusion from wrong livelihood and the misconduct of body and speech; who maintain tranquility and restraint, neither acting nor performing [evil], not practicing it, not transgressing it, and not destroying the boundaries, embankments, bridges, or rafts [of virtue]; who abandon improper conduct, remaining without violating or overstepping it—this is called right livelihood.
What is right effort?

It refers to the noble disciple who contemplates suffering as suffering, the origin as the origin, cessation as cessation, and the path as the path; it consists of all diligent efforts associated with untainted mental attention (*anāsrava-manasikāra*), which are courageous, powerful, fierce, intense, difficult to restrain, and characterized by an unremitting application of the will and a nature of mental fortitude—this is called right effort.

What is right mindfulness? It refers to noble disciples who, regarding suffering, contemplate it as suffering; regarding its origin, contemplate it as its origin; regarding its cessation, contemplate it as its cessation; and regarding the path, contemplate it as the path. It consists of mindfulness, recollection, distinct mindfulness, and remembrance associated with untainted attention (*anāsrava-manasikāra*), which is non-forgetful, non-loss, non-neglectful, and non-leaking; it is the nature of not forgetting the dharma-nature and the nature of the mind’s clear recording. This is called right mindfulness.

What is right concentration (*samyak-samādhi*)? It refers to the noble disciples who, regarding suffering, contemplate it as suffering; regarding its origin, contemplate it as its origin; regarding its cessation, contemplate it as its cessation; and regarding the path, contemplate it as the path. It is the state of mental one-pointedness consisting of the attention associated with the untainted (*anāsrava*), which causes the mind to abide, abide evenly, abide securely, abide closely, abide firmly, and which is non-distraction, non-dispersion, gathering, calming, and meditative absorption (*samādhi*). This is called right concentration.
What is the fetter of attachment?
It refers to craving within the three realms.
What is the fetter of aversion?
This refers to that which can cause harm to sentient beings.
What is the fetter of pride?
It refers to the seven types of pride.
What is the fetter of ignorance (*avidyā-saṃyojana*)?
It refers to a lack of wisdom regarding the three realms.
What is the fetter of views (*dṛṣṭi-saṃyojana*)?
That is to say, the three views.
What is the fetter of grasping?
That is to say, the two graspings.
What is the fetter of doubt?
It refers to perplexity, uncertainty, and hesitation regarding the truths.
What is the fetter of envy?
That is to say, envy and jealousy.
What is the fetter of avarice?
It is the mind’s stinginess and parsimony.
What is the first abode of sentient beings?
It refers to those sentient beings possessing form who have diverse bodies and diverse perceptions, such as humans and some classes of devas; this is the first abode of sentient beings.
Regarding this, "the first" refers to that which stands at the very beginning according to the sequence of calculation, the gradual progression, the serial order, and the continuous succession.

As for "abodes of sentient beings" (*sattvāvāsa*), it means that various sentient beings dwell within them, each dwelling separately; because this reveals their place of rebirth, they are called "abodes of sentient beings."
What is the second abode of sentient beings?

It refers to those sentient beings who possess form, whose bodies are diverse but whose perceptions are uniform, such as the gods of the Brahma-group at the beginning of a kalpa; this is the second abode of sentient beings.
Regarding "the second among these," this refers to its position as the second according to the gradual, sequential, continuous, and successive order of enumeration.
As for the term "abodes of sentient beings" (*sattvāvāsa*), the meaning is as previously explained.
What is the third abode of sentient beings?
It refers to those sentient beings who possess form, being uniform in body but diverse in perception, such as the gods of the Ābhāsvara Heaven; this is the third abode of sentient beings.
Regarding "the third" herein: it refers to the third position according to the gradual, sequential, continuous, and successive order of calculation.
As for the term "abodes of sentient beings," its meaning is as previously explained.
What is the fourth abode of sentient beings?
It refers to sentient beings who possess form, being uniform in body and uniform in perception, such as the gods of the Universal Purity Heaven; this is the fourth abode of sentient beings.
Regarding "the fourth among these": it refers to being situated as the fourth according to the gradual, sequential, continuous, and successive order of calculation.
As for the term "abode of sentient beings" (*sattvāvāsa*), its meaning is as previously explained.
What is the fifth abode of sentient beings?

It refers to those sentient beings who possess form, yet are without perception and without differentiated perception, such as the gods of the realm of non-percipient beings; this is the fifth abode of sentient beings.
Regarding "the fifth among these," it refers to the sequence of calculation, the gradual progression, the regular succession, and the serial order;
this [state] occupies the fifth position.
As for the term "abodes of sentient beings" (*sattvāvāsa*), its meaning is as previously explained.
What is the sixth abode of sentient beings?

It refers to formless sentient beings who have transcended all perceptions of form, extinguished perceptions of sensory resistance, and do not attend to perceptions of diversity; they enter the sphere of infinite space and dwell in its full accomplishment, just like the gods of the Sphere of Infinite Space. This is the sixth abode of sentient beings.
Regarding "the sixth among these," it refers to its position as the sixth according to the progressive enumeration, the sequential order, and the continuous succession;
"abode of sentient beings" has the same meaning as previously explained.
What is the seventh abode of sentient beings?

It refers to formless sentient beings who, transcending the entire sphere of infinite space, enter the sphere of infinite consciousness and dwell fully therein; like the devas of the sphere of infinite consciousness, this is the seventh abode of sentient beings.
Regarding "the seventh among these": it refers to the seventh position according to the gradual, sequential, continuous, and successive order of counting.
As for the term "abodes of sentient beings" (*sattvāvāsa*), its meaning is as previously explained.
What is the eighth abode of sentient beings?

It refers to formless sentient beings who, having transcended the sphere of infinite consciousness, enter and dwell fully in the sphere of nothingness, just like the gods of the sphere of nothingness; this is the eighth abode of sentient beings.
Regarding "the eighth herein": this refers to its position as the eighth according to the progressive enumeration, the sequential order, and the continuous succession;
"abode of sentient beings" has the meaning previously explained.
What is the ninth abode of sentient beings?

It refers to formless sentient beings who, having transcended the sphere of nothingness, enter and dwell fully in the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, such as the gods of the heaven of neither-perception-nor-non-perception; this is the ninth abode of sentient beings.
Regarding "the ninth herein," this refers to its position as the ninth according to the progressive, sequential, continuous, and orderly enumeration;
"abode of sentient beings" has the meaning explained previously.
What is the first *kṛtsnāyatana*?
It refers to the perception of earth as all-pervasive, extending upward, downward, and across, without duality and immeasurable;
this is the first *kṛtsnāyatana*. Herein, "first" means that according to the gradual, sequential, continuous, and orderly progression of enumeration, this stands at the very beginning.
Furthermore, according to the gradual, sequential, continuous, and successive order of entering meditative absorption, this is foremost at the beginning.
Thus, all wholesome form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness within such concentration are called "totalities" (kṛtsnāyatana).
The same applies to the spheres of totality (kṛtsnāyatana) of water, fire, wind, blue, yellow, red, and white.
What is the ninth sphere of totality?
It is the perception of a single class [of object] as empty, pervading above, below, and across, non-dual and immeasurable; this is the ninth sphere of totality.
Regarding "the ninth herein": it refers to being the ninth according to the gradual, sequential, continuous, and orderly progression of numerical calculation;
furthermore, it is the ninth according to the gradual, sequential, continuous, and orderly progression of entering meditative absorption.
In this way, all wholesome feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness within meditative concentration are called "totalities" (kṛtsnāyatana).
The same applies to the totality of the sphere of infinite consciousness.

The right view, right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration of one beyond training (aśaikṣa) are as explained in the discourse on the Noble Eightfold Path.
What is right resolute confidence of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa-samyak-adhimokṣa*)?

It refers to noble disciples and others who, regarding suffering, contemplate it as suffering; regarding its origin, contemplate it as its origin; regarding its cessation, contemplate it as its cessation; and regarding the path, contemplate it as the path—possessing mental attention associated with the state beyond training, they have already attained, are currently attaining, or will attain resolute confidence. This is called right resolute confidence of one beyond training.
What is the right knowledge of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa-samyagjñāna*)?
It refers to the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) and the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*); this is called the right knowledge of one beyond training.
What is contaminated form (*sāsrava-rūpa*)?

That is to say, if there are various forms that are with outflows and subject to grasping, and regarding these forms—whether past, future, or present—if desire, greed, hatred, or delusion, or any individual secondary affliction associated with the mind, arises when it ought to arise, this is called "form with outflows."
What is untainted form (*anāsrava-rūpa*)?

It refers to those forms that are untainted and without grasping (*anupādāna*). Regarding these forms—whether past, future, or present—if desire, greed, hatred, or delusion, or any individual secondary affliction (*upakleśa*) associated with the mind, should arise but does not arise, this is called untainted form.
The same applies to the contaminated and uncontaminated aggregates of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness.
What are unconditioned phenomena?
They are the three unconditioned phenomena, namely: space, cessation not through deliberation, and cessation through deliberation.
The twelve bases (*āyatana*) and eighteen elements (*dhātu*) have already been explained in the "Chapter on Distinguishing the Seven Matters.
What is the eye-faculty (*cakṣur-indriya*)?
It refers to that by which the eye has seen, is seeing, or will see forms, as well as its "homogeneous part" (*sabhāga*).
What is the ear faculty?
It refers to the ear’s having heard, its currently hearing, or its about-to-hear of sounds, as well as its homogeneous part (sabhāga).
What is the nose faculty?
This refers to the nose having already smelled, currently smelling, or about to smell an odor, as well as its corresponding faculty (sabhāga).
What is the tongue faculty?
It refers to the tongue having already tasted, currently tasting, or about to taste a flavor, as well as its corresponding faculty.
What is the body faculty (*kāyendriya*)?
It refers to the body in relation to tangibles—those already contacted, those currently being contacted, and those of its corresponding class (*sabhāga*).
What is the female faculty (*strīndriya*)?
It refers to a portion of the body faculty (*kāyendriya*).
What is the male faculty (*puruṣendriya*)?
It refers to a portion of the body faculty.
What is the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*)?
It refers to the life-span (*āyus*) of the three realms.
What is the mind-faculty (*manendriya*)?
This refers to the six groups of consciousness.
What is the faculty of pleasure (*sukhendriya*)?

It refers to the physical and mental pleasure, the even feeling (*vedanā*) that arises when one is touched by a contact conducive to pleasant experience; being comprised within feeling, it is called the faculty of pleasure.
What is the faculty of suffering (*duḥkhendriya*)?
It refers to the physical sensation of unease that arises when one is touched by a contact conducive to painful feeling; being comprised within feeling, it is called the faculty of suffering.
What is the faculty of joy (*saumanasyendriya*)?
It refers to the mental joy and equanimous feeling that arises when one is touched by contact conducive to joyful feeling; being comprised within feeling, it is called the faculty of joy.
What is the faculty of grief (*daurmanasyendriya*)?

It refers to the mental state of grief and uneven feeling that arises when one is touched by contact conducive to the experience of grief; being comprised within feeling, it is called the faculty of grief.
What is the faculty of equanimity (*upekṣendriya*)?

It refers to the bodily equanimity and mental equanimity that arise when one is touched by a contact conducive to the feeling of equanimity—a feeling that is neither balanced nor unbalanced, and which is comprised within feeling; this is called the faculty of equanimity.
What is the faculty of faith (*śraddhendriya*)?

It refers to the various forms of faith, the nature of faith, and the nature of superior faith that arise based on wholesome dharmas born of renunciation and seclusion; it is the state of acceptance, the desire to act, the desire to perform, the desire to undertake, and the clarity and purity of the mind. This is called the faculty of faith.
What is the faculty of diligence (*vīryendriya*)?

It refers to the nature of mental fortitude—the state of being diligent, energetic, courageous, powerful, intense, unyielding, and resolute without ceasing—arising from wholesome dharmas born of renunciation and seclusion; this is called the faculty of diligence.
What is the faculty of mindfulness (*smṛtīndriya*)?

It refers to the various forms of mindfulness, recollection, distinct recollection, and memory regarding the wholesome dharmas born of renunciation and seclusion—being without forgetfulness, without loss, without omission, and without leakage; it is the non-forgetfulness of the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) and the mind’s quality of clear recording. This is called the faculty of mindfulness.
What is the faculty of concentration (*samādhīndriya*)?

It refers to the state of mental one-pointedness (*cittaikāgratā*), which consists of mindfulness, abiding, even abiding, firm abiding, close abiding, steadfast abiding, non-distraction, non-dispersion, withdrawal, and meditative equipoise (*samādhi*), arising from wholesome states born of renunciation and seclusion; this is called the faculty of concentration.
What is the faculty of wisdom (*prajñendriya*)?

It refers to the discernment, thorough discernment, and supreme discernment of phenomena; the understanding, equal understanding, pervasive understanding, and proximate understanding based on wholesome states born of renunciation and seclusion; as well as acuity, penetration, investigation, sagacity, the practice of awakening and clarity, and *vipaśyanā*. This is called the faculty of wisdom.
What is the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (*anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīndriya*)?

It refers to the various faculties of wisdom and so forth belonging to a person (*pudgala*) who has already entered into the state of rightness and departure from birth (*samyaktva-niyāma*). By means of these faculties, those who practice through faith or through dharma (*śraddhānusārin* and *dharmānusārin*) are able to realize the four noble truths that have not yet been realized; this is called the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown."
What is the faculty of "I have known" (*ājñātendriya*)?

It refers to the faculties of wisdom, understanding, and so forth, belonging to a person who has already seen and realized [the truths] and is still in training (*śaikṣa*). By means of these faculties—namely, faith, resolve, and vision—one attains the realization of the four noble truths and proceeds toward the superior qualities to be realized; this is called the faculty of "I have known."
What is the faculty of one who has already known?

It refers to the wisdom and the faculties such as wisdom belonging to Arhats who have exhausted their outflows and are beyond training; by means of these faculties, they attain liberation through wisdom and liberation through both [wisdom and concentration], and achieve dwelling in happiness in the present life. This is called the faculty of one who has already known.
The ninety-eight latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) are as previously explained.

The dharmas that are objects of knowledge, objects of cognition, objects of thorough penetration, objects of focus, and predominant dharmas are subsumed within the eighteen elements (*dhātu*), the twelve bases (*āyatana*), and the five aggregates (*skandha*). They are known by the ten knowledges (*jñāna*) and cognized by the six consciousnesses (*vijñāna*); all latent dispositions increase in relation to them.

Material phenomena (rūpadharma) are subsumed under eleven elements (dhātu), eleven bases (āyatana), and one aggregate (skandha). They are known by eight cognitions—excluding the cognition of others' minds and the cognition of cessation—and are cognized by the six consciousnesses. The latent dispositions (anuśaya) that are universal in the desire and form realms, as well as those to be abandoned through cultivation, increase in relation to them.

Non-material phenomena (*arūpadharma*) are subsumed under eight elements (*dhātu*), two bases (*āyatana*), and four aggregates (*skandha*); they are known by ten knowledges (*jñāna*) and cognized by one consciousness (*vijñāna*); all latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) increase therein.

Visible phenomena (*sanidarśanadharma*) are subsumed under one element, one base, and one aggregate; they are known by seven knowledges—excluding the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*), the knowledge of cessation (*nirodhajñāna*), and the knowledge of the path (*mārgajñāna*)—and cognized by two consciousnesses; the universal latent dispositions of the desire and form realms (*kāma-rūpa-dhātu-sarvatraga-anuśaya*) and those to be abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya-anuśaya*) increase therein.

Non-visible phenomena (*anidarśana-dharma*) are subsumed under seventeen elements (*dhātu*), eleven bases (*āyatana*), and five aggregates (*skandha*); they are known by ten cognitions (*jñāna*) and cognized by the six consciousnesses (*vijñāna*); all latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) increase in relation to them.

Resistible phenomena (*sapratigha-dharma*) are subsumed under ten elements, ten bases, and one aggregate; they are known by seven cognitions—excluding the cognition of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*), the cognition of cessation (*nirodhajñāna*), and the cognition of the path (*mārgajñāna*)—and cognized by six consciousnesses; the universal latent dispositions (*sarvatraga-anuśaya*) of the desire and form realms (*kāma-rūpa-dhātu*) and those to be abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) increase in relation to them.

Non-obstructive (*apratigha*) phenomena are subsumed under eight elements (*dhātu*), two bases (*āyatana*), and five aggregates (*skandha*); they are known by ten cognitions (*jñāna*) and cognized by one consciousness (*vijñāna*); all latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) increase therein.

Phenomena with outflows (*sāsrava*) are subsumed under eighteen elements, twelve bases, and five aggregates; they are known by eight cognitions—excluding the cognition of cessation (*nirodha-jñāna*) and the cognition of the path (*mārga-jñāna*)—and cognized by six consciousnesses; all latent dispositions increase therein.

The untainted dharmas (*anāsrava-dharma*) are subsumed within the three realms, two bases, and five aggregates; they are known by eight knowledges, excluding the knowledge of suffering and the knowledge of origin; they are cognized by one consciousness, and the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) do not increase therein.

Conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*) are subsumed under the eighteen elements (*dhātu*), the twelve bases (*āyatana*), and the five aggregates (*skandha*). They are known by nine cognitions, excluding the cognition of cessation (*nirodhajñāna*); they are cognized by the six consciousnesses; and all latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) increase in accordance with them.

Unconditioned phenomena (asaṃskṛta-dharma) are comprised of one element (dhātu), one base (āyatana), and are not included within the aggregates (skandha). They are known by six types of knowledge—excluding the knowledge of others' minds, the knowledge of suffering, the knowledge of origin, and the knowledge of the path—and are cognized by one consciousness. Latent dispositions (anuśaya) do not increase therein.

The phenomena associated with contention (*saraṇa-dharma*) are subsumed within the eighteen elements (*dhātu*), the twelve bases (*āyatana*), and the five aggregates (*skandha*). They are known by eight cognitions, excluding the cognition of cessation (*nirodha-jñāna*) and the cognition of the path (*mārga-jñāna*), and are cognized by the six consciousnesses. All latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) increase in accordance with them.

The dharma of non-contention (araṇā) is subsumed under the three realms, two bases, and five aggregates; it is known by eight knowledges, excluding the knowledges of suffering and its origin; it is cognized by one consciousness; and it is not the locus where latent dispositions (anuśaya) increase.

The same applies to mundane and supramundane phenomena, phenomena that fall within the realm and those that do not, phenomena with attachment and those without attachment, and phenomena based on indulgence and those based on renunciation.

Mental phenomena (*citta-dharma*) are subsumed under seven elements (*dhātu*), one base (*āyatana*), and one aggregate (*skandha*); they are known by nine cognitions (*jñāna*), excluding the cognition of cessation (*nirodha-jñāna*); they are cognized by one consciousness (*vijñāna*); and all latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) increase therein.

Non-mental phenomena (*a-citta-dharma*) are subsumed under eleven elements, eleven bases, and four aggregates; they are known by ten cognitions; they are cognized by six consciousnesses; and all latent dispositions increase therein.

Mental concomitants (citta-saṃprayukta-dharma) are subsumed under one element, one base, and three aggregates; they are known by nine knowledges, excluding the knowledge of cessation; they are cognized by one consciousness; and all latent proclivities (anuśaya) increase in relation to them.

Non-mental factors are subsumed within the eighteen elements, twelve bases, and three aggregates; they are known by ten cognitions, cognized by six consciousnesses, and all latent tendencies increase therein.
The same applies to mental concomitants (*cittasaṃprayukta*) and non-mental concomitants (*cittaviprayukta*).

Phenomena coexistent with the mind (*cittasahabhū*) are subsumed under eleven elements (*dhātu*), eleven bases (*āyatana*), and four aggregates (*skandha*); they are known by nine cognitions, excluding the cognition of cessation (*nirodhajñāna*); they are cognized by the six consciousnesses; and all latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) increase therein.

Dharmas that do not coexist with the mind are subsumed within eighteen elements (dhātus), twelve bases (āyatanas), and three aggregates (skandhas); they are known by ten knowledges (jñānas), cognized by six consciousnesses (vijñānas), and all latent dispositions (anuśayas) increase in relation to them.

The phenomena that follow the mind (cittānuvartin) are subsumed under one element, one base, and four aggregates; they are known by nine knowledges, excluding the knowledge of cessation, and are cognized by one consciousness; all latent dispositions (anuśaya) increase therein.

Dharmas that do not follow the mind are subsumed within eighteen elements, twelve bases, and three aggregates; they are known by ten cognitions and cognized by six consciousnesses; all latent dispositions increase in relation to them.

Dharmas having mind as their cause are subsumed within the eighteen elements, the twelve bases, and the five aggregates; they are known by nine knowledges, excluding the knowledge of cessation, and are cognized by the six consciousnesses; all latent dispositions increase in relation to them.

Dharmas that do not have mind as their cause are subsumed within thirteen elements (*dhātu*), twelve bases (*āyatana*), and three aggregates (*skandha*); they are known by ten cognitions (*jñāna*) and cognized by six consciousnesses (*vijñāna*); and the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) that are universal throughout the three realms, as well as those to be abandoned through cultivation, increase therein.

The mind is a dharma that serves as an equal-and-immediate condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*); it is subsumed under eight elements (*dhātu*), two bases (*āyatana*), and four aggregates (*skandha*). It is known by nine cognitions, excluding the cognition of cessation (*nirodha-jñāna*), and is cognized by one consciousness; all latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) increase in accordance with it.

That which is not mind as an immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*) is comprised within the eighteen elements (*dhātu*), the twelve bases (*āyatana*), and the five aggregates (*skandha*); it is known by ten knowledges (*jñāna*), cognized by six consciousnesses (*vijñāna*), and all latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) increase therein.

The mind is a dharma that serves as an object of cognition; it is subsumed under three realms, two bases, and four aggregates. It is known by nine knowledges, excluding the knowledge of cessation, and is cognized by one consciousness. The latent dispositions (anuśaya) that take conditioned phenomena of the three realms as their objects increase in relation to it.

Non-mental phenomena that serve as objects of cognition are comprised within the eighteen elements, the twelve bases, and the five aggregates; they are known by ten types of knowledge, cognized by six consciousnesses, and all latent dispositions increase in relation to them.

The mind as the predominant factor (*adhipati-dharma*) is subsumed within the eighteen elements (*dhātu*), the twelve bases (*āyatana*), and the five aggregates (*skandha*). It is known by nine cognitions (*jñāna*), excluding the cognition of cessation (*nirodha-jñāna*), and is cognized by the six consciousnesses (*vijñāna*). All latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) increase in accordance with it.

The phenomena that do not have mind as their predominant condition consist of one element, one base, and are not included within the aggregates. They are known by six types of knowledge—excluding the knowledge of others' minds, the knowledge of suffering, the knowledge of origin, and the knowledge of the path—and are cognized by one consciousness. Latent dispositions do not increase therein.

Phenomena that are the fruits of mind (*cittaphala*) are subsumed within the eighteen elements (*dhātu*), the twelve bases (*āyatana*), and the five aggregates (*skandha*); they are known by ten knowledges (*jñāna*) and cognized by six consciousnesses (*vijñāna*), and all latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) increase therein.

Phenomena that are not the fruits of mind are subsumed within one element, one base, and are not subsumed within any aggregate; they are known by one knowledge, namely conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*), and cognized by one consciousness, and no latent dispositions increase therein.

The dharmas that are the maturation of mind are subsumed within seventeen elements, eleven bases, and five aggregates; they are known by eight knowledges, excluding the knowledge of cessation and the knowledge of the path; they are cognized by five consciousnesses; and the latent dispositions (anuśaya) to be abandoned through cultivation, as well as the universal [dispositions] of the three realms, increase in association with them, with the exception of those associated with ear-consciousness.

Dharmas that are not the maturation of mind are subsumed within the eighteen elements, twelve bases, and five aggregates; they are known by ten cognitions, cognized by six consciousnesses, and all latent dispositions increase in relation to them.

The dharma of karma is subsumed under the three realms, three bases, and two aggregates; it is known by nine knowledges, excluding the knowledge of cessation; it is cognized by three consciousnesses, namely those of the eye, ear, and mind; and all latent dispositions increase in association with it.

Non-karmic phenomena (*akarmadharma*) are subsumed under eighteen elements (*dhātu*), twelve bases (*āyatana*), and five aggregates (*skandha*); they are known by ten knowledges (*jñāna*) and cognized by six consciousnesses (*vijñāna*); all latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) increase in relation to them.

Phenomena associated with karma (*karmasaṃprayuktadharma*) are subsumed under eight elements, two bases, and four aggregates; they are known by nine knowledges—excluding the knowledge of cessation (*nirodhajñāna*)—and cognized by one consciousness; all latent dispositions increase in relation to them.

Dharmas dissociated from karma are subsumed under eleven elements (dhātu), eleven bases (āyatana), and two aggregates (skandha); they are known by ten cognitions (jñāna), cognized by six consciousnesses (vijñāna), and all latent tendencies (anuśaya) increase therein.

Dharmas coexistent with karma are subsumed within the eighteen elements (*dhātu*), the twelve bases (*āyatana*), and the five aggregates (*skandha*). They are known by nine cognitions, excluding the cognition of cessation (*nirodha-jñāna*); they are cognized by the six consciousnesses; and all latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) increase therein.

Non-concomitant factors with karma are subsumed under eleven elements (dhātu), eleven bases (āyatana), and two aggregates (skandha); they are known by ten cognitions (jñāna) and cognized by six consciousnesses (vijñāna), and all latent dispositions (anuśaya) increase therein.

The phenomena that follow the transformation of karma are subsumed under eight elements (dhātus), two bases (āyatanas), and five aggregates (skandhas). They are known by nine knowledges (jñānas), excluding the knowledge of cessation (nirodha-jñāna), and are cognized by one consciousness (vijñāna). All latent dispositions (anuśayas) increase in accordance with them.

The factors that do not follow the transformation of karma are subsumed under eleven elements (dhātu), eleven bases (āyatana), and two aggregates (skandha); they are known by ten cognitions (jñāna) and cognized by six consciousnesses (vijñāna), and all latent dispositions (anuśaya) increase therein.

Phenomena that have karma as their cause are subsumed within the eighteen elements, the twelve bases, and the five aggregates; they are known by nine knowledges—excluding the knowledge of cessation—and are cognized by the six consciousnesses; all latent dispositions increase in relation to them.

Dharmas that do not have karma as their cause are subsumed under eleven elements (dhātu), eleven bases (āyatana), and two aggregates (skandha); they are known by ten knowledges (jñāna) and cognized by six consciousnesses (vijñāna); and the latent dispositions (anuśaya) that are universal throughout the three realms and those to be abandoned through cultivation increase therein.

Karma is subsumed under eight elements (dhātu), two bases (āyatana), and four aggregates (skandha) as its immediately preceding condition (samanantaradharma). It is known by nine knowledges (jñāna), excluding the knowledge of cessation (nirodhajñāna), and is cognized by one consciousness (vijñāna). All latent dispositions (anuśaya) increase in accordance with it.

Non-karmic dharmas that serve as equal-and-immediate conditions (*samanantara-pratyaya*) are subsumed within the eighteen elements (*dhātu*), the twelve bases (*āyatana*), and the five aggregates (*skandha*); they are known by ten cognitions (*jñāna*), cognized by six consciousnesses (*vijñāna*), and all latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) increase therein.

Karma as an object-condition (ālambana-dharma) is subsumed under five elements (dhātu), two bases (āyatana), and four aggregates (skandha). It is known by nine knowledges (jñāna), excluding the knowledge of cessation (nirodha-jñāna); it is cognized by one consciousness (vijñāna); and the latent dispositions (anuśaya) that take conditioned phenomena of the three realms as their objects increase therein.

Dharmas that are not objects of karma are subsumed within the eighteen elements, the twelve bases, and the five aggregates; they are known by ten cognitions, cognized by six consciousnesses, and all latent dispositions increase in relation to them.

Karma as the predominant factor (*adhipati-dharma*) is subsumed within the eighteen elements (*dhātu*), the twelve bases (*āyatana*), and the five aggregates (*skandha*). It is known by nine types of knowledge, excluding the knowledge of cessation (*nirodha-jñāna*); it is cognized by the six consciousnesses (*vijñāna*), and all latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) increase in accordance with it.

The dharma that has non-action as its predominant condition is comprised of one element, one base, and is not included within the aggregates. It is known by six types of knowledge—excluding the knowledge of others' minds, the knowledge of suffering, the knowledge of origin, and the knowledge of the path—and is cognized by one consciousness. Latent dispositions do not increase therein.

Phenomena that are the results of karma (*karmaphala*) are subsumed within the eighteen elements (*dhātu*), the twelve bases (*āyatana*), and the five aggregates (*skandha*); they are known by ten types of knowledge (*jñāna*) and cognized by six consciousnesses (*vijñāna*); all latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) increase in accordance with them.

Phenomena that are not the results of karma are subsumed within one element, one base, and are not included among the aggregates; they are known by one type of knowledge, namely conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*), and cognized by one consciousness; no latent dispositions increase in accordance with them.

The phenomena that are the maturation of karma (*karmavipāka*) are subsumed within seventeen elements (*dhātu*), eleven bases (*āyatana*), and five aggregates (*skandha*). They are known by eight types of knowledge (*jñāna*), excluding the knowledge of cessation (*nirodhajñāna*) and the knowledge of the path (*mārgajñāna*). They are cognized by five types of consciousness (*vijñāna*), excluding the ear-consciousness (*śrotravijñāna*). The latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) to be abandoned through universal cultivation (*sarvatragabhāvanāheya*) and those to be abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanāheya*) increase in relation to them.

Dharmas that are not the maturation of karma are subsumed within the eighteen elements (*dhātu*), the twelve bases (*āyatana*), and the five aggregates (*skandha*); they are known by ten cognitions (*jñāna*) and cognized by six consciousnesses (*vijñāna*), and all latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) increase therein.

There are phenomena subsumed within the eighteen elements, the twelve bases, and the five aggregates; they are known by eight knowledges—excluding the knowledge of cessation and the knowledge of the path—and are cognized by the six consciousnesses; all latent dispositions increase in relation to them.

Non-existent phenomena (*abhāvadharma*) are subsumed under three realms, two bases, and five aggregates; they are known by eight knowledges, excluding the knowledges of suffering and its origin; they are cognized by one consciousness, and latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) do not increase therein.

Associated dharmas are subsumed under eight elements, two bases, and four aggregates; they are known by eight knowledges—excluding the knowledge of cessation and the knowledge of the path—and are cognized by one consciousness; all latent dispositions increase in relation to them.

There are dissociated phenomena (viprayukta-dharma), which are subsumed within thirteen elements (dhātu), twelve bases (āyatana), and five aggregates (skandha); they are known by ten knowledges (jñāna) and cognized by six consciousnesses (vijñāna); and the latent tendencies (anuśaya) with outflows (sāsrava) that take the three realms as their object increase therein.

There are co-existent phenomena (*sahabhū-dharma*), which are subsumed under the eighteen elements (*dhātu*), the twelve bases (*āyatana*), and the five aggregates (*skandha*). They are known by nine types of knowledge, excluding the knowledge of cessation (*nirodha-jñāna*); they are cognized by the six consciousnesses; and all latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) increase in relation to them.

The non-existent coexistent dharma (*asat-sahabhū-dharma*) is subsumed under three realms (*dhātu*), two bases (*āyatana*), and five aggregates (*skandha*). It is known by eight knowledges (*jñāna*), excluding the knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-jñāna*) and the knowledge of origin (*samudaya-jñāna*); it is cognized by one consciousness (*vijñāna*), and no latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) increase therein.

The phenomena that arise in accordance with existence (*bhava*) and those that are conditioned by existence (*bhava-hetuka*) are subsumed within the eighteen elements (*dhātu*), the twelve bases (*āyatana*), and the five aggregates (*skandha*). They are known by eight cognitions, excluding the cognition of cessation (*nirodha-jñāna*) and the cognition of the path (*mārga-jñāna*), and are cognized by the six consciousnesses (*vijñāna*). All latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) increase in relation to them.

Those phenomena that do not have concomitant factors and those that do not have conditioned factors as their cause are subsumed within the three realms, three bases, and five aggregates; they are known by eight knowledges—excluding the knowledges of suffering and origin—and are cognized by one consciousness; they are not sites where latent dispositions increase.

Conditioned *samanantara-dharmas* (dharmas that arise immediately after) are subsumed under eight elements (*dhātus*), two bases (*āyatanas*), and four aggregates (*skandhas*). They are known by nine knowledges (*jñānas*), excluding the knowledge of cessation (*nirodha-jñāna*), and are cognized by one consciousness (*vijñāna*). All latent dispositions (*anuśayas*) increase in accordance with them.

Non-conditioned dharmas that are not immediate antecedents (samanantara-pratyaya) are subsumed within the eighteen elements (dhātu), the twelve bases (āyatana), and the five aggregates (skandha); they are known by ten knowledges (jñāna), cognized by six consciousnesses (vijñāna), and all latent dispositions (anuśaya) increase therein.

Conditioned phenomena as objects of cognition are subsumed under eight elements, two bases, and four aggregates; they are known by nine knowledges, excluding the knowledge of cessation; they are cognized by one consciousness; and the latent dispositions with outflows directed toward the three realms increase therein.

Non-conditioned phenomena as objects of cognition are subsumed within thirteen elements, twelve bases, and five aggregates; they are known by ten cognitions and cognized by six consciousnesses, and all latent dispositions increase in relation to them.

Conditioned phenomena as the predominant factor are subsumed within the eighteen elements, the twelve bases, and the five aggregates; they are known by nine knowledges, excluding the knowledge of cessation, and are cognized by the six consciousnesses; all latent dispositions increase in relation to them.

The non-conditioned *adhipati-dharma* is comprised of one element (*dhātu*), one base (*āyatana*), and is not included within the aggregates (*skandha*). It is known by six types of knowledge—excluding the knowledge of others' minds, the knowledge of suffering, the knowledge of origin, and the knowledge of the path—and is cognized by one consciousness. Latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) do not increase therein.

Dharmas that possess fruit are subsumed within the eighteen elements, the twelve bases, and the five aggregates; they are known by nine knowledges—excluding the knowledge of the path—and are cognized by the six consciousnesses; all latent dispositions increase in relation to them.

Dharmas that do not possess a fruit are subsumed within the three realms, two bases, and five aggregates; they are known by eight knowledges—excluding the knowledges of suffering and origin—and are cognized by one consciousness; they are not increased by underlying tendencies.

There are dharmas with maturation (vipāka), which are subsumed under seventeen elements (dhātu), eleven bases (āyatana), and five aggregates (skandha). They are known by eight knowledges (jñāna), excluding the knowledge of cessation (nirodhajñāna) and the knowledge of the path (mārgajñāna); they are cognized by five consciousnesses (vijñāna), excluding the ear-consciousness; and the pervasive latent dispositions (anuśaya) of the three realms, as well as those to be abandoned through cultivation (bhāvanā-heya), increase therein.

Dharmas that do not possess maturation (avipāka) are subsumed within the eighteen elements (dhātus), the twelve bases (āyatanas), and the five aggregates (skandhas); they are known by ten knowledges (jñānas), cognized by six consciousnesses (vijñānas), and all latent dispositions (anuśayas) increase therein.

The phenomena to be fully known by wisdom are subsumed within the eighteen elements, the twelve bases, and the five aggregates; they are known by the ten knowledges, cognized by the six consciousnesses, and all latent tendencies increase in relation to them.

It is not a phenomenon to be fully known by the knowledge of full comprehension; it is not subsumed under the elements, the sense bases, or the aggregates; it is not known by cognition, nor is it cognized by consciousness; and the latent dispositions do not increase therein, because such a phenomenon is unattainable.

The phenomena to be fully known through the thorough knowledge of abandonment (*prahāṇa-parijñā*) are precisely those phenomena that ought to be abandoned. These phenomena are subsumed within the eighteen elements (*dhātu*), the twelve bases (*āyatana*), and the five aggregates (*skandha*). They are known by eight cognitions—excluding the cognition of cessation (*nirodha-jñāna*) and the cognition of the path (*mārga-jñāna*)—and are cognized by the six consciousnesses (*vijñāna*); all latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) increase in accordance with them.

Those phenomena not to be fully known through the full knowledge of abandonment (*prahāṇa-parijñā*) are precisely those that are not to be abandoned. These phenomena are subsumed within the three realms, two bases, and five aggregates; they are known by eight knowledges—excluding the knowledges of suffering and origin—and are cognized by one consciousness; they are not subject to the increase of latent dispositions (*anuśaya*).

The dharmas that should be cultivated are subsumed within ten elements (*dhātu*), four bases (*āyatana*), and five aggregates (*skandha*). They are known by nine knowledges—excluding the knowledge of cessation—and cognized by three consciousnesses. The latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) that increase in relation to them are those that are omnipresent throughout the three realms and those to be abandoned through cultivation.

Dharmas that are not to be cultivated are subsumed within the eighteen elements, the twelve bases, and the five aggregates; they are known by nine cognitions, excluding the cognition of the path, and are cognized by the six consciousnesses; all latent dispositions increase in relation to them.

The dharmas that are to be realized through the realization of wisdom are subsumed within the eighteen elements, the twelve bases, and the five aggregates; they are known by ten types of knowledge, cognized by six consciousnesses, and all latent dispositions increase in relation to them.

It is not a dharma to be realized through the realization of wisdom; it is not subsumed under the elements, the sense bases, or the aggregates; it is not known by wisdom, nor cognized by consciousness, nor do latent tendencies increase therein, because such a dharma is unattainable.

The dharmas that should be realized through direct realization are subsumed within the twelve bases (*āyatana*), the six sense-fields (*āyatana*), and the five aggregates (*skandha*). They are known by ten knowledges (*jñāna*) and cognized by three consciousnesses (*vijñāna*). The latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) that are universal throughout the three realms and those to be abandoned through cultivation increase in relation to them.

Non-acquisition (*aprāpti*) is comprised within the eighteen elements (*dhātu*), the twelve bases (*āyatana*), and the five aggregates (*skandha*). It is known by eight cognitions (*jñāna*), excluding the cognition of cessation (*nirodhajñāna*) and the cognition of the path (*mārgajñāna*). It is cognized by the six consciousnesses (*vijñāna*), and all latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) increase in accordance with it.

The dharmas that should be cultivated are subsumed within ten elements (dhātu), four bases (āyatana), and five aggregates (skandha). They are known by nine knowledges (jñāna), excluding the knowledge of cessation (nirodhajñāna), and are cognized by three consciousnesses (vijñāna). The latent dispositions (anuśaya) that are universal throughout the three realms and those to be abandoned through cultivation increase in relation to them.

Dharmas that are not to be cultivated are subsumed within the eighteen elements, the twelve bases, and the five aggregates; they are known by nine knowledges, excluding the knowledge of the path, and are cognized by the six consciousnesses; all latent dispositions increase in association with them.

Dharmas that are associated with outflows (sāsrava) are subsumed within ten elements (dhātu), four bases (āyatana), and five aggregates (skandha). They are known by eight knowledges (jñāna), excluding the knowledge of cessation (nirodhajñāna) and the knowledge of the path (mārgajñāna), and are cognized by three consciousnesses (vijñāna). All latent dispositions (anuśaya) increase in association with them.

The faultless phenomena (*anavadya-dharma*) are subsumed within the eighteen elements (*dhātu*), the twelve bases (*āyatana*), and the five aggregates (*skandha*); they are known by ten cognitions (*jñāna*) and cognized by six consciousnesses (*vijñāna*); and the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) that are universal throughout the three realms as well as those to be abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) increase therein.

The same applies to wholesome and unwholesome dharmas, obscured and unobscured-neutral dharmas, and dharmas conducive to decline and those not conducive to decline. As for conditioned dharmas (*vijñapti-dharma*), they are subsumed under ten elements (*dhātu*), four bases (*āyatana*), and five aggregates (*skandha*);

they are known by ten cognitions (*jñāna*) and perceived by three consciousnesses (*vijñāna*). The latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) that increase in relation to them include all [dispositions] of the desire realm, as well as the universal and those to be abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) of the form and formless realms.

Indeterminate phenomena (*avyākṛta-dharma*) are subsumed within the eighteen elements (*dhātu*), the twelve bases (*āyatana*), and the five aggregates (*skandha*). They are known by eight cognitions (*jñāna*), excluding the cognition of cessation (*nirodha-jñāna*) and the cognition of the path (*mārga-jñāna*). They are cognized by the six consciousnesses (*vijñāna*). Regarding their underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*), they are increased by all [tendencies] of the form and formless realms, as well as by the two categories of the desire realm, and by the pervasive underlying tendencies (*sarvatraga-anuśaya*) to be abandoned through the vision of origin (*samudaya-darśana-prahātavya*).

Phenomena that have already arisen are subsumed within the eighteen elements (*dhātu*), the twelve bases (*āyatana*), and the five aggregates (*skandha*). They are known by nine types of knowledge, excluding the knowledge of cessation (*nirodha-jñāna*); they are cognized by the six consciousnesses (*vijñāna*), and all latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) increase in relation to them.

Non-arisen phenomena (*anutpanna-dharma*) are subsumed within the eighteen elements (*dhātu*), the twelve bases (*āyatana*), and the five aggregates (*skandha*); they are known by ten knowledges (*jñāna*), cognized by six consciousnesses (*vijñāna*), and all latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) increase in relation to them.

The same applies to phenomena that are currently arising and those not currently arising, phenomena already ceased and those not yet ceased, and phenomena currently ceasing and those not currently ceasing.

Conditioned phenomena (*pratītyasamutpāda*) are subsumed within the eighteen elements (*dhātu*), the twelve bases (*āyatana*), and the five aggregates (*skandha*). They are known by nine types of knowledge, excluding the knowledge of cessation (*nirodhajñāna*); they are cognized by the six consciousnesses (*vijñāna*), and all latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) increase therein.

That which is not a dependently originated phenomenon (apratītyasamutpanna-dharma) is comprised within one element (dhātu), one base (āyatana), and is not included among the aggregates (skandha). It is known by six types of knowledge—excluding the knowledge of others' minds (paracittajñāna), the knowledge of suffering (duḥkhajñāna), the knowledge of origin (samudayajñāna), and the knowledge of the path (mārgajñāna)—and is cognized by one consciousness (vijñāna). It is not a condition for the increase of latent dispositions (anuśaya).

The same applies to: arisen phenomena that are not conditioned by what has already arisen; causal phenomena that are not causal phenomena; phenomena with causes that are not phenomena with causes; and caused phenomena that have arisen which are not caused phenomena that have arisen.

Dharmas associated with causes are subsumed under eight elements, two bases, and four aggregates; they are known by nine knowledges, excluding the knowledge of cessation; they are cognized by one consciousness, and all latent dispositions increase therein.

The dissociated factors (viprayukta-dharma) are subsumed under eleven elements (dhātu), eleven bases (āyatana), and two aggregates (skandha). They are known by nine cognitions, excluding the cognition of others' minds (paracittajñāna), and are cognized by the six consciousnesses. The latent dispositions (anuśaya) that have the outflow-bound (sāsrava) objects of the three realms as their objective support increase in relation to them.

Regarding the dharma of fetters (*saṃyojana*): it is subsumed under one element (*dhātu*), one base (*āyatana*), and one aggregate (*skandha*). It is known by eight knowledges (*jñāna*), excluding the knowledge of cessation (*nirodhajñāna*) and the knowledge of the path (*mārgajñāna*). It is cognized by one consciousness (*vijñāna*). With the exception of the untainted object (*anāsravālambana*) and the unique ignorance (*āveṇikāvidyā*), all other latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) increase in association with it.

Dharmas that are not fetters (*asaṃyojana*) are comprised within the eighteen elements (*dhātu*), the twelve bases (*āyatana*), and the five aggregates (*skandha*); they are known by ten knowledges (*jñāna*) and cognized by six consciousnesses (*vijñāna*); all latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) increase therein.

Dharmas that are conducive to fetters (*anuloma-saṃyojana*) are comprised within the eighteen elements, the twelve bases, and the five aggregates; they are known by eight knowledges—excluding the knowledge of cessation (*nirodha-jñāna*) and the knowledge of the path (*mārga-jñāna*)—and cognized by six consciousnesses; all latent dispositions increase therein.

The factors not concordant with the fetters (*an-anuśaya-dharma*) are subsumed under two bases and five aggregates within the three realms; they are known by eight knowledges, excluding the knowledge of suffering and the knowledge of origin; they are cognized by one consciousness, and no latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) increase therein.

The appropriated phenomena (*upādāna-dharma*) are subsumed under one element (*dhātu*), one base (*āyatana*), and one aggregate (*skandha*); they are known by eight knowledges (*jñāna*), excluding the knowledge of cessation (*nirodha-jñāna*) and the knowledge of the path (*mārga-jñāna*); they are cognized by one consciousness (*vijñāna*); and all latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) increase therein.

Non-appropriated phenomena (*anupāttadharma*) are subsumed under the eighteen elements (*dhātu*), twelve bases (*āyatana*), and five aggregates (*skandha*); they are known by ten cognitions (*jñāna*) and cognized by six consciousnesses (*vijñāna*); all latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) increase in relation to them.

Appropriated phenomena (*upāttadharma*) are subsumed under nine elements, nine bases, and one aggregate; they are known by seven cognitions—excluding the cognition of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*) and the cognitions of cessation (*nirodhajñāna*) and the path (*mārgajñāna*)—and cognized by five consciousnesses; the universal latent dispositions (*sarvatragānuśaya*) of the desire and form realms, as well as those to be abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanāheya*), increase in relation to them.

Non-appropriated phenomena (*anupāttadharma*) are subsumed within the eighteen elements (*dhātu*), the twelve bases (*āyatana*), and the five aggregates (*skandha*); they are known by ten types of knowledge (*jñāna*) and cognized by six consciousnesses (*vijñāna*); all latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) increase in relation to them.

Dharmas that are *anugrāhaka* (favorable to grasping) are comprised within the eighteen *dhātus*, the twelve *āyatanas*, and the five *skandhas*. They are known by eight types of knowledge—excluding the knowledge of cessation (*nirodha-jñāna*) and the knowledge of the path (*mārga-jñāna*)—and are cognized by the six consciousnesses.

All underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) increase in accordance with them. Dharmas that are not *anugrāhaka* are comprised within the three realms, two *āyatanas*, and five *skandhas*. They are known by eight types of knowledge—excluding the knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-jñāna*) and the knowledge of origin (*samudaya-jñāna*)—and are cognized by one consciousness. Underlying tendencies do not increase in accordance with them.

The phenomena of affliction (*kleśa-dharma*) are subsumed under one element (*dhātu*), one base (*āyatana*), and one aggregate (*skandha*); they are known by eight cognitions (*jñāna*), excluding the cognition of cessation (*nirodha-jñāna*) and the cognition of the path (*mārga-jñāna*); they are cognized by one consciousness (*vijñāna*); and all latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) increase in accordance with them.

Non-afflicted phenomena (*akliṣṭadharma*) are subsumed within the eighteen elements (*dhātu*), the twelve bases (*āyatana*), and the five aggregates (*skandha*); they are known by ten knowledges (*jñāna*) and cognized by the six consciousnesses (*vijñāna*); all latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) increase in relation to them. Afflicted phenomena (*kliṣṭadharma*) are subsumed within ten elements, four bases, and five aggregates; they are known by eight knowledges—excluding the knowledge of cessation (*nirodhajñāna*) and the knowledge of the path (*mārgajñāna*)—and cognized by three consciousnesses; all latent dispositions increase in relation to them.

Non-defiled phenomena are subsumed within the eighteen elements, twelve bases, and five aggregates; they are known by ten cognitions and cognized by six consciousnesses; and the latent dispositions (anuśaya) that are universal throughout the three realms, as well as those to be abandoned through cultivation, increase therein.

Defiled phenomena (*kliṣṭa-dharma*) are subsumed within eighteen elements (*dhātu*), twelve bases (*āyatana*), and five aggregates (*skandha*). They are known by eight types of knowledge, excluding the knowledge of cessation (*nirodha-jñāna*) and the knowledge of the path (*mārga-jñāna*), and are cognized by the six consciousnesses (*vijñāna*). All latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) increase in association with them.

Non-defiled phenomena (*asaṃkleśa-dharma*) are subsumed under three realms, two bases, and five aggregates; they are known by eight knowledges, excluding the knowledge of suffering and the knowledge of origin; they are cognized by one consciousness; and latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) do not increase therein. Enveloping phenomena (*paryavasthāna-dharma*) are subsumed under one realm, one base, and one aggregate; they are known by eight knowledges, excluding the knowledge of cessation and the knowledge of the path; they are cognized by one consciousness; and all latent dispositions increase therein.

Dharmas that are not bound (*asaṃyukta*) are subsumed under eighteen elements (*dhātu*), twelve bases (*āyatana*), and five aggregates (*skandha*); they are known by ten knowledges (*jñāna*) and cognized by six consciousnesses (*vijñāna*); all latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) increase therein.

Dharmas that are bound (*saṃyukta*) are subsumed under eight elements, two bases, and four aggregates; they are known by eight knowledges—excluding the knowledge of cessation (*nirodhajñāna*) and the knowledge of the path (*mārgajñāna*)—and cognized by one consciousness; all latent dispositions increase therein.

Dharmas that are not bound by the fetters are subsumed within the eighteen elements, the twelve bases, and the five aggregates; they are known by ten types of knowledge and cognized by six consciousnesses; and the latent dispositions (anuśaya) with outflows pertaining to the three realms increase in relation to them as their objects.

The factors that accord with the fetters (*paryavasthāna*) are subsumed within the eighteen elements (*dhātu*), the twelve bases (*āyatana*), and the five aggregates (*skandha*); they are known by eight cognitions, excluding the cognition of cessation (*nirodhajñāna*) and the cognition of the path (*mārgajñāna*); they are cognized by the six consciousnesses; and all latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) increase in accordance with them.

The factors that are not concordant with the fetters (*paryavasthāna*) are subsumed under two bases and five aggregates within the three realms; they are known by eight knowledges—excluding the knowledge of suffering and the knowledge of origin—and cognized by one consciousness; they are neither concomitant nor do they increase [in intensity].

Dharmas that have an object (sālambana) are subsumed under two elements (dhātu), two bases (āyatana), and four aggregates (skandha). They are known by nine knowledges (jñāna), excluding the knowledge of cessation (nirodhajñāna); they are cognized by one consciousness (vijñāna), and all latent dispositions (anuśaya) increase therein.

Dharmas that have no object of cognition (*anālambana*) are subsumed under eleven elements (*dhātu*), eleven bases (*āyatana*), and two aggregates (*skandha*). They are known by nine cognitions (*jñāna*), excluding the cognition of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*); they are cognized by the six consciousnesses (*vijñāna*); and the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) with outflows (*sāsrava*) belonging to the three realms increase in relation to them as their objects.

Dharmas with vitarka are subsumed under eight elements, two bases, and four aggregates; they are known by nine knowledges, excluding the knowledge of cessation; they are cognized by one consciousness; and all latent dispositions (anuśaya) belonging to the desire and form realms increase therein.

Dharmas without vitarka are subsumed within thirteen elements, twelve bases, and five aggregates; they are known by ten knowledges and cognized by six consciousnesses; all latent dispositions increase in relation to them.
The same applies to dharmas with vicāra and without vicāra.

The phenomena associated with joy (*somanassadhamma*) are subsumed under three realms, two bases, and three aggregates; they are known by nine knowledges, excluding the knowledge of cessation (*nirodha-ñāṇa*), and are cognized by one consciousness. They comprise everything in the form realm; with respect to the desire realm, all latent dispositions (*anusaya*) increase except for doubt directed toward the outflow-free (*anāsava*) and the ignorance associated with that doubt. As for the phenomena not associated with joy (*asomanassadhamma*), they are subsumed under eighteen elements, twelve bases, and five aggregates; they are known by ten knowledges and cognized by six consciousnesses, and all latent dispositions increase therein.

There are factors that are subject to vigilance (*sasaṃvedana*); they are subsumed under eight elements (*dhātu*), two bases (*āyatana*), and four aggregates (*skandha*). They are known by nine knowledges (*jñāna*), excluding the knowledge of cessation (*nirodhajñāna*), and are cognized by one consciousness (*vijñāna*). All latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) increase in relation to them.

Dharmas that are not objects of mental application (*amanasikāra*) are subsumed under eleven elements (*dhātu*), eleven bases (*āyatana*), and two aggregates (*skandha*); they are known by ten knowledges (*jñāna*), cognized by six consciousnesses (*vijñāna*), and all latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) increase therein.

There are phenomena with objects, phenomena with conditions, and phenomena that have a superior; they are subsumed within the eighteen elements, the twelve bases, and the five aggregates; they are known by nine knowledges, excluding the knowledge of cessation, and are cognized by the six consciousnesses.

All latent dispositions (anuśaya) increase with respect to phenomena that are without a basis (avastuka), without an object (anālambana), and unsurpassed (anuttara). These are comprised within one element (dhātu), one base (āyatana), and are not included within the aggregates (skandha). They are known by six types of knowledge—excluding the knowledge of others' minds, the knowledge of suffering, the knowledge of origin, and the knowledge of the path—and are cognized by one consciousness. Latent dispositions do not increase with respect to them.

Distant phenomena (*dūradharma*) are subsumed within the eighteen elements (*dhātu*), the twelve bases (*āyatana*), and the five aggregates (*skandha*). They are known by nine cognitions (*jñāna*), excluding the cognition of cessation (*nirodhajñāna*); they are cognized by the six consciousnesses (*vijñāna*), and all latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) increase in relation to them.

The "near-dharmas" (pratyāsanna-dharma) are subsumed within the eighteen elements (dhātu), the twelve bases (āyatana), and the five aggregates (skandha); they are known by ten cognitions (jñāna) and cognized by the six consciousnesses (vijñāna), and all latent dispositions (anuśaya) increase therein.
The same applies to finite and infinite dharmas.

The view of phenomena (*dṛṣṭi-dharma*) is subsumed under two elements (*dhātu*), two bases (*āyatana*), and two aggregates (*skandha*). It is known by nine knowledges (*jñāna*), excluding the knowledge of cessation (*nirodha-jñāna*), and is cognized by one consciousness (*vijñāna*). Regarding the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*), the ignorance associated with views (*dṛṣṭi-samprayukta-avidyā-anuśaya*) increases in relation to the outflow-tainted objects (*sāsrava-ālambana*) and the outflow-free objects (*anāsrava-ālambana*) of the three realms.

Non-view phenomena (*adṛṣṭi-dharma*) are subsumed under seventeen elements (*dhātu*), eleven bases (*āyatana*), and five aggregates (*skandha*); they are known by ten knowledges (*jñāna*) and cognized by six consciousnesses (*vijñāna*); all latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) increase therein.

View-basis phenomena (*dṛṣṭisthāna-dharma*) are subsumed under eighteen elements, twelve bases, and five aggregates; they are known by eight knowledges—excluding the knowledge of cessation (*nirodha-jñāna*) and the knowledge of the path (*mārga-jñāna*)—and cognized by six consciousnesses; all latent dispositions increase therein.

The phenomena that are not objects of vision (*adṛṣṭa-sthāna-dharma*) are subsumed under the three realms, two bases, and five aggregates; they are known by eight knowledges, excluding the knowledge of suffering and the knowledge of origin; they are cognized by one consciousness, and the underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) do not increase therein.

The phenomena associated with views (*dṛṣṭi-saṃprayukta-dharma*) are subsumed under three realms, two bases, and four aggregates; they are known by nine knowledges, excluding the knowledge of cessation (*nirodha-jñāna*); they are cognized by one consciousness; and the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) of views and their associated ignorance (*avidyā*), which take as their objects both the outflow-tainted (*sāsrava*) and the outflow-free (*anāsrava*) within the three realms, increase therein.

Dharmas dissociated from vision (*dṛṣṭi-viprayukta*) are subsumed under eighteen elements (*dhātu*), eleven bases (*āyatana*), and five aggregates (*skandha*). They are known by ten cognitions (*jñāna*) and cognized by six consciousnesses (*vijñāna*). With the exception of those latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) that take the untainted as their object, all other latent dispositions increase in association with them.

Chapter Six, Part Five: On the Dharmas of Ordinary Beings (*pṛthagjana*). These dharmas are subsumed within the eighteen elements (*dhātu*), the twelve bases (*āyatana*), and the five aggregates (*skandha*). They are known by eight cognitions, excluding the cognition of cessation (*nirodhajñāna*) and the cognition of the path (*mārgajñāna*). They are cognized by the six consciousnesses (*vijñāna*), and all latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) belonging to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) and the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) increase in relation to them.

The phenomena that are not the factors of ordinary beings (pṛthagjana-dharma) are subsumed under eleven elements (dhātu), ten bases (āyatana), and five aggregates (skandha); they are known by ten cognitions (jñāna), cognized by four consciousnesses (vijñāna), and are the locus where the latent dispositions (anuśaya) to be abandoned through cultivation and those that are universal within the three realms increase.

The factors shared with ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) are subsumed within the eighteen elements (*dhātu*), the twelve bases (*āyatana*), and the five aggregates (*skandha*). They are known by eight types of knowledge, excluding the knowledge of cessation (*nirodhajñāna*) and the knowledge of the path (*mārgajñāna*), and are cognized by the six consciousnesses. All latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) increase in association with them.

The dharmas not shared with ordinary beings (*āveṇika-asādhāraṇa*) are subsumed under eleven elements (*dhātu*), ten bases (*āyatana*), and five aggregates (*skandha*); they are known by ten cognitions (*jñāna*), perceived by four consciousnesses (*vijñāna*), and are the locus for the increase of the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) that are universal throughout the three realms as well as those to be abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*).

The determined dharma (*niyata-dharma*) is subsumed under five elements (*dhātu*), four bases (*āyatana*), and five aggregates (*skandha*). It is known by nine knowledges (*jñāna*), excluding the knowledge of cessation (*nirodha-jñāna*); it is cognized by three consciousnesses (*vijñāna*). The latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) that are universal in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) and those to be abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) increase in association with it.

The non-fixed dharmas are subsumed within the eighteen elements, the twelve bases, and the five aggregates; they are known by nine knowledges, excluding the knowledge of the path, and are cognized by the six consciousnesses; all latent dispositions increase in relation to them.

The phenomena conducive to heat and affliction (*paritāpaniya-dharma*) are subsumed under ten elements (*dhātu*), four bases (*āyatana*), and five aggregates (*skandha*). They are known by eight cognitions (*jñāna*), excluding the cognition of cessation (*nirodha-jñāna*) and the cognition of the path (*mārga-jñāna*), and are cognized by three consciousnesses (*vijñāna*). All latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) increase in accordance with them.

That which is not a dharma conducive to the affliction of heat is comprised within the eighteen elements, the twelve bases, and the five aggregates; it is known by ten cognitions and cognized by six consciousnesses; and the latent dispositions (anuśaya) that are universal throughout the three realms and those to be abandoned through cultivation increase therein.

Root phenomena (*indriya-dharma*) are subsumed within thirteen elements (*dhātu*), seven bases (*āyatana*), and four aggregates (*skandha*); they are known by nine knowledges (*jñāna*), excluding the knowledge of cessation (*nirodha-jñāna*), and are cognized by one consciousness (*vijñāna*). All latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) increase in accordance with them.

Non-faculty phenomena (*anindriya-dharma*) are subsumed within six elements (*dhātu*), six bases (*āyatana*), and three aggregates (*skandha*); they are known by ten knowledges (*jñāna*), cognized by six consciousnesses (*vijñāna*), and all latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) increase therein.

Phenomena subsumed under the Noble Truths (*āryasatya*) are subsumed within eighteen elements, twelve bases, and five aggregates; they are known by ten knowledges, cognized by six consciousnesses, and all latent dispositions increase therein.

Dharmas not included within the Noble Truths are comprised of one element, one base, and are not comprised of any aggregate; they are known by one wisdom, namely conventional wisdom (*saṃvṛtijñāna*), and are cognized by one consciousness; they are not the locus for the increase of latent dispositions (*anuśaya*).

Coexistent phenomena (*sahabhū-dharma*) are subsumed within the eighteen elements (*dhātu*), the twelve bases (*āyatana*), and the five aggregates (*skandha*). They are known by nine cognitions, excluding the cognition of cessation (*nirodha-jñāna*), and are cognized by the six consciousnesses (*vijñāna*). All latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) increase in accordance with them.

It is not a coexistent dharma; it is comprised within one element, one base, and is not included in any aggregate. It is known by six types of knowledge—excluding the knowledge of others' minds, the knowledge of suffering, the knowledge of origin, and the knowledge of the path—and is cognized by one consciousness. Latent dispositions do not increase in accordance with it.

Associated phenomena (saṃprayukta-dharma) are subsumed under eight elements (dhātu), two bases (āyatana), and four aggregates (skandha). They are known by nine knowledges (jñāna), excluding the knowledge of cessation (nirodha-jñāna), and are cognized by one consciousness (vijñāna). All latent dispositions (anuśaya) increase in accordance with them.

Dissociated phenomena (viprayukta-dharma) are subsumed under eleven elements (dhātu), eleven bases (āyatana), and two aggregates (skandha). They are known by nine cognitions, excluding the cognition of others' minds (paracittajñāna); they are cognized by the six consciousnesses; and the latent dispositions (anuśaya) that take the outflow-tainted (sāsrava) objects of the three realms as their object increase therein.

Fruitional phenomena (*phala-dharma*) are subsumed within the eighteen elements (*dhātu*), the twelve bases (*āyatana*), and the five aggregates (*skandha*); they are known by ten types of knowledge (*jñāna*) and cognized by six consciousnesses (*vijñāna*); all latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) increase in association with them.

Non-fruitional phenomena are subsumed within one element, one base, and are not included among the aggregates; they are known by one type of knowledge, namely conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*), and cognized by one consciousness; no latent dispositions increase in association with them.

Dharmas that possess fruit are subsumed within the eighteen elements (dhātus), the twelve bases (āyatanas), and the five aggregates (skandhas). They are known by nine types of knowledge—excluding the knowledge of cessation—and are cognized by the six consciousnesses. All latent dispositions (anuśayas) increase in relation to them.

Dharmas that are without fruit (avipāka) are comprised of one element (dhātu), one base (āyatana), and are not included within the aggregates (skandha). They are known by six types of knowledge—excluding the knowledge of others' minds, the knowledge of suffering, the knowledge of origin, and the knowledge of the path—and are cognized by one consciousness. Latent dispositions (anuśaya) do not increase therein.

Vipāka-dharmas are subsumed under seventeen elements (dhātus), eleven bases (āyatanas), and five aggregates (skandhas). They are known by eight knowledges, excluding the knowledge of cessation (nirodha-jñāna) and the knowledge of the path (mārga-jñāna); they are cognized by the five consciousnesses (vijñānas). The latent dispositions (anuśayas) that are universal throughout the three realms and those to be abandoned through cultivation (bhāvanā-heya) increase in association with them.

Non-resultant phenomena are subsumed within the eighteen elements, twelve bases, and five aggregates; they are known by ten cognitions, cognized by six consciousnesses, and all latent dispositions increase in relation to them.

There are dharmas with maturation (vipāka), which are subsumed under ten elements (dhātu), four bases (āyatana), and five aggregates (skandha). They are known by eight knowledges (jñāna), excluding the knowledge of cessation (nirodha-jñāna) and the knowledge of the path (mārga-jñāna), and are cognized by three consciousnesses (vijñāna). The latent dispositions (anuśaya) of the desire realm (kāmadhātu) in their entirety, as well as those of the form and formless realms that are universal (sarvatraga) and to be abandoned through cultivation (bhāvanā-heya), increase in association with them.

Dharmas that lack maturation (*avipāka*) are subsumed within the eighteen elements (*dhātu*), the twelve bases (*āyatana*), and the five aggregates (*skandha*). They are known by ten cognitions (*jñāna*) and cognized by six consciousnesses (*vijñāna*). Regarding their latent tendencies (*anuśaya*), all [tendencies] of the form and formless realms, as well as those of the two categories of the desire realm—namely, those abandoned through the vision of suffering and origination and the universal [tendencies] abandoned through the vision of origination—increase in association with them.

Conditioned phenomena (*pratītyasamutpāda*) are subsumed within the eighteen elements (*dhātu*), the twelve bases (*āyatana*), and the five aggregates (*skandha*); they are known by the ten knowledges (*jñāna*) and cognized by the six consciousnesses (*vijñāna*), and all latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) increase therein.
