Non-conditioned phenomena are not subsumed within the elements, the bases, or the aggregates; they are not known by any knowledge, not cognized by any consciousness, and no latent tendencies increase therein, because such phenomena cannot be apprehended.

Conditioned phenomena by causes and conditions are subsumed within the eighteen elements (*dhātu*), the twelve bases (*āyatana*), and the five aggregates (*skandha*). They are known by nine types of knowledge—excluding the knowledge of cessation—and are cognized by the six consciousnesses. All latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) increase in accordance with them.

The dharma that is without cause or condition (ahetuka-dharma) is comprised of one element (dhātu), one base (āyatana), and is not included within the aggregates (skandha). It is known by six types of knowledge—excluding the knowledge of others' minds, the knowledge of suffering, the knowledge of origin, and the knowledge of the path—and is cognized by one consciousness. Latent dispositions (anuśaya) do not increase therein.

The dissociated dharma (*visamyukta-dharma*) is subsumed under five elements (*dhātu*), four bases (*āyatana*), and five aggregates (*skandha*); it is known by ten cognitions (*jñāna*) and cognized by three consciousnesses (*vijñāna*); and the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) that are universal throughout the three realms as well as those to be abandoned through cultivation increase therein.

That which is not dissociated from phenomena is subsumed within the eighteen elements, the twelve bases, and the five aggregates; it is known by eight knowledges—excluding the knowledge of cessation and the knowledge of the path—and is cognized by the six consciousnesses; all latent dispositions increase in association with it.

There is a phenomenon of dissociation (*vippayutta-dhamma*), which is comprised within the eighteen elements (*dhātu*), the twelve bases (*āyatana*), and the five aggregates (*skandha*). It is known by nine cognitions (*jñāna*), excluding the cognition of cessation (*nirodha-jñāna*); it is cognized by the six consciousnesses (*vijñāna*), and all latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) increase therein.

The dharma of non-separation (avisaṃyoga-dharma) is comprised of one element (dhātu), one base (āyatana), and is not included within the aggregates (skandha). It is known by six types of knowledge—excluding the knowledge of others' minds, the knowledge of suffering, the knowledge of origin, and the knowledge of the path—and is cognized by one consciousness. Latent dispositions (anuśaya) do not increase therein.

The dharma of continuity is subsumed within the eighteen elements (dhātus), the twelve bases (āyatanas), and the five aggregates (skandhas). It is known by nine types of knowledge, excluding the knowledge of cessation (nirodha-jñāna), and is cognized by the six consciousnesses. All latent dispositions (anuśayas) increase in accordance with it.

Non-continuous phenomena are subsumed within the eighteen elements, the twelve bases, and the five aggregates; they are known by ten cognitions, cognized by six consciousnesses, and all latent dispositions increase in relation to them.
The same applies to phenomena that have continuity and those that lack continuity.

Wholesome phenomena (*kuśala-dharma*) are subsumed under ten bases (*dhātu*), four spheres (*āyatana*), and five aggregates (*skandha*); they are known by ten cognitions (*jñāna*) and cognized by three consciousnesses (*vijñāna*). The latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) that are universal throughout the three realms and those to be abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) increase in association with them.

Unwholesome phenomena (*akuśala-dharma*) are subsumed within ten elements (*dhātu*), four bases (*āyatana*), and five aggregates (*skandha*). They are known by seven types of knowledge—excluding the knowledge of similarity (*anvaya-jñāna*), the knowledge of cessation (*nirodha-jñāna*), and the knowledge of the path (*mārga-jñāna*)—and are cognized by three types of consciousness. All latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) increase in association with them.

Indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) phenomena are subsumed within the eighteen elements (*dhātu*), twelve bases (*āyatana*), and five aggregates (*skandha*). They are known by eight cognitions, excluding the cognition of cessation (*nirodha-jñāna*) and the cognition of the path (*mārga-jñāna*). They are cognized by the six consciousnesses. The latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) that increase in relation to them include all [tendencies] of the form and formless realms, as well as those of two categories in the desire realm, and the universal (*sarvatraga*) latent tendencies to be abandoned through the vision of origin (*samudaya-darśana-prahātavya*).

The dharmas of those in training and those beyond training are subsumed within the three realms, two bases, and five aggregates; they are known by seven knowledges—excluding the knowledges of suffering, origin, and cessation—and are cognized by one consciousness; latent dispositions do not increase therein.

Dharmas that are neither-learner-nor-non-learner are subsumed within the eighteen elements, the twelve bases, and the five aggregates; they are known by nine knowledges, excluding the knowledge of the path, and are cognized by the six consciousnesses; all latent dispositions increase in relation to them.

The factors to be abandoned by insight (*darśana-heya*) are subsumed under the three realms, two bases, and four aggregates; they are known by eight knowledges, excluding the knowledge of cessation and the knowledge of the path, and are cognized by one consciousness. All latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) to be abandoned by insight within the three realms increase in relation to them.

The factors to be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) are subsumed within the eighteen elements (*dhātu*), the twelve bases (*āyatana*), and the five aggregates (*skandha*). They are known by eight types of knowledge (*jñāna*), excluding the knowledge of cessation (*nirodha-jñāna*) and the knowledge of the path (*mārga-jñāna*), and are cognized by the six consciousnesses (*vijñāna*). All pervasive (*sarvatraga*) and cultivation-abandoned latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) of the three realms increase in association with them.

Dharmas not to be abandoned are subsumed under the three realms, two bases, and five aggregates; they are known by eight knowledges—excluding the knowledges of suffering and origin—and cognized by one consciousness; they are not increased by latent dispositions.

Dharmas that have as their cause those to be abandoned by insight (*darśana-heya*) are subsumed within the eighteen elements (*dhātu*), the twelve bases (*āyatana*), and the five aggregates (*skandha*). They are known by eight cognitions (*jñāna*), excluding the cognition of cessation (*nirodha-jñāna*) and the cognition of the path (*mārga-jñāna*), and are cognized by the six consciousnesses (*vijñāna*). All latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) increase in accordance with them.

Phenomena that have as their cause those to be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) are subsumed within the eighteen elements (*dhātu*), the twelve bases (*āyatana*), and the five aggregates (*skandha*). They are known by eight knowledges (*jñāna*), excluding the knowledge of cessation (*nirodha-jñāna*) and the knowledge of the path (*mārga-jñāna*), and are cognized by the six consciousnesses (*vijñāna*). All latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) to be abandoned by cultivation in the three realms, as well as the universal (*sarvatraga*) ones, increase in association with them.

Dharmas that have non-abandonable factors as their cause are subsumed under the three realms, two bases, and five aggregates; they are known by seven cognitions—excluding the cognitions of suffering, origin, and cessation—and are cognized by one consciousness; the latent dispositions do not increase therein.

The phenomena that are visible and resistant are subsumed under one element, one base, and one aggregate; they are known by seven knowledges—excluding the knowledge of others' minds, the knowledge of cessation, and the knowledge of the path—and are cognized by two consciousnesses; the pervasive proclivities of the desire and form realms, as well as those abandoned through cultivation, increase in relation to them.

The non-visible and obstructive dharmas are subsumed under nine elements, nine bases, and one aggregate; they are known by seven cognitions—excluding the cognition of others' minds, the cognition of cessation, and the cognition of the path—and are cognized by the five consciousnesses; the latent dispositions (anuśaya) that are universal in the desire and form realms, as well as those to be abandoned through cultivation, increase therein.

Non-visible and non-obstructive phenomena (*anidarśana-apratigha-dharma*) are subsumed under eight elements (*dhātu*), two bases (*āyatana*), and five aggregates (*skandha*); they are known by ten cognitions (*jñāna*) and cognized by one consciousness (*vijñāna*); all latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) increase therein.

Resultant phenomena (*vipāka-dharma*) are subsumed under seventeen elements, eleven bases, and five aggregates; they are known by eight cognitions—excluding the cognition of cessation (*nirodha-jñāna*) and the cognition of the path (*mārga-jñāna*)—and cognized by five consciousnesses; the universal latent dispositions (*sarvatraga-anuśaya*) of the three realms and those to be abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya-anuśaya*) increase therein.

The dharma that is a resultant phenomenon (*vipākaja-dharma*) is subsumed within ten elements (*dhātu*), four bases (*āyatana*), and five aggregates (*skandha*). It is known by eight knowledges (*jñāna*), excluding the knowledge of cessation (*nirodha-jñāna*) and the knowledge of the path (*mārga-jñāna*), and is cognized by three consciousnesses (*vijñāna*). The latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) of the entire desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), as well as those pervasive (*sarvatraga*) and those to be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) in the form and formless realms (*rūpa-ārūpyadhātu*), increase in association with it.

That which is neither maturation nor a dharma that is not maturation is subsumed within the eighteen elements, the twelve bases, and the five aggregates; it is known by ten cognitions and cognized by six consciousnesses. It includes all [dharmas] of the form and formless realms, as well as those of the desire realm belonging to the two categories and the pervasive latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) to be abandoned through the vision of the origin [of suffering]. It is accompanied by the increase of these latent dispositions.

Inferior phenomena (*hīna-dharma*) are subsumed within ten bases (*dhātu*), four spheres (*āyatana*), and five aggregates (*skandha*); they are known by eight knowledges (*jñāna*), excluding the knowledge of cessation (*nirodha-jñāna*) and the knowledge of the path (*mārga-jñāna*); they are cognized by three consciousnesses (*vijñāna*); and all latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) increase in accordance with them.

The intermediate dharma is subsumed under the eighteen elements (dhātus), the twelve bases (āyatanas), and the five aggregates (skandhas). It is known by eight cognitions, excluding the cognition of cessation and the cognition of the path; it is cognized by the six consciousnesses. The latent dispositions (anuśayas) that are universal throughout the three realms and those to be abandoned through cultivation increase in relation to it.

The "Sublime Dharma" (saddharma) is subsumed within the three realms, two bases, and five aggregates; it is known by eight knowledges, excluding the knowledge of suffering and the knowledge of origin; it is cognized by one consciousness; and no latent dispositions (anuśaya) increase therein.

The "Minor Dharma" and "Great Dharma" are subsumed within the eighteen elements, twelve bases, and five aggregates; they are known by nine knowledges, excluding the knowledge of cessation; they are cognized by six consciousnesses; and all latent dispositions increase therein.

Immeasurable phenomena (*apramāṇa-dharma*), agreeable phenomena (*manojña-dharma*), disagreeable phenomena (*amanojña-dharma*), and neither-agreeable-nor-disagreeable phenomena (*naivamanojñānāmanojña-dharma*) are subsumed within the eighteen elements (*dhātu*), the twelve bases (*āyatana*), and the five aggregates (*skandha*). They are known by ten cognitions (*jñāna*) and cognized by six consciousnesses (*vijñāna*); all latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) increase in accordance with them.

Dharmas associated with pleasure (*sukha-sahagata*) are subsumed under eight elements (*dhātu*), two bases (*āyatana*), and three aggregates (*skandha*). They are known by nine knowledges (*jñāna*), excluding the knowledge of cessation (*nirodha-jñāna*); they are cognized by one consciousness (*vijñāna*). All [defilements] of the form realm (*rūpa-dhātu*) increase in relation to them; all latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) of the desire realm (*kāma-dhātu*) increase in relation to them, except for doubt (*vicikitsā*) that takes the untainted (*anāsrava*) as its object and the ignorance (*avidyā*) associated therewith. Dharmas associated with suffering (*duḥkha-sahagata*) are subsumed under eight elements, two bases, and three aggregates. They are known by seven knowledges, excluding the subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*), the knowledge of cessation, and the knowledge of the path (*mārga-jñāna*); they are cognized by one consciousness. All latent dispositions of the desire realm increase in relation to them.

Dharmas associated with neither-suffering-nor-pleasure are subsumed under eight elements, two bases, and three aggregates; they are known by nine knowledges, excluding the knowledge of cessation; they are cognized by one consciousness; and all latent dispositions increase therein.

Dharmas that arise together, abide together, and cease together are subsumed within the eighteen elements, the twelve bases, and the five aggregates; they are known by nine knowledges, excluding the knowledge of cessation; they are cognized by the six consciousnesses; and all latent dispositions increase in relation to them.

It is not a dharma that arises simultaneously [with others], nor one that abides simultaneously, nor one that ceases simultaneously; it is comprised within one element, one base, and is not included among the aggregates. It is known by six types of knowledge—excluding the knowledge of others' minds, the knowledge of suffering, the knowledge of origin, and the knowledge of the path—and is cognized by one consciousness. Latent dispositions do not increase in accordance with it.

The factors co-arising with the mind are subsumed within eleven elements, eleven bases, and four aggregates; they are known by nine knowledges, excluding the knowledge of cessation, and are cognized by the six consciousnesses; all latent dispositions increase in relation to them.

The phenomena co-residing with the mind are comprised within one element, one base, and four aggregates; they are known by nine knowledges, excluding the knowledge of cessation, and are cognized by one consciousness; all latent dispositions increase in relation to them.

Phenomena that perish simultaneously with the mind are subsumed within ten elements, ten bases, and four aggregates; they are known by nine knowledges, excluding the knowledge of cessation, and are cognized by the five consciousnesses; all latent dispositions increase in relation to them.

Those phenomena that do not arise together with the mind, do not abide together with the mind, and do not cease together with the mind are subsumed within the eighteen elements (*dhātu*), the twelve bases (*āyatana*), and the three aggregates (*skandha*); they are known by ten cognitions (*jñāna*) and cognized by six consciousnesses (*vijñāna*), and all latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) increase in accordance with them.

The desire realm (kāmadhātu) is subsumed under ten elements (dhātu), four bases (āyatana), and five aggregates (skandha). It is known by seven knowledges (jñāna)—excluding the knowledge of subsequent realization (anvaya-jñāna), the knowledge of cessation (nirodha-jñāna), and the knowledge of the path (mārga-jñāna)—and is cognized by three consciousnesses (vijñāna). The latent dispositions (anuśaya) that have outflows (sāsrava) and take the desire realm as their object increase therein.
The element of ill will (*vyāpādadhātu*) is also like this.

The element of cruelty (*vihiṃsādhātu*) is subsumed under five elements, four bases, and five aggregates; it is known by seven knowledges—excluding the knowledge of similarity (*anvayajñāna*), the knowledge of cessation (*nirodhajñāna*), and the knowledge of the path (*mārgajñāna*)—and is cognized by three consciousnesses. The latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) that are omnipresent in the desire realm and those to be abandoned through cultivation increase in association with it.

The element of renunciation is subsumed under ten elements, four bases, and five aggregates; it is known by ten cognitions and cognized by three consciousnesses; and the latent dispositions (anuśaya) that are universal throughout the three realms, as well as those to be abandoned through cultivation, increase therein.

The realm of non-ill will (*avyāpādadhātu*) and the realm of non-harming (*avihiṃsādhātu*) are subsumed under ten elements (*dhātu*), four bases (*āyatana*), and five aggregates (*skandha*). They are known by nine knowledges (*jñāna*), excluding the knowledge of cessation (*nirodhajñāna*); they are cognized by three consciousnesses (*vijñāna*); and the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) that are universal within the three realms (*traidhātuka-sarvatraga*) and those to be abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) increase therein.

The desire realm (kāmadhātu) is subsumed within the eighteen elements (dhātus), the twelve bases (āyatanas), and the five aggregates (skandhas). It is known by seven types of knowledge—excluding the knowledge of subsequent realization (anvaya-jñāna), the knowledge of cessation (nirodha-jñāna), and the knowledge of the path (mārga-jñāna)—and is cognized by the six consciousnesses (vijñānas). All latent dispositions (anuśayas) of the desire realm increase in association with it.

The form realm (rūpadhātu) is subsumed under fourteen elements (dhātu), ten bases (āyatana), and five aggregates (skandha). It is known by seven knowledges (jñāna), excluding the knowledge of cessation (nirodhajñāna) and the knowledge of the path (mārgajñāna). It is cognized by four consciousnesses (vijñāna), and all latent dispositions (anuśaya) of the form realm increase therein.

The formless realm (ārūpyadhātu) is subsumed under three elements (dhātu), two bases (āyatana), and four aggregates (skandha). It is known by six knowledges (jñāna), excluding the knowledge of others' minds (paracittajñāna), the knowledge of cessation (nirodhajñāna), and the knowledge of the path (mārgajñāna). It is cognized by one consciousness (vijñāna), and all latent dispositions (anuśaya) of the formless realm increase therein.

That which is called the "form realm" (rūpadhātu) within the desire realm and the form realm is comprised of eighteen elements (dhātu), twelve bases (āyatana), and five aggregates (skandha). It is known by eight knowledges (jñāna), excluding the knowledge of cessation (nirodhajñāna) and the knowledge of the path (mārgajñāna); it is cognized by six consciousnesses (vijñāna), and all latent tendencies (anuśaya) of the desire and form realms increase therein.

The four formless states (ārūpya) are called the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu). They are subsumed under three realms, two bases (āyatana), and four aggregates (skandha). They are known by six types of knowledge—excluding the knowledge of others' minds, the knowledge of cessation, and the knowledge of the path—and are cognized by one consciousness. All latent dispositions (anuśaya) of the formless realm increase therein.

Regarding the designation of *pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha* (cessation through deliberation) and *apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha* (cessation not through deliberation) as the "element of cessation" (*nirodhadhātu*): it is comprised of one element, one base, and is not included within the aggregates. It is known by six types of knowledge—excluding the knowledge of others' minds, the knowledge of suffering, the knowledge of origin, and the knowledge of the path—and is cognized by one consciousness. Latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) do not increase therein.

Furthermore, that which is collectively termed the "form realm" (*rūpadhātu*)—referring to all form-phenomena (*rūpadharma*)—is comprised of eleven elements (*dhātu*), eleven bases (*āyatana*), and one aggregate (*skandha*). It is known by eight cognitions (*jñāna*), excluding the cognition of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*) and the cognition of cessation (*nirodhajñāna*); it is cognized by the six consciousnesses (*vijñāna*); and the pervasive (*sarvatraga*) and cultivation-abandoned (*bhāvanā-heya*) latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) of the desire and form realms increase therein.

Excluding both cessation through deliberation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) and cessation not through deliberation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*), all remaining non-material phenomena (*arūpa-dharma*) are collectively termed the formless realm (*ārūpya-dhātu*). They are subsumed under eight elements (*dhātu*), two bases (*āyatana*), and four aggregates (*skandha*); they are known by nine cognitions (*jñāna*), excluding the cognition of cessation (*nirodha-jñāna*); they are cognized by one consciousness (*vijñāna*); and all latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) increase therein.

Cessation through deliberation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) and cessation not through deliberation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) are collectively termed the element of cessation (*nirodha-dhātu*), as previously explained.

The realm of desire (*kāmadhātu*) is subsumed within the eighteen elements (*dhātus*), the twelve bases (*āyatanas*), and the five aggregates (*skandhas*). It is known by seven cognitions—excluding the cognition of subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*) and the cognition of the path (*mārga-jñāna*)—and is cognized by the six consciousnesses (*vijñānas*). All latent dispositions (*anuśayas*) of the desire realm increase therein.

The existence of form (*rūpabhava*) is comprised of fourteen elements (*dhātu*), ten bases (*āyatana*), and five aggregates (*skandha*). It is known by seven cognitions—excluding the cognition of cessation (*nirodhajñāna*) and the cognition of the path (*mārgajñāna*)—and is cognized by the four consciousnesses. All latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) belonging to the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*) increase therein.

The formless existence (ārūpyabhava) is comprised of three realms, two bases, and four aggregates; it is known by six knowledges—excluding the knowledge of others' minds, the knowledge of cessation, and the knowledge of the path—and is cognized by one consciousness; all latent dispositions (anuśaya) of the formless realm increase therein.

The outflow of desire (*kāma-āsrava*) is comprised of one element, one base, and one aggregate; it is known by seven knowledges—excluding the knowledge of subsequent realization, the knowledge of cessation, and the knowledge of the path—and is cognized by one consciousness. All latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) of the desire realm increase in association with it.

The contaminated (sāsrava) is subsumed under one element, one base, and one aggregate; it is known by seven knowledges—excluding the knowledge of cessation and the knowledge of the path—and is cognized by one consciousness. All latent dispositions (anuśaya) belonging to the realms of form and formlessness increase in relation to it.

The outflow of ignorance (avidyā-āsrava) is comprised of one element (dhātu), one base (āyatana), and one aggregate (skandha). It is known by eight knowledges (jñāna), excluding the knowledge of cessation (nirodha-jñāna) and the knowledge of the path (mārga-jñāna); it is cognized by one consciousness (vijñāna). With the exception of that ignorance which takes the untainted (anāsrava) as its object, all other latent dispositions (anuśaya) increase in association with it.

The three statements regarding the three periods of time are subsumed under the eighteen elements (*dhātu*), the twelve bases (*āyatana*), and the five aggregates (*skandha*). They are known by nine cognitions, excluding the cognition of cessation (*nirodhajñāna*); they are cognized by the six consciousnesses; and all latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) increase in accordance with them.

Regarding the fact that the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) is suffering due to the suffering of suffering (*duḥkhaduḥkhatā*): it is comprised within eighteen elements (*dhātu*), twelve bases (*āyatana*), and five aggregates (*skandha*); it is known by seven cognitions (*jñāna*), excluding the cognition of subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*), the cognition of cessation (*nirodhajñāna*), and the cognition of the path (*mārgajñāna*); it is cognized by the six consciousnesses (*vijñāna*); and all latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) of the desire realm increase therein.

Regarding the fact that the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) is suffering by virtue of the suffering of change (*vipariṇāmaduḥkha*): it is comprised of fourteen elements (*dhātu*), ten bases (*āyatana*), and five aggregates (*skandha*); it is known by seven cognitions (*jñāna*), excluding the cognition of cessation (*nirodhajñāna*) and the cognition of the path (*mārgajñāna*); it is cognized by four consciousnesses (*vijñāna*); and all latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) of the form realm increase therein.

Regarding the statement that the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) is suffering by virtue of the suffering inherent in conditioned formations (*saṃskāra-duḥkhatā*): it is comprised of three realms, two bases (*āyatana*), and four aggregates (*skandha*). It is known by six types of knowledge—excluding the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*), the knowledge of cessation (*nirodhajñāna*), and the knowledge of the path (*mārgajñāna*)—and is cognized by one consciousness. All latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) of the formless realm increase therein.

Furthermore, unwholesome conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are suffering by way of the suffering of suffering (*duḥkhaduḥkhatā*); wholesome conditioned phenomena are suffering by way of the suffering of change (*vipariṇāmaduḥkhatā*); and neutral conditioned phenomena—neither wholesome nor unwholesome—are suffering by way of the suffering inherent in formations (*saṃskāraduḥkhatā*). All these are subsumed within the eighteen elements (*dhātu*), the twelve bases (*āyatana*), and the five aggregates (*skandha*). They are known by eight cognitions, excluding the cognition of cessation (*nirodhajñāna*) and the cognition of the path (*mārgajñāna*); they are cognized by the six consciousnesses (*vijñāna*), and all latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) increase therein.

Furthermore, regarding the fact that painful feeling is suffering by way of the suffering of suffering (*duḥkha-duḥkhatā*): it is comprised within one element, one base, and one aggregate; it is known by seven knowledges—excluding the knowledge of subsequent realization, the knowledge of cessation, and the knowledge of the path—and is cognized by one consciousness; all latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) of the desire realm increase in association with it.

Regarding the statement that pleasant feeling is suffering by virtue of the suffering of change (*vipariṇāma-duḥkha*): it is comprised of one element (*dhātu*), one base (*āyatana*), and one aggregate (*skandha*). It is known by eight knowledges (*jñāna*), excluding the knowledge of cessation (*nirodha-jñāna*) and the knowledge of the path (*mārga-jñāna*). It is cognized by one consciousness (*vijñāna*). It includes all [factors] of the form realm (*rūpa-dhātu*). Excluding the doubt (*vicikitsā*) that takes the untainted (*anāsrava*) as its object in the desire realm, along with the ignorance (*avidyā*) associated therewith, all other latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) of the desire realm increase in association with it.

That which is neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling is suffering by virtue of the suffering of conditioned formations (*saṃskāra-duḥkhatā*); it is comprised within one element, one base, and one aggregate; it is known by eight knowledges—excluding the knowledge of cessation and the knowledge of the path—and is cognized by one consciousness; all latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) increase therein.

Dharmas with vitarka and vicāra are subsumed under eight elements, two bases, and four aggregates; they are known by nine knowledges, excluding the knowledge of cessation; they are cognized by one consciousness; and all latent dispositions (anuśaya) belonging to the desire and form realms increase in relation to them.

The dharmas that are without vitarka and with only vicāra are subsumed under three realms, two bases, and four aggregates; they are known by nine knowledges, excluding the knowledge of cessation; they are cognized by one consciousness; and all latent dispositions (anuśaya) belonging to the desire and form realms increase therein.

Dharmas without vitarka and without vicāra are subsumed under thirteen elements (dhātus), twelve bases (āyatanas), and five aggregates (skandhas). They are known by ten knowledges (jñānas) and cognized by six consciousnesses (vijñānas). The latent dispositions (anuśayas) of the form and formless realms, as well as those in the desire realm that have outflowing objects (sāsrava-ālambana), increase in relation to them.

The stage with vitarka and vicāra is subsumed within the eighteen dhātus, the twelve āyatanas, and the five skandhas; it is known by nine jñānas, excluding the knowledge of cessation (nirodha-jñāna); it is cognized by the six vijñānas; and all latent proclivities (anuśaya) belonging to the desire realm and the form realm increase therein.

The stage of no-vitarka and only-vicāra is subsumed under three realms, two bases, and five aggregates; it is known by nine knowledges excluding the knowledge of cessation, and is cognized by one consciousness; the pervasive latent dispositions of the form realm and those to be abandoned through cultivation increase therein.

The stage without vitarka and vicāra is subsumed under eleven elements (dhātu), ten bases (āyatana), and five aggregates (skandha). It is known by nine knowledges (jñāna), excluding the knowledge of cessation (nirodhajñāna), and is cognized by four consciousnesses (vijñāna). All latent dispositions (anuśaya) belonging to the realms of form and formlessness increase therein.

The bodily action (kāyakarman) is subsumed under two elements (dhātu), two bases (āyatana), and one aggregate (skandha). It is known by eight knowledges (jñāna), excluding the knowledge of others' minds (paracittajñāna) and the knowledge of cessation (nirodhajñāna). It is cognized by two consciousnesses (vijñāna). The latent dispositions (anuśaya) that are universal in the desire and form realms, as well as those to be abandoned through cultivation (bhāvanā-heya), increase in relation to it.
The same applies to verbal karma.

As for mental karma, it is subsumed under one element, one base, and one aggregate; it is known by nine knowledges, excluding the knowledge of cessation; it is cognized by one consciousness; and all latent dispositions increase in relation to it.

Wholesome karma is subsumed under three realms, three bases, and two aggregates; it is known by nine knowledges, excluding the knowledge of cessation; it is cognized by three consciousnesses; and the latent dispositions (anuśaya) that are universal throughout the three realms and those to be abandoned through cultivation increase in association with it.

Unwholesome karma is subsumed under the three realms, three bases, and two aggregates; it is known by seven knowledges—excluding the knowledge of similarity, the knowledge of cessation, and the knowledge of the path—and is cognized by three consciousnesses. All latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) of the desire realm increase in association with it.

Indeterminate karma is subsumed under the three realms, three bases, and two aggregates; it is known by eight knowledges—excluding the knowledge of cessation and the knowledge of the path—and is cognized by three consciousnesses. It is associated with the increase of all latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) belonging to the form and formless realms, those of the three categories in the desire realm, and the universal latent dispositions abandoned through the vision of origin.

The *śaikṣa* (trainee) and *aśaikṣa* (non-trainee) karmas are subsumed under one element (*dhātu*), one base (*āyatana*), and two aggregates (*skandha*). They are known by seven cognitions—excluding the cognitions of suffering, origin, and cessation—and are cognized by one consciousness. Latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) do not increase therein.

Karma that is neither-learner-nor-non-learner is subsumed under the three realms, three bases, and two aggregates; it is known by eight knowledges—excluding the knowledge of cessation and the knowledge of the path—and is cognized by the three consciousnesses; all latent dispositions increase in accordance with it.

Karma to be abandoned by insight (darśana-heya) is subsumed under one element (dhātu), one base (āyatana), and one aggregate (skandha). It is known by eight knowledges (jñāna), excluding the knowledge of cessation (nirodha-jñāna) and the knowledge of the path (mārga-jñāna); it is cognized by one consciousness (vijñāna). All latent dispositions (anuśaya) to be abandoned by insight in the three realms increase in relation to it.

Karma to be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) is subsumed under the three realms, three bases, and two aggregates; it is known by eight knowledges—excluding the knowledge of cessation (*nirodha-jñāna*) and the knowledge of the path (*mārga-jñāna*)—and is cognized by three consciousnesses. All pervasive (*sarvatraga*) and cultivation-abandoned latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) of the three realms increase in association with it.

Karma that is not to be abandoned is subsumed under one element, one base, and two aggregates; it is known by seven knowledges—excluding the knowledges of suffering, origin, and cessation—and is cognized by one consciousness; it is not increased by underlying tendencies.

Karma to be experienced in the present life (*dṛṣṭadharmavedanīya*), karma to be experienced in the next life (*upapadyavedanīya*), and karma to be experienced in subsequent lives (*aparaparyāyavedanīya*) are subsumed under the three realms, three bases, and two aggregates. They are known by eight knowledges, excluding the knowledge of cessation (*nirodhajñāna*) and the knowledge of the path (*mārgajñāna*); they are cognized by three consciousnesses. All latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) belonging to the entire desire realm, the pervasive [dispositions] of the form and formless realms, and those to be abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanāheya*) increase in association with them.

Karma conducive to pleasant feeling is subsumed under the three realms, three bases, and two aggregates; it is known by eight knowledges, excluding the knowledge of cessation and the knowledge of the path; it is cognized by three consciousnesses; and the pervasive latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) of the desire and form realms, as well as those to be abandoned through cultivation, increase in association with it.

Karma conducive to painful feeling (*duḥkhavedanīya-karman*) is subsumed under the three realms (*dhātu*), three bases (*āyatana*), and two aggregates (*skandha*). It is known by seven knowledges (*jñāna*), excluding the knowledge of similarity (*anvaya-jñāna*), the knowledge of cessation (*nirodha-jñāna*), and the knowledge of the path (*mārga-jñāna*); it is cognized by three consciousnesses (*vijñāna*). All latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) increase in association with it.

Karma that is neither painful nor pleasant is subsumed under one element, one base, and two aggregates; it is known by seven cognitions—excluding the cognition of cessation and the cognition of the path—and is cognized by one consciousness. The pervasive and cultivation-abandoned latent dispositions (anuśaya) of the form and formless realms increase in association with it.

The application of mindfulness to the body (kāyasmṛtyupasthāna) is subsumed under eleven elements (dhātu), eleven bases (āyatana), and one aggregate (skandha). It is known by eight knowledges (jñāna), excluding the knowledge of others' minds (paracittajñāna) and the knowledge of cessation (nirodhajñāna). It is cognized by the six consciousnesses (vijñāna). The latent dispositions (anuśaya) that are universal in the desire and form realms (kāma- and rūpadhātu) and those to be abandoned through cultivation (bhāvanāheya) increase in association with it.

The foundation of mindfulness of feeling is subsumed under one element, one base, and one aggregate; it is known by nine knowledges, excluding the knowledge of cessation; it is cognized by one consciousness; and all latent dispositions increase therein.

The mindfulness of mind is subsumed under seven elements, one base, and one aggregate; it is known by nine knowledges, excluding the knowledge of cessation; it is cognized by one consciousness; and all latent dispositions increase therein.

The foundation of mindfulness of phenomena (*dharmasmṛtyupasthāna*) is subsumed under one element, one base, and two aggregates; it is known by ten knowledges and cognized by one consciousness; all latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) increase therein.

Furthermore, the wholesome, outflow-tainted (*sāsrava*) and untainted (*anāsrava*) paths arising through the predominance of body, feeling, mind, and phenomena are subsumed under three elements, two bases, and five aggregates; they are known by nine knowledges—excluding the knowledge of cessation—and cognized by one consciousness; the universal latent dispositions of the three realms and those to be abandoned by cultivation increase therein.

Furthermore, the wholesome, outflow-tainted (*sāsrava*) and outflow-free (*anāsrava*) wisdom arising from taking body, feeling, mind, and phenomena as objects is subsumed under one element, one base, and one aggregate; it is known by nine knowledges, excluding the knowledge of cessation (*nirodhajñāna*); it is cognized by one consciousness; and the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) that are universal throughout the three realms and those to be abandoned through cultivation increase therein.

The four right efforts (*samyakprahāṇa*) and the four bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*) are subsumed under three elements (*dhātu*), two bases (*āyatana*), and five aggregates (*skandha*). They are known by nine knowledges (*jñāna*), excluding the knowledge of cessation (*nirodhajñāna*), and are cognized by one consciousness (*vijñāna*). The latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) that are universal throughout the three realms and those to be abandoned through cultivation increase in relation to them.

The four dhyānas are subsumed under three realms, two bases, and five aggregates; they are known by nine cognitions, excluding the cognition of cessation; they are cognized by one consciousness; and the pervasive latent dispositions of the form realm, as well as those to be abandoned through cultivation, increase therein.

The Noble Truth of the Origin of Suffering is subsumed within the eighteen elements (dhātus), the twelve bases (āyatanas), and the five aggregates (skandhas). It is known by eight types of knowledge—excluding the knowledge of cessation and the knowledge of the path—and is cognized by the six consciousnesses. All latent dispositions (anuśayas) increase in accordance with it.

The Noble Truth of Cessation is comprised of one element, one base, and is not included within the aggregates. It is known by six types of knowledge—excluding the knowledge of others' minds, the knowledge of suffering, the knowledge of origination, and the knowledge of the path—and is cognized by one consciousness. Latent dispositions do not increase in accordance with it.

The Noble Truth of the Path is subsumed under three realms, two bases, and five aggregates; it is known by seven knowledges—excluding the knowledges of suffering, origin, and cessation—and is cognized by one consciousness; it is not the locus where latent dispositions increase.

The four immeasurables (*apramāṇa*) are subsumed under three realms, two bases (*āyatana*), and five aggregates (*skandha*). They are known by seven knowledges—excluding the knowledge of cessation (*nirodhajñāna*) and the knowledge of the path (*mārgajñāna*)—and are cognized by one consciousness. The latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) that are omnipresent in the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) and those to be abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) increase in association with them.

The base of infinite space, the base of infinite consciousness, and the base of nothingness are subsumed under three elements, two bases, and four aggregates. They are known by seven knowledges—excluding the knowledge of others' minds and the knowledge of cessation—and are cognized by one consciousness. All latent dispositions (anuśaya) of the formless realm increase in association with them.

The sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception is subsumed under three realms, two bases, and four aggregates. It is known by six types of knowledge—excluding the knowledge of others' minds, the knowledge of cessation, and the knowledge of the path—and is cognized by one consciousness. All latent dispositions (anuśaya) of the formless realm increase therein.

The four noble lineages (āryavaṃśa) are subsumed within the three realms, two bases, and five aggregates; they are known by nine knowledges, excluding the knowledge of cessation; they are cognized by one consciousness; and the latent dispositions (anuśaya) that are universal throughout the three realms and those to be abandoned through cultivation increase therein.

The four conditioned fruits of śrāmaṇya are subsumed under three realms, two bases, and five aggregates; they are known by seven knowledges—excluding the knowledges of suffering, origin, and cessation—and are cognized by one consciousness; they are not the locus for the increase of latent dispositions (*anuśaya*).

The four fruits of śrāmaṇya that are unconditioned (asaṃskṛta) are comprised within one element, one base, and are not included among the aggregates. They are known by six types of knowledge—excluding the knowledge of others' minds, the knowledge of suffering, the knowledge of origin, and the knowledge of the path—and are cognized by one consciousness. They are not the locus for the increase of latent dispositions (anuśaya).

Dharma-knowledge (dharma-jñāna) is subsumed under one element (dhātu), one base (āyatana), and one aggregate (skandha). It is known by six knowledges—excluding the knowledge of subsequent realization (anvaya-jñāna) and the knowledges of suffering, origin, and cessation—and is cognized by one consciousness. Latent dispositions (anuśaya) do not increase therein.

Subsequent knowledge (anvaya-jñāna) is comprised within one element, one base, and one aggregate; it is known by six knowledges—excluding the knowledges of dharma, suffering, origin, and cessation—and is cognized by one consciousness; it is not increased by underlying tendencies (anuśaya).

The knowledge of others' minds is subsumed under one element, one base, and one aggregate; it is known by nine knowledges—excluding the knowledge of cessation—and is cognized by one consciousness. The pervasive latent dispositions of the form realm and those to be abandoned through cultivation increase in association with it.

Conventional knowledge (saṃvṛtijñāna) is subsumed under one element, one base, and one aggregate; it is known by eight knowledges—excluding the knowledge of cessation and the knowledge of the path—and is cognized by one consciousness. With the exception of those latent dispositions (anuśaya) that take the untainted as their object, all other latent dispositions increase in association with it.

The knowledge of suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path is subsumed under one element, one base, and one aggregate; it is known by seven knowledges—excluding the knowledges of suffering, its origin, and its cessation—and is cognized by one consciousness; latent dispositions do not increase therein.

The analytical knowledge of phenomena (dharma-pratisaṃvid) is subsumed under one element, one base, and one aggregate; it is known by eight knowledges, excluding the knowledge of cessation and the knowledge of the path; it is cognized by one consciousness; and the pervasive latent dispositions (anuśaya) of the desire and form realms, as well as those to be abandoned through cultivation, increase therein.
The analytical knowledge of language (nirukti-pratisaṃvid) is also like this.

The analytical knowledge of meaning (artha-pratisaṃvid) is comprised within one element, one base, and one aggregate; it is known by nine knowledges, excluding the knowledge of cessation; it is cognized by one consciousness; and the latent dispositions (anuśaya) that are universal throughout the three realms and those to be abandoned through cultivation increase therein.
The same applies to the analytical knowledge of non-obstruction (*pratibhāna-pratisaṃvid*).

It is comprised within the eighteen elements (*dhātu*), the twelve bases (*āyatana*), and the five aggregates (*skandha*). It is known by nine knowledges, excluding the knowledge of cessation (*nirodha-jñāna*). It is cognized by the six consciousnesses, and all latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) increase therein.

The immediately preceding condition (samanantara-pratyaya) is subsumed under eight elements (dhātu), two bases (āyatana), and four aggregates (skandha). It is known by nine knowledges (jñāna), excluding the knowledge of cessation (nirodha-jñāna); it is cognized by one consciousness (vijñāna), and all latent dispositions (anuśaya) increase therein.

The object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*) and the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*) are subsumed within the eighteen elements (*dhātu*), the twelve bases (*āyatana*), and the five aggregates (*skandha*). They are known by ten types of knowledge (*jñāna*) and cognized by the six consciousnesses (*vijñāna*); all latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) increase in association with them.

Edible food (*kavaḍīkāra-āhāra*) is subsumed under the three realms, three bases, and one aggregate; it is known by six knowledges—excluding the knowledge of types (*anvaya-jñāna*), the knowledge of others' minds (*paracitta-jñāna*), the knowledge of cessation (*nirodha-jñāna*), and the knowledge of the path (*mārga-jñāna*); it is cognized by four consciousnesses; and the pervasive (*sarvatraga*) and cultivation-abandoned (*bhāvanā-heya*) latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) of the desire realm increase in relation to it.

The nutriment of contact and the nutriment of mental volition are subsumed under one element, one base, and one aggregate; they are known by eight knowledges—excluding the knowledge of cessation and the knowledge of the path—and are cognized by one consciousness; all latent dispositions increase in relation to them.

The consciousness nutriment (vijñānāhāra) is subsumed under seven elements (dhātu), one base (āyatana), and one aggregate (skandha). It is known by eight knowledges (jñāna), excluding the knowledge of cessation (nirodhajñāna) and the knowledge of the path (mārgajñāna); it is cognized by one consciousness (vijñāna), and all latent dispositions (anuśaya) increase therein.

The flood of sensual desire (kāma-ogha) is comprised of one element, one base, and one aggregate; it is known by seven knowledges—excluding the knowledge of subsequent realization, the knowledge of cessation, and the knowledge of the path—and is cognized by one consciousness; all latent dispositions (anuśaya) of the desire realm increase in association with it.

The flood of existence (*bhava-ogha*) is comprised of one element (*dhātu*), one base (*āyatana*), and one aggregate (*skandha*). It is known by seven cognitions—excluding the cognition of cessation (*nirodha-jñāna*) and the cognition of the path (*mārga-jñāna*)—and is cognized by one consciousness. All latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) belonging to the form and formless realms increase in association with it.

The flood of views (*dṛṣṭi-ogha*) is comprised of one element (*dhātu*), one base (*āyatana*), and one aggregate (*skandha*). It is known by eight knowledges (*jñāna*), excluding the knowledge of cessation (*nirodha-jñāna*) and the knowledge of the path (*mārga-jñāna*), and is cognized by one consciousness (*vijñāna*). It consists of the outflow-tainted objects (*sāsrava-ālambana*) abandoned through the vision of the three realms, as well as the increase of the underlying tendency of ignorance (*avidyā-anuśaya*) associated with views that takes untainted objects (*anāsrava-ālambana*).

The flood of ignorance (*avidyā-ogha*) is comprised of one element (*dhātu*), one base (*āyatana*), and one aggregate (*skandha*). It is known by eight knowledges (*jñāna*), excluding the knowledge of cessation (*nirodha-jñāna*) and the knowledge of the path (*mārga-jñāna*); it is cognized by one consciousness (*vijñāna*). All other latent dispositions (*anuśaya*), with the exception of those that take the untainted as their object, increase in association with it.
As with the four floods (*ogha*), so it is with the four yokes (*yoga*).

The grasping of desire (*kāma-upādāna*) is comprised of one element, one base, and one aggregate; it is known by seven knowledges—excluding the knowledge of subsequent realization, the knowledge of cessation, and the knowledge of the path—and is cognized by one consciousness. All latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) of the desire realm increase in association with it.

The adherence to views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*) is comprised of one element (*dhātu*), one base (*āyatana*), and one aggregate (*skandha*). It is known by eight knowledges, excluding the knowledge of cessation (*nirodhajñāna*) and the knowledge of the path (*mārgajñāna*), and is cognized by one consciousness. It consists of the outflow-conditioned (*sāsrava*) objects of the three realms that are abandoned by vision, as well as the ignorance (*avidyā-anuśaya*) associated with vision that takes the outflow-free (*anāsrava*) as its object; these increase [in association with it].

The clinging to rules and observances (śīlavrataparāmarśa) is subsumed under one element (dhātu), one base (āyatana), and one aggregate (skandha). It is known by eight knowledges, excluding the knowledge of cessation (nirodhajñāna) and the knowledge of the path (mārgajñāna); it is cognized by one consciousness. All latent dispositions (anuśaya) that are abandoned through the vision of suffering (duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya) within the three realms, as well as the universal [dispositions] abandoned through the vision of origination (samudaya-darśana-prahātavya) and those with outflow-objects (sāsrava-ālambana) abandoned through the vision of the path, increase in association with it.

The grasping at the doctrine of self (ātmavādopādāna) is subsumed under one element, one base, and one aggregate; it is known by seven types of knowledge—excluding the knowledge of cessation and the knowledge of the path—and is cognized by one consciousness. All latent dispositions (anuśaya) belonging to the form and formless realms increase in association with it.

Past phenomena, future phenomena, and present phenomena are subsumed within the eighteen elements (dhātus), the twelve bases (āyatanas), and the five aggregates (skandhas). They are known by nine types of knowledge, excluding the knowledge of cessation (nirodha-jñāna), and are cognized by the six consciousnesses; all latent dispositions (anuśayas) increase in accordance with them.

Dharmas that are neither past, nor future, nor present are comprised within one element, one base, and are not included among the aggregates; they are known by six types of knowledge—excluding the knowledge of others' minds, the knowledge of suffering, the knowledge of origin, and the knowledge of the path—and are cognized by one consciousness; they are not the locus for the increase of underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*).

Dharmas bound to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*) are subsumed within the eighteen elements (*dhātu*), the twelve bases (*āyatana*), and the five aggregates (*skandha*). They are known by seven cognitions—excluding the cognition of subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*), the cognition of cessation (*nirodha-jñāna*), and the cognition of the path (*mārga-jñāna*)—and are cognized by the six consciousnesses (*vijñāna*). All latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) belonging to the desire realm increase in association with them.

Dharmas bound to the form realm (*rūpadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*) are subsumed under fourteen elements (*dhātu*), ten bases (*āyatana*), and five aggregates (*skandha*). They are known by seven cognitions—excluding the cognition of cessation (*nirodhajñāna*) and the cognition of the path (*mārgajñāna*)—and are cognized by the four consciousnesses. All latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) belonging to the form realm increase in relation to them.

Dharmas associated with the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*) are subsumed under three realms, two bases, and four aggregates; they are known by six knowledges—excluding the knowledge of others' minds, the knowledge of cessation, and the knowledge of the path—and are cognized by one consciousness; all latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) of the formless realm increase in relation to them.

The unconditioned (apratisaṃyukta) dharmas are subsumed under the three realms, two bases, and five aggregates; they are known by eight knowledges, excluding the knowledges of suffering and origin; they are cognized by one consciousness, and no latent dispositions (anuśaya) increase therein.

Dharmas that have the wholesome as their cause are subsumed within the eighteen elements (dhātus), the twelve bases (āyatanas), and the five aggregates (skandhas). They are known by nine cognitions, excluding the cognition of cessation (nirodha-jñāna); they are cognized by the six consciousnesses; and the latent dispositions (anuśayas) that are universal throughout the three realms, as well as those to be abandoned through cultivation, increase in relation to them.

Dharmas that have unwholesome states as their cause are subsumed within the eighteen elements (dhātus), the twelve bases (āyatanas), and the five aggregates (skandhas). They are known by seven types of knowledge—excluding the knowledge of subsequent realization (anvaya-jñāna), the knowledge of cessation (nirodha-jñāna), and the knowledge of the path (mārga-jñāna)—and are cognized by the six consciousnesses. All latent dispositions (anuśayas) belonging to the desire realm increase in association with them.

Dharmas that have the indeterminate as their cause are comprised within the eighteen elements, the twelve bases, and the five aggregates; they are known by eight cognitions—excluding the cognition of cessation and the cognition of the path—and are cognized by the six consciousnesses; all latent dispositions increase in relation to them.

Dharmas that do not have the wholesome as their cause, nor the unwholesome as their cause, nor the indeterminate as their cause, are comprised within one element, one base, and are not included among the aggregates. They are known by six cognitions—excluding the cognition of others' minds, the cognition of suffering, the cognition of origin, and the cognition of the path—and are cognized by one consciousness. Latent dispositions do not increase with respect to them.

The dharma of having an object as its condition is subsumed under three realms, two bases, and four aggregates; it is known by nine knowledges, excluding the knowledge of cessation; it is cognized by one consciousness; and the latent dispositions with conditioned objects in the three realms increase therein.

The dharma that has non-objectification as its object is subsumed within eight elements, two bases, and four aggregates; it is known by nine knowledges, excluding the knowledge of cessation, and is cognized by one consciousness; all latent dispositions increase in relation to it.

Conditioned by that which has an object and conditioned by that which lacks an object, these are subsumed under three realms, two bases, and four aggregates; they are known by nine knowledges excluding the knowledge of cessation; they are cognized by one consciousness; and the latent dispositions (anuśaya) that take conditioned phenomena of the three realms as their objects increase therein.

Those phenomena that do not take as their object either that which has an object or that which lacks an object are subsumed under eleven elements (*dhātu*), eleven bases (*āyatana*), and two aggregates (*skandha*). They are known by nine cognitions, excluding the cognition of others' minds, and are cognized by the six consciousnesses. The latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) associated with the three realms increase in relation to them when they have outflowing objects.

The aggregate of form (rūpaskandha) is subsumed under eleven elements (dhātu), eleven bases (āyatana), and one aggregate. It is known by eight cognitions—excluding the cognition of others' minds (paracittajñāna) and the cognition of cessation (nirodhajñāna)—and is cognized by the six consciousnesses (vijñāna). The latent dispositions (anuśaya) that are universal in the desire realm (kāmadhātu) and the form realm (rūpadhātu), as well as those to be abandoned through cultivation (bhāvanā-heya), increase in relation to it.

The aggregate of feeling (vedanā-skandha) is subsumed under one element, one base, and one aggregate; it is known by nine cognitions, excluding the cognition of cessation (nirodha-jñāna), and is cognized by one consciousness; all latent dispositions (anuśaya) increase therein.
The same applies to the aggregate of perception (saṃjñā-skandha) and the aggregate of formations (saṃskāra-skandha).

The aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*) is subsumed under seven elements (*dhātu*), one base (*āyatana*), and one aggregate; it is known by nine knowledges (*jñāna*), excluding the knowledge of cessation (*nirodha-jñāna*); it is cognized by one consciousness (*vijñāna*); and all latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) increase therein.

The aggregate of form-clinging (*rūpa-upādāna-skandha*) is subsumed under eleven elements, eleven bases, and one aggregate; it is known by seven knowledges, excluding the knowledge of others' minds (*paracitta-jñāna*), the knowledge of cessation, and the knowledge of the path (*mārga-jñāna*); it is cognized by six consciousnesses; and the universal latent dispositions (*sarvatraga-anuśaya*) of the desire and form realms, as well as those to be abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*), increase therein.

The aggregate of feeling (vedanā-skandha) is subsumed under one element, one base, and one aggregate; it is known by eight knowledges, excluding the knowledge of cessation and the knowledge of the path; it is cognized by one consciousness; and all latent dispositions (anuśaya) increase therein.
The same applies to the appropriation-aggregate of perception and the appropriation-aggregate of formations.

The appropriation-aggregate of consciousness is subsumed under seven elements, one base, and one aggregate; it is known by eight knowledges, excluding the knowledge of cessation and the knowledge of the path; it is cognized by one consciousness; and all latent dispositions increase therein.

The hell realm is comprised of the eighteen elements (*dhātu*), the twelve bases (*āyatana*), and the five aggregates (*skandha*). It is known by seven cognitions—excluding the cognition of similarity (*anvaya-jñāna*), the cognition of cessation (*nirodha-jñāna*), and the cognition of the path (*mārga-jñāna*)—and is cognized by the six consciousnesses. All latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) of the desire realm increase in association with it.
The same applies to the realms of animals, hungry ghosts, and humans.

The realm of gods is comprised of the eighteen elements (*dhātu*), the twelve bases (*āyatana*), and the five aggregates (*skandha*); it is known by eight knowledges—excluding the knowledge of cessation (*nirodha-jñāna*) and the knowledge of the path (*mārga-jñāna*)—and is cognized by the six consciousnesses; all latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) of the three realms increase therein.

The category of afflictions to be abandoned through the vision of suffering (duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya) is subsumed under one element (dhātu), one base (āyatana), and one aggregate (skandha). It is known by eight cognitions, excluding the cognition of cessation (nirodha-jñāna) and the cognition of the path (mārga-jñāna); it is cognized by one consciousness. All pervasive latent dispositions (anuśaya) to be abandoned through the vision of suffering and all pervasive ones to be abandoned through the vision of origin (samudaya) increase in association with it.

The category of afflictions abandoned through the vision of the origin (samudaya-darśana-prahātavya) is subsumed under one element (dhātu), one base (āyatana), and one aggregate (skandha). It is known by eight knowledges, excluding the knowledge of cessation (nirodha-jñāna) and the knowledge of the path (mārga-jñāna), and is cognized by one consciousness. All pervasive (sarvatraga) latent dispositions (anuśaya) abandoned through the vision of suffering (duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya) and all [latent dispositions] abandoned through the vision of the origin increase in association with this category.

The category of afflictions to be abandoned by the vision of cessation is comprised of one element, one base, and one aggregate; it is known by eight knowledges—excluding the knowledge of cessation and the knowledge of the path—and is cognized by one consciousness. All pervasive and universal proclivities (anuśaya) belonging to the three realms that are to be abandoned by the vision of cessation increase in association with it.

The category of afflictions abandoned through the path of seeing is subsumed under one element, one base, and one aggregate; it is known by eight knowledges—excluding the knowledge of cessation and the knowledge of the path—and is cognized by one consciousness. All pervasive and universal latent dispositions (anuśaya) belonging to the three realms that are abandoned through the path of seeing increase in association with it.

The category of afflictions to be abandoned by cultivation is subsumed under one element, one base, and one aggregate; it is known by eight knowledges—excluding the knowledge of cessation and the knowledge of the path—and is cognized by one consciousness. All pervasive and non-pervasive latent dispositions (anuśaya) belonging to all three realms that are to be abandoned by cultivation increase in association with it.

Matter-dharmas (rūpa-dharma) are subsumed under eleven elements (dhātu), eleven bases (āyatana), and one aggregate (skandha). They are known by eight cognitions—excluding the cognition of others' minds and the cognition of cessation—and are cognized by the six consciousnesses. The pervasive latent dispositions (anuśaya) of the desire and form realms, as well as those to be abandoned through cultivation, increase in relation to them.

Mental phenomena (*citta-dharma*) are subsumed under seven elements (*dhātu*), one base (*āyatana*), and one aggregate (*skandha*); they are known by nine knowledges (*jñāna*), excluding the knowledge of cessation (*nirodha-jñāna*); they are cognized by one consciousness (*vijñāna*); and all latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) increase therein.

Mental concomitants (*caitta-dharma*) are subsumed under one element, one base, and three aggregates; they are known by nine knowledges, excluding the knowledge of cessation; they are cognized by one consciousness; and all latent dispositions increase therein.

The formations dissociated from mind (*cittaviprayuktasaṃskāradharma*) are subsumed under one element, one base, and one aggregate; they are known by eight knowledges—excluding the knowledge of others' minds and the knowledge of cessation—and are cognized by one consciousness; the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) that take the outflow-tainted objects of the three realms as their object increase therein.

Unconditioned phenomena (asaṃskṛta-dharma) are comprised of one element (dhātu), one base (āyatana), and are not included within the aggregates (skandha). They are known by six types of knowledge—excluding the knowledge of others' minds, the knowledge of suffering, the knowledge of origin, and the knowledge of the path—and are cognized by one consciousness. Latent dispositions (anuśaya) do not increase therein.

The earth element is subsumed under one element, one base, and one aggregate; it is known by seven knowledges—excluding the knowledge of others' minds, the knowledge of cessation, and the knowledge of the path—and is cognized by two consciousnesses; the latent dispositions (anuśaya) that are universal in the desire and form realms, as well as those to be abandoned through cultivation, increase in relation to it.
The same applies to the elements of water, fire, wind, and space.

The consciousness element (*vijñānadhātu*) is subsumed under seven elements, one base (*āyatana*), and one aggregate (*skandha*); it is known by eight knowledges, excluding the knowledge of cessation (*nirodhajñāna*) and the knowledge of the path (*mārgajñāna*); it is cognized by one consciousness; and all latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) increase therein.

The phenomena abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya*) are subsumed within the three realms, two bases, and four aggregates. They are known by eight knowledges, excluding the knowledge of cessation and the knowledge of the path, and are cognized by one consciousness. All pervasive latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) abandoned through the vision of suffering in the three realms, as well as those abandoned through the vision of the origin, increase in relation to them.

The phenomena abandoned through the vision of the origin (samudaya-darśana-prahātavya) are subsumed under the three realms, two bases, and four aggregates. They are known by eight knowledges—excluding the knowledge of cessation and the knowledge of the path—and cognized by one consciousness. All pervasive latent dispositions (anuśaya) abandoned through the vision of suffering and all [latent dispositions] abandoned through the vision of the origin increase in relation to them.

The phenomena to be abandoned by the vision of cessation (*nirodhadarśana-prahātavya*) are subsumed within the three realms, two bases, and four aggregates. They are known by eight cognitions, excluding the cognition of cessation (*nirodhajñāna*) and the cognition of the path (*mārgajñāna*), and are cognized by one consciousness. All pervasive (*sarvatraga*) and non-pervasive (*asarvatraga*) latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) to be abandoned by the vision of cessation in the three realms increase in relation to them.

The dharmas abandoned by the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) are subsumed under the three realms, two bases (*āyatana*), and four aggregates (*skandha*). They are known by eight knowledges (*jñāna*), excluding the knowledge of cessation (*nirodhajñāna*) and the knowledge of the path (*mārgajñāna*), and are cognized by one consciousness (*vijñāna*). All pervasive (*sarvatraga*) and universal (*anuvartaka*) latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) belonging to the three realms that are abandoned by the path of seeing increase [in relation to them].

The factors to be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) are subsumed within the eighteen elements (*dhātu*), the twelve bases (*āyatana*), and the five aggregates (*skandha*). They are known by eight cognitions, excluding the cognition of cessation (*nirodha-jñāna*) and the cognition of the path (*mārga-jñāna*), and are cognized by the six consciousnesses. All pervasive (*sarvatraga*) and cultivation-abandoned latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) of the three realms increase in association with them.

Dharmas not to be abandoned (*apraheya*) are subsumed under the three realms (*dhātu*), two bases (*āyatana*), and five aggregates (*skandha*). They are known by eight knowledges (*jñāna*), excluding the knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-jñāna*) and the knowledge of origin (*samudaya-jñāna*); they are cognized by one consciousness (*vijñāna*), and the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) do not increase therein.

The latent tendency of sensual desire (*kāmarāgānuśaya*) and the latent tendency of aversion (*pratighānuśaya*) are subsumed within one element, one base, and one aggregate. They are known by seven cognitions—excluding the cognition of subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*), the cognition of cessation (*nirodhajñāna*), and the cognition of the path (*mārgajñāna*)—and are cognized by one consciousness. They are the latent tendencies that increase with respect to the outflow-tainted objects (*sāsravālambana*) of the desire realm.

The latent tendency of sensual desire (*kāmarāgānuśaya*) is comprised within one element, one base, and one aggregate; it is known by seven cognitions—excluding the cognition of cessation and the cognition of the path—and is cognized by one consciousness. It is the latent tendency that increases in relation to the outflow-tainted objects of the form and formless realms.

The latent tendency of pride (mānānuśaya) is subsumed under one element, one base, and one aggregate; it is known by eight knowledges, excluding the knowledge of cessation and the knowledge of the path; it is cognized by one consciousness; and the latent tendencies with outflows directed toward the three realms increase in association with it.

The latent tendency of ignorance (avidyā-anuśaya) is subsumed under one element (dhātu), one base (āyatana), and one aggregate (skandha). It is known by eight knowledges (jñāna), excluding the knowledge of cessation (nirodha-jñāna) and the knowledge of the path (mārga-jñāna); it is cognized by one consciousness (vijñāna). With the exception of that ignorance which takes the untainted (anāsrava) as its object, all other latent tendencies increase in association with it.

The latent tendency of views (dṛṣṭyanuśaya) is subsumed under one element, one base, and one aggregate; it is known by eight knowledges, excluding the knowledge of cessation and the knowledge of the path; it is cognized by one consciousness; and the latent tendency of ignorance associated with views that has outflows and takes as its object the three realms, as well as that which takes the outflow-free as its object, increases therein.

The latent tendency of doubt (vicikitsā-anuśaya) is subsumed under one element (dhātu), one base (āyatana), and one aggregate (skandha). It is known by eight knowledges, excluding the knowledge of cessation (nirodha-jñāna) and the knowledge of the path (mārga-jñāna), and is cognized by one consciousness. The latent tendencies of ignorance (avidyā-anuśaya) associated with doubt—which are to be abandoned by insight (darśana-heya) within the three realms and which take both contaminated (sāsrava) and uncontaminated (anāsrava) objects as their conditions—increase [in association] with it.

The first station of consciousness is subsumed within the eighteen elements, the twelve bases, and the five aggregates. It is known by seven types of knowledge—excluding the knowledge of subsequent realization, the knowledge of cessation, and the knowledge of the path—and is cognized by the six consciousnesses. All latent dispositions of the desire realm increase in association with it.

The second station of consciousness is comprised of fourteen elements, ten bases, and five aggregates; it is known by seven knowledges—excluding the knowledge of cessation and the knowledge of the path—and is cognized by four consciousnesses; all latent dispositions of the form realm increase therein.

The third and fourth stations of consciousness are subsumed under eleven elements, ten bases, and five aggregates; they are known by seven knowledges—excluding the knowledge of cessation and the knowledge of the path—and are cognized by four consciousnesses; all latent dispositions of the form realm increase therein.

The fifth, sixth, and seventh stations of consciousness (*vijñānasthiti*) are subsumed under three realms (*dhātu*), two bases (*āyatana*), and four aggregates (*skandha*). They are known by six types of knowledge (*jñāna*), excluding the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*), the knowledge of cessation (*nirodhajñāna*), and the knowledge of the path (*mārgajñāna*). They are cognized by one type of consciousness (*vijñāna*), and all latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) of the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) increase therein.
Abhidharmaprakaraṇapādaśāstra, Volume Nine of the Sarvāstivādins;
Abhidharmaprakaraṇapādaśāstra, Volume Ten,
composed by the Venerable Vasumitra.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang by Imperial Decree. The Remainder of Chapter Six: The Analysis of the Factors of Enlightenment (*bodhipakṣa-dharma*).

If taken individually, the seven factors of enlightenment are subsumed under one element (*dhātu*), one base (*āyatana*), and one aggregate (*skandha*); if taken collectively, they are subsumed under one element, one base, and two aggregates. They are known by seven types of knowledge—excluding the knowledges of suffering, origin, and cessation—and are cognized by one consciousness. Latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) do not increase therein.

The first, second, and third liberations (vimokṣa) are subsumed under three realms, two bases, and five aggregates. They are known by seven knowledges—excluding the knowledge of cessation (nirodha-jñāna) and the knowledge of the path (mārga-jñāna)—and are cognized by one consciousness. The latent dispositions (anuśaya) that are universal in the form realm and those to be abandoned through cultivation increase therein.

The fourth, fifth, and sixth liberations are subsumed under three realms, two bases, and four aggregates. They are known by seven knowledges—excluding the knowledge of others' minds and the knowledge of cessation—and are cognized by one consciousness. The latent dispositions (anuśaya) that are omnipresent in the formless realm and those to be abandoned through cultivation increase therein.

The seventh liberation is subsumed under three realms, two bases, and four aggregates; it is known by six knowledges—excluding the knowledge of others' minds, the knowledge of cessation, and the knowledge of the path—and is cognized by one consciousness. The latent dispositions (anuśaya) that are universal in the formless realm and those to be abandoned through cultivation increase in relation to it.

The liberation through the cessation of perception and feeling is subsumed under one element, one base, and one aggregate; it is known by six types of knowledge—excluding the knowledge of others' minds, the knowledge of cessation, and the knowledge of the path—and is cognized by one consciousness. The latent dispositions (anuśaya) that are universal in the formless realm and those to be abandoned through cultivation increase in relation to it.

The eight spheres of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*) are subsumed under the three realms, three bases (*āyatana*), and five aggregates (*skandha*). They are known by seven knowledges, excluding the knowledge of cessation (*nirodhajñāna*) and the knowledge of the path (*mārgajñāna*); they are cognized by one consciousness. The latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) that are universal in the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) and those to be abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) increase therein.

Among the eight factors of the Noble Path, right speech, right action, and right livelihood are subsumed under one element, one base, and one aggregate; they are known by six types of knowledge—excluding the knowledge of others' minds and the knowledges of suffering, origin, and cessation—and are cognized by one consciousness; latent dispositions do not increase therein.

The remaining five factors of the noble path are subsumed under one element, one base, and one aggregate; they are known by seven knowledges—excluding the knowledges of suffering, origin, and cessation—and are cognized by one consciousness; they are not increased by underlying tendencies.

The fetter of craving (*rāga-saṃyojana*) and the fetter of conceit (*māna-saṃyojana*) are subsumed under one element (*dhātu*), one base (*āyatana*), and one aggregate (*skandha*). They are known by eight knowledges, excluding the knowledge of cessation (*nirodha-jñāna*) and the knowledge of the path (*mārga-jñāna*), and are cognized by one consciousness. The latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) that take the outflows of the three realms as their object increase in association with them.

The fetter of ill-will (*pratigha-saṃyojana*) is subsumed under one element, one base, and one aggregate; it is known by seven knowledges—excluding the knowledge of subsequent realization, the knowledge of cessation, and the knowledge of the path—and is cognized by one consciousness; the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) with outflows that take the objects of the desire realm as their condition increase therein.

The fetter of ignorance (avidyā-saṃyojana) is subsumed under one element (dhātu), one base (āyatana), and one aggregate (skandha). It is known by eight knowledges (jñāna), excluding the knowledge of cessation (nirodha-jñāna) and the knowledge of the path (mārga-jñāna); it is cognized by one consciousness (vijñāna). With the exception of those latent tendencies (anuśaya) that take the untainted as their object, all other latent tendencies increase in association with it.

The fetter of views (*dṛṣṭi-saṃyojana*) is subsumed under one element (*dhātu*), one base (*āyatana*), and one aggregate (*skandha*). It is known by eight knowledges, excluding the knowledge of cessation (*nirodha-jñāna*) and the knowledge of the path (*mārga-jñāna*); it is cognized by one consciousness. The latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) of ignorance (*avidyā*) associated with views that have outflows (*sāsrava*) as their object and those that have no outflows (*anāsrava*) as their object—both of which are to be abandoned by insight (*darśana-prahātavya*) within the three realms—are present therein.

The fetter of grasping (*parāmarśa-saṃyojana*) is comprised within one element, one base, and one aggregate; it is known by eight knowledges, excluding the knowledge of cessation and the knowledge of the path; it is cognized by one consciousness; and the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) associated with the outflows that are to be abandoned by vision in the three realms increase therein.

The fetter of doubt (*vicikitsā-saṃyojana*) is comprised within one element, one base, and one aggregate; it is known by eight knowledges, excluding the knowledge of cessation and the knowledge of the path; it is cognized by one consciousness; and the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) of ignorance (*avidyā*) associated with doubt—which are to be abandoned by insight into the three realms and which take both contaminated and uncontaminated objects as their conditions—increase therein.
