The fetter of envy (*īrṣyā-saṃyojana*) and the fetter of avarice (*mātsarya-saṃyojana*) are subsumed under one element (*dhātu*), one base (*āyatana*), and one aggregate (*skandha*). They are known by seven cognitions—excluding the cognition of subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*), the cognition of cessation (*nirodha-jñāna*), and the cognition of the path (*mārga-jñāna*)—and are cognized by one consciousness. The latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) that are universal in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) and those to be abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) increase in association with them.

The first abode of sentient beings is subsumed within the eighteen elements (dhātus), the twelve bases (āyatanas), and the five aggregates (skandhas). It is known by seven cognitions—excluding the cognition of subsequent knowledge (anvaya-jñāna), the cognition of cessation (nirodha-jñāna), and the cognition of the path (mārga-jñāna)—and is cognized by the six consciousnesses. All latent dispositions (anuśayas) of the desire realm increase therein.

The second abode of sentient beings is subsumed under fourteen elements, ten bases, and five aggregates; it is known by seven knowledges—excluding the knowledge of cessation and the knowledge of the path—and is cognized by four consciousnesses; all latent dispositions of the form realm increase therein.

The third, fourth, and fifth abodes of sentient beings are subsumed under eleven elements (dhātu), ten bases (āyatana), and five aggregates (skandha). They are known by seven knowledges (jñāna), excluding the knowledge of cessation (nirodhajñāna) and the knowledge of the path (mārgajñāna). They are cognized by four consciousnesses (vijñāna), and all latent dispositions (anuśaya) belonging to the form realm (rūpadhātu) increase therein.

The remaining four abodes of sentient beings (*sattvāvāsa*) are subsumed under two bases (*āyatana*), four aggregates (*skandha*), and two realms (*dhātu*). They are known by six knowledges (*jñāna*), excluding the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*), the knowledge of cessation (*nirodhajñāna*), and the knowledge of the path (*mārgajñāna*). They are cognized by one consciousness (*vijñāna*), and all latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) of the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) increase therein.

The first eight bases of mastery (*kṛtsnāyatana*) are subsumed under three realms, two bases, and five aggregates. They are known by seven knowledges—excluding the knowledge of cessation (*nirodhajñāna*) and the knowledge of the path (*mārgajñāna*)—and are cognized by one consciousness. The latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) that are universal in the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) and those to be abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) increase in relation to them.

The latter two *kṛtsnāyatana*s (totalities) are subsumed under three realms, two bases, and four aggregates. They are known by six types of knowledge—excluding the knowledge of others' minds, the knowledge of cessation, and the knowledge of the path—and are cognized by one consciousness. The latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) of the universal [defilements] of the formless realm and those to be abandoned through cultivation increase in relation to them.

Among the ten factors of one beyond training (*aśaikṣadharma*), right speech, right action, and right livelihood are subsumed under one element, one base, and one aggregate; they are known by six types of knowledge—excluding the knowledge of others' minds and the knowledges of suffering, origin, and cessation; they are cognized by one consciousness; and no latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) increase therein.

The remaining seven dharmas of one beyond training (aśaikṣa) are subsumed under one element, one base, and one aggregate; they are known by seven knowledges—excluding the knowledges of suffering, origin, and cessation—and are cognized by one consciousness; the latent dispositions (anuśaya) do not increase therein.

Contaminated form (*sāsrava-rūpa*) is subsumed under eleven elements (*dhātu*), eleven bases (*āyatana*), and one aggregate (*skandha*). It is known by seven cognitions—excluding the cognition of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*), the cognition of cessation (*nirodhajñāna*), and the cognition of the path (*mārgajñāna*)—and is cognized by the six consciousnesses (*vijñāna*). The pervasive (*sarvatraga*) and cultivation-abandoned (*bhāvanā-heya*) latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) and the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) increase in association with it.

The contaminated (sāsrava) feeling, perception, and formations are subsumed under one element, one base, and one aggregate; they are known by eight knowledges, excluding the knowledge of cessation and the knowledge of the path; they are cognized by one consciousness, and all latent dispositions (anuśaya) increase therein.

Contaminated consciousness (*sāsrava-vijñāna*) is subsumed under seven elements (*dhātu*), one base (*āyatana*), and one aggregate (*skandha*); it is known by eight knowledges (*jñāna*), excluding the knowledge of cessation (*nirodha-jñāna*) and the knowledge of the path (*mārga-jñāna*); it is cognized by one consciousness (*vijñāna*); and all latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) increase therein.

Untainted form (anāsrava-rūpa) is subsumed under one element, one base, and one aggregate; it is known by six types of knowledge—excluding the knowledge of others' minds and the knowledges of suffering, origin, and cessation—and is cognized by one consciousness; latent dispositions do not increase therein.

The untainted (anāsrava) feeling, perception, and formations are subsumed under one element, one base, and one aggregate; they are known by seven cognitions—excluding the cognitions of suffering, origin, and cessation—and are cognized by one consciousness; the underlying tendencies (anuśaya) do not increase therein.

Untainted consciousness (*anāsrava-vijñāna*) is subsumed under two elements (*dhātu*), one base (*āyatana*), and one aggregate (*skandha*); it is known by seven knowledges (*jñāna*), excluding the knowledges of suffering, origin, and cessation; it is cognized by one consciousness (*vijñāna*); and it is not the locus where latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) increase.

Unconditioned phenomena (asaṃskṛta-dharma) are comprised of one element (dhātu), one base (āyatana), and are not included within the aggregates (skandha). They are known by six types of knowledge—excluding the knowledge of others' minds, the knowledge of suffering, the knowledge of origin, and the knowledge of the path—and are cognized by one consciousness; they are not the locus for the increase of latent dispositions (anuśaya).

The eye-base (cakṣur-āyatana) is subsumed under one element, one base, and one aggregate; it is known by seven cognitions—excluding the cognition of others' minds, the cognition of cessation, and the cognition of the path—and is cognized by one consciousness; the pervasive latent dispositions (anuśaya) of the desire and form realms, as well as those to be abandoned through cultivation, increase in relation to it.
As with the sense-base of the eye, so it is with the sense-bases of the ear, nose, tongue, and body.

The sense-base of visible form is comprised within one element, one base, and one aggregate; it is known by seven cognitions—excluding the cognition of others' minds and the cognitions of cessation and the path—and is cognized by two consciousnesses. The latent dispositions that are universal in the desire and form realms, as well as those to be abandoned through cultivation, increase in relation to it.
As with the sense-base of visible form (*rūpāyatana*), so it is with the sense-bases of sound and tangibles.

The sense-base of odors and the sense-base of tastes are subsumed under one element, one base, and one aggregate; they are known by six types of knowledge—excluding the knowledge of subsequent realization (*anvayajñāna*), the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*), the knowledge of cessation (*nirodhajñāna*), and the knowledge of the path (*mārgajñāna*)—and are cognized by two types of consciousness. The latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) that are universal in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) and those to be abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) increase in association with them.

The mind base (*manāyatana*) is subsumed under seven elements (*dhātu*), one base, and one aggregate (*skandha*); it is known by nine knowledges, excluding the knowledge of cessation (*nirodhajñāna*); it is cognized by one consciousness; and all latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) increase therein.

The phenomena base (*dharmāyatana*) is subsumed under one element, one base, and four aggregates; it is known by seven knowledges; it is cognized by one consciousness; and all latent dispositions increase therein.

The eye-element (cakṣurdhātu) is subsumed under one element, one base, and one aggregate; it is known by seven knowledges—excluding the knowledge of others' minds, the knowledge of cessation, and the knowledge of the path—and is cognized by one consciousness; the latent dispositions (anuśaya) that are universal in the desire and form realms, as well as those to be abandoned through cultivation, increase in relation to it.
The same applies to the elements of ear, nose, tongue, and body.

The element of visible form (*rūpa-dhātu*) is subsumed under one element, one base, and one aggregate; it is known by seven cognitions—excluding the cognition of others' minds, the cognition of cessation, and the cognition of the path—and is cognized by two consciousnesses. The proclivities (*anuśaya*) that are universal in the desire and form realms, as well as those to be abandoned through cultivation, increase in relation to it. The same applies to the elements of sound and tangibles.

The fragrance element (gandhadhātu) and the taste element (rasadhātu) are subsumed under one element, one base, and one aggregate. They are known by six types of knowledge—excluding the knowledge of types (anvayajñāna), the knowledge of others' minds (paracittajñāna), the knowledge of cessation (nirodhajñāna), and the knowledge of the path (mārgajñāna)—and are cognized by two types of consciousness. The pervasive (sarvatraga) and cultivation-abandoned (bhāvanā-heya) latent dispositions (anuśaya) of the desire realm increase in association with them.

The mind-element (*manodhātu*) is subsumed under seven elements, one base, and one aggregate; it is known by nine knowledges, excluding the knowledge of cessation (*nirodhajñāna*); it is cognized by one consciousness; and all latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) increase therein.

The phenomena-element (*dharmadhātu*) is subsumed under one element, one base, and four aggregates; it is known by ten knowledges; it is cognized by one consciousness; and all latent dispositions increase therein.

The eye-consciousness element is subsumed under two elements, one base, and one aggregate; it is known by eight knowledges, excluding the knowledge of cessation and the knowledge of the path; it is cognized by one consciousness; and the pervasive latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) of the desire and form realms, as well as those to be abandoned through cultivation, increase therein.
The same applies to the ear, body, and consciousness elements.

The nose and tongue consciousness elements are subsumed under two elements, one base, and one aggregate; they are known by seven cognitions—excluding the cognition of similarity (*anvaya-jñāna*), the cognition of cessation (*nirodha-jñāna*), and the cognition of the path (*mārga-jñāna*)—and are cognized by one consciousness. The latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) that are universal in the desire realm and those to be abandoned through cultivation increase in association with them.

The mind-consciousness element (manovijñānadhātu) is subsumed under two elements, one base, and one aggregate; it is known by nine knowledges, excluding the knowledge of cessation (nirodhajñāna); it is cognized by one consciousness; and all latent dispositions (anuśaya) increase therein.

The eye-faculty is comprised within one element, one base, and one aggregate; it is known by seven cognitions—excluding the cognition of others' minds and the cognitions of cessation and the path—and is cognized by one consciousness; the latent dispositions (anuśaya) that are universal in the desire and form realms, as well as those to be abandoned through cultivation, increase in relation to it.
The faculties of the ear, nose, tongue, and body are also thus.

The female faculty and male faculty are comprised within one element, one base, and one aggregate; they are known by six types of knowledge—excluding the knowledge of types, the knowledge of others' minds, the knowledge of cessation, and the knowledge of the path—and are cognized by one consciousness. The latent dispositions (anuśaya) that are universal in the desire realm and those to be abandoned through cultivation increase in relation to them.

The life-faculty (jīvitendriya) is subsumed under one element, one base, and one aggregate; it is known by seven knowledges—excluding the knowledge of others' minds, the knowledge of cessation, and the knowledge of the path—and is cognized by one consciousness; the latent dispositions (anuśaya) that are universal throughout the three realms and those to be abandoned through cultivation increase in association with it.

The mind-faculty (*manendriya*) is subsumed under seven elements (*dhātu*), one base (*āyatana*), and one aggregate (*skandha*); it is known by nine knowledges (*jñāna*), excluding the knowledge of cessation (*nirodhajñāna*); it is cognized by one consciousness; and all latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) increase in accordance with it.

The faculty of pleasure (*sukhendriya*) is subsumed under one element, one base, and one aggregate; it is known by nine knowledges, excluding the knowledge of cessation; it is cognized by one consciousness; and the latent dispositions belonging to the entire form realm (*rūpadhātu*), the universal [defilements] of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), and those to be abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanāheya*) increase in accordance with it.

The faculty of suffering (*duḥkhendriya*) is comprised within one element, one base, and one aggregate; it is known by seven types of knowledge—excluding the knowledge of dharma (*dharmajñāna*), the knowledge of cessation (*nirodhajñāna*), and the knowledge of the path (*mārgajñāna*)—and is cognized by one consciousness. The latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) that are universal in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) and those to be abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) increase in association with it.

The faculty of joy (*somanassindriya*) is subsumed under one element, one base, and one aggregate; it is known by nine knowledges, excluding the knowledge of cessation (*nirodha-jñāna*); it is cognized by one consciousness. It comprises all [factors] of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), with the exception of doubt directed toward the untainted (*anāsrava*) objects in the desire realm, as well as the ignorance (*avidyā*) associated therewith; all other latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) of the desire realm increase in association with it.

The faculty of sorrow (*daurmanasyendriya*) is comprised within one element, one base, and one aggregate; it is known by seven knowledges—excluding the knowledge of subsequent realization, the knowledge of cessation, and the knowledge of the path—and is cognized by one consciousness; all latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) of the desire realm increase in association with it.

The faculty of equanimity (*upekṣendriya*) is comprised within one element, one base, and one aggregate; it is known by nine knowledges, excluding the knowledge of cessation (*nirodhajñāna*); it is cognized by one consciousness; and all latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) increase in relation to it.

The faculty of faith (*śraddhendriya*) is comprised within one element, one base, and one aggregate; it is known by nine knowledges, excluding the knowledge of cessation; it is cognized by one consciousness; and the universal latent dispositions of the three realms (*tridhātuka-sarvatraga-anuśaya*) as well as those to be abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya-anuśaya*) increase in relation to it.
The faculties of energy, mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom are likewise.

The faculty of "knowing what is not yet known" (anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīndriya) is comprised within the three realms, two bases, and two aggregates; it is known by seven knowledges—excluding the knowledges of suffering, origin, and cessation—and is cognized by one consciousness. Latent dispositions do not increase therein.
The faculty of one who has already known (*ājñātendriya*) and the faculty of one who has fully known (*ājñātāvīndriya*) are likewise.

The latent tendency of the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi-anuśaya*) bound to the desire realm is comprised within one element, one base, and one aggregate; it is known by seven cognitions—excluding the cognition of subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*), the cognition of cessation (*nirodhajñāna*), and the cognition of the path (*mārgajñāna*)—and is cognized by one consciousness. It is augmented by all [defilements] abandoned through the vision of suffering and by the pervasive latent tendencies abandoned through the vision of the origin in the desire realm.

The same applies to the view of extreme attachment (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*) bound to the desire realm and the other eight latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya*).

Regarding the latent disposition of false view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*) abandoned through the vision of origin (*samudaya-darśana-prahātavya*) bound to the desire realm: it is comprised within one element, one base, and one aggregate; it is known by seven knowledges—excluding the knowledge of subsequent realization (*anvaya-jñāna*), the knowledge of cessation (*nirodha-jñāna*), and the knowledge of the path (*mārga-jñāna*); it is cognized by one consciousness; and all [dispositions] abandoned through the vision of origin and the pervasive (*sarvatraga*) latent dispositions abandoned through the vision of suffering increase in relation to it.

The same applies to the remaining six latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) abandoned through the vision of the origin (*samudaya-darśana-prahātavya*) that are bound to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*).

As for the latent disposition of wrong view (*mithyā-dṛṣṭi-anuśaya*) abandoned through the vision of cessation (*nirodha-darśana-prahātavya*) that is bound to the desire realm, it is subsumed under one element (*dhātu*), one base (*āyatana*), and one aggregate (*skandha*). It is known by seven cognitions (*jñāna*), excluding the cognition of similarity (*anvaya-jñāna*), the cognition of cessation (*nirodha-jñāna*), and the cognition of the path (*mārga-jñāna*). It is cognized by one consciousness (*vijñāna*). The outflow-conditions (*sāsrava-ālambana*) abandoned through the vision of cessation in the desire realm, as well as the ignorance (*avidyā*) associated with wrong view, and the pervasive latent dispositions (*sarvatraga-anuśaya*) increase in relation to it.

The latent tendency of view-attachment (*dṛṣṭi-parāmarśa-anuśaya*) associated with the desire realm and to be abandoned by the vision of cessation is subsumed under one element, one base, and one aggregate; it is known by seven knowledges—excluding the knowledge of subsequent realization, the knowledge of cessation, and the knowledge of the path—and is cognized by one consciousness. It is augmented by the outflow-conditioned objects and the universal latent tendencies to be abandoned by the vision of cessation within the desire realm.
The same applies to the latent tendencies of greed, hatred, and pride associated with the desire realm that are to be abandoned by the vision of cessation.

The latent tendency of doubt associated with the desire realm that is to be abandoned by the vision of cessation is subsumed under one element, one base, and one aggregate; it is known by seven knowledges—excluding the knowledge of subsequent realization, the knowledge of cessation, and the knowledge of the path—and is cognized by one consciousness. It is augmented by the outflow-conditions (sāsrava-ālambana) to be abandoned by the vision of cessation in the desire realm, as well as by the ignorance associated with doubt and the universal latent tendencies.

The latent tendency of ignorance (*avidyā-anuśaya*) bound to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*) and to be abandoned by the vision of cessation (*nirodha-darśana-heya*) is subsumed under one element (*dhātu*), one base (*āyatana*), and one aggregate (*skandha*). It is known by seven knowledges—excluding the knowledge of subsequent realization (*anvaya-jñāna*), the knowledge of cessation (*nirodha-jñāna*), and the knowledge of the path (*mārga-jñāna*)—and is cognized by one consciousness. With the exception of the ignorance associated with the desire realm that is to be abandoned by the vision of cessation and which takes the untainted (*anāsrava*) as its object, all other factors to be abandoned by the vision of cessation in the desire realm, as well as the pervasive latent tendencies (*sarvatraga-anuśaya*), increase in association with it.

The latent tendency of false view (*mithyādṛṣṭi-anuśaya*) to be abandoned by the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) pertaining to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*) is comprised within one element, one base, and one aggregate. It is known by seven knowledges—excluding the knowledge of subsequent realization (*anvayajñāna*), the knowledge of cessation (*nirodhajñāna*), and the knowledge of the path (*mārgajñāna*)—and is cognized by one consciousness. It consists of the outflow-conditioned (*sāsrava-ālambana*) factors to be abandoned by the path of seeing in the desire realm, as well as the ignorance (*avidyā*) associated with false view, along with the pervasive latent tendencies (*sarvatraga-anuśaya*) that increase therein.

The latent tendency of dogmatic attachment to views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa-anuśaya*) belonging to the desire realm and abandoned through the path of seeing (*darśanamārga-prahātavya*) is subsumed under one element (*dhātu*), one base (*āyatana*), and one aggregate (*skandha*). It is known by seven cognitions—excluding the cognition of subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*), the cognition of cessation (*nirodhajñāna*), and the cognition of the path (*mārgajñāna*)—and is cognized by one consciousness. The outflow-tainted objects (*sāsravālambana*) abandoned through the path of seeing in the desire realm, as well as the universal latent tendencies (*sarvatragānuśaya*), increase in association with it.

The same applies to the underlying tendencies of adherence to precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*), greed (*rāga*), hatred (*dveṣa*), and pride (*māna*) that are bound to the desire realm and abandoned through the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*).

The underlying tendency of doubt (*vicikitsā*) that is bound to the desire realm and abandoned through the path of seeing is subsumed under one element (*dhātu*), one base (*āyatana*), and one aggregate (*skandha*). It is known by seven knowledges—excluding the knowledge of subsequent realization (*anvayajñāna*), the knowledge of cessation (*nirodhajñāna*), and the knowledge of the path (*mārgajñāna*)—and is cognized by one consciousness. It consists of the outflow-conditions (*sāsravālambana*) abandoned through the path of seeing in the desire realm, as well as the ignorance (*avidyā*) associated with doubt; furthermore, the universal underlying tendencies (*sarvatragānuśaya*) increase in relation to it.

The latent tendency of ignorance (*avidyā-anuśaya*) bound to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*) and abandoned through the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga-prahātavya*) is comprised within one element (*dhātu*), one base (*āyatana*), and one aggregate (*skandha*). It is known by seven knowledges (*jñāna*), excluding the knowledge of subsequent realization (*anvaya-jñāna*), the knowledge of cessation (*nirodha-jñāna*), and the knowledge of the path (*mārga-jñāna*); it is cognized by one consciousness (*vijñāna*). With the exception of the outflow-free object (*anāsrava-ālambana*) ignorance abandoned through the path of seeing in the desire realm, all other [ignorance] abandoned through the path of seeing in the desire realm, as well as the pervasive latent tendencies (*sarvatraga-anuśaya*), increase in association with it.

The latent tendency of attachment (*rāgānuśaya*) bound to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*) and abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) is subsumed under one element (*dhātu*), one base (*āyatana*), and one aggregate (*skandha*). It is known by seven cognitions—excluding the cognition of subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*), the cognition of cessation (*nirodha-jñāna*), and the cognition of the path (*mārga-jñāna*)—and is cognized by one consciousness. All latent tendencies abandoned through cultivation in the desire realm, as well as the universal (*sarvatraga*) latent tendencies, increase in association with it.
The same applies to the latent tendencies of hatred, pride, and ignorance that are bound to the desire realm and abandoned through cultivation.

The latent tendency of the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) bound to the form realm is comprised of one element, one base, and one aggregate; it is known by seven cognitions—excluding the cognition of cessation, the cognition of the path, and [the three types of] cognition [of the desire realm]—and is cognized by one consciousness. It is augmented by all [defilements] abandoned through the vision of suffering and by the universal latent tendencies abandoned through the vision of origin within the form realm.

The view of extreme attachment (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*) bound to the form realm (*rūpadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*), as well as the other seven latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya*), are likewise [to be understood].

The latent tendency of false view (*mithyādṛṣṭi-anuśaya*) abandoned through the vision of origin (*samudaya-darśana-prahātavya*) bound to the form realm is comprised within one element, one base, and one aggregate; it is known by seven cognitions, excluding the cognition of cessation (*nirodha-jñāna*) and the cognition of the path (*mārga-jñāna*); it is cognized by one consciousness; and all [defilements] abandoned through the vision of origin and the pervasive (*sarvatraga*) latent tendencies abandoned through the vision of suffering increase in relation to it.
The same applies to the remaining five latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) abandoned through the vision of the origin (*samudaya-darśana-prahātavya*) that are bound to the realm of form (*rūpāvacara*).

The latent disposition of wrong view (*mithyādṛṣṭi-anuśaya*) abandoned through the vision of cessation (*nirodha-darśana-prahātavya*) that is bound to the realm of form is subsumed under one element (*dhātu*), one base (*āyatana*), and one aggregate (*skandha*). It is known by seven knowledges (*jñāna*), excluding the knowledge of cessation (*nirodha-jñāna*) and the knowledge of the path (*mārga-jñāna*). It is cognized by one consciousness (*vijñāna*). It consists of the outflow-conditioned (*sāsrava*) objects abandoned through the vision of cessation in the realm of form, as well as the ignorance (*avidyā*) associated with wrong view, along with the pervasive latent dispositions (*sarvatraga-anuśaya*) that increase therein.

The latent tendency of views (dṛṣṭi-anuśaya) consisting of dogmatic clinging (parāmarśa) to be abandoned through the vision of the cessation [of suffering] and bound to the form realm (rūpadhātu-pratisaṃyukta) is comprised within one element, one base, and one aggregate; it is known by seven cognitions—excluding the cognition of cessation, the cognition of the path, and the conventional cognition—and is cognized by one consciousness. It is augmented by the outflow-conditions (sāsrava-ālambana) and the universal latent tendencies (sarvatraga-anuśaya) to be abandoned through the vision of cessation within the form realm.
The latent tendencies of greed and pride associated with the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) and to be abandoned by the vision of cessation (*nirodhadarśana-prahātavya*) are likewise.

The latent tendency of doubt (*vicikitsā-anuśaya*) associated with the form realm and to be abandoned by the vision of cessation is subsumed under one element, one base, and one aggregate; it is known by seven knowledges—excluding the knowledge of cessation (*nirodhajñāna*) and the knowledge of the path (*mārgajñāna*)—and is cognized by one consciousness. It is the object of outflow (*sāsrava*) conditions to be abandoned by the vision of cessation in the form realm, as well as the ignorance (*avidyā*) associated with doubt, and the pervasive latent tendencies (*sarvatraga-anuśaya*) increase therein.

The latent tendency of ignorance (*avidyā-anuśaya*) associated with the form realm (*rūpadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*) and to be abandoned by the vision of cessation (*nirodha-darśana-heya*) is comprised within one element (*dhātu*), one base (*āyatana*), and one aggregate (*skandha*). It is known by seven cognitions—excluding the cognition of cessation (*nirodha-jñāna*) and the cognition of the path (*mārga-jñāna*)—and is cognized by one consciousness. With the exception of the outflow-free object (*anāsrava-ālambana*) ignorance to be abandoned by the vision of cessation in the form realm, all other [ignorance] to be abandoned by the vision of cessation in the form realm, as well as the universal latent tendencies (*sarvatraga-anuśaya*), increase in association with it.

The latent tendency of wrong view (*mithyādṛṣṭi-anuśaya*) to be abandoned by the path of seeing (*darśanamārga-prahātavya*) pertaining to the realm of form (*rūpadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*) is subsumed under one element (*dhātu*), one base (*āyatana*), and one aggregate (*skandha*). It is known by seven cognitions—excluding the cognition of cessation (*nirodhajñāna*) and the cognition of the path (*mārgajñāna*)—and is cognized by one consciousness. It consists of the outflow-conditioned (*sāsrava-ālambana*) objects to be abandoned by the path of seeing in the realm of form, as well as the ignorance (*avidyā*) associated with wrong view, along with the increase of the universal latent tendencies (*sarvatraga-anuśaya*).

The latent tendency of views (dṛṣṭi-parāmarśa-anuśaya) associated with the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) and abandoned through the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) is comprised within one element, one base, and one aggregate; it is known by seven knowledges—excluding the knowledge of cessation (*nirodhajñāna*) and the knowledge of the path (*mārgajñāna*)—and is cognized by one consciousness. It is augmented by the outflow-bound (*sāsrava-ālambana*) and universal (*sarvatraga*) latent tendencies abandoned through the path of seeing in the form realm.

The same applies to the latent tendencies of adherence to precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*), greed (*rāga*), and pride (*māna*) bound to the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) and abandoned through the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*).

The latent tendency of doubt (*vicikitsā*) bound to the form realm and abandoned through the path of seeing is subsumed under one element (*dhātu*), one base (*āyatana*), and one aggregate (*skandha*). It is known by seven cognitions—excluding the cognition of cessation (*nirodhajñāna*) and the cognition of the path (*mārgajñāna*)—and is cognized by one consciousness. It consists of that which is associated with outflows (*sāsrava*) and serves as an object for the path of seeing in the form realm, as well as the ignorance (*avidyā*) associated with doubt, along with the pervasive latent tendencies (*sarvatragānuśaya*) that increase therein.

The latent tendency of ignorance (*avidyā-anuśaya*) belonging to the form realm (*rūpadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*) and abandoned through the path of seeing (*darśanamārga-prahātavya*) is comprised within one element, one base, and one aggregate; it is known by seven cognitions—excluding the cognition of cessation (*nirodhajñāna*) and the cognition of the path (*mārgajñāna*)—and is cognized by one consciousness. With the exception of the ignorance associated with the form realm that takes the outflow-free (*anāsrava*) as its object, all other instances of ignorance abandoned through the path of seeing in the form realm, as well as the pervasive latent tendencies (*sarvatraga-anuśaya*), increase in association with it.

The latent tendency of attachment (*rāgānuśaya*) bound to the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) and abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) is comprised within one element (*dhātu*), one base (*āyatana*), and one aggregate (*skandha*). It is known by seven knowledges (*jñāna*), excluding the knowledge of cessation (*nirodhajñāna*) and the knowledge of the path (*mārgajñāna*), and is cognized by one consciousness (*vijñāna*). All latent tendencies abandoned through cultivation in the form realm, as well as the universal (*sarvatraga*) latent tendencies, increase (*anuśerate*) in relation to it.
The same applies to the latent tendencies of pride and ignorance that are bound to the form realm and abandoned through cultivation.
Just as there are thirty-one latent tendencies bound to the form realm, it should be understood that there are likewise thirty-one latent tendencies bound to the formless realm.
Regarding the distinctions: six knowledges are excluded from the knowledge of others' minds and the knowledges of cessation and the path.
The training rules, purity, fruits, practices, and noble lineages; The right abandonments, bases of power, foundations of mindfulness, and truths;
The meditative absorptions, immeasurables, and formless attainments; The factors of enlightenment, faculties, bases, aggregates, elements, and discourses.
The training rules refer to the five precepts of a lay follower (*upāsaka*).
Purity refers to the four kinds of verified confidence (*avetyaprasāda*).
The fruits refer to the four fruits of the ascetic life (*śrāmaṇyaphala*).
The "practices" refer to the four paths of practice (*pratipad*).
The "noble lineages" refer to the four noble lineages (*āryavaṃśa*).
The "right abandonments" refer to the four right abandonments (*samyakprahāṇa*).
The bases of supernormal power refer to the four bases of supernormal power.
The foundations of mindfulness refer to the four foundations of mindfulness.
The truths refer to the four noble truths.
Dhyāna refers to the four dhyānas.
The Immeasurables refer to the four immeasurables.
The Formless refers to the four formless attainments.
Concentration refers to the four types of cultivated concentration.
Factors of enlightenment refer to the seven factors of awakening.
Faculties refer to the twenty-two faculties.
"Āyatana" refers to the twelve āyatanas.
"Skandha" refers to the five skandhas.
"Dhātu" refers to the eighteen dhātus.
Regarding the "Sūtras," this refers to the nine preceding and nine following verses within the stanzas, each group being taken as one, totaling twenty sūtras.
Based on each individual sūtra, there are the first fifty questions.
Furthermore, based on the Sūtra on the Five Training Precepts of a Lay Follower (*Upāsaka-śikṣāpada-sūtra*), there are fifty questions.

That is to say: among the five training precepts, how many are with form (*rūpin*) and how many are without form; how many are visible (*sanidarśana*) and how many are invisible; how many are resistant (*sapratigha*) and how many are non-resistant; how many are with outflows (*sāsrava*) and how many are without outflows; how many are conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) and how many are unconditioned; how many have maturation (*savipāka*) and how many are without maturation; how many are produced by conditions, produced by causes, and included within the world (*loka-saṃgṛhīta*), and how many are not produced by conditions, not produced by causes, and not included within the world; how many are included within form and how many are included within name (*nāman*); how many are included within the internal bases (*ādhyātmika-āyatana*) and how many are included within the external bases; and how many are to be fully known through knowledge (*jñāna-parijñeya*) and how many are not to be fully known through knowledge.

How many are to be fully known through the thorough knowledge of abandonment, and how many are not to be fully known through the thorough knowledge of abandonment? How many should be abandoned, and how many should not be abandoned? How many should be cultivated, and how many should not be cultivated? How many are defiled, and how many are undefiled? How many are fruits but not possessors of fruit, and how many are possessors of fruit but not fruits? How many are both fruits and possessors of fruit, and how many are neither fruits nor possessors of fruit? How many are appropriated, and how many are unappropriated? How many are derived from the primary elements, and how many are not derived from the primary elements? How many are surpassable, and how many are unsurpassable? How many are conditioned, and how many are unconditioned? How many are associated with causes, and how many are dissociated from causes?
There are six bases that subsume what is wholesome (*kuśalāyatana*), namely, the five wholesome aggregates (*skandha*) and analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyānirodha*).
Do these six wholesome bases subsume the five precepts (*śikṣāpada*), or do the five precepts subsume the six wholesome bases?
There are five unwholesome bases, namely the five unwholesome aggregates (*pañcākuśalaskandha*).
Do the five precepts (*pañcaśikṣāpada*) subsume the five unwholesome bases, or do the five unwholesome bases subsume the five precepts?
There are seven bases of the indeterminate (avyākṛta), namely: the five indeterminate aggregates, space, and non-analytical cessation (apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha).
Do these seven bases of the indeterminate subsume the five bases of training (śikṣāpada), or do the five bases of training subsume the seven bases of the indeterminate?

There are three bases for the outflows (*āsrava-sthāna*), namely: the outflow of sensual desire (*kāma-āsrava*), the outflow of existence (*bhava-āsrava*), and the outflow of ignorance (*avidyā-āsrava*).
Do these three bases for the outflows subsume the five precepts (*śikṣāpada*), or do the five precepts subsume the three bases for the outflows?
There are five bases that subsume the tainted (*sāsrava*) states, namely, the five tainted aggregates (*skandha*).
Do the five bases for the tainted subsume the five precepts (*śikṣāpada*), or do the five precepts subsume the five bases for the tainted?
There are eight untainted bases (*anāsrava-sthāna*), namely the five untainted aggregates (*skandha*) and the three unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*).
Do these eight untainted bases subsume the five bases of training (*śikṣāpada*), or do the five bases of training subsume the eight untainted bases?
Regarding these five precepts: how many are past, how many are future, how many are present, and how many are neither past, nor future, nor present?
How many are wholesome, how many are unwholesome, and how many are indeterminate?
How many are bound to the desire realm, how many are bound to the form realm, how many are bound to the formless realm, and how many are unbound?
How many are in training, how many are beyond training, and how many are neither in training nor beyond training?
How many are abandoned by vision, how many are abandoned by cultivation, and how many are not to be abandoned?
How many are neither mind, nor mental factors, nor associated with mind; how many are mental factors associated with mind; and how many are exclusively mind?

How many are concomitant with the mind but not associated with feeling? How many are associated with feeling but not concomitant with the mind? How many are both concomitant with the mind and associated with feeling? How many are neither concomitant with the mind nor associated with feeling?

How many are concomitant with the mind but are not associated with perception and formations? How many are associated with perception and formations but are not concomitant with the mind? How many are both concomitant with the mind and associated with perception and formations? How many are neither concomitant with the mind nor associated with perception and formations?

How many follow the movement of vitarka (applied thought) but are not associated with vicāra (sustained thought)? How many are associated with vicāra but do not follow the movement of vitarka? How many both follow the movement of vitarka and are associated with vicāra? How many neither follow the movement of vitarka nor are associated with vicāra?
How many views are not the locus of views? How many are the locus of views but are not views? How many are both views and the locus of views? How many are neither views nor the locus of views?

How many have the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) as their cause but do not have the view of a self-identity as their cause? How many have the view of a self-identity as their cause but do not have the view of a self-identity as their cause? How many have the view of a self-identity as their cause and also have the view of a self-identity as their cause? How many do not have the view of a self-identity as their cause and do not have the view of a self-identity as their cause?

How many karmas are not karmic maturation (*vipāka*), how many are karmic maturation but not karma, how many are both karma and karmic maturation, and how many are neither karma nor karmic maturation? How many karmas do not follow along with karma (*anuvartaka*), how many follow along with karma but are not karma, how many are both karma and follow along with karma, and how many are neither karma nor follow along with karma?
How many derived forms are not visible forms? How many visible forms are not derived forms? How many are both derived forms and visible forms? How many are neither derived forms nor visible forms?

How many derived forms are not resistant forms? How many resistant forms are not derived forms? How many are both derived forms and resistant forms? How many are neither derived forms nor resistant forms?
How many are profound because they are difficult to see? How many are difficult to see because they are profound? How many are wholesome but do not have wholesomeness as their cause?

How many have wholesomeness as their cause but are not wholesome? How many are both wholesome and have wholesomeness as their cause? How many are neither wholesome nor have wholesomeness as their cause? How many are unwholesome but do not have unwholesomeness as their cause? How many have unwholesomeness as their cause but are not unwholesome? How many are both unwholesome and have unwholesomeness as their cause? How many are neither unwholesome nor have unwholesomeness as their cause?

How many are indeterminate but do not have indeterminacy as their cause? How many have indeterminacy as their cause but are not themselves indeterminate? How many are both indeterminate and have indeterminacy as their cause? How many are neither indeterminate nor have indeterminacy as their cause?

How many *hetu-pratyayas* (causal conditions) are not *sahetu* (having a cause)? How many *sahetu* are not *hetu-pratyaya*? How many are both *hetu-pratyaya* and *sahetu*? How many are neither *hetu-pratyaya* nor *sahetu*?

How many *samanantara* (immediately preceding) are not *samanantara-pratyaya* (condition as immediate antecedent)? How many *samanantara-pratyaya* are not *samanantara*? How many are both *samanantara* and *samanantara-pratyaya*? How many are neither *samanantara* nor *samanantara-pratyaya*?

How many are object-conditions (ālambana-pratyaya) but not having an object (anālambaka)? How many have an object but are not object-conditions? How many are both object-conditions and have an object? How many are neither object-conditions nor have an object?

How many are adhipati-conditions but do not possess adhipati-power? How many possess adhipati-power but are not adhipati-conditions? How many are both adhipati-conditions and possess adhipati-power? How many are neither adhipati-conditions nor possess adhipati-power?

How many are floods that are not favorable to the floods? How many are favorable to the floods but are not floods? How many are both floods and favorable to the floods? How many are neither floods nor favorable to the floods?
Just as there are fifty questions based on the training rules (*śikṣāpada*), so too are there questions based on the remaining nineteen.
As for the five training rules: first, to abstain from taking life for as long as one lives;
second, to abstain from taking what is not given for as long as one lives.
3. For as long as life lasts, abstain from sexual misconduct;
4. For as long as life lasts, abstain from false speech;
5. For as long as life lasts, abstain from drinking various intoxicants.
These five are called the training precepts (*śikṣāpada*) of the lay follower (*upāsaka*).
Regarding these five training precepts, as to how many possess form (*rūpin*): all of them possess form.

As to how many are visible (*sanidarśana*): one is invisible; four should be analyzed—namely, if they are informative (*vijñapti*), they are visible; if they are non-informative (*avijñapti*), they are invisible.

Regarding how many are with resistance (*sapratigha*) and so forth: all should be analyzed. That is to say, if it is manifest action (*vijñapti*), it is with resistance; if it is non-manifest action (*avijñapti*), it is without resistance.
Regarding how many are with outflows (*sāsrava*) and so forth: all are with outflows.
Regarding how many are conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) and so forth: all are conditioned.
Regarding how many have maturation (*vipāka*) and so forth: all have maturation.
Regarding how many are dependently originated (*pratītyasamutpanna*) and so forth: all are dependently originated, produced by causes, and included within the world (*loka*).
Regarding how many are subsumed under form (*rūpa*): all are subsumed under form.
Regarding how many are subsumed under internal bases (*ādhyātmikāyatana*): all are subsumed under external bases (*bāhyāyatana*).
Regarding how many are to be fully known through the thorough knowledge of wisdom (*jñānaparijñāparijñeya*): all are to be fully known through the thorough knowledge of wisdom.
Regarding these five training rules, as for how many are to be fully known through abandonment (*prahāṇa-parijñā*) and so forth: all are to be fully known through abandonment.
As for how many are to be abandoned and so forth: all are to be abandoned.
Regarding how many are to be cultivated (*bhāvanīya*) and so forth: all are to be cultivated.
Regarding how many are defiled (*kliṣṭa*) and so forth: none are defiled.
Regarding how many are results (*phala*) but not possessing results (*saphala*) and so forth: all are both results and possess results.
Regarding how many are appropriated (*upātta*) and so forth: all are unappropriated.
Regarding how many are derived from the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) and so forth: all are derived from the primary elements.
Regarding how many have something superior (*sottara*) and so forth: all have something superior.
Regarding the question "How many are existent (*sat*) and so forth?", all are existent.
Regarding the question "How many are associated with causes (*hetu-saṃprayukta*) and so forth?", all are not associated with causes.

As for the inclusion of these five training rules (*śikṣāpada*) within the six wholesome bases (*kuśala-sthāna*): one wholesome base partially includes the five training rules, and the five training rules also include a portion of one wholesome base.
Regarding their inclusion within the five unwholesome bases (*akuśalasthāna*), they do not mutually include one another.
Regarding their inclusion within the seven indeterminate bases (*avyākṛtasthāna*), they do not mutually include one another.
Regarding their inclusion within the three taints (*āsravasthāna*), they do not mutually include one another.

Regarding the inclusion within the five bases of outflows (*āsravasthāna*): one part of a single base of outflows includes the five precepts of training (*śikṣāpada*), and the five precepts of training likewise include one part of a single base of outflows.
Regarding their mutual inclusion with the eight untainted bases (*anāsrava-āyatana*), they do not include one another.
As for how many are past and so forth, all are either past, future, or present.
Regarding how many are wholesome and so forth: all are wholesome.
Regarding how many are bound to the desire realm and so forth: all are bound to the desire realm.
Regarding how many are of the stage of training and so forth: all are neither of the stage of training nor of the stage beyond training.
Regarding these five precepts (*śikṣāpada*), how many are abandoned by vision (*darśana-prahātavya*) and so forth? All are abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-prahātavya*).
How many are not mind (*citta*) and so forth? All are neither mind, nor mental factors (*caitta*), nor associated with mind (*cittasaṃprayukta*).
Regarding how many are concomitant with the mind (*cittānuvartin*) but not associated with feeling (*vedanā-saṃprayukta*), etc.: all are neither concomitant with the mind nor associated with feeling.

Regarding how many are concomitant with the mind but not associated with perception (*saṃjñā*) or mental formations (*saṃskāra*), etc.: all are neither concomitant with the mind nor associated with perception or mental formations.

Regarding how many follow the movement of vitarka (applied thought) but are not associated with vicāra (sustained thought), etc.: none follow the movement of vitarka and none are associated with vicāra.
Regarding how many are views but are not the locus of views, etc.: all are the locus of views but are not views themselves.

Regarding how many have the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) as their cause but are not themselves causes of the view of a self-identity: all [of these] do not have the view of a self-identity as their cause, nor are they causes of the view of a self-identity.
Regarding how many are karma but not the maturation of karma: all are karma, but not the maturation of karma.
Regarding the question of how many types of karma do not follow along with karma (*karmānuvartin*), all [of them] are karma but do not follow along with karma.

Regarding the question of how many types of derived matter (*upādāya-rūpa*) are not visible matter (*sanidarśana-rūpa*), one is derived matter but not visible matter; four should be analyzed: that is to say, if it is informative action (*vijñapti*), it is both derived matter and visible matter; if it is non-informative action (*avijñapti*), it is derived matter but not visible matter.

Regarding these five precepts, as to how many are derived matter (*upādāya-rūpa*) but not resistant matter (*sapratigha-rūpa*), all should be analyzed as follows: if they are informative (*vijñapti*), they are both derived matter and resistant matter; if they are non-informative (*avijñapti*), they are derived matter but not resistant matter.
Regarding the statement "How many are profound because they are difficult to see," etc.: all are profound because they are difficult to see, and they are difficult to see because they are profound.
Regarding the statement "How many are wholesome and have the wholesome as their cause," etc.: all are wholesome and have the wholesome as their cause.
Regarding the question of how many unwholesome states are not caused by the unwholesome and so forth: all [such states] are neither unwholesome nor caused by the unwholesome.
Regarding the question of how many indeterminate states are not caused by the indeterminate and so forth: all [such states] are neither indeterminate nor caused by the indeterminate.
Regarding how many are object-conditions (*ālambana-pratyaya*) but not causes (*hetu*), etc.: all are object-conditions and also causes.

Regarding how many are equal-and-immediate conditions (*samanantara-pratyaya*) but not equal-and-immediate conditions, etc.: all are neither equal-and-immediate conditions nor equal-and-immediate conditions.
Regarding how many object-conditions (ālambana-pratyaya) are not possessed of an object (sālambana): all are object-conditions but are not possessed of an object.
Regarding how many predominant conditions (adhipati-pratyaya) are not possessed of predominance (ādhipatya): all are predominant conditions and also possess predominance.
Regarding the question of how many floods (*ogha*) are not favorable to the floods and so forth: all [factors] favorable to the floods are not themselves floods.

The four kinds of verified confidence (*avetyaprasāda*) are: verified confidence in the Buddha, verified confidence in the Dharma, verified confidence in the Saṃgha, and verified confidence in the precepts beloved by the noble ones (*āryakānta-śīla*).
Regarding these four forms of verified confidence (*avetyaprasāda*), how many possess form (*rūpin*) and so forth? One possesses form; three are formless (*arūpin*).
How many are visible (*sanidarśana*) and so forth? All are invisible (*anidarśana*).
Regarding how many are with resistance (*sapratigha*) and so forth: all are without resistance (*apratigha*).
Regarding how many are with outflows (*sāsrava*) and so forth: all are without outflows (*anāsrava*).
Regarding how many are conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) and so forth: all are conditioned.
Regarding how many have maturation (*vipāka*) and so forth: none have maturation.
Regarding how many are dependently originated (*pratītyasamutpanna*) and so forth: all are dependently originated, produced by causes, and included within the world (*loka*).
Regarding how many are included within form (*rūpa*) and so forth: one is included within form, and three are included within name (*nāman*).
Regarding how many are included within internal bases (*ādhyātmikāyatana*) and so forth: all are included within external bases (*bāhyāyatana*).
Regarding how many are to be fully known through the thorough knowledge of wisdom (*jñānaparijñāparijñeya*) and so forth: all are to be fully known through the thorough knowledge of wisdom.

Regarding these four forms of verified confidence (*avetyaprasāda*), as for how many are to be fully known through the thorough knowledge of abandonment (*prahāṇa-parijñā*) and so forth: none of them are to be fully known through the thorough knowledge of abandonment.
As for how many are to be abandoned and so forth: none of them are to be abandoned.
Regarding how many are to be cultivated (*bhāvanīya*) and so forth: all are to be cultivated.
Regarding how many are afflicted (*kliṣṭa*) and so forth: none are afflicted.
Regarding how many are results (*phala*) but not possessors of results (*saphala*) and so forth: all are both results and possessors of results.
Regarding how many are appropriated (*upātta*) and so forth: all are unappropriated.
Regarding how many are derived from the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) and so forth: one is derived from the primary elements, and three are not derived from the primary elements.
Regarding how many are "with superior" (*sottara*): all are with superior.
Regarding how many are "existent" (*sat*): none are existent.
Regarding how many are "associated with causes" (*hetu-saṃprayukta*): one is not associated with causes; three are associated with causes.

Regarding the inclusion of these four forms of verified confidence (avetyaprasāda) within the six bases of wholesomeness (ṣad-kuśala-sthāna): two of the bases of wholesomeness partially include the four forms of verified confidence, and the four forms of verified confidence also partially include two of the bases of wholesomeness.
Regarding their inclusion within the five unwholesome bases (*akuśalasthāna*), they do not mutually include one another.
Regarding their inclusion within the seven indeterminate bases (*avyākṛtasthāna*), they do not mutually include one another.
Regarding their inclusion within the three outflows bases (*āsravasthāna*), they do not mutually include one another.
Regarding their inclusion within the five contaminated bases (*sāsrava-āyatana*), they do not include one another.

Regarding their inclusion within the eight uncontaminated bases (*anāsrava-āyatana*), one entire uncontaminated base and a portion of another uncontaminated base include the four types of verified confidence (*avetyaprasāda*); likewise, the four types of verified confidence include one entire uncontaminated base and a portion of another uncontaminated base.
Regarding how many are past and so forth: all are either past, future, or present.
Regarding how many are wholesome and so forth: all are wholesome.
Regarding how many are bound to the desire realm and so forth: all are unbound.

Regarding how many are "in training" (*śaikṣa*) and so forth, all should be analyzed as follows: the clarity of conviction regarding the Buddha (*buddha-prasāda*) is either in training or beyond training (*aśaikṣa*).
What is in training?
It refers to the clarity of conviction regarding the Buddha associated with the attention (*manasikāra*) of one in training.
What is that which pertains to those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*)?
It refers to the verified confidence in the Buddha associated with the mental attention of one beyond training.
The same applies to the verified confidence in the Dharma and the Sangha.
The verified clarity regarding the precepts beloved by the Noble Ones is either of the trainee (śaikṣa) or of the one beyond training (aśaikṣa).
What is that of the trainee?
It refers to the bodily and vocal actions of the trainee.
What is that which is beyond training (*aśaikṣa*)?
It refers to the bodily and vocal actions of one beyond training.
Regarding how many of these four types of verified clarity (*avetyaprasāda*) are abandoned by vision (*darśana-prahātavya*) and so forth: none of them are to be abandoned.
Regarding "how many are not mind, etc.": one is neither mind nor mental factors nor associated with mind; three are mental factors associated with mind.
Regarding "how many follow the mind and are not associated with feeling, etc.": one follows the mind but is not associated with feeling; three follow the mind and are also associated with feeling.

Regarding how many follow the mind (*cittānuvartin*), are not associated with perception (*saṃjñā*), and are associated with formations (*saṃskāra*): one follows the mind and is not associated with perception; three follow the mind and are also associated with perception.
One [type] evolves with the mind but is not associated with volition; three evolve with the mind and are also associated with volition, excluding their own nature.

Regarding how many evolve with vitarka but are not associated with vicāra, and so forth—all should be analyzed as follows: the "verified clarity regarding the Buddha" may be with both vitarka and vicāra, or without vitarka and with vicāra only, or without both vitarka and vicāra.
What is that which is accompanied by both vitarka (applied thought) and vicāra (sustained thought)?
It refers to the clarity of faith in the Buddha associated with mental attention accompanied by both vitarka and vicāra.
What is that which is without vitarka and possesses only vicāra?
This refers to the verified confidence in the Buddha associated with attention that is without vitarka and with only vicāra.
What is meant by "without vitarka and without vicāra"?
It refers to the verified confidence in the Buddha associated with attention that is without vitarka and without vicāra.
The same applies to the verified clarity regarding the Dharma and the Saṅgha.

Regarding the verified clarity of the precepts cherished by the noble ones, it either follows vitarka and is not associated with vicāra, or it does not follow vitarka and is not associated with vicāra.
What is that which follows the movement of vitarka (applied thought) but is not associated with vicāra (sustained thought)?
It refers to untainted bodily and vocal actions that follow the movement of vitarka.
What is that which neither follows the movement of vitarka nor is associated with vicāra?
This refers to untainted bodily and vocal actions that do not proceed in accordance with discursive thought (*vitarka*).
Regarding the question of how many are "not views" and "not bases for views," all are neither views nor bases for views.

Regarding the question of how many have the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) as their cause but are not themselves causes of the view of a self-identity, all do not have the view of a self-identity as their cause and are not causes of the view of a self-identity.
Regarding how many karmas are not karmic maturation (*vipāka*), etc.: one is karma but not karmic maturation; three are neither karma nor karmic maturation.
Regarding how many karmas do not follow along with karma (*anuvartaka*), etc.: one is both karma and follows along with karma; three follow along with karma but are not karma.

Regarding the question of how many derived forms (*upādāya-rūpa*) are not visible forms (*sanidarśana-rūpa*), one is a derived form that is not a visible form, and three are neither derived forms nor visible forms.
*Abhidharma-prakaraṇapāda-śāstra*, Fascicle Ten.
*Abhidharma-prakaraṇapāda-śāstra*, Fascicle Eleven.
Composed by the Venerable Vasumitra.
