Chapter Seven, Part Two: Discerning the Thousand Questions. Regarding these four kinds of verified purity (*avetyaprasāda*): how many are derived matter (*upādāyarūpa*) and non-obstructive matter (*apratigha-rūpa*), and so forth? One is derived matter and non-obstructive matter; three are neither derived matter nor obstructive matter.
Regarding the phrase "difficult to see, therefore profound," etc.: because all [phenomena] are difficult to see, they are profound; because they are profound, they are difficult to see.
Regarding the question "how many are wholesome and have the wholesome as their cause," etc.: all are wholesome and also have the wholesome as their cause.
Regarding the question of how many unwholesome factors are not caused by the unwholesome and so forth: all [factors] are neither unwholesome nor caused by the unwholesome.
Regarding the question of how many indeterminate factors are not caused by the indeterminate and so forth: all [factors] are neither indeterminate nor caused by the indeterminate.
Regarding how many are causes and how many are not causes with a cause, etc.: all are causal conditions (*hetu-pratyaya*) and also possess a cause.

Regarding how many are equal-and-immediate [conditions] and how many are not equal-and-immediate conditions, etc.: one is neither an equal-and-immediate condition nor an equal-and-immediate condition; three should be analyzed as follows: namely, the verified confidence in the Buddha may be an equal-and-immediate condition but not an equal-and-immediate condition, or it may be both an equal-and-immediate condition and an equal-and-immediate condition, or it may be neither an equal-and-immediate condition nor an equal-and-immediate condition.
What is that which is an immediate antecedent but not an immediately preceding condition?
It refers to the future, present-arising, and currently manifesting *buddha-prasāda* (clarity of faith in the Buddha).
What is that which is both an immediate antecedent and an immediately preceding condition?
This refers to the verified clarity regarding the Buddhas of the past and present.
What is that which is neither an equal-and-immediate [condition] nor an equal-and-immediate object-condition?
It refers to all other future verified clarities regarding the Buddhas, excluding those future verified clarities regarding the Buddhas that are currently arising and manifesting.
The same applies to the verified clarity regarding the Dharma and the Sangha.

As for how many are object-conditions (*ālambana-pratyaya*) but do not possess an object (*sālambana*), one is an object-condition but does not possess an object, while three are both object-conditions and possess objects.
Regarding the question of how many are dominant conditions (*adhipati-pratyaya*) but not possessing dominance (*ādhipatya*), all are dominant conditions and also possess dominance.
Regarding the question of how many are floods (*ogha*) but not favorable to the floods (*anugata-ogha*), none are floods and none are favorable to the floods.
The four fruits of śrāmaṇya are: the fruit of stream-entry, the fruit of once-returning, the fruit of non-returning, and the fruit of arhatship.

Regarding how many of these four fruits of śrāmaṇya possess form (*rūpa*) and so forth, all must be analyzed as follows: those comprised within the fruits of śrāmaṇya that consist of bodily and vocal actions possess form; the remainder are all without form (*arūpa*).
Regarding how many are "with visibility" (*sanidarśana*) and so forth: all are "without visibility.
Regarding how many are "with resistance" (*sapratigha*) and so forth: all are "without resistance.
Regarding how many are "with outflows" (*sāsrava*) and so forth: all are "without outflows" (*anāsrava*).
Regarding how many are conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) and so forth, all should be analyzed as follows: the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpatti-phala*) is either conditioned or unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
What is conditioned?
It refers to the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) subsumed under the fruit of stream-entry.
What is the unconditioned?
It refers to the analytical cessation (pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha) included within the fruit of stream-entry.
The same applies to the fruits of once-returning, non-returning, and arhatship.
Regarding how many have maturation (*vipāka*) and so forth: none have maturation. Regarding how many are dependently originated (*pratītyasamutpanna*) and so forth:

all should be analyzed as follows. Conditioned fruits of asceticism (*saṃskṛta-śrāmaṇyaphala*) are dependently originated, produced by causes, and included within the world (*loka*). If they are unconditioned fruits of asceticism (*asaṃskṛta-śrāmaṇyaphala*), they are not dependently originated, not produced by causes, and not included within the world.

Regarding how many [categories of] form they are subsumed under, all should be analyzed as follows: those bodily and vocal actions subsumed within the fruits of śramaṇaship are subsumed under form; all others are subsumed under name (nāman).

Regarding the inclusion within the sense bases (*āyatana*), all such cases should be analyzed as follows: that which is included within the fruits of asceticism (*śrāmaṇyaphala*)—namely, the mind, mental consciousness, and their associated states—is included within the internal sense bases; all others are included within the external sense bases.
Regarding the question of how many are fully known by the thorough knowledge of wisdom (*jñāna-parijñā*): all of them are fully known by the thorough knowledge of wisdom.

Regarding the question of how many of these four fruits of the ascetic life (*śrāmaṇyaphala*) are fully known by the thorough knowledge of abandonment (*prahāṇa-parijñā*): none of them are fully known by the thorough knowledge of abandonment.
Regarding the question "How many should be abandoned? and so forth: none should be abandoned.

Regarding the question "How many should be cultivated? and so forth: all should be analyzed; that is to say, the conditioned fruits of śrāmaṇya should be cultivated, whereas the unconditioned fruits of śrāmaṇya should not be cultivated.
Regarding how many are defiled and so forth: all are undefiled.

Regarding how many are results but do not have results and so forth: all should be analyzed. That is to say, conditioned fruits of śrāmaṇya are both results and possess results; if they are unconditioned fruits of śrāmaṇya, they are results but do not possess results.
Regarding how many are appropriated (*upātta*) and so forth: all are unappropriated.

Regarding how many are derived from the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) and so forth: all should be analyzed. That is to say, the bodily and vocal actions subsumed under the fruits of asceticism (*śrāmaṇyaphala*) are derived from the primary elements; the rest are not derived from the primary elements.

Regarding the question "How many are with superior [attainments]? all should be analyzed as follows: conditioned fruits of śrāmaṇya are with superior, while unconditioned fruits of śrāmaṇya are unsurpassed.
Regarding the question "How many are non-existent, etc.?", all are non-existent.

Regarding the question "How many are associated with causes, etc.?", all should be analyzed as follows: the bodily and vocal actions, the formations dissociated from mind (*citta-viprayukta-saṃskāra*), and the cessation through deliberation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) that are included within the fruits of asceticism (*śrāmaṇya-phala*) are not associated with causes; all others are associated with causes.

Regarding the inclusion of these four fruits of śrāmaṇya within the six wholesome bases: a portion of the six wholesome bases includes the four fruits of śrāmaṇya, and the four fruits of śrāmaṇya also include a portion of the six wholesome bases.
Regarding their inclusion within the five unwholesome bases, they do not mutually include one another.
Regarding their inclusion within the seven indeterminate bases, they do not mutually include one another.
Regarding their inclusion within the three outflows bases, they do not mutually include one another.
Regarding their inclusion within the five contaminated bases (*āsravasthāna*), they do not mutually include one another.

Regarding their inclusion within the eight untainted bases (*anāsravasthāna*), the six untainted bases partially include the four fruits of śramaṇaship, and the four fruits of śramaṇaship also partially include the six untainted bases.

Regarding how many are past and so forth, all should be analyzed as follows: the conditioned fruits of śrāmaṇya are either past, future, or present; whereas the unconditioned fruit of śrāmaṇya is neither past, nor future, nor present.
Regarding how many are wholesome and so forth: all are wholesome.
Regarding how many are bound to the desire realm and so forth: all are unbound.

Regarding how many are of the path of training (*śaikṣa*) and so forth: all should be analyzed; that is to say, the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpatti-phala*) is either of the path of training, or neither of the path of training nor of the path beyond training (*aśaikṣa*).
What is the state of training (*śaikṣa*)?
It refers to the conditioned fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpatti-phala*).
What is that which is neither training nor beyond training (*naivaśaikṣanāśaikṣa*)?
That is to say, the fruit of stream-entry is unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
The same applies to the fruits of once-returning and non-returning.
The fruit of arhatship is either beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) or neither-in-training-nor-beyond-training (*naivaśaikṣanāśaikṣa*).
What is "beyond training" (*aśaikṣa*)?
It refers to the conditioned fruit of arhatship.
What is "neither training nor beyond training" (*naivaśaikṣanāśaikṣa*)?
This refers to the unconditioned fruit of arhatship.
Regarding these four fruits of śrāmaṇya, how many are abandoned by vision (*darśana-prahātavya*) and so forth? All are not to be abandoned (*aprahātavya*).

How many are not mind (*acitta*) and so forth? All should be analyzed as follows: the bodily and vocal actions, the formations dissociated from mind (*cittaviprayukta-saṃskāra*), and cessation through deliberation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) included within the fruits of śrāmaṇya are neither mind, nor mental factors (*caitta*), nor associated with mind (*cittasaṃprayukta*).
If it refers to the aggregate of feeling, the aggregate of perception, and the associated aggregate of formations, these are mental factors that are associated with the mind;
if it refers to mind, thought, and consciousness, these are exclusively mind itself.

Regarding how many [factors] follow the mind in their transformation but are not associated with feeling, and so forth—all such cases should be analyzed. Specifically, for the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpatti-phala*), there are four permutations (*catuṣkoṭi*).

Some are concomitant with the mind but not associated with feeling, namely: the bodily and vocal actions subsumed under the fruit of stream-entry, as well as the formations dissociated from mind that are concomitant with the mind; or they are associated with feeling but not concomitant with the mind, namely: the mind, mental consciousness, and intellect subsumed under the fruit of stream-entry.

Some are both concomitant with the mind (*cittānuvartin*) and associated with feeling (*vedanā-saṃprayukta*), namely, the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*) and the associated aggregate of formations (*saṃprayukta-saṃskāra-skandha*) included within the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpatti-phala*).

Others are neither concomitant with the mind nor associated with feeling, namely, all other formations dissociated from the mind (*citta-viprayukta-saṃskāra*) included within the fruit of stream-entry—excluding those that are concomitant with the mind—as well as cessation through deliberation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).
The same applies to the fruits of once-returner, non-returner, and arhatship.

Regarding how many [factors] follow the mind (*cittānuvartin*), are not associated with perception (*saṃjñā*) or formations (*saṃskāra*), and so forth—all these should be analyzed; that is to say, excluding their own intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), they should be understood in the same way as feeling (*vedanā*).

Regarding the question of how many [factors] follow the movement of vitarka (initial application) but are not associated with vicāra (sustained application), all such cases should be analyzed. Specifically, there are four permutations concerning the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpatti-phala*).

First, there are those that follow the movement of vitarka but are not associated with vicāra: namely, the bodily and vocal actions (*kāya-vāk-karman*) comprised within the fruit of stream-entry, as well as the formations dissociated from mind (*citta-viprayukta-saṃskāra*) that follow the movement of vitarka, together with vicāra itself.

Alternatively, there are those associated with investigation (*vicāra*) that do not follow the movement of initial inquiry (*vitarka*), namely, the *vitarka* subsumed under the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpatti-phala*).

Alternatively, there are those that follow the movement of initial inquiry and are also associated with investigation, namely, the mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta*) associated with both *vitarka* and *vicāra* that are subsumed under the fruit of stream-entry.

Or, it is neither that which follows the movement of vitarka nor associated with vicāra; this refers to all other formations dissociated from mind included within the fruit of stream-entry (srotāpattiphala), excluding those formations dissociated from mind that follow the movement of vitarka, as well as cessation through deliberation (pratisaṃkhyānirodha).
The fruit of once-returning is also like this.
Regarding the fruit of non-returning, there are four propositions.

First, there are those that follow vitarka (initial inquiry) but are not associated with vicāra (sustained investigation), namely: the bodily and vocal karma subsumed under the fruit of non-returning that follows vitarka, the formations dissociated from mind that follow vitarka, and the vicāra associated with vitarka.

Or, there are those associated with investigation (*vicāra*) but not proceeding with initial inquiry (*vitarka*), namely: the *vitarka* subsumed under the fruit of non-returning (*anāgāmiphala*), as well as the mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta-dharma*) that are dissociated from *vitarka* but associated with *vicāra*.

Either they follow the movement of vitarka and are associated with vicāra—namely, those mental states and mental factors associated with vitarka and vicāra that are subsumed under the fruit of an Anāgāmin;

or they do not follow the movement of vitarka and are not associated with vicāra—namely, all other bodily and vocal actions and formations dissociated from mind subsumed under the fruit of an Anāgāmin (excluding those bodily and vocal actions and formations dissociated from mind that follow the movement of vitarka), as well as the vicāra dissociated from vitarka subsumed under the fruit of an Anāgāmin, and finally, those mental states and mental factors that are without both vitarka and vicāra, along with cessation through deliberation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).
The fruit of arhatship is also like this.

Regarding the question of how many are "view" (*dṛṣṭi*) and not "the locus of view" (*dṛṣṭisthāna*), all should be analyzed as follows: the wisdom (*prajñā*) subsumed under the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpattiphala*) is "view" and not "the locus of view," while all the rest are neither "view" nor "the locus of view."
The same applies to the fruits of Once-returner and Non-returner.

Regarding the fruit of Arhatship, the wisdom included therein that is not included within the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) and the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*) is vision but not a basis for vision; all other [wisdom] is neither vision nor a basis for vision.

Regarding how many have the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) as their cause but are not themselves causes of the view of a self-identity, etc.: all [factors] neither have the view of a self-identity as their cause nor are they causes of the view of a self-identity.

Regarding how many are karma but not the maturation of karma (*karmavipāka*), etc.: all should be analyzed. That is to say, bodily and vocal karma and volition (*cetanā*) comprised within the fruits of asceticism (*śrāmaṇyaphala*) are karma but not the maturation of karma; the remainder are neither karma nor the maturation of karma.
Regarding the question of how many karmas are not "concomitant with karma" (karma-anuvartin) and so forth, all cases should be analyzed.
Specifically, there are four propositions concerning the fruit of stream-entry (srotāpatti-phala).
First, there may be karma that is not concomitant with karma, namely, the volition (cetanā) comprised within the fruit of stream-entry.

Some are concomitants of karma but are not karma itself; this refers to the aggregates of feeling, perception, and consciousness included within the fruit of stream-entry, as well as the aggregate of formations included therein that are concomitants of karma but are not themselves volition.
Some are both karma and concomitants of karma; this refers to the bodily and vocal actions included within the fruit of stream-entry.

Or [there are those] that are neither karma nor concomitants of karma; this refers to all other formations dissociated from mind included within the fruit of stream-entry, with the exception of those formations dissociated from mind that are concomitants of karma, as well as cessation through deliberation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).
The same applies to the fruits of once-returning, non-returning, and arhatship.

Regarding how many derived forms (*upādāya-rūpa*) are not visible forms (*sanidarśana-rūpa*), all should be analyzed as follows: those bodily and vocal actions (*kāya-vāk-karman*) subsumed under the fruits of the religious life (*śrāmaṇyaphala*) are derived forms that are not visible forms; all others are neither derived forms nor visible forms.

Regarding these four fruits of śrāmaṇya, as to how many are derived matter (*upādāyarūpa*) and not resistant matter (*sapratigharūpa*), all should be analyzed as follows: those comprised within the fruits of śrāmaṇya that are bodily and vocal actions are derived matter and not resistant matter; the remainder are neither derived matter nor resistant matter.
Regarding the phrase "difficult to see, therefore profound," etc.: all things are profound because they are difficult to see, and they are difficult to see because they are profound.

Regarding the question of how many are wholesome and have the wholesome as their cause, etc.: all should be analyzed. That is to say, the conditioned fruits of śrāmaṇya are both wholesome and have the wholesome as their cause; the unconditioned fruits of śrāmaṇya are wholesome but do not have the wholesome as their cause.
Regarding the question of how many unwholesome factors are not caused by the unwholesome and so forth: all are neither unwholesome nor caused by the unwholesome.
Regarding the question of how many indeterminate factors are not caused by the indeterminate and so forth: all are neither indeterminate nor caused by the indeterminate.

Regarding the phrase "how many conditions are not having-cause, etc.," all should be analyzed as follows: if it is a conditioned fruit of śramaṇaship, it is both a condition and has a cause; if it is an unconditioned fruit of śramaṇaship, it is neither a condition nor does it have a cause.

Regarding the question of how many are equal-immediate [conditions] but not equal-immediate conditions, all should be analyzed as follows: namely, the fruits of asceticism (śrāmaṇyaphala) may be equal-immediate but not equal-immediate conditions; or they may be both equal-immediate and equal-immediate conditions; or they may be neither equal-immediate nor equal-immediate conditions.

Those which are equal-immediate but not equal-immediate conditions refer to the minds and mental factors comprised within the fruits of asceticism (*śrāmaṇyaphala*) that are currently arising in the future.
Those which are both equal-immediate and equal-immediate conditions refer to the minds and mental factors comprised within the fruits of asceticism in the past and present.

That which is neither an equal-and-immediate [condition] nor an equal-and-immediate condition refers to all other future mind and mental factors included within the fruits of śramaṇaship—excluding those that are currently arising and manifesting in the future—as well as bodily and vocal actions, formations dissociated from mind, and analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).

Regarding how many object-conditions (ālambana-pratyaya) are not possessed of an object (sālambana), all should be analyzed as follows: namely, bodily and vocal actions, formations dissociated from mind (citta-viprayukta-saṃskāra), and analytical cessation (pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha) included within the category of the ascetic life are object-conditions but are not possessed of an object; all others are both object-conditions and possessed of an object.

Regarding the question of how many are predominant conditions (*adhipati-pratyaya*) but do not possess predominance (*adhipatya*), all should be analyzed as follows: conditioned fruits of asceticism (*saṃskṛta-śrāmaṇyaphala*) are both predominant conditions and possess predominance; unconditioned fruits of asceticism (*asaṃskṛta-śrāmaṇyaphala*) are predominant conditions but do not possess predominance.
Regarding how many floods (*ogha*) are not favorable to the floods and so forth: all of them are neither floods nor favorable to the floods.

As for the four paths of practice (*pratipad*), they are: the painful practice with slow progress, the painful practice with quick progress, the pleasant practice with slow progress, and the pleasant practice with quick progress.

Regarding how many of these four paths of practice (*pratipad*) possess form (*rūpin*), all should be analyzed as follows: those comprised within the paths of practice that consist of bodily and vocal actions (*kāya-vāk-karman*) possess form, while all others are without form (*arūpin*).
Regarding how many are "with visibility" (*sanidarśana*) and so forth: all are "without visibility.
Regarding how many are "with resistance" (*sapratigha*) and so forth: all are "without resistance.
Regarding how many are "with outflows" (*sāsrava*) and so forth: all are "without outflows" (*anāsrava*).
Regarding how many are conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) and so forth: all are conditioned.
Regarding how many have maturation (*vipāka*) and so forth: none have maturation.
Regarding how many are dependently originated (*pratītyasamutpanna*) and so forth: all are dependently originated, produced by causes, and included within the world (*loka*).

Regarding how many [factors] are comprised within "form" (*rūpa*) and so forth, all should be analyzed as follows: those bodily and vocal actions (*kāya-vāk-karman*) included within the "universal path" (*sarvatraga-mārga*) are comprised within form; all others are comprised within "name" (*nāman*).

Regarding the inclusion within the sense bases (*āyatana*), all [factors] should be analyzed as follows: those included in the "path of practice" (i.e., the mental states associated with it) are included within the internal sense bases (*ādhyātmikāyatana*), while the remainder are all included within the external sense bases (*bāhyāyatana*).
Regarding the question of how many are fully known by the thorough knowledge of wisdom (*jñāna-parijñā-parijñeya*), all are fully known by the thorough knowledge of wisdom.

Regarding the question of how many of these four paths of practice (*pratipad*) are fully known by the thorough knowledge of abandonment (*prahāṇa-parijñā-parijñeya*), none are fully known by the thorough knowledge of abandonment.
Regarding how many should be abandoned and so forth: none should be abandoned.
Regarding how many should be cultivated and so forth: all should be cultivated.
Regarding how many are defiled and so forth: none are defiled.
Regarding the question of how many are results but not possess results, and so forth: all are results and also possess results.
Regarding the question of how many are appropriated (*upātta*), and so forth: all are non-appropriated.

Regarding the question of how many are derived from the primary elements (*mahābhūta*), and so forth: all should be analyzed. That is to say, bodily and vocal actions included within the "universal path" (*pratipad*) are derived from the primary elements; the rest are all not derived from the primary elements.
Regarding "how many have the superior" (*sottara*): all have the superior.
Regarding "how many are with existence" (*bhava-saṃprayukta*): none are with existence.

Regarding "how many are associated with causes" (*hetu-saṃprayukta*): all should be analyzed. That is to say, the bodily and vocal actions included within the "path of practice" (*pratipad*) and the formations dissociated from mind (*citta-viprayukta-saṃskāra*) are not associated with causes; the rest are all associated with causes.

Regarding the inclusion of these four paths of practice within the six bases of wholesome action: a portion of the five bases of wholesome action includes the four paths of practice, and the four paths of practice also include a portion of the five bases of wholesome action.
Regarding their mutual inclusion with the five unwholesome bases (*akuśalasthāna*), they do not mutually include one another.
Regarding their mutual inclusion with the seven indeterminate bases (*avyākṛtasthāna*), they do not mutually include one another.
Regarding their mutual inclusion with the three outflow bases (*āsravasthāna*), they do not mutually include one another.
Regarding their inclusion within the five contaminated bases (*āsravasthāna*), they do not include one another.

Regarding their inclusion within the eight uncontaminated bases (*anāsravasthāna*), the five uncontaminated bases include the four paths of practice (*pratipad*), and the four paths of practice also include the five uncontaminated bases.
Regarding how many are past and so forth: all are either past, future, or present.
Regarding how many are wholesome and so forth: all are wholesome.
Regarding how many are bound to the desire realm and so forth: all are unbound.
Regarding "how many are training" (*śaikṣa*) and so forth, all should be analyzed: namely, the four paths of practice (*pratipad*) are either training or beyond-training (*aśaikṣa*).
What is training? It refers to the five aggregates (*skandha*) of one in training.
What is the state of no-more-learning?
It refers to the five aggregates of one beyond learning.
Regarding these four paths of practice, how many are to be abandoned by vision and so forth? All of them are not to be abandoned.

Regarding "how many are not mind, etc.," all should be analyzed as follows: bodily and vocal actions subsumed under the "common path" (pratipad) and the formations dissociated from mind (*cittaviprayuktasaṃskāra*) are neither mind, nor mental factors (*caitta*), nor associated with mind;

if they belong to the aggregate of feeling (*vedanā-skandha*), the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*), or the associated portion of the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*), they are mental factors associated with mind;
if they are mind, mentation, or consciousness (*manovijñāna*), they are exclusively mind.

Regarding how many [factors] follow the mind (*cittānuvartin*) but are not associated with feeling (*vedanā-saṃprayukta*), all should be analyzed; that is, each of the various paths of practice (*pratipad*) has its own fourfold permutation (*catuṣkoṭi*).

First, those that follow the mind but are not associated with feeling: these include bodily and vocal actions (*kāya-vāk-karman*) subsumed under the paths of practice, as well as the mind-dissociated formations (*citta-viprayukta-saṃskāra*) that follow the mind, and feeling itself.
Some are associated with feeling but do not follow the mind, namely the mind, mental faculty, and mental consciousness as included within the "path of practice" (pratipad).
Some both follow the mind and are associated with feeling, namely the aggregate of perception and the associated aggregate of formations as included within the "path of practice."

Or [those] that do not follow the mind and are not associated with feeling: namely, with the exception of the formations dissociated from mind that follow the mind and are included within the modes of practice (pratipad), all other formations dissociated from mind included within the modes of practice.

Regarding how many [factors] follow the mind (*cittānuvartin*), are not associated with perception (*saṃjñā*) or formations (*saṃskāra*), and so forth—all should be analyzed. That is to say, excluding their own intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), they should be understood in the same manner as feeling (*vedanā*).

Regarding how many [factors] follow vitarka (*vitarkānuvartin*), are not associated with vicāra (*vicāra*), and so forth—all should be analyzed. That is to say, regarding the path of sluggish progress (*duḥkhā pratipat*), there are four permutations (*catuṣkoṭi*).

Or, there are those that follow vitarka but are not associated with vicāra; these refer to the bodily and vocal actions and the formations dissociated from mind that are subsumed under the "difficult progress with sluggish intuition" and which follow vitarka, as well as the vicāra that is associated with vitarka.

Or, there are those associated with examination (*vicāra*) but not functioning in accordance with initial inquiry (*vitarka*), namely: the initial inquiry subsumed under the path of sluggish progress (*duḥkhā pratipad dhandhābhijñā*), as well as the mental states and mental factors (*citta-caitta-dharma*) that are dissociated from initial inquiry but associated with examination.

Some are concomitant with vitarka and also associated with vicāra, namely those mental states and mental factors associated with vitarka and vicāra that are subsumed under the practice of painful and slow progress (duḥkhā pratipad dhandhābhijñā).

Some are neither concomitant with vitarka nor associated with vicāra, namely: excluding those bodily and vocal actions and formations dissociated from mind that are concomitant with vitarka and are subsumed under the practice of painful and slow progress, all other bodily and vocal actions and formations dissociated from mind subsumed under the practice of painful and slow progress; as well as vicāra not associated with vitarka; and all mental states and mental factors that are without both vitarka and vicāra.
The same applies to the path of swift progress with suffering.
Regarding the path of slow progress with pleasure, there are also four permutations.

There are cases that follow the movement of vitarka (applied thought) but are not associated with vicāra (sustained thought), namely: the bodily and vocal karma, the formations dissociated from mind, and vicāra itself, which are subsumed under the path of slow progress with pleasure and follow the movement of vitarka.
Alternatively, there are those associated with vicāra that do not follow vitarka, namely the vitarka subsumed under the path of practice characterized by ease and slowness.

Alternatively, there are those that follow vitarka and are also associated with vicāra, namely the mind and mental factors associated with both vitarka and vicāra that are subsumed under the path of practice characterized by ease and slowness.

Or [there are those] that neither follow after vitarka nor are associated with vicāra; namely, with the exception of the bodily and vocal karma and the formations dissociated from mind that accompany vitarka and are included within the practice of difficult progress with ease, all other bodily and vocal karma and formations dissociated from mind included within the practice of difficult progress with ease, as well as the minds and mental factors that are without vitarka and without vicāra.
The same applies to the "pleasant swift practice" (*sukhā pratipad*).

Regarding how many are views (*dṛṣṭi*) and not bases of view (*na dṛṣṭisthāna*), all should be analyzed as follows: the wisdom (*prajñā*) included within the practices that is not included within the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) and the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*) is a view and is a base of view; all others are neither views nor bases of view.

Regarding how many have the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) as their cause but are not causes of the view of a self-identity, etc.: all [factors] neither have the view of a self-identity as their cause nor are they causes of the view of a self-identity.

Regarding how many are karma but not the maturation of karma (*karmavipāka*), etc.: all should be analyzed. That is to say, bodily and vocal karma and volition (*cetanā*) included within the "paths of practice" (*pratipad*) are karma but not the maturation of karma; all others are neither karma nor the maturation of karma.

Regarding the question of how many types of karma are not "concomitant with karma" (karmānuvartin) and so forth, all should be analyzed; that is, each of the various paths of practice (pratipad) has four permutations (catuṣkoṭi).
There may be karma that is not concomitant with karma, namely, volition (cetanā) included within the paths of practice.

Some are concomitants of karma but are not karma itself; this refers to the aggregates of feeling, perception, and consciousness as included within the pervasive courses of action, as well as the aggregate of formations that are concomitants of karma but are not themselves subsumed under volition (*cetanā*).
Some are both karma and concomitants of karma; this refers to bodily and vocal actions as included within the pervasive courses of action.

Or [there are those] that are neither karma nor concomitants of karma, namely: with the exception of the non-concomitant formations associated with mind that are included within the "path of practice" (pratipad) and are concomitants of karma, all other non-concomitant formations associated with mind included within the path of practice.

Regarding the question of how many derived forms (*upādāya-rūpa*) are not visible forms (*sanidarśana-rūpa*), all such cases should be analyzed as follows: those bodily and vocal actions (*kāya-vāk-karman*) included within the "universal paths" (*sarvatraga-mārga*) are derived forms that are not visible forms; all others are neither derived forms nor visible forms.

Regarding these four paths of practice (*pratipad*), as to how many are derived matter (*upādāyarūpa*) and not resistant matter (*sapratigha-rūpa*), all should be analyzed as follows: those bodily and vocal actions (*kāya-vāk-karman*) subsumed under the paths of practice are derived matter and not resistant matter; the remainder are neither derived matter nor resistant matter.
Regarding the phrase "how many are difficult to see and profound," etc.: all are difficult to see because they are profound, and they are profound because they are difficult to see.
Regarding the phrase "how many are wholesome and have the wholesome as their cause," etc.: all are wholesome and also have the wholesome as their cause.
Regarding the question, "How many are unwholesome and not caused by the unwholesome, etc.?"—all are neither unwholesome nor caused by the unwholesome.
Regarding the question, "How many are indeterminate and not caused by the indeterminate, etc.?"—all are neither indeterminate nor caused by the indeterminate.
Regarding the question of how many conditions are not "having a cause" (*sahetu*) and so forth: all are conditions and also have a cause.

Regarding the question of how many are "immediately preceding" (*samanantara*) but not "immediately preceding conditions" (*samanantarapratyaya*) and so forth: all should be analyzed as follows. That is to say, among the various paths of practice (*pratipad*), some are immediately preceding but not immediately preceding conditions; some are both immediately preceding and immediately preceding conditions; and some are neither immediately preceding nor immediately preceding conditions.
Those which are equal-immediate but not equal-immediate conditions refer to the minds and mental factors included within the "path of progress" (*pratipad*) that are currently arising in the future.
Those which are both equal-immediate and equal-immediate conditions refer to the minds and mental factors included within the "path of progress" in the past and present.

Those that are neither equal-and-immediate nor equal-and-immediate conditions refer to all other future mind and mental factors included within the path of practice, as well as bodily and vocal actions and formations dissociated from mind included within the path of practice—excluding those mind and mental factors included within the path of practice that are currently arising and present in the future.

Regarding how many object-conditions (ālambana-pratyaya) are not possessed of an object (sālambana), all should be analyzed as follows: namely, bodily and vocal karma and formations dissociated from mind (citta-viprayukta-saṃskāra) that are subsumed under the "universal path" (sarvatraga-mārga) are object-conditions but are not possessed of an object; all others are both object-conditions and possessed of an object.
Regarding the question of how many are dominant conditions (*adhipati-pratyaya*) but not possess dominant power (*ādhipatya*), all are dominant conditions and also possess dominant power.
Regarding the question of how many are floods (*ogha*) but not favorable to the floods (*anugata-ogha*), none are floods and none are favorable to the floods.

The four noble lineages (āryavaṃśa) are: the noble lineage of contentment with whatever robes one obtains, the noble lineage of contentment with whatever food one obtains, the noble lineage of contentment with whatever bedding and seats one obtains, and the noble lineage of delighting in abandonment and delighting in cultivation.

Regarding how many of these four noble lineages (āryavaṃśa) possess form and so forth: all should be analyzed. That is to say, the bodily and vocal actions subsumed within the noble lineages possess form; the remainder are all without form.
Regarding how many are "with visibility" (*sanidarśana*) and so forth: all are "without visibility.
Regarding how many are "with resistance" (*sapratigha*) and so forth: all are "without resistance.
Regarding how many are "with outflows" (*sāsrava*) and so forth: all should be analyzed; that is to say, the noble lineages (*āryavaṃśa*) are either with outflows or without outflows.
What are the outflows (sāsrava)?
They are the five aggregates (pañcaskandha) that are outflowed and included within the noble lineages (āryavaṃśa).
What are the non-outflows (anāsrava)?
This refers to the five untainted aggregates (*anāsrava-skandha*).
Regarding how many are conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) and so forth: all are conditioned.

Regarding how many have maturation (*savipāka*) and so forth: all should be analyzed; that is, if the noble lineages (*āryavaṃśa*) are tainted (*sāsrava*), they have maturation; if they are untainted (*anāsrava*), they have no maturation.
Regarding how many are dependently originated (*pratītyasamutpanna*), and so forth: all are dependently originated, produced by causes, and included within the world (*loka*).

Regarding how many are included among the material (*rūpa*), and so forth: all should be analyzed. That is to say, those bodily and vocal actions included among the noble lineages (*āryavaṃśa*) are included among the material; the rest are all included among the nominal (*nāman*).

Regarding the inclusion within the sense bases (*āyatana*), all [factors] should be analyzed as follows: those included among the noble lineages (*āryavaṃśa*) are comprised within the internal sense bases of mind, intellect, and consciousness; the remainder are all comprised within the external sense bases.
Regarding the question of how many are fully known by the thorough knowledge of wisdom (*jñāna-parijñā*): all of them are fully known by the thorough knowledge of wisdom.

Regarding the question of how many of these four noble lineages (*ārya-vaṃśa*) are fully known by the thorough knowledge of abandonment (*prahāṇa-parijñā*): all should be analyzed. That is to say, among the noble lineages, those that are with outflows (*sāsrava*) are fully known by the thorough knowledge of abandonment, while those that are without outflows (*anāsrava*) are not fully known by the thorough knowledge of abandonment.

Regarding "how many are to be abandoned" and so forth, all should be analyzed as follows: among the noble lineages (*āryavaṃśa*), those that are with outflows (*sāsrava*) are to be abandoned, while those that are without outflows (*anāsrava*) are not to be abandoned.
Regarding how many are to be cultivated (*bhāvayitavya*) and so forth: all are to be cultivated.
Regarding how many are defiled (*kliṣṭa*) and so forth: none are defiled.
Regarding how many are results (*phala*) but not possessing results (*saphala*) and so forth: all are results and also possess results.
Regarding how many are appropriated (*upātta*) and so forth: all are unappropriated.

Regarding how many are derived from the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) and so forth: all should be analyzed. That is to say, bodily and vocal karma included within the noble lineages (*āryavaṃśa*) are derived from the primary elements; the rest are not derived from the primary elements.
Regarding the question "How many are with superior [objects] (*sottara*)?", all are with superior objects.

Regarding the question "How many are existence (*bhava*)?", all should be analyzed: that is to say, among the noble lineages (*āryavaṃśa*), if they are contaminated (*sāsrava*), they are existence; if they are uncontaminated (*anāsrava*), they are not existence.

Regarding the phrase "associated with how many causes" and so forth, all should be analyzed as follows: namely, bodily and vocal actions subsumed under the noble lineages (*āryavaṃśa*), as well as formations dissociated from mind (*cittaviprayuktasaṃskāra*), are not associated with causes; all others are associated with causes.

Regarding the inclusion of these four noble lineages within the six bases of wholesome qualities: a portion of the five bases of wholesome qualities includes the four noble lineages, and the four noble lineages likewise include a portion of the five bases of wholesome qualities.
Regarding their inclusion within the five unwholesome bases (*akuśalasthāna*), they do not include one another.
Regarding their inclusion within the seven indeterminate bases (*avyākṛtasthāna*), they do not include one another.
Regarding their inclusion within the three outflows bases (*āsravasthāna*), they do not include one another.
Regarding the mutual inclusion with the five outflow-tainted bases (*āsravasthāna*), one should formulate four permutations (*catuṣkoṭi*).
There may be an outflow-tainted base that is not a noble lineage (*āryavaṃśa*), namely, the outflow-tainted five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*) not included within the noble lineages.
Either they are noble lineages (*āryavaṃśa*) but not bases of outflows (*sāsravasthāna*), namely the four untainted noble lineages;
or they are both bases of outflows and noble lineages, namely the four tainted noble lineages.
Alternatively, there are those that are neither tainted bases nor noble lineages, namely space and the two types of cessation.
Regarding their mutual inclusion with the eight untainted bases, one should formulate four permutations.
Alternatively, there are things that belong to the untainted sphere (*anāsrava-dhātu*) but are not the noble lineages (*ārya-vaṃśa*), namely: space and the two types of cessation (*nirodha*).
Alternatively, there are things that are the noble lineages but do not belong to the untainted sphere, namely: the four untainted noble lineages that are associated with outflows (*sāsrava*).
Either they are untainted bases and also noble lineages— namely, the four untainted noble lineages—
or they are neither untainted bases nor noble lineages— namely, the tainted five aggregates not subsumed within the noble lineages.
Regarding how many are past and so forth: all are either past, future, or present.
Regarding how many are wholesome and so forth: all are wholesome.

Regarding how many are bound to the desire realm and so forth: all should be analyzed; that is to say, the noble lineages (āryavaṃśa) are either bound to the desire realm, or bound to the form realm, or bound to the formless realm, or unbound.
What is that which is bound to the desire realm?
It refers to the five aggregates of the desire realm comprised within the noble lineages (*āryavaṃśa*).
What is that which is bound to the form realm?
This refers to the five aggregates of the form realm subsumed under the noble lineages (*āryavaṃśa*).
What is that which is bound to the formless realm?
It refers to the four aggregates of the formless realm subsumed under the noble lineages.
What is "unbound" (*asaṃyukta*)?
It refers to the five untainted aggregates (*anāsrava-skandha*).

Regarding how many are "in training" (*śaikṣa*) and so forth, all should be analyzed: namely, the noble lineages (*āryavaṃśa*) are either in training, or beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), or neither in training nor beyond training (*naivaśaikṣanāśaikṣa*).
What is "in training" (śaikṣa)?
It refers to the five aggregates of one in training.
What is "beyond training" (aśaikṣa)?
That is to say, the five aggregates of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*).
What are those that are neither of training nor beyond training?
That is to say, the contaminated (*sāsrava*) five aggregates included within the noble lineages (*āryavaṃśa*).

Regarding how many of these four noble lineages (*āryavaṃśa*) are to be abandoned by insight (*darśana-prahātavya*), and so forth: all must be analyzed. That is to say, among the noble lineages, those that are contaminated (*sāsrava*) are to be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-prahātavya*), while those that are uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) are not to be abandoned.

Regarding how many are not mind (*citta*) and so forth, all should be analyzed as follows: namely, the bodily and vocal actions (*kāya-vāk-karman*) and the formations dissociated from mind (*citta-viprayukta-saṃskāra*) included within the noble lineages (*āryavaṃśa*) are neither mind, nor mental factors (*caitta*), nor associated with mind;

the aggregate of feeling (*vedanā-skandha*), the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*), and the associated aggregate of formations (*saṃprayukta-saṃskāra-skandha*) included within the noble lineages are mental factors associated with mind;
and the mind, intellect, and consciousness (*mano-vijñāna*) included within the noble lineages are exclusively mind.

Regarding how many follow the mind (*cittānuvartin*) but are not associated with feeling (*vedanā-saṃprayukta*), all should be analyzed; that is, each of the noble lineages (*āryavaṃśa*) has four permutations (*catuṣkoṭi*).

First, those that follow the mind but are not associated with feeling: these include the bodily and vocal actions (*kāyavākkarman*) subsumed under the noble lineages that follow the mind, as well as the formations dissociated from mind (*cittaviprayuktasaṃskāra*) and feeling itself.
Some are associated with feeling but do not follow the mind; this refers to the mind, mental consciousness, and their concomitants subsumed under the noble lineages (*āryavaṃśa*).

Some both follow the mind and are associated with feeling; this refers to the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*) and the associated aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) subsumed under the noble lineages.

Or, it is neither concomitant with the mind nor associated with feeling; this refers to all other bodily and vocal actions and formations dissociated from mind that are included within the noble lineages (āryavaṃśa), excluding those bodily and vocal actions and formations dissociated from mind that are themselves included within the noble lineages.

Regarding how many [factors] follow the mind (*cittānuvartin*), are not associated with perception (*saṃjñā*) or formations (*saṃskāra*), and so forth: all should be analyzed; that is to say, excluding their own intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), they should be understood in the same manner as feeling (*vedanā*).

Regarding how many [factors] follow discursive thought (*vitarkānuvartin*), are not associated with sustained thought (*vicāra*), and so forth: all should be analyzed; that is to say, for each of the noble lineages (*āryavaṃśa*), there are four permutations (*catuṣkoṭi*).

Or, there are those that follow vitarka (initial inquiry) but are not associated with vicāra (sustained investigation), namely: bodily and vocal karma, and formations dissociated from mind, which are included within the noble lineages (āryavaṃśa) and follow vitarka; as well as vicāra itself when it is associated with vitarka.

Alternatively, there are those associated with *vicāra* (sustained thought) but not following *vitarka* (applied thought), namely: the *vitarka* included within the noble lineages (*āryavaṃśa*), as well as the mind and mental factors associated with *vicāra* but dissociated from *vitarka*.

Alternatively, there are those that follow *vitarka* and are also associated with *vicāra*, namely: the mind and mental factors associated with both *vitarka* and *vicāra* that are included within the noble lineages.

Or [there are those] that neither follow the movement of vitarka nor are associated with vicāra; namely, excluding those bodily and vocal actions and formations dissociated from mind that are included within the noble lineages (āryavaṃśa) and follow the movement of vitarka, all other bodily and vocal actions and formations dissociated from mind included within the noble lineages, as well as vicāra that is not associated with vitarka, and all mental states and mental factors (citta-caitta-dharma) that are without both vitarka and vicāra.

Regarding the question of how many views are not bases for views (*adṛṣṭisthāna*) and so forth, all should be analyzed; that is, each of the noble lineages (*āryavaṃśa*) has four permutations (*catuṣkoṭi*).

There may be that which is a view but not a base for views: namely, untainted wisdom (*anāsravaprajñā*) not subsumed under the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) and the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*).
Alternatively, there are cases that are "bases of views" but not "views," namely, the four noble lineages (*āryavaṃśa*) that are tainted (*sāsrava*) and not subsumed under "view.
Alternatively, there are cases that are both "views" and "bases of views," namely, mundane right view (*laukikī samyagdṛṣṭi*) that is subsumed under the noble lineages.
Or that which is neither view nor the locus of view, namely, the four noble lineages (āryavaṃśa) that are untainted (anāsrava) and not subsumed under view.

Regarding the question of how many have the view of a self-identity (satkāyadṛṣṭi) as their cause but are not themselves the cause of the view of a self-identity: all of them do not have the view of a self-identity as their cause, nor are they the cause of the view of a self-identity.

Regarding how many karmas are not karmic maturations (karmavipāka) and so forth, all should be analyzed as follows: bodily and vocal karma, as well as volition (cetanā), that are subsumed under the noble lineages (āryavaṃśa) are karma but not karmic maturations; all others are neither karma nor karmic maturations.

Regarding the question of how many types of karma do not follow along with karma (*karmānuvartin*), all cases should be analyzed; that is, each of the noble lineages (*āryavaṃśa*) has four permutations.

There may be karma that is not followed by karma, namely: excluding those bodily and vocal karmas included within the noble lineages that are themselves followed by karma, all other bodily and vocal karmas included within the noble lineages, as well as volition (*cetanā*).

Some are concomitants of karma but are not karma itself; this refers to the aggregates of feeling, perception, and consciousness included within the noble lineages (*āryavaṃśa*), as well as the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāraskandha*) that are concomitants of karma but are not comprised by volition (*cetanā*).
Some are both karma and concomitants of karma; this refers to the bodily and vocal actions included within the noble lineages that are concomitants of karma.

Or they are neither karma nor concomitants of karma; that is to say, with the exception of those formations dissociated from mind included within the noble lineages (*āryavaṃśa*) that are concomitants of karma, all other formations dissociated from mind included within the noble lineages.

Regarding the question of how many derived forms (*upādāya-rūpa*) are not visible forms (*sanidarśana-rūpa*), all should be analyzed as follows: bodily and vocal actions (*kāya-vāk-karman*) subsumed under the noble lineages (*ārya-vaṃśa*) are derived forms that are not visible forms; all others are neither derived forms nor visible forms.

Regarding these four noble lineages (*āryavaṃśa*), as to how many are derived matter (*upādāyarūpa*) but not resistant matter (*sapratigharūpa*), all should be analyzed as follows: those comprised within the noble lineages that are bodily and vocal actions are derived matter but not resistant matter; the remainder are neither derived matter nor resistant matter.
Regarding the statement "difficult to see, therefore profound," etc.: all things are profound because they are difficult to see, and they are difficult to see because they are profound.
Regarding the statement "how many are wholesome and have the wholesome as their cause," etc.: all are wholesome and also have the wholesome as their cause.
Regarding the question of how many are unwholesome but do not have the unwholesome as their cause, and so forth: all are neither unwholesome nor have the unwholesome as their cause.
Regarding the question of how many are indeterminate but do not have the indeterminate as their cause, and so forth: all are neither indeterminate nor have the indeterminate as their cause.
Regarding "how many are object-conditions (*ālambana-pratyaya*) but not causes (*hetu*)," etc.: all are both object-conditions and causes.

Regarding "how many are equal-immediate conditions (*samanantara-pratyaya*) but not equal-immediate conditions," etc.: all should be analyzed as follows—namely, the noble lineages (*ārya-vaṃśa*) may be equal-immediate conditions but not equal-immediate conditions, or they may be both equal-immediate conditions and equal-immediate conditions, or they may be neither equal-immediate conditions nor equal-immediate conditions.

Those that are equal-immediate but not equal-immediate conditions refer to the future mental states and mental factors subsumed under the noble lineages (*āryavaṃśa*) that are currently arising before one.
Those that are both equal-immediate and equal-immediate conditions refer to the past and present mental states and mental factors subsumed under the noble lineages.

Those that are neither equal-and-immediate [conditions] nor equal-and-immediate conditions refer to all other future mental states and mental factors included within the noble lineages (*āryavaṃśa*), as well as bodily and vocal actions and formations dissociated from mind included within the noble lineages—excluding those future mental states and mental factors included within the noble lineages that are currently arising and manifesting.

Regarding how many object-conditions (*ālambana-pratyaya*) are not possessed of an object (*sālambana*), all should be analyzed as follows: those comprised within the noble lineages (*āryavaṃśa*), namely bodily and vocal karma and formations dissociated from mind (*cittaviprayukta-saṃskāra*), are object-conditions but are not possessed of an object; all others are both object-conditions and possessed of an object.
Regarding the question of how many *adhipati-pratyaya* (dominant conditions) are not *adhipati* [conditions], all are *adhipati-pratyaya* and also possess *adhipati* [status].

Regarding the question of how many *ogha* (floods) are not *anu-ogha* (conducive to floods), all should be analyzed as follows: among the noble lineages (*ārya-vaṃśa*), if they are with outflows (*sāsrava*), they are conducive to floods but are not floods; if they are without outflows (*anāsrava*), they are neither floods nor conducive to floods.
As with the four noble lineages, so it is with the four right endeavors and the four bases of psychic power.
As for the four foundations of mindfulness, they are: mindfulness of the body, mindfulness of feelings, mindfulness of the mind, and mindfulness of phenomena.
What is the application of mindfulness to the body?
It is wholesome, with-outflows (sāsrava) and without-outflows (anāsrava) wisdom that takes the body as its object.
What is the application of mindfulness to feelings?
That is to say, it is wholesome, outflow-tainted, and outflow-free wisdom that takes feeling as its object.
What is the application of mindfulness to the mind?
It is wholesome, outflow-tainted, and outflow-free wisdom that takes the mind as its object.
What is the application of mindfulness to phenomena (*dharmasmṛtyupasthāna*)?
It is wholesome, with-outflows (*sāsrava*) or without-outflows (*anāsrava*), wisdom (*prajñā*) that takes phenomena as its object.
Regarding these four applications of mindfulness, how many possess form (*rūpin*) and so forth? All of them are without form.
Regarding how many are "with visibility" (*sanidarśana*) and so forth: all are "without visibility" (*anidarśana*).
Regarding how many are "with resistance" (*sapratigha*) and so forth: all are "without resistance" (*apratigha*).
Regarding how many are "with outflows" (*sāsrava*) and so forth: all should be analyzed; the wisdom that takes the body as its object may be either with outflows or without outflows (*anāsrava*).
What is with outflows (*sāsrava*)?
It refers to wisdom that takes the body as its object and is associated with attention that has outflows.
What is without outflows (*anāsrava*)?
This refers to the wisdom associated with untainted mental attention (*anāsrava-manasikāra*) that takes the body as its object.
The same applies to the wisdom that takes feeling, mind, and phenomena as its objects.
Regarding how many are conditioned (*saṃskṛta*), all of them are conditioned.

Regarding the question of how many have maturation (*savipāka*) and so forth, all should be analyzed as follows: namely, if the applications of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) are contaminated (*sāsrava*), they have maturation; if they are uncontaminated (*anāsrava*), they have no maturation.

Regarding how many are dependently originated (*pratītyasamutpanna*) and so forth: all are dependently originated, produced by causes (*hetusamutpanna*), and included within the world (*loka-saṃgṛhīta*).
Regarding how many are included within form (*rūpa*) and so forth: all are included within the mental (*nāma*).
Regarding how many are included among the bases (*āyatana*): they are all included among the external bases.
Regarding how many are to be fully known through the thorough knowledge of wisdom (*jñāna-parijñā*): they are all to be fully known through the thorough knowledge of wisdom.
*Abhidharma-prakaraṇapāda-śāstra*, Fascicle Eleven.

Chapter Seven on the Examination of the Thousand Questions, Part Three. Regarding the question of how many of these four foundations of mindfulness (smṛtyupasthāna) are to be fully known through the complete knowledge of abandonment (prahāṇa-parijñā), all should be analyzed as follows: those foundations of mindfulness that are with outflows (sāsrava) are to be fully known through the complete knowledge of abandonment; those that are without outflows (anāsrava) are not to be fully known through the complete knowledge of abandonment.

Regarding the phrase "how many should be abandoned" and so forth, all [factors] should be analyzed as follows: among the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*), those that are with outflows (*sāsrava*) should be abandoned, while those that are without outflows (*anāsrava*) should not be abandoned.
Regarding how many are to be cultivated (*bhāvanīya*) and so forth: all are to be cultivated.
Regarding how many are defiled (*kliṣṭa*) and so forth: none are defiled.
Regarding how many are fruits (*phala*) but do not possess fruits (*saphala*) and so forth: all are both fruits and possess fruits.
Regarding how many are appropriated (*upātta*) and so forth: all are unappropriated.
Regarding how many are derived from the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) and so forth: all are not derived from the primary elements.
Regarding how many have something superior (*sottara*) and so forth: all have something superior.

Regarding the question "How many are 'existent' (*sattva*) and so forth?", all should be analyzed as follows: among the applications of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*), those that are with outflows (*sāsrava*) are existent, while those that are without outflows (*anāsrava*) are not existent.
Regarding the question "How many are associated with causes (*hetu-saṃprayukta*) and so forth?", all are associated with causes.

Regarding the inclusion of these four foundations of mindfulness within the six bases of wholesomeness: one base of wholesomeness includes a portion of the four foundations of mindfulness, and the four foundations of mindfulness also include a portion of one base of wholesomeness.
Regarding their mutual inclusion with the five unwholesome bases, they do not mutually include one another.
Regarding their mutual inclusion with the seven indeterminate bases, they do not mutually include one another.
Regarding their mutual inclusion with the three outflow bases, they do not mutually include one another.
Regarding the mutual inclusion with the five outflowing bases (*sāsrava-āyatana*), one should formulate four permutations (*catuṣkoṭi*).

There may be outflowing bases that are not applications of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*); namely, the outflowing aggregates of form, feeling, perception, and consciousness, as well as the outflowing aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) not included within the applications of mindfulness.
Some foundations of mindfulness are not objects of the outflows, namely, the four untainted foundations of mindfulness.
Some are both objects of the outflows and foundations of mindfulness, namely, the four tainted foundations of mindfulness.

Or, there are things that are neither outflow-tainted bases nor foundations of mindfulness; namely, the untainted aggregates of form, feeling, perception, and consciousness, as well as the untainted aggregate of formations not subsumed under the foundations of mindfulness, and the unconditioned.
Regarding the mutual inclusion between the eight untainted bases (*anāsrava-āyatana*) and the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*), one should formulate four permutations (*catuṣkoṭi*).

First, there are those that are untainted bases but not foundations of mindfulness: namely, the untainted aggregates of form, feeling, perception, and consciousness; the untainted aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) not included within the foundations of mindfulness; and the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
Either the foundations of mindfulness are not the untainted bases, namely the tainted four foundations of mindfulness;
or they are both untainted bases and foundations of mindfulness, namely the untainted four foundations of mindfulness.

Or, there are those that are neither untainted bases nor applications of mindfulness; namely, the tainted aggregates of form, feeling, perception, and consciousness, as well as the tainted aggregate of formations not subsumed under the applications of mindfulness.
Regarding how many are past and so forth: all are either past, future, or present.
Regarding how many are wholesome and so forth: all are wholesome.

Regarding how many are bound to the desire realm and so forth: all should be analyzed. That is to say, wisdom that takes the body as its object is either bound to the desire realm, or bound to the form realm, or bound to the formless realm, or unbound.
What is bound to the desire realm?
It refers to wisdom that takes the body as its object and is associated with mental attention belonging to the desire realm.
What is bound to the form realm?
This refers to wisdom that takes the body as its object and is associated with mental attention belonging to the form realm (*rūpadhātu*).
What is bound to the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*)?
It refers to wisdom that takes the body as its object and is associated with mental attention belonging to the formless realm.
What is meant by "unbound"?
It refers to wisdom that takes the body as its object and is associated with untainted mental attention (*anāsrava-manasikāra*).
Wisdom that takes feeling, mind, and phenomena as its objects is likewise so.

Regarding "how many are trainings" (*śaikṣa*) and so forth, all should be analyzed as follows: wisdom that takes the body as its object is either a training, or beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), or neither-training-nor-beyond-training.
What is a training?
It refers to the wisdom that takes the body as its object and is associated with the attention of one in training (*śaikṣa*).
What is that of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*)?
It refers to the wisdom that takes the body as its object and is associated with the attention of one beyond training.
What is that which is neither-learner-nor-non-learner?
It refers to wisdom associated with tainted attention (*sāsrava-manasikāra*) that takes the body as its object.
Wisdom that takes feeling, mind, and phenomena as its objects is likewise.

Regarding how many of these four foundations of mindfulness are to be abandoned by insight (*darśana-heya*), and so forth: all should be analyzed. That is to say, among the foundations of mindfulness, those that are contaminated (*sāsrava*) are to be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*), while those that are uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) are not to be abandoned.
Regarding "how many are not associated with mind, etc.": all are mental factors (*caitta*) that are associated with the mind (*cittasaṃprayukta*).
Regarding "how many follow the mind and are not associated with feeling, etc.": all follow the mind and are also associated with feeling (*vedanāsaṃprayukta*).

Regarding how many [factors] follow the mind (*cittānuvartin*), are associated with perception (*saṃjñā-samprayukta*), and are associated with formations (*saṃskāra-samprayukta*): all that follow the mind are also associated with perception; all that follow the mind are also associated with formations, excluding their own self-nature (*svabhāva*).

Regarding the question of how many [factors] proceed with vitarka (applied thought) but are not associated with vicāra (sustained thought), all such cases should be analyzed as follows: wisdom that takes the body as its object may be accompanied by both vitarka and vicāra, or it may be without vitarka and with vicāra only, or it may be without both vitarka and vicāra.
What is that which is accompanied by vitarka and vicāra?
It refers to wisdom that takes the body as its object and is associated with attention accompanied by vitarka and vicāra.
What is that which is without vitarka and with only vicāra?
This refers to wisdom that takes the body as its object and is associated with attention that is without vitarka and accompanied only by vicāra.
What is meant by "without vitarka and without vicāra"?
It refers to wisdom that takes the body as its object and is associated with attention that is without vitarka and without vicāra.
The same applies to the wisdom that takes feeling, mind, and phenomena as its objects.
Regarding how many are views but not bases of views and so forth, all should be analyzed as follows: the wisdom that takes the body as its object consists of four permutations.

Or, there is that which is not a basis for vision (*na dṛṣṭi-sthāna*), namely, untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-prajñā*) directed toward the body that is not subsumed under the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣaya-jñāna*) and the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpāda-jñāna*).

Or, there is that which is a basis for vision but is not vision itself (*na dṛṣṭi*), namely, wholesome wisdom associated with the five groups of sensory consciousness (*pañca-vijñāna-kāya-saṃprayukta-kuśala-prajñā*).
Either it is vision and also a basis for vision, namely, mundane right view;
or it is neither vision nor a basis for vision, namely, untainted wisdom directed toward the body that is not subsumed under [mundane] vision.

Wisdom that takes feeling as its object is, in some cases, vision but not a basis for vision; in some cases, both vision and a basis for vision; and in some cases, neither vision nor a basis for vision.

That which is vision but not a basis for vision refers to untainted wisdom taking feeling as its object that is not subsumed within the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) and the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*).
That which is both a view and a basis for views refers to mundane right view.
That which is neither a view nor a basis for views refers to untainted wisdom that takes feeling as its object and is not subsumed under the category of views.
The same applies to the mind that takes phenomena as its object and to the wisdom regarding phenomena.

As for the question of how many [factors] have the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) as their cause but are not themselves causes of the view of a self-identity: all of them do not have the view of a self-identity as their cause, nor are they causes of the view of a self-identity.
Regarding how many are karma but not the maturation of karma: all are neither karma nor the maturation of karma.
Regarding how many are karma but do not follow along with karma: all follow along with karma but are not karma.
Regarding the question of how many derived forms (*upādāya-rūpa*) are not visible forms (*sanidarśana-rūpa*), etc.: none of them are derived forms that are not visible forms.

Regarding these four foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*), how many derived forms are not resistant forms (*sapratigha-rūpa*), etc.: none of them are derived forms that are not resistant forms.
Regarding the phrase "difficult to see, therefore profound," etc.: all things are profound because they are difficult to see, and they are difficult to see because they are profound.
Regarding the question "how many are wholesome and have the wholesome as their cause," etc.: all are wholesome and also have the wholesome as their cause.
Regarding the question of how many are unwholesome but not having the unwholesome as their cause, and so forth: all are neither unwholesome nor have the unwholesome as their cause.
Regarding the question of how many are indeterminate but not having the indeterminate as their cause, and so forth: all are neither indeterminate nor have the indeterminate as their cause.
Regarding the question of how many conditions are not "having a cause" (*sahetu*) and so forth: all are conditions and also have causes.

Regarding the question of how many are "equal-immediate" (*samanantara*) but not "equal-and-immediate conditions" (*samanantarapratyaya*) and so forth: all should be analyzed as follows. That is to say, wisdom based on the body may be equal-immediate but not an equal-and-immediate condition; or it may be both equal-immediate and an equal-and-immediate condition; or it may be neither equal-immediate nor an equal-and-immediate condition.
Those that are equal-immediate but not equal-immediate conditions refer to the wisdom that takes the body as its object when it is about to arise in the future and is currently manifesting.
Those that are both equal-immediate and equal-immediate conditions refer to the wisdom that takes the body as its object in the past and present.

That which is neither an equal-and-immediate [condition] nor an equal-and-immediate object-condition refers to all other future wisdoms taking the body as their object, excluding those future wisdoms that are currently arising and present before one.
The same applies to the wisdom regarding feeling, mind, and phenomena.
As for how many are object-conditions (ālambana-pratyaya) but do not have an object (ālambana), all of them are both object-conditions and possess an object.
Regarding the question, "How many are dominant conditions (*adhipati-pratyaya*) but not possessing dominance (*ādhipatya*)? and so forth: all are dominant conditions and also possess dominance.

Regarding the question, "How many are floods (*ogha*) but not favorable to the floods (*anugata*)? and so forth: all should be analyzed as follows. That is to say, among the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*), if they are with outflows (*sāsrava*), they are favorable to the floods but not floods; if they are without outflows (*anāsrava*), they are neither floods nor favorable to the floods.
Furthermore, what is the application of mindfulness to the body (*kāyasmṛtyupasthāna*)?
It refers to the ten bases of form (*rūpāyatana*) and the form included within the base of mental objects (*dharmāyatana*).
What is the application of mindfulness to feelings (*vedanāsmṛtyupasthāna*)?
This refers to the six groups of feeling.
What is the application of mindfulness to the mind?
It refers to the six groups of consciousness.
What is the application of mindfulness to phenomena (*dharmasmṛtyupasthāna*)?
It refers to the sphere of non-material phenomena (*arūpadharmāyatana*) not included within sensation (*vedanā*).
Regarding how many of these four applications of mindfulness possess form (*rūpin*) and so forth: one possesses form, and three are formless (*arūpin*).

Regarding how many are with-visual-perception (*sadarśana*) and so forth: three are without-visual-perception (*adarśana*), and one should be analyzed. That is to say, the mindfulness-establishment of the body (*kāyasmṛtyupasthāna*) is either with-visual-perception or without-visual-perception.
What is with-visual-perception?
It refers to one base.
What is the invisible?
It refers to nine bases and a portion of one base.

Regarding how many are with resistance (*sapratigha*) and so forth: three are without resistance, while one should be analyzed. That is to say, the mindfulness-establishment of the body may be with resistance or without resistance.
What is with resistance?
This refers to ten bases (*āyatana*).
What is non-resistant (*apratigha*)?
It refers to a portion of one base.

Regarding how many are with outflows (*sāsrava*) and so forth, all should be analyzed as follows: the application of mindfulness to the body (*kāyasmṛtyupasthāna*) is either with outflows or without outflows (*anāsrava*).
What is with outflows?
It refers to ten bases (*āyatana*) and a portion of one base.
What is the untainted?
It refers to a small portion of one base.
The application of mindfulness to sensation may be either tainted or untainted.
What is the tainted?
It refers to the aggregate of feeling associated with tainted attention (*manasikāra*).
What is the untainted?
This refers to the aggregate of feeling associated with untainted (anāsrava) attention.
The same applies to the application of mindfulness to the mind.
The application of mindfulness to phenomena (dharmasmṛtyupasthāna) may be either tainted or untainted.
What are the outflows (sāsrava)?
They are the aggregates of perception (saṃjñā-skandha) and mental formations (saṃskāra-skandha) that are associated with outflows.
What are the outflow-free (anāsrava)?
This refers to the untainted (anāsrava) aggregates of perception and formations, as well as the three unconditioned (asaṃskṛta) phenomena.

Regarding how many are conditioned (saṃskṛta) and so forth: three are conditioned; one should be analyzed, namely the application of mindfulness to phenomena (dharmasmṛtyupasthāna), which may be either conditioned or unconditioned.
What is conditioned?
It refers to the aggregates of perception and mental formations.
What is unconditioned?
This refers to the three unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*).

Regarding how many have maturation (*savipāka*) and so forth, all should be analyzed as follows: the application of mindfulness to the body (*kāyasmṛtyupasthāna*) may either have maturation or be without maturation.
What possesses maturation?
It refers to the unwholesome and the wholesome-with-outflows (sāsrava) aggregate of form (rūpaskandha).
What lacks maturation?
This refers to the indeterminate and untainted (*anāsrava*) aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*).
The same applies to the applications of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) regarding feeling, mind, and phenomena (*dharma*).

As for how many are dependently originated (*pratītyasamutpanna*), etc.: three are dependently originated, produced by causes, and included within the world (*loka*); one should be analyzed. That is to say, if the application of mindfulness regarding phenomena is conditioned (*saṃskṛta*), it is dependently originated, produced by causes, and included within the world; if it is unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), it is not dependently originated, not produced by causes, and not included within the world.
Regarding how many are subsumed under the category of form (*rūpa*), etc.: one is subsumed under form, and three are subsumed under name (*nāman*).

Regarding how many are subsumed under the internal bases (*ādhyātmikāyatana*), etc.: one is subsumed under the internal bases, two are subsumed under the external bases (*bāhyāyatana*), and one should be analyzed—that is, the mindfulness-establishment of the body (*kāyasmṛtyupasthāna*) is either subsumed under the internal bases or subsumed under the external bases.
What is included within the internal bases?
It refers to the five internal bases.
What is included within the external bases?
This refers to the five external bases (*bāhyāyatana*) and a portion of one external base.

Regarding the question of how many are to be fully known through the thorough knowledge of wisdom (*jñānaparijñā-parijñeya*), all of them are to be fully known through the thorough knowledge of wisdom.

Regarding the question of how many of these four foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) are to be fully known through the thorough knowledge of abandonment (*prahāṇa-parijñā*), all should be analyzed as follows: those that are contaminated (*sāsrava*) are to be fully known through the thorough knowledge of abandonment; those that are uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) are not to be fully known through the thorough knowledge of abandonment.

Regarding "how many are to be abandoned" and so forth, all should be analyzed as follows: among the applications of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*), those that are contaminated (*sāsrava*) are to be abandoned, while those that are uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) are not to be abandoned.
Regarding "how many should be cultivated" and so forth, all should be analyzed as follows: the application of mindfulness to the body may either be cultivated or not cultivated.
How should it be cultivated?
This refers to the aggregate of form that is wholesome.
What is not to be cultivated?
This refers to the aggregate of form that is unwholesome or indeterminate.
