The same applies to the applications of mindfulness regarding feelings and the mind.
Regarding the application of mindfulness regarding phenomena (*dharmasmṛtyupasthāna*), it may be cultivated or it may not be cultivated.
How is it to be cultivated?
This refers to the wholesome aggregates of perception and formations.
What is not to be cultivated?
This refers to the unwholesome and indeterminate aggregates of perception and formations, as well as the three unconditioned phenomena.
Regarding "how many are defiled," etc., all should be analyzed: that is to say, the application of mindfulness to the body may be either defiled or undefiled. What is defiled?
This refers to the obscured aggregate of form.
What is non-defiled?
It refers to the unobscured aggregate of form.
The same applies to the applications of mindfulness regarding feelings, the mind, and phenomena (*vedanā-, citta-, and dharma-smṛtyupasthāna*).

Regarding how many are results (*phala*) but not possessors of results (*saphala*), etc.: three are both results and possessors of results; one should be analyzed as follows: the application of mindfulness regarding phenomena may be a result but not a possessor of results, or it may be both a result and a possessor of results, or it may be neither a result nor a possessor of results.
That which is a fruit but does not possess a fruit refers to analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).
That which is both a fruit and possesses a fruit refers to the aggregates of perception and formations (*saṃjñā-saṃskāra-skandha*).
That which is neither a fruit nor possesses a fruit refers to space (*ākāśa*) and non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).

Regarding how many are appropriated (*upātta*) and so forth: three are unappropriated; one should be analyzed—that is, the application of mindfulness to the body (*kāyasmṛtyupasthāna*) may be either appropriated or unappropriated.
What is appropriated?
It refers to the aggregate of form (rūpaskandha) that is comprised within one's own personal continuity.
What is non-appropriated?

Regarding the question of which of the form aggregates (*rūpaskandha*) not included within their own nature are derived from the primary elements (*mahābhūta*), three are not derived from the primary elements, while one should be analyzed: namely, the mindfulness-establishment of the body (*kāyasmṛtyupasthāna*) is either derived from the primary elements or not derived from the primary elements.
What is derived from the great elements?
It refers to nine bases and a portion of two bases.
What is not derived from the great elements?

Regarding the question, "In how many places is there that which has something superior (*sottara*)? there are three that have something superior, and one should be analyzed: namely, the application of mindfulness to phenomena (*dharmasmṛtyupasthāna*) may either have something superior or be unsurpassed (*anuttara*).
What is "surpassable"?
It refers to the aggregates of perception and formations, as well as space and non-analytical cessation.
What is "unsurpassable"?
This refers to analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).

Regarding how many are "existent" (*bhava*) and so forth, all should be analyzed as follows: among the applications of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*), those that are contaminated (*sāsrava*) are existent, while those that are uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) are not existent.

Regarding how many factors they are associated with, etc.: first, one is not associated with any factor; second, two are associated. One [category] should be analyzed: namely, the application of mindfulness to phenomena (*dharmasmṛtyupasthāna*). If it is a mental concomitant (*caitta*), it is associated with factors; if it is not a mental concomitant, it is not associated with factors.

Regarding the inclusion of these four foundations of mindfulness within the six bases of wholesome qualities: the six bases of wholesome qualities include a portion of the four foundations of mindfulness, and a portion of the four foundations of mindfulness also includes the six bases of wholesome qualities.

Regarding their mutual inclusion with the five unwholesome bases: the five unwholesome bases include a portion of the four foundations of mindfulness, and a portion of the four foundations of mindfulness also includes the five unwholesome bases.

Regarding the inclusion of the seven indeterminate bases (*avyākṛtasthāna*): the seven indeterminate bases include a portion of the four foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*), and a portion of the four foundations of mindfulness also includes the seven indeterminate bases.

Regarding their mutual inclusion with the three bases of outflows (*āsravasthāna*): the three bases of outflows include a portion of one application of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*), and a portion of one application of mindfulness also includes the three bases of outflows.

Regarding their mutual inclusion with the five bases of outflows (*sāsravasthāna*): the five bases of outflows include a portion of the four applications of mindfulness, and a portion of the four applications of mindfulness also includes the five bases of outflows.

Regarding their mutual inclusion with the eight untainted bases (*anāsrava-āyatana*): the eight untainted bases include a portion of the four foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*), and a portion of the four foundations of mindfulness also includes the eight untainted bases.

Regarding how many are past and so forth: three are either past, future, or present; one should be analyzed. That is, the mindfulness-establishment of phenomena (*dharmasmṛtyupasthāna*) is, if conditioned (*saṃskṛta*), either past, future, or present; if unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), it is neither past, nor future, nor present.
Regarding how many are wholesome and so forth, all should be analyzed as follows: the application of mindfulness to the body may be wholesome, unwholesome, or indeterminate.
What is wholesome and what is unwholesome?
This refers to a portion of three bases.
What is the indeterminate?
It refers to eight bases and a portion of two bases.
The foundation of mindfulness of feeling is either wholesome, unwholesome, or indeterminate.
What is wholesome?
It refers to the aggregate of feeling associated with wholesome attention.
What is unwholesome?
It refers to the aggregate of feeling associated with unwholesome attention.
What is indeterminate?
This refers to the aggregate of feeling associated with indeterminate attention (*avyākṛta-manasikāra*).
The same applies to the mindfulness of mind (*cittasmṛtyupasthāna*).
As for the mindfulness of phenomena (*dharmasmṛtyupasthāna*), it may be wholesome (*kuśala*), unwholesome (*akuśala*), or indeterminate (*avyākṛta*).
What is wholesome?
It refers to the wholesome aggregates of perception and formations, as well as analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).
What is unwholesome?
This refers to the unwholesome aggregates of perception and formations.
What is the indeterminate?
It refers to the indeterminate aggregates of perception and formations, as well as space and non-analytical cessation.
Regarding how many are bound to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu-saṃprayukta*) and so forth, all should be analyzed as follows:
the application of mindfulness to the body (*kāyasmṛtyupasthāna*) is either bound to the desire realm, bound to the form realm (*rūpadhātu-saṃprayukta*), or not bound (*asaṃprayukta*).
What is bound to the desire realm?
It refers to two bases and a portion of nine bases.
What is bound to the form realm?
This refers to a portion of nine bases (*āyatana*).
What is not bound?
This refers to a portion of one base.
The foundation of mindfulness of feelings is either bound to the desire realm, or bound to the form realm, or bound to the formless realm, or unbound.
What is bound to the desire realm?
This refers to the aggregate of feeling associated with mental attention of the desire realm.
What is bound to the form realm?
It refers to the aggregate of feeling associated with mental attention of the form realm.
What is that which is bound to the formless realm?
It refers to the aggregate of feeling associated with mental attention belonging to the formless realm.
What is that which is unbound?
This refers to the aggregate of feeling associated with untainted mental attention (*anāsrava-manasikāra*).
The same applies to the application of mindfulness to the mind (*cittasmṛtyupasthāna*).

As for the application of mindfulness to phenomena (*dharmasmṛtyupasthāna*), it may be bound to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*), the form realm (*rūpadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*), the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*), or unbound (*apratisaṃyukta*).
What is bound to the desire realm?
It refers to the aggregates of perception and formations belonging to the desire realm.
What is bound to the form realm?
This refers to the aggregates of perception and formations belonging to the form realm (*rūpadhātu*).
What belongs to the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*)?
This refers to the aggregates of perception and formations belonging to the formless realm.
What is not bound?
It refers to the untainted (anāsrava) aggregates of perception and formations, as well as unconditioned phenomena (asaṃskṛta-dharma).
Regarding how many are "in training" (śaikṣa) and so forth, all should be analyzed accordingly.
This refers to the application of mindfulness to the body, which may be of the learner (śaikṣa), the one beyond learning (aśaikṣa), or neither learner nor one beyond learning.
What is meant by "learner" and "beyond learning"?
It refers to a small portion of one [of the four] foundations.
What is neither-learner-nor-non-learner?
It refers to ten bases (*āyatana*) and a portion of one base.
The application of mindfulness to feeling (*vedanā-smṛtyupasthāna*) is either learner (*śaikṣa*), or non-learner (*aśaikṣa*), or neither-learner-nor-non-learner.
What is that which pertains to training (*śaikṣa*)?
It refers to the aggregate of feeling (*vedanā-skandha*) associated with the mental attention of one in training.
What is that which pertains to no-more-training (*aśaikṣa*)?
This refers to the aggregate of feeling associated with the mental attention (*manasikāra*) of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*).
What is neither-learner-nor-non-learner?
This refers to the aggregate of feeling associated with tainted (*sāsrava*) mental attention.
The same applies to the mindfulness of mind.
As for the mindfulness of phenomena (*dharmasmṛtyupasthāna*), it may be of the learner (*śaikṣa*), of the non-learner (*aśaikṣa*), or neither of the learner nor the non-learner.
What is that of the learner?
This refers to the aggregates of perception and formations of those in training (*śaikṣa*).
What are those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*)?
This refers to the aggregates of perception and formations of those beyond training.
What are those that are neither-learner-nor-non-learner?
They are the contaminated aggregates of perception and formations, as well as unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*).
Regarding these four foundations of mindfulness, as to how many are abandoned by vision (*darśana-prahātavya*) and so forth, all should be analyzed accordingly.
This refers to the foundation of mindfulness of the body, which is either to be abandoned by cultivation or not to be abandoned.
What is to be abandoned by cultivation?
It refers to ten bases and a portion of one base.
What is not to be abandoned?
It refers to a small portion of one base.
The application of mindfulness to sensation may be abandoned by seeing, abandoned by cultivation, or not to be abandoned.
What is abandoned by insight?
It refers to that which is abandoned by the patiences at the limit of clear realization for those who practice through faith or through dharma within the application of mindfulness of feeling.
Furthermore, what is this?
This refers to the aggregate of feeling associated with the eighty-eight proclivities (*anuśaya*) abandoned through seeing.
What is abandoned through cultivation?
It refers to the application of mindfulness to feeling that is abandoned through cultivation by those in training who have seen the path.

What, then, is this? It refers to the aggregate of feeling associated with the ten proclivities (*anuśaya*) to be abandoned through cultivation, as well as the undefiled contaminated (*sāsrava*) aggregate of feeling.
What is not to be abandoned?
This refers to the untainted aggregate of feeling (*vedanā-skandha*).
The same applies to the application of mindfulness to the mind (*citta-smṛtyupasthāna*).

As for the application of mindfulness to phenomena (*dharma-smṛtyupasthāna*), it is either to be abandoned by seeing (*darśana-heya*), or to be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*), or not to be abandoned at all (*aheya*).
What is abandoned by insight?
It refers to that which is abandoned by the patiences at the limit of clear realization for those practicing through faith or through dharma within the application of mindfulness of phenomena.
What, furthermore, is this?

This refers to the eighty-eight latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) abandoned through seeing, along with their associated aggregates of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*) and mental formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*), as well as the non-associated formations (*citta-viprayukta-saṃskāra*) arising together with them.
What is abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*)?
This refers to the dharma-smṛtyupasthāna of those in training who have seen the tracks [of the path], which is to be abandoned through cultivation. What, then, is this?

It refers to the ten underlying tendencies (anuśaya) to be abandoned through cultivation, along with their associated aggregates of perception (saṃjñā-skandha) and formations (saṃskāra-skandha), as well as the non-associated formations (citta-viprayukta-saṃskāra) arising from them, and the non-defiled, out-flowing (sāsrava) aggregates of perception and formations.

What are those not to be abandoned? They are the untainted (anāsrava) aggregates of perception (saṃjñā-skandha) and formations (saṃskāra-skandha), as well as unconditioned phenomena (asaṃskṛta-dharma).

Regarding how many are not mind (*citta*), etc.: one is neither mind, nor mental factor (*caitta*), nor associated with mind; one is a mental factor associated with mind; one is exclusively mind; and one should be analyzed.

That is to say, regarding the application of mindfulness to phenomena (*dharmasmṛtyupasthāna*): if it has an object of focus, it is a mental factor associated with the mind; if it lacks an object of focus, it is neither mind nor mental factor, nor is it associated with the mind.

Regarding how many follow the mind (cittānuvartin) but are not associated with feeling (vedanā-samprayukta), and so forth: one follows the mind but is not associated with feeling; one is associated with feeling but does not follow the mind; these two cases should be analyzed separately.

This refers to the foundation of mindfulness of the body (*kāyasmṛtyupasthāna*), which is either concomitant with the mind but not associated with feeling, or not concomitant with the mind and not associated with feeling.

That which is concomitant with the mind but not associated with feeling refers to bodily and vocal actions that follow the mind; all other remaining aggregates of form (*rūpaskandha*) are neither concomitant with the mind nor associated with feeling.

The application of mindfulness to phenomena (dharmasmṛtyupasthāna) either follows the mind but is not associated with feeling, or both follows the mind and is associated with feeling, or neither follows the mind nor is it associated with feeling.
Those that follow the mind but are not associated with feeling refer to the formations dissociated from mind that follow the mind.
Those that both follow the mind and are associated with feeling refer to the aggregate of perception and the associated aggregate of formations.

Those that do not follow the mind and are not associated with feeling refer to all other formations dissociated from the mind, as well as unconditioned phenomena, excluding those formations dissociated from the mind that do follow the mind.

Regarding how many [factors] follow the mind (*cittānuvartin*), are not associated with perception (*saṃjñā*) or formations (*saṃskāra*), and so forth: with the exception of their own intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), they should be understood in the same manner as feeling (*vedanā*).
Regarding how many [factors] follow applied thought (*vitarkānuvartin*), are not associated with sustained thought (*vicāra*), and so forth: all [of these] should be analyzed.

This refers to the foundation of mindfulness of the body; it either follows after vitarka (applied thought) and is not associated with vicāra (sustained thought), or it does not follow after vitarka and is not associated with vicāra.

That which follows after vitarka and is not associated with vicāra refers to bodily and vocal karma that follows after vitarka; all other remaining aggregates of form (rūpa-skandha) do not follow after vitarka and are not associated with vicāra.
The foundation of mindfulness of feeling may be accompanied by vitarka and vicāra, or without vitarka and with only vicāra, or without both vitarka and vicāra.
What is "accompanied by vitarka and vicāra"?
It refers to the aggregate of feeling associated with attention (manasikāra) that is accompanied by vitarka and vicāra.
What is "without vitarka and with vicāra"?
It refers to the aggregate of feeling associated with mental attention that is without vitarka and with vicāra.
What is "without vitarka and without vicāra"?
This refers to the aggregate of feeling associated with attention that is without vitarka and without vicāra.
The same applies to the application of mindfulness to the mind. Regarding the application of mindfulness to phenomena (dharmasmṛtyupasthāna), there are four propositions.

Either it follows the movement of vitarka but is not associated with vicāra—namely, the formations dissociated from mind that follow the movement of vitarka, as well as the vicāra associated with vitarka;
or it is associated with vicāra but does not follow the movement of vitarka—namely, vitarka itself, and the saṃjñā- and saṃskāra-skandhas associated with vicāra that are dissociated from vitarka.
Some follow the movement of vitarka and are also associated with vicāra; that is, the aggregates of perception (saṃjñā-skandha) and formations (saṃskāra-skandha) associated with vitarka and vicāra.

Some do not follow the movement of vitarka and are not associated with vicāra; that is, with the exception of those formations dissociated from mind (citta-viprayukta-saṃskāra) that follow the movement of vitarka, all other formations dissociated from mind, as well as vicāra that is not associated with vitarka, those mental factors dissociated from feeling (vedanā) that are neither accompanied by vitarka nor vicāra, and unconditioned phenomena (asaṃskṛta-dharma).
Regarding the question of how many [of the foundations of mindfulness] are "views" (*dṛṣṭi*) and how many are "bases for views" (*dṛṣṭisthāna*), all should be analyzed as follows:
namely, the foundation of mindfulness of the body (*kāyasmṛtyupasthāna*) is either a base for views but not a view, or both a view and a base for views, or neither a view nor a base for views.
That which is a locus of views but not a view refers to nine bases (*āyatana*) and a portion of one base.
That which is both a view and a locus of views refers to one base.
That which is neither a view nor a locus of views refers to a portion of one base.

Regarding the application of mindfulness to feelings (*vedanā-smṛtyupasthāna*): if it is with outflows (*sāsrava*), it is a locus for views (*dṛṣṭisthāna*) but is not a view; if it is without outflows (*anāsrava*), it is neither a view nor a locus for views.

The same applies to the application of mindfulness to the mind (*citta-smṛtyupasthāna*). Regarding the application of mindfulness to phenomena (*dharma-smṛtyupasthāna*), there are four permutations (*catuṣkoṭi*).

Or it is that which is the locus of vision but not vision itself: namely, untainted wisdom (*anāsravaprajñā*) not included within the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) and the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*).

Or it is that which is the locus of vision but not vision itself: namely, the tainted aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*), and the tainted aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) not included within vision.
Or it is both view and the basis for views, namely the five defiled views and mundane right view.
Or it is neither view nor the basis for views, namely the untainted aggregate of perception, the untainted aggregate of formations not included within views, and unconditioned phenomena.

Regarding the question of how many [factors] have the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) as their cause but are not themselves causes of the view of a self-identity, all such cases should be analyzed.

That is to say, regarding the application of mindfulness to the body (*kāyasmṛtyupasthāna*): if it is defiled, it has the view of a self-identity as its cause but is not itself a cause of the view of a self-identity; if it is undefiled, it neither has the view of a self-identity as its cause nor is it itself a cause of the view of a self-identity.

Regarding the foundation of mindfulness of feeling, some have the view of a self-identity as their cause but are not causes for the view of a self-identity; some have the view of a self-identity as their cause and are also causes for the view of a self-identity; and some neither have the view of a self-identity as their cause nor are causes for the view of a self-identity.

Regarding those things that have the view of a self (satkāyadṛṣṭi) as their cause but are not causes of the view of a self: this refers to all other defiled aggregates of feeling (vedanā-skandha), excluding the aggregates of feeling associated with the proclivities (anuśaya) abandoned through the vision of suffering (duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya) in the past and present, excluding the aggregates of feeling associated with the universal proclivities abandoned through the vision of origination (samudaya-darśana-prahātavya) in the past and present, and also excluding the aggregates of feeling associated with the view of a self in the future.
That which has the view of a self as its cause and is also a cause for the view of a self refers to the aggregate of feeling (vedanā-skandha) previously excluded.
That which neither has the view of a self as its cause nor is a cause for the view of a self refers to the non-defiled aggregate of feeling.
The same applies to the mindfulness of mind.

Regarding the mindfulness of phenomena (*dharmasmṛtyupasthāna*), some have the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) as their cause but are not themselves causes for the view of a self-identity; some have the view of a self-identity as their cause and are also causes for the view of a self-identity; and some neither have the view of a self-identity as their cause nor are they causes for the view of a self-identity.

Regarding those things that have the view of a self (satkāyadṛṣṭi) as their cause but are not themselves causes of the view of a self: these refer to all other defiled aggregates of perception (saṃjñā-skandha) and formations (saṃskāra-skandha), excluding the latent dispositions (anuśaya) abandoned through the vision of suffering (duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya) in the past and present, along with their associated and co-existent factors; excluding the universal latent dispositions abandoned through the vision of the origin (samudaya-darśana-prahātavya) in the past and present, along with their associated and co-existent aggregates of perception and formations; excluding the future aggregates of perception and formations associated with the view of a self; and excluding the future arising, aging, duration, and impermanence of the view of a self and its associated factors. All other such defiled aggregates of perception and formations [are what is meant].

That which has the view of a self (satkāyadṛṣṭi) as its cause and is also a cause for the view of a self refers to the aggregates of perception (saṃjñā-skandha) and formations (saṃskāra-skandha) previously excluded [from the view of a self].

That which neither has the view of a self as its cause nor is a cause for the view of a self refers to the undefiled aggregates of perception and formations, as well as unconditioned phenomena (asaṃskṛta-dharma).
Regarding how many are karma and not karmic maturation, and so forth, all should be analyzed as follows:
the application of mindfulness to the body is either (1) karma and not karmic maturation, (2) karmic maturation and not karma, or (3) neither karma nor karmic maturation.
That which is action but not the maturation of action refers to bodily and vocal actions.
That which is the maturation of action but not action refers to the aggregate of form born from the maturation of action.
That which is neither action nor the maturation of action refers to all other aggregates of form, excluding both action and the aggregate of form that is the maturation of action.
The application of mindfulness to feelings (vedanā-smṛtyupasthāna) is either karmic maturation that is not karma, or neither karma nor karmic maturation.
That which is karmic maturation but not karma refers to the aggregate of feeling born of karmic maturation.
The remaining aggregates of feeling are neither karma nor the maturation of karma;
the same applies to the mindfulness-establishment of mind (*cittasmṛtyupasthāna*). Regarding the mindfulness-establishment of phenomena (*dharmasmṛtyupasthāna*), there are four cases.
Alternatively, there are those that are not karma but are the maturation of karma, namely: volition (*cetanā*) that is not included within the maturation of karma.

Alternatively, there are those that are the maturation of karma but are not karma, namely: the aggregates of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*) and formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) born from the maturation of karma that are not included within volition.
Some are both karma and the maturation of karma (*karmavipāka*), namely, volition (*cetanā*) born from the maturation of karma.

Some are neither karma nor the maturation of karma, namely, with the exception of karma and the aggregates of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*) and formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) that are maturations of karma, all other aggregates of perception and formations, as well as unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*).
Regarding the question of how many *karmas* do not follow along with *karma* (*anuvartaka*), two [foundations] follow along with *karma* but are not *karma*, while two should be analyzed.

That is to say, the application of mindfulness to the body (*kāyasmṛtyupasthāna*) consists of three propositions: either it is *karma* but does not follow along with *karma*, which refers to all other bodily and vocal actions except for those bodily and vocal actions that follow along with *karma*.
Some are both karma and concomitants of karma, namely, bodily and vocal karma that follow along with [primary] karma.
Some are neither karma nor concomitants of karma, namely, all other members of the aggregate of form (rūpaskandha) excluding karma and its concomitants.
The application of mindfulness to phenomena (dharmasmṛtyupasthāna) consists of three categories:
either it is karma but not concomitant with karma, namely volition (cetanā);

or it is concomitant with karma but not karma itself, namely the aggregate of perception (saṃjñāskandha) and those factors of the aggregate of formations (saṃskāraskandha) that are concomitant with karma but are not subsumed under volition.

Or [there are those] that are neither karma nor concomitants of karma: namely, with the exception of karma and the formations that are concomitants of karma, all other formations (saṃskāra-skandha) as well as unconditioned phenomena (asaṃskṛta-dharma).

Regarding how many are derived matter (upādāya-rūpa) but not visible matter (sanidarśana-rūpa), etc.: three are not derived matter and are not visible matter; one should be analyzed, meaning that the mindfulness foundation of the body (kāya-smṛtyupasthāna) consists of three propositions.
Some derived matter is not visible matter, namely the eight bases and a portion of two bases;
some derived matter is also visible matter, namely one base.
Or, there are those that are neither derived matter nor visible matter, namely a small portion of one base (*āyatana*).

Regarding these four foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*), how many are derived matter and non-obstructive matter, and so forth? Three are neither derived matter nor obstructive matter; one should be analyzed, namely the foundation of mindfulness of the body (*kāyasmṛtyupasthāna*), which consists of three propositions.
Either derived matter is not resistant matter, namely a portion of one base;
or resistant matter is not derived matter, namely a portion of one base.
Furthermore, derived matter (*upādāya-rūpa*) may also be resistant matter (*sapratigha-rūpa*), namely the nine bases (*āyatana*) and a portion of one base.
Regarding the question of how many are profound because they are difficult to see, all are profound because they are difficult to see, and they are difficult to see because they are profound.

Regarding the question of how many wholesome factors have non-wholesome factors as their cause and so forth, all should be analyzed. Specifically, the application of mindfulness to the body consists of three propositions.
First, there are those that have wholesome factors as their cause but are not themselves wholesome; this refers to the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*) born from the maturation of wholesome karma.
Either it is wholesome and has the wholesome as its cause, namely, the wholesome aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*);

or it is neither wholesome nor has the wholesome as its cause, namely, all other indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) and unwholesome aggregates of form, excluding those that are wholesome and born of maturation (*vipākaja*).
The same applies to the applications of mindfulness regarding feeling and mind.
Regarding the application of mindfulness regarding phenomena (dharma-smṛtyupasthāna), there are four possibilities:
it may be wholesome and not have wholesomeness as its cause, namely, analytical cessation (pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha).

Some are wholesome as their cause but not wholesome themselves; this refers to the aggregates of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*) and formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) that arise from the maturation (*vipāka*) of wholesome karma. Some are both wholesome and have wholesome causes; this refers to the wholesome aggregates of perception and formations.

Some are neither wholesome nor have wholesome causes; this refers to all remaining neutral (*avyākṛta*) phenomena—excluding those aggregates of perception and formations arising from the maturation of wholesome karma—as well as unwholesome aggregates of perception and formations, along with space (*ākāśa*) and cessation not through deliberation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).
Regarding the question of how many are unwholesome (*akuśala*) and not caused by the unwholesome, all such cases should be analyzed.
That is to say, the application of mindfulness to the body (*kāyasmṛtyupasthāna*) consists of three propositions.
First, there are those that are caused by the unwholesome but are not themselves unwholesome; namely, the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*) born from the maturation (*vipāka*) of the unwholesome.
Either it is unwholesome and has the unwholesome as its cause, namely, the unwholesome aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*);

or it is neither unwholesome nor has the unwholesome as its cause, namely, all other indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) and wholesome aggregates of form, excluding those aggregates of form born of the maturation (*vipākaja*) of the unwholesome.
The application of mindfulness to feelings (vedanā-smṛtyupasthāna) consists of three propositions.

First, there are those that have unwholesome roots as their cause but are not themselves unwholesome; namely, the aggregate of feeling born of the maturation of unwholesome karma, and the aggregate of feeling associated with the view of a self-identity (satkāyadṛṣṭi) and the view of extreme adherence (antagrāhadṛṣṭi) within the desire realm.
Or it is unwholesome and has the unwholesome as its cause, namely, the aggregate of feeling that is unwholesome.

Or it is neither unwholesome nor has the unwholesome as its cause, namely, all other indeterminate and wholesome aggregates of feeling, excluding those aggregates of feeling born of the maturation of the unwholesome, and excluding those aggregates of feeling associated with the view of a self-identity and the view of extremes belonging to the desire realm.
The same applies to the application of mindfulness of the mind (*cittasmṛtyupasthāna*). Regarding the application of mindfulness of phenomena (*dharmasmṛtyupasthāna*), there are three propositions.

First, that which has unwholesome causes but is not itself unwholesome: namely, the aggregates of perception and formations born from the maturation of the unwholesome; as well as the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and the view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*) within the desire realm, together with their associated and co-existent aggregates of perception and formations.
Or [they are] unwholesome and also have the unwholesome as their cause, namely, the unwholesome aggregates of perception and formations (*saṃjñā-saṃskāra-skandha*).

Or [they are] neither unwholesome nor have the unwholesome as their cause, namely, with the exception of the unwholesome aggregates of perception and formations born of maturation (*vipākaja*), and with the exception of the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and the view of extreme adherence (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*) in the desire realm along with their associated and co-existent aggregates of perception and formations, all other indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) and wholesome aggregates of perception and formations, as well as the three unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*).

Regarding the question of how many are indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) but not having indeterminacy as their cause, all such cases should be analyzed. That is to say, the application of mindfulness to the body (*kāyasmṛtyupasthāna*) consists of three propositions.
First, there are those that have indeterminacy as their cause but are not themselves indeterminate; these are the unwholesome (*akuśala*) aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*).
Either it is indeterminate and has an indeterminate cause, namely the indeterminate aggregate of form;
or it is neither indeterminate nor has an indeterminate cause, namely the wholesome aggregate of form.
The same applies to the mindfulness establishments of sensation and mind.
Regarding the mindfulness establishment of phenomena (*dharmasmṛtyupasthāna*), there are four propositions:
that which is indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) but does not have indeterminacy as its cause, namely, space (*ākāśa*) and cessation not through deliberation (*apratisaṃkhyānirodha*).
Either that which has an indeterminate cause but is not itself indeterminate— namely, the unwholesome aggregates of perception and formations—
or that which is both indeterminate and has an indeterminate cause— namely, the indeterminate aggregates of perception and formations.

Some are neither indeterminate nor have indeterminacy as their cause; namely, the wholesome aggregates of perception (*saṃjñā*) and formations (*saṃskāra*), as well as analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).
Regarding how many are conditions (*pratyaya*) but not having a cause (*sahetuka*), three are both conditions and have a cause, while one should be analyzed.

That is to say, regarding the application of mindfulness to phenomena (*dharmasmṛtyupasthāna*): if it is conditioned (*saṃskṛta*), it is both a causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*) and possesses a cause; if it is unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), it is neither a causal condition nor does it possess a cause.

As for the question of how many are equivalent immediate conditions (*samanantara-pratyaya*) but not equivalent immediate objects (*samanantarālambana*), one is neither an equivalent immediate condition nor an equivalent immediate object, while three should be analyzed accordingly.
That is to say, the mindfulness of feeling (vedanā-smṛtyupasthāna) consists of three categories:

those that are immediate antecedents but not equal-and-immediate conditions; namely, the aggregate of feeling that is yet to arise in the future and is currently manifesting, as well as the aggregate of feeling at the moment of an Arhat’s death in the past or present.

Some are both equal-immediate [condition] and equal-immediate object-condition; that is, with the exception of the aggregate of sensation at the moment of death of past and present Arhats, all other past and present aggregates of sensation.

Or, there are those that are neither equal-and-immediate [condition] nor equal-and-immediate condition: namely, with the exception of the aggregate of feeling that is currently arising in the present within the future, all other remaining aggregates of feeling in the future.
The same applies to the mindfulness-establishment of mind (*cittasmṛtyupasthāna*).
The mindfulness-establishment of phenomena has three propositions.

First, there are those that are immediately antecedent conditions but not equal-and-immediate conditions: namely, future mental factors that are currently arising and are not associated with feeling; past and present mental factors not associated with feeling at the moment of an Arhat’s death; and the mental factors not associated with feeling that have already arisen or are currently arising during the attainment of non-conception or the attainment of cessation.

Some are both equal-immediate [conditions] and equal-immediate conditions: namely, with the exception of the non-feeling mental factors at the moment of death of a past or present Arhat, all other past and present non-feeling mental factors.

Or [there are those] that are neither equal-immediate [condition] nor equal-immediate condition, namely: with the exception of future mental factors not associated with feeling that are currently arising before one, all other future mental factors not associated with feeling; and with the exception of the mind-dissociated formations that are equal-immediate conditions, all other mind-dissociated formations as well as unconditioned phenomena.

Regarding the question of how many object-conditions (ālambana-pratyaya) do not possess an objective referent (ālambana), there are two cases: first, those object-conditions that do not possess an objective referent; second, those object-conditions that also possess an objective referent. These should be analyzed individually.

That is to say, regarding the application of mindfulness to phenomena (*dharmasmṛtyupasthāna*): if it is a mental factor (*caitta*), it is both a condition as an object-condition (*ālambanapratyaya*) and possesses an object; if it is not a mental factor, it is a condition as an object-condition but does not possess an object.

Regarding the question of how many predominant conditions (*adhipati-pratyaya*) are not themselves predominant, there are three that are both predominant conditions and predominant, while one should be analyzed as follows:

namely, the mindfulness-establishment of phenomena (*dharma-smṛtyupasthāna*). If it is conditioned (*saṃskṛta*), it is both a predominant condition and predominant; if it is unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), it is a predominant condition but not itself predominant.
Regarding how many floods (*ogha*) are not conducive to the floods (*anugata-ogha*), all should be analyzed as follows:

that is to say, the mindfulness-establishment of the body (*kāyasmṛtyupasthāna*), if it is with outflows (*sāsrava*), is conducive to the floods but is not itself a flood; if it is without outflows (*anāsrava*), it is neither a flood nor conducive to the floods.
The same applies to the applications of mindfulness regarding feelings and the mind.
Regarding the application of mindfulness regarding phenomena (*dharmasmṛtyupasthāna*), there are three categories:

some are conformable to the floods (*ogha*) but are not themselves floods; these refer to the contaminated aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*) and those contaminated aggregates of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) that are not subsumed within the floods.
Some are both floods (*ogha*) and favorable to the floods, namely the four floods.
Others are neither floods nor favorable to the floods, namely the untainted (*anāsrava*) aggregates of perception and formations, as well as unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛtadharma*).
The Four Noble Truths are the noble truth of suffering, the noble truth of the origin, the noble truth of cessation, and the noble truth of the path.
Regarding these four noble truths, how many possess form and so forth? One is formless; three should be analyzed.
That is to say, the Noble Truth of Suffering is either with form or without form.
What is with form?
It refers to ten bases (*āyatana*) and a portion of one base.
What is the formless?
It refers to one base and a small portion of another base.
The Noble Truth of Origination is also like this.
The bodily and vocal actions subsumed under the Noble Truth of the Path are material; all others are immaterial.
Regarding how many are visible and so forth: two are invisible, while two should be analyzed.
That is to say, regarding the Noble Truth of Suffering, there is both that which is seen and that which is not seen.
What is meant by "that which is seen"?
It refers to one location.
What is the "unseen"?
It refers to the eleven bases (*āyatana*).
The Noble Truth of Origination (*samudaya-satya*) is likewise.
Regarding "how many are with resistance" (*sapratigha*) and so forth: two are without resistance (*apratigha*), and two should be analyzed.
That is to say, the Noble Truth of Suffering is either with resistance or without resistance.
What is with resistance?
This refers to the ten bases.
What is non-resistant?
It refers to the two bases.
The Noble Truth of Origination is also like this.
Regarding how many are with outflows (*sāsrava*) and so forth: two are with outflows, and two are without outflows (*anāsrava*).
Regarding how many are conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) and so forth: three are conditioned, and one is unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
Regarding how many possess maturation (*savipāka*) and so forth: two have no maturation, while two should be analyzed.
That is to say, the Noble Truth of Suffering may either possess maturation or lack maturation.
What has maturation?
It refers to wholesome and unwholesome [phenomena] within the Truth of Suffering.
What lacks maturation?
This refers to the indeterminate *duḥkha-satya*.
The *samudaya-āryasatya* is likewise.

As for how many are dependently originated (*pratītyasamutpanna*), etc.: three are dependently originated, produced by causes (*hetuja*), and included within the world (*loka-saṃgṛhīta*); one is not dependently originated, not produced by causes, and not included within the world.
Regarding the question of how many [categories of] form (*rūpa*) it comprises and so forth: first, there is inclusion by name (*nāma*). Three [of the truths] should be analyzed.
That is to say, the Noble Truth of Suffering is either comprised of form or comprised of name.
What is comprised of form?
This refers to ten bases (*āyatana*) and a portion of one base.
What is meant by "inclusion" (*saṃgraha*)?
It refers to one base and a portion of another base.
The noble truth of origination is likewise.
Within the noble truth of the path, bodily and vocal actions are subsumed under form (*rūpa*); the remainder are all subsumed under name (*nāma*).
As for how many are subsumed under the internal bases (*ādhyātmikāyatana*), one is subsumed under the external bases (*bāhyāyatana*), and three should be analyzed.
That is to say, the Noble Truth of Suffering is either comprised within the internal bases or the external bases.
What is comprised within the internal bases?
It refers to the six internal bases.
What is included within the external bases?
It refers to the six external bases.
The Noble Truth of Origination is also like this.

That which is subsumed under the Noble Truth of the Path is included within the internal bases of mind, mental consciousness, and the [six] sense bases; all else is included within the external bases.

Regarding the question of how many types of knowledge constitute the thorough knowledge that is to be fully understood: all of them are the thorough knowledge that is to be fully understood by means of knowledge.
Abhidharmaprakaraṇapādaśāstra, Volume Twelve, Part on the Sarvāstivādins;
Abhidharmaprakaraṇapādaśāstra, Volume Thirteen.
Composed by the Venerable Vasumitra.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang by Imperial Decree.

Chapter Seven: Discerning the Thousand Questions, Part Four. Regarding the question of how many of these four noble truths are to be fully known through abandonment (*prahāṇa-parijñā*), two are to be fully known through abandonment, while two are not to be fully known through abandonment.
Regarding "how many should be abandoned," etc.: two should be abandoned, and two should not be abandoned.

Regarding "how many should be cultivated," etc.: one should be cultivated, one should not be cultivated, and two should be analyzed—namely, the Noble Truth of Suffering may either be cultivated or not be cultivated.
How should one cultivate?
It refers to the noble truth of suffering. How should one not cultivate? [It refers to that which is not the noble truth of suffering.]
This refers to the unwholesome and the indeterminate aspects of the Truth of Suffering;
the Truth of Origination is likewise.
Regarding how many are defiled and so forth: two are non-defiled, while two should be analyzed. That is to say, the Noble Truth of Suffering may be either defiled or non-defiled.
What is defiled?
It refers to the obscured truth of suffering (*saṃvṛta-duḥkhasatya*). What is undefiled?
This refers to the undefiled truth of suffering (*duḥkha-satya*).
The noble truth of origination (*samudaya-āryasatya*) is likewise.
Regarding how many are results (*phala*) but not possessors of results (*saphala*), three are both results and possessors of results, while one is a result but not a possessor of results.
Regarding how many are appropriated (*upātta*) and so forth: two are unappropriated; two should be analyzed. That is to say, the Noble Truth of Suffering is either appropriated or unappropriated.
What is that which is appropriated?
It refers to the Truth of Suffering comprised within one's own personal existence.
What is that which is not appropriated?
This refers to the Truth of Suffering that is not comprised within its own intrinsic nature;
the Noble Truth of Origination is likewise.
Regarding how many are derived from the great elements (*mahābhūta*) and so forth: one is not derived from the great elements, while three should be analyzed.
It refers to the Noble Truth of Suffering, which is either derived from the great elements (mahābhūta) or not derived from the great elements.
What is derived from the great elements?
It refers to nine bases (āyatana) and a portion of two bases.
What is not derived from the great elements?
It refers to one base and a portion of two bases.
The Noble Truth of Origination is also like this.
The bodily and vocal actions subsumed under the Noble Truth of the Path are derived from the primary elements (*mahābhūta*); all others are not derived from the primary elements.
Regarding how many have something superior: three have something superior, and one is unsurpassed.
Regarding how many are "existent" and so forth: two are existent, and two are non-existent.
Regarding how many are associated with causes and so forth: one is not associated with causes, and three should be analyzed.
That is to say, the matter and formations dissociated from mind subsumed under the Noble Truth of Suffering are dissociated from causes; all others are associated with causes.
The same applies to the Noble Truth of Origination.
Bodily and vocal actions and formations dissociated from mind that are subsumed under the Noble Truth of the Path are not associated with causes; all others are associated with causes.

Regarding the inclusion of these Four Noble Truths within the six wholesome bases (*ṣaḍ-kuśalāyatana*): the six wholesome bases include two truths and a portion of two truths, and those two truths and portions of two truths also include the six wholesome bases.

Regarding their mutual inclusion with the five unwholesome bases: the five unwholesome bases include a portion of the two truths, and a portion of the two truths also includes the five unwholesome bases.
Regarding the mutual inclusion with the seven indeterminate bases (*avyākṛtasthāna*), one should formulate four permutations (*catuṣkoṭi*).
First, there are those that are indeterminate bases but not truths (*satya*): namely, space (*ākāśa*) and cessation not through deliberation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).
Second, there are those that are truths but not indeterminate bases: namely, the two truths and a portion of the other two truths.
Alternatively, there are indeterminate bases that are also truths, namely a portion of two truths.
Or, there are things that are neither indeterminate bases nor truths; such a thing cannot be found.

Regarding their mutual inclusion with the three bases of outflows (*āsrava-sthāna*): the three bases of outflows include a portion of two truths, and a portion of two truths also includes the three bases of outflows.
Regarding their mutual inclusion with the five contaminated bases (*āsravasthāna*): the five contaminated bases include the two truths, and the two truths also include the five contaminated bases.
Regarding their mutual inclusion with the eight uncontaminated bases (*anāsravasthāna*), one should formulate four alternatives (*catuṣkoṭi*).
Either there are instances that are uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) but not truths (*satya*), namely space (*ākāśa*) and cessation not through deliberation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*);
or there are instances that are truths but not uncontaminated, namely the two truths;
or there are instances that are both uncontaminated and truths, namely the [other] two truths.
It is impossible for there to be that which is neither an untainted state (*anāsrava*) nor a truth (*satya*).
Regarding how many are past and so forth: three are either past, future, or present; one is neither past, nor future, nor present.
Regarding "how many are wholesome," etc.: two are wholesome, and two should be analyzed.
That is to say, the Noble Truth of Suffering may be wholesome, unwholesome, or indeterminate.
What is wholesome?
It refers to the five aggregates that are wholesome and subsumed under the truth of suffering.
What is unwholesome?
This refers to the unwholesome five aggregates subsumed under the truth of suffering.
What are the indeterminate?
This refers to the indeterminate five aggregates subsumed under the truth of suffering.
The Noble Truth of Origination is also like this.
Regarding how many are bound to the desire realm and so forth: two are not bound, and two should be analyzed.
That is to say, the Noble Truth of Suffering is either bound to the desire realm, or bound to the form realm, or bound to the formless realm.
What is that which is bound to the desire realm?
It refers to the five aggregates of the desire realm subsumed under the truth of suffering.
What is that which is bound to the form realm?
This refers to the five aggregates of the form realm (rūpadhātu) subsumed under the truth of suffering (duḥkhasatya).
What is that which is bound to the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu)?
It refers to the four aggregates of the formless realm subsumed under the truth of suffering.
The same applies to the noble truth of origination (*samudaya-satya*).
Regarding how many are "in training" (*śaikṣa*) and so forth: three are neither in training nor beyond training (*naiva-śaikṣa-nāśaikṣa*), while one should be analyzed.
That is to say, the noble truth of the path (*mārga-satya*) is either in training or beyond training.
What is the "learner" (*śaikṣa*)? It refers to the five aggregates of the learner.
What is the "one beyond learning" (*aśaikṣa*)? It refers to the five aggregates of one beyond learning.
Regarding these four noble truths, how many are to be abandoned by vision (*darśana-prahātavya*), and so forth? Two are not to be abandoned; two should be analyzed.
That is to say, the noble truth of suffering is either to be abandoned by seeing or to be abandoned by cultivation.
What is to be abandoned by seeing?

It refers to that which is abandoned by the patiences at the limit of clear realization for those who practice in accordance with faith or in accordance with the Dharma regarding the truth of suffering.

What, then, is this? It refers to the eighty-eight latent dispositions (anuśaya) abandoned through insight, the Truth of Suffering associated with them, and the non-associated formations (citta-viprayukta-saṃskāra) that arise together with them.
What is abandoned through cultivation?
It refers to that which is abandoned through cultivation by those in training who have seen the tracks of the Truth of Suffering.
Furthermore, what is this?

This refers to the ten latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) to be abandoned through cultivation, the truth of suffering (*duḥkhasatya*) associated with them, as well as the bodily and vocal actions arising from them, the formations dissociated from mind (*cittaviprayuktasaṃskāra*), and non-defiled suffering.
The noble truth of origination is also like this.
Regarding how many are not mind (*citta*), etc.: one is neither mind, nor mental factor (*caitta*), nor associated with mind; three should be analyzed.

That is to say, the form (*rūpa*) and formations dissociated from mind (*cittaviprayuktasaṃskāra*) included within the noble truth of suffering are neither mind, nor mental factors, nor associated with mind.
The aggregates of feeling, perception, and the associated aggregate of formations are mental factors that are associated with the mind;
the mind, intellect, and consciousness are exclusively the mind itself.
The Noble Truth of Origination is likewise.
The bodily and vocal actions, as well as the formations dissociated from mind, subsumed under the Noble Truth of the Path are neither mind, nor mental factors, nor associated with mind;
the aggregate of feeling, the aggregate of perception, and the associated aggregate of formations are mental factors associated with mind;
and mind, intellect, and consciousness are exclusively mind.

Regarding how many follow the mind (*cittānuvartin*) but are not associated with feeling (*vedanā-saṃprayukta*), one does not follow the mind and is not associated with feeling; three should be analyzed.
That is to say, regarding the Noble Truth of Suffering (*duḥkha-āryasatya*), there are four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*).

Some are concomitant with the mind but not associated with feeling, namely: bodily and vocal karma that is concomitant with the mind, the formations dissociated from mind (*citta-viprayukta-saṃskāra*), and feeling itself.
Some are associated with feeling but not concomitant with the mind, namely: mind, thought, and consciousness (*manovijñāna*).

Some are both concomitant with the mind and associated with feeling, namely the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*) and the associated factors of the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*).

Others are neither concomitant with the mind nor associated with feeling, namely all other material phenomena and non-associated formations, excluding those bodily and vocal actions that are concomitant with the mind and the formations dissociated from the mind (*citta-viprayukta-saṃskāra*).
The noble truth of cessation is also like this.
Regarding the noble truth of the path, there are four categories:

some are concomitant with the mind but not associated with feeling, namely bodily and vocal actions, as well as mental formations dissociated from the mind that are concomitant with the mind, together with feeling itself.
Some are associated with feeling but do not follow the mind, namely, the mind, mental faculty, and consciousness.
Some both follow the mind and are associated with feeling, namely, the aggregate of perception and the associated aggregate of formations.

Or [those factors] that do not follow the mind (*cittānuvartin*) and are not associated with feeling (*vedanā-saṃprayukta*): these refer to all other formations dissociated from mind (*citta-viprayukta-saṃskāra*), excluding those formations dissociated from mind that do follow the mind.

Regarding how many follow the mind and are associated with perception (*saṃjñā*) and formations (*saṃskāra*), one should understand this as being like the case of feeling, with the exception of their own intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).

Regarding the question of how many [factors] follow the movement of vitarka (applied thought) but are not associated with vicāra (sustained thought), and so forth: one is neither following the movement of vitarka nor associated with vicāra; three should be analyzed.
That is to say, the Noble Truth of Suffering consists of four propositions.

Some follow *vitarka* (initial inquiry) but are not associated with *vicāra* (sustained investigation), namely: bodily and vocal karma that follow *vitarka*, the formations dissociated from mind (*citta-viprayukta-saṃskāra*), and *vicāra* itself when it is associated with *vitarka*.

Some are associated with *vicāra* but do not follow *vitarka*, namely: *vitarka* itself, and those mental states and mental factors associated with *vicāra* that are not associated with *vitarka*, as well as the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkha-satya*).

Some follow the movement of vitarka (applied thought) and are also associated with vicāra (sustained thought), namely, the suffering truth consisting of mind and mental factors associated with vitarka and vicāra.

Others do not follow the movement of vitarka and are not associated with vicāra, namely, all remaining matter and formations dissociated from mind—excluding those bodily and vocal actions and formations dissociated from mind that follow the movement of vitarka—as well as vicāra that is not associated with vitarka, and the suffering truth consisting of mind and mental factors that are neither accompanied by vitarka nor vicāra.
The noble truth of cessation is also like this.
Regarding the noble truth of the path, there are four categories:

some follow the movement of vitarka (applied thought) but are not associated with vicāra (sustained thought), namely, bodily and vocal karma that follow the movement of vitarka, as well as formations dissociated from mind, and vicāra that is associated with vitarka.

Or, there are those associated with investigation (*vicāra*) that do not follow the movement of applied thought (*vitarka*), namely: applied thought itself and those mental states and mental factors associated with investigation but not associated with applied thought.

Or, there are those that follow the movement of applied thought and are also associated with investigation, namely: those mental states and mental factors associated with both applied thought and investigation.

Or [there are those] that neither follow after vitarka nor are associated with vicāra; namely, excluding those bodily and vocal actions and formations dissociated from mind that follow after vitarka, all other remaining bodily and vocal actions and formations dissociated from mind, as well as vicāra not associated with vitarka, and all mental states and mental factors (citta-caitta) that are without both vitarka and vicāra.
Regarding the question of how many [of the four truths] are views but not bases for views (*dṛṣṭi-sthāna*), one is neither a view nor a base for views, while three should be analyzed.
That is to say, the Noble Truth of Suffering is either both a view and a base for views, or a base for views but not a view.
"Or that which is both view and the locus of view" refers to the five defiled views and mundane right view; all others are loci of view but are not themselves views.
The Noble Truth of Origination is likewise.

The wisdom included within the Noble Truth of the Path that is not included within the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣaya-jñāna*) and the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpāda-jñāna*) is vision but not a basis for vision; all others are neither vision nor a basis for vision.

Regarding how many have the view of a self-identity (*satkāya-dṛṣṭi*) as their cause but are not causes of the view of a self-identity: two are not caused by the view of a self-identity and are not causes of the view of a self-identity; two should be analyzed.

That is to say, regarding the Noble Truth of Suffering: some have the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) as their cause but are not themselves causes for the view of a self-identity; some have the view of a self-identity as their cause and are also causes for the view of a self-identity; and some neither have the view of a self-identity as their cause nor are they causes for the view of a self-identity.

That which has the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) as its cause, but is not itself a cause of the view of a self-identity, refers to: (1) all other afflicted truths of suffering (*duḥkhasatya*), excluding the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkhadarśana-prahātavya*) in the past and present, along with their associated and co-existent factors; (2) excluding the pervasive latent tendencies (*sarvatragānuśaya*) abandoned through the vision of the origin (*samudayadarśana-prahātavya*) in the past and present, along with their associated and co-existent truths of suffering; (3) excluding the truths of suffering associated with the future view of a self-identity as its cause; and (4) excluding the future view of a self-identity, its associated factors, and their arising, aging, duration, and impermanence. All remaining afflicted truths of suffering are included.
That which has the view of a self as its cause and also has the view of a self as its cause refers to the truth of suffering previously excluded [from the category of the view of a self].
That which neither has the view of a self as its cause nor has the view of a self as its cause refers to the undefiled truth of suffering.
The Noble Truth of Origination is likewise.
Regarding how many are karma but not karmic maturation, and so forth: one is neither karma nor karmic maturation; three should be analyzed.
That is to say, the Noble Truth of Suffering consists of four propositions.
Either it is karma but not the maturation of karma, namely: bodily and vocal karma, as well as volition (*cetanā*) that is not subsumed under the maturation of karma;
or it is the maturation of karma but not karma, namely: the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkha-satya*) born from the maturation of karma that is not subsumed under volition.
Some are both karma and the maturation of karma (*karmavipāka*), namely, volition (*cetanā*) born of the maturation of karma.
Some are neither karma nor the maturation of karma, namely, all other truths of suffering (*duḥkhasatya*) excluding karma and the suffering born of the maturation of karma.
The noble truth of origination is also like this.

Regarding the noble truth of the path, bodily and vocal actions as well as volition (cetanā) subsumed within it are karma but not the maturation of karma; all others are neither karma nor the maturation of karma.
Regarding the question of how many karmas are not "concomitant with karma" (karma-anuvartin) and so forth: one is neither karma nor concomitant with karma; three should be analyzed.
That is to say, the Noble Truth of Suffering consists of four propositions.

Alternatively, there are those that are not concomitant with karma (*karmānuvartin*), namely: all other bodily and vocal actions—excluding those bodily and vocal actions that are concomitant with karma—as well as volition (*cetanā*).

Alternatively, there are those that are concomitant with karma but are not karma itself, namely: the aggregates of feeling (*vedanā-skandha*), perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*), and consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*), as well as those factors of the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) that are concomitant with karma but are not included within volition.
Some are both karma and follow along with karma, namely, bodily and vocal karma that follow along with karma.
Some are neither karma nor follow along with karma, namely, all other instances of the truth of suffering (duḥkhasatya) excluding both karma and that which follows along with karma.
The noble truth of origination is also like this.
Regarding the noble truth of the path, there are four propositions:
there are instances that are karma but do not follow along with karma, namely, volition (*cetanā*).

Some are concomitants of karma but are not karma itself; this refers to the aggregates of feeling, perception, and consciousness, as well as those factors of the aggregate of formations that are concomitants of karma but are not included within volition (*cetanā*).
Some are both karma and concomitants of karma; this refers to bodily and vocal karma.

Or [there are those] that are neither karma nor concomitants of karma: namely, with the exception of the formations dissociated from mind that are concomitants of karma, all other formations dissociated from mind.
Regarding how many are derived matter and not visible matter, etc.: one is neither derived matter nor visible matter; three should be analyzed.
That is to say, the Noble Truth of Suffering consists of three categories:
(1) derived matter that is not visible matter, namely the eight bases and a portion of two bases;
(2) derived matter that is also visible matter, namely one base.
Or, there are those that are neither derived matter nor visible matter; these refer to one base and a portion of two bases.
It is the same for the noble truth of cessation.
As for the noble truth of the path, the bodily and vocal actions subsumed within it are derived matter but not visible matter; all others are neither derived matter nor visible matter.

Regarding these Four Noble Truths, as for how many are derived matter (upādāya-rūpa) and non-obstructive matter (apratigha-rūpa), one is neither derived matter nor obstructive matter, while three should be analyzed.
That is to say, the Noble Truth of Suffering has four propositions:
either derived matter that is not resistant matter, which refers to a small portion of one base;
or resistant matter that is not derived matter, which refers to a small portion of one base.
Either it is derived matter that is also resistant matter— namely, the nine bases and a portion of one base—
or it is neither derived matter nor resistant matter— namely, one base and a portion of another base.
The noble truth of cessation is also like this.

Regarding the noble truth of the path, bodily and vocal actions subsumed within it are derived matter (*upādāya-rūpa*) but not obstructive matter (*sapratigha-rūpa*); all others are neither derived matter nor obstructive matter.
Regarding the statement "How many are profound because they are difficult to see," etc.: all are profound because they are difficult to see, and they are difficult to see because they are profound.

Regarding the question "How many are wholesome with non-wholesome as their cause," etc.: one is wholesome with non-wholesome as its cause, one is wholesome with wholesome as its cause, and two should be analyzed.
That is to say, the Noble Truth of Suffering has three categories:
(1) that which is caused by the wholesome but is not itself wholesome, namely, suffering that arises as the maturation (*vipāka*) of the wholesome;
(2) that which is both wholesome and caused by the wholesome, namely, the wholesome aspect of the Truth of Suffering.

Or [it is] neither wholesome nor has the wholesome as its cause; that is to say, with the exception of the Truth of Suffering born of the maturation of the wholesome, all other indeterminate and unwholesome Truths of Suffering.
The Noble Truth of Origination is also like this.
Regarding the question of how many are unwholesome and not caused by the unwholesome, etc.: two are neither unwholesome nor caused by the unwholesome; two should be analyzed.
That is to say, the Noble Truth of Suffering consists of three propositions.

Or, that which has the unwholesome as its cause but is not itself unwholesome refers to the truth of suffering born from the maturation of the unwholesome, as well as the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and the view of extreme adherence (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*) bound to the desire realm, along with the truths of suffering consisting of their associated and co-existent factors.
Or, it is unwholesome and has the unwholesome as its cause, namely, the unwholesome *duḥkhasatya* (truth of suffering).

Or, it is neither unwholesome nor has the unwholesome as its cause, namely, with the exception of the *duḥkhasatya* born of the maturation (*vipākaja*) of the unwholesome, and with the exception of the *satkāyadṛṣṭi* (view of a self-identity) and *antagrāhadṛṣṭi* (view of extremes) bound to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) along with their associated and co-existent factors and so forth, all other neutral (*avyākṛta*) and wholesome *duḥkhasatya*.
The same applies to the noble truth of origination (*samudaya-satya*).
Regarding how many are indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) yet not caused by the indeterminate, and so forth: two are not indeterminate and are not caused by the indeterminate; two should be analyzed.
That is to say, the Noble Truth of Suffering has three categories.
First, that which is indeterminate in its cause but not itself indeterminate: namely, unwholesome suffering.
Second, that which is both indeterminate and has an indeterminate cause: namely, indeterminate suffering.
Or [there are things] that are neither indeterminate nor have indeterminacy as their cause; this refers to the wholesome Truth of Suffering.
The Noble Truth of Origination is also like this.
Regarding how many causal conditions are not "having causes" and so forth: three are causal conditions and also have causes, while one is neither a causal condition nor has a cause.

Regarding the question of how many are equal-immediate [conditions] but not equal-immediate conditions, there is one that is neither an equal-immediate nor an equal-immediate condition, and three that should be analyzed.
That is to say, the Noble Truth of Suffering consists of three propositions.

Or, there are those that are equal-and-immediate [conditions] but not equal-and-immediate conditions: namely, future mind and mental factors of the truth of suffering that are currently arising; the mind and mental factors of the truth of suffering at the moment of death of a past or present Arhat; and the non-conceptual attainment (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*) and the cessation attainment (*nirodha-samāpatti*) when they have already arisen or are currently arising.

Or, there are those that are both samanantara and samanantarapratyaya; namely, with the exception of the past and present citta and caitta factors of the *duḥkhasatya* at the moment of the final death of an Arhat, all other past and present citta and caitta factors of the *duḥkhasatya*.

Or [there are those things] that are neither immediate antecedents nor equivalent immediate conditions: namely, with the exception of future mind and mental factors of the truth of suffering that are currently arising before one, all other remaining future mind and mental factors of the truth of suffering; with the exception of the immediately antecedent formations dissociated from mind, all other remaining formations dissociated from mind; and the matter of the truth of suffering.
The noble truth of cessation is also like this.
Regarding the noble truth of the path, there are three categories:

some are equal-and-immediate [conditions] but not equal-and-immediate objects. This refers to the future mind and mental factors of the noble truth of the path that are currently arising and about to manifest.
Some are both immediate antecedents and immediate conditions, namely: past and present minds and mental factors, as well as the Truth of the Path (*mārgasatya*).

Some are neither immediate antecedents nor immediate conditions, namely: with the exception of future minds and mental factors that are currently arising and the Truth of the Path, all other remaining future minds and mental factors, the Truth of the Path, and bodily and vocal actions and formations dissociated from mind (*cittaviprayuktasaṃskāra*) that are the Truth of the Path.

Regarding the question of how many are object-conditions (*ālambana-pratyaya*) but do not possess an object (*sālambana*), one is an object-condition that does not possess an object, while three should be analyzed.

Specifically, the form (*rūpa*) and the formations dissociated from mind (*citta-viprayukta-saṃskāra*) subsumed under the Noble Truth of Suffering are object-conditions but do not possess an object; all other [factors] subsumed under the Truth of Suffering are both object-conditions and possess an object.
The noble truth of cessation is also like this.

Those bodily and vocal actions and formations dissociated from mind included within the noble truth of the path are object-conditions (*ālambana-pratyaya*) but do not possess an object; all other [factors] included in the noble truth of the path are both object-conditions and possess an object.

Regarding the question of how many are dominant conditions (*adhipati-pratyaya*) but do not possess dominance (*adhipatitva*), one is a dominant condition but does not possess dominance, while three are both dominant conditions and possess dominance.
Regarding how many floods (*ogha*) are not concomitants of the floods (*anugata*), there is one that is neither a flood nor a concomitant of the floods, and two that should be analyzed.
That is to say, the Noble Truth of Suffering is either both a flood and a concomitant of the floods, or a concomitant of the floods but not a flood.
Regarding "these are the floods and also that which is conducive to the floods," this refers to the four floods.
All other portions of the truth of suffering (duḥkha-satya) are conducive to the floods but are not themselves floods.
The same applies to the noble truth of origination (samudaya-āryasatya).
Regarding the four dhyānas: they are the first dhyāna, the second dhyāna, the third dhyāna, and the fourth dhyāna.

As for how many of these four dhyānas possess form (*rūpa*) and so forth, all should be analyzed as follows: those bodily and vocal actions subsumed under the various dhyānas possess form; all others are without form (*arūpa*).
Regarding how many are "with visibility" (*sanidarśana*) and so forth: all are "without visibility.
Regarding how many are "with resistance" (*sapratigha*) and so forth: all are "without resistance.
Regarding how many are "with outflows" (*sāsrava*) and so forth: all should be analyzed; that is to say, the various dhyānas are either with outflows or without outflows.
What are the outflows (sāsrava)?
They are the five aggregates (pañcaskandha) associated with outflows that are subsumed within meditative absorption (dhyāna).
What are the outflow-free (anāsrava)?
This refers to the five untainted aggregates (anāsrava-skandha) subsumed under meditative absorption (dhyāna).
Regarding how many are conditioned (saṃskṛta): all are conditioned.

Regarding how many have maturation (savipāka): all should be analyzed; that is to say, those meditative absorptions which are tainted (sāsrava) have maturation, while those which are untainted (anāsrava) have no maturation.
Regarding the question "How many are dependently originated (*pratītyasamutpanna*) and so forth?"—all are dependently originated, produced by causes, and included within the worldly (*laukika*).

Regarding the question "How many are included within form (*rūpa*) and so forth?"—all should be analyzed as follows: those bodily and vocal actions (*kāyavākkarman*) included within the meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*) are included within form; all others are included within the mental (*nāman*).

Regarding the inclusion within the sense bases (*āyatana*), all such cases should be analyzed as follows: those comprised within the meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*)—namely, mind (*citta*), mental faculty (*manas*), and mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*)—are included within the internal sense bases; all others are included within the external sense bases.

Regarding the question of how many knowledges (*jñāna*) have as their object of thorough knowledge (*parijñeya*) that which is thoroughly known by the knowledge of all (*sarvajña-parijñā*), it is all [of them].

Regarding the question of how many of these four dhyānas have as their object of thorough knowledge that which is thoroughly known by the abandonment-knowledge (*prahāṇa-parijñā*), all should be analyzed: namely, those dhyānas that are with outflows (*sāsrava*) have as their object that which is thoroughly known by abandonment-knowledge, while those that are without outflows (*anāsrava*) do not have as their object that which is thoroughly known by abandonment-knowledge.

Regarding "how many should be abandoned," all [factors] should be analyzed: that is to say, those meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*) which are with outflows (*sāsrava*) should be abandoned, while those which are without outflows (*anāsrava*) should not be abandoned.
Regarding "how many should be cultivated," all [factors] are to be cultivated.
Regarding how many are defiled and so forth: all are non-defiled.
Regarding how many are results but do not possess results and so forth: all are both results and possess results.
Regarding how many are appropriated and so forth: all are non-appropriated.

Regarding the question of how many primary elements (*mahābhūta*) they are derived from, all cases should be analyzed as follows: bodily and vocal actions subsumed under the meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*) are derived from the primary elements; all others are not derived from the primary elements.
Regarding the question "How many are with superior?"—all are with superior.

Regarding the question "How many are existent?"—all should be analyzed: that is to say, among the dhyānas, those that are with outflows (sāsrava) are existent, while those that are without outflows (anāsrava) are not existent.

Regarding how many causes they are associated with and so forth, all should be analyzed as follows: those bodily and vocal actions and formations dissociated from mind that are subsumed under the dhyānas are not associated with causes; all others are associated with causes.

Regarding the inclusion of these four dhyānas within the six wholesome bases (*ṣaḍ-kuśala-sthāna*): a portion of the five wholesome bases includes the four dhyānas, and the four dhyānas likewise include a portion of the five wholesome bases.
Regarding their mutual inclusion with the five unwholesome bases (*akuśalasthāna*), they do not mutually include one another.
Regarding their mutual inclusion with the seven indeterminate bases (*avyākṛtasthāna*), they do not mutually include one another.
