Regarding their mutual inclusion with the three outflows bases (*āsravasthāna*), they do not mutually include one another.
Regarding the mutual inclusion between the five bases of outflows (*āsravasthāna*) and meditative absorption (*dhyāna*), one should formulate four permutations (*catuṣkoṭi*).
There may be bases of outflows that are not meditative absorption, namely, the five outflowing aggregates (*skandha*) not included within meditative absorption.
Either there are dhyānas that are not impure bases, namely the four untainted (anāsrava) dhyānas;
or there are impure bases that are also dhyānas, namely the four tainted (sāsrava) dhyānas.

Alternatively, there are cases that are neither tainted bases nor meditative absorptions; these refer to the untainted five aggregates not subsumed under the meditative absorptions, as well as unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*).
Regarding their mutual inclusion with the eight untainted bases (*anāsrava-āyatana*), one should formulate four permutations (*catuṣkoṭi*).

Alternatively, there are instances that are untainted (anāsrava) but not meditative absorption (dhyāna), namely: the untainted five aggregates not subsumed under meditative absorption, as well as unconditioned phenomena (asaṃskṛtadharma).
Alternatively, there are instances that are meditative absorption but not untainted, namely: the four tainted (sāsrava) meditative absorptions.
Either they are untainted bases and also meditative absorptions, namely the four untainted meditative absorptions;
or they are neither untainted bases nor meditative absorptions, namely the tainted five aggregates not subsumed under the meditative absorptions.
Regarding how many are past and so forth: all are either past, future, or present.
Regarding how many are wholesome and so forth: all are wholesome.

Regarding how many are bound to the desire realm and so forth: all should be analyzed; that is to say, the various dhyānas are bound to the form realm if they are with outflows (*sāsrava*), and are unbound (*apratisaṃyukta*) if they are without outflows (*anāsrava*).

Regarding how many are associated with training (*śaikṣa*), all should be analyzed as follows: the various dhyānas are either associated with training, or associated with no-more-training (*aśaikṣa*), or associated with neither-training-nor-no-more-training (*naivaśaikṣanāśaikṣa*).
What is the learner (śaikṣa)?
It refers to the five aggregates of the learner as comprised within meditative concentration (dhyāna).
What is the non-learner (aśaikṣa)?
This refers to the five aggregates of one beyond training (aśaikṣa) as comprised within meditative concentration (dhyāna).
What are those that are neither of training nor beyond training?
This refers to the five contaminated (sāsrava) aggregates as comprised within meditative concentration.

Regarding how many of these four dhyānas are abandoned by insight (*darśana-prahātavya*) and so forth: all should be analyzed. That is to say, those dhyānas that are with outflows (*sāsrava*) are abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-prahātavya*), while those that are without outflows (*anāsrava*) are not to be abandoned.

Regarding how many are not mind (*citta*) and so forth, all should be analyzed as follows: bodily and vocal actions (*kāya-vāk-karman*) subsumed under meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), as well as formations dissociated from mind (*citta-viprayukta-saṃskāra*), are neither mind, nor mental factors (*caitta*), nor associated with mind;

the aggregate of feeling (*vedanā-skandha*), the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*), and the associated portion of the aggregate of formations are mental factors that are associated with mind;
and mind, thought, and consciousness (*mano-vijñāna*) are exclusively mind.
Regarding how many [factors] follow the mind (*cittānuvartin*) but are not associated with feeling (*vedanā-samprayukta*), all should be analyzed as having four permutations (*catuṣkoṭi*).

First, those that follow the mind but are not associated with feeling: these include bodily and vocal actions (*kāya-vāk-karman*) subsumed under meditative absorption (*dhyāna*), as well as the mind-dissociated formations (*citta-viprayukta-saṃskāra*) that follow the mind, together with feeling itself.
Some are associated with feeling but do not follow the mind, namely, the mind-consciousness complex (manovijñāna) subsumed under dhyāna.
Some both follow the mind and are associated with feeling, namely, the aggregate of perception (saṃjñā-skandha) and the associated aggregate of formations (saṃskāra-skandha) subsumed under dhyāna.

Or [those factors] that neither follow the mind nor are associated with feeling: namely, with the exception of the formations dissociated from mind that follow the mind and are included within dhyāna, all other formations dissociated from mind included within dhyāna.

Regarding how many [factors] follow the mind (*cittānuvartin*), are not associated with perception (*saṃjñā*) or formations (*saṃskāra*), and so forth: excluding their own intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), they should be understood in the same manner as sensation (*vedanā*).

Regarding how many [factors] follow discursive thought (*vitarkānuvartin*), are not associated with sustained thought (*vicāra*), and so forth: three do not follow discursive thought and are not associated with sustained thought; one should be analyzed.
Regarding the first dhyāna, four permutations should be established.

There are cases that follow the movement of vitarka (applied thought) but are not associated with vicāra (sustained thought), namely: bodily and vocal karma subsumed under the first dhyāna, as well as formations dissociated from mind that follow the movement of vitarka, and vicāra itself.
Alternatively, there are those associated with investigation (*vicāra*) but not proceeding with applied thought (*vitarka*), namely, the applied thoughts included within the first dhyāna.

Alternatively, there are those that proceed with applied thought and are also associated with investigation, namely, the mental states and mental factors associated with both applied thought and investigation included within the first dhyāna.

Or, there are those that neither follow after vitarka nor are associated with vicāra; namely, all other formations dissociated from mind included within the first dhyāna, excluding those formations dissociated from mind that follow after vitarka and are included within the first dhyāna.
Regarding the question of how many views are not the locus of views (*na-dṛṣṭi-sthāna*) and so forth, all should be analyzed; that is, each has four permutations (*catuṣkoṭika*).

First, there are those that are views but not the locus of views: namely, untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-prajñā*) included within the dhyānas that is not subsumed under the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣaya-jñāna*) or the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpāda-jñāna*).
Or there are those that are views but not view-spheres, namely the four contaminated meditative absorptions (dhyāna) not included within "view.
Or there are those that are both views and view-spheres, namely the contaminated wisdom (prajñā) included within the meditative absorptions.
Or that which is neither view nor the locus of view, namely the four untainted (anāsrava) dhyānas not subsumed under view.

Regarding the question of how many have the view of a self-identity (satkāyadṛṣṭi) as their cause but are not causes of the view of a self-identity: all of them do not have the view of a self-identity as their cause, nor are they causes of the view of a self-identity.

Regarding the question of how many karmas are not karmic maturation (*vipāka*), all [categories] should be analyzed as follows: bodily and vocal karma subsumed under the meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*), as well as volition (*cetanā*), are karma but not karmic maturation; all others are neither karma nor karmic maturation.
Regarding the question of how many types of karma are not "concomitant with karma" (karmānuvartin) and so forth, all should be analyzed as having four permutations (catuṣkoṭi).
One permutation is: karma that is not concomitant with karma, namely, volition (cetanā) included within dhyāna.

Some are concomitants of karma but are not karma itself; this refers to the aggregates of feeling, perception, and consciousness included within meditative concentration (dhyāna), as well as the aggregate of formations (saṃskāra-skandha) that are concomitants of karma but are not themselves encompassed by volition (cetanā).
Some are both karma and concomitants of karma; this refers to bodily and vocal karma included within meditative concentration.

Or they are neither karma nor concomitants of karma; that is to say, with the exception of those formations dissociated from mind included within dhyāna that are concomitants of karma, all other formations dissociated from mind included within dhyāna.

Regarding the question of how many derived forms (*upādāyarūpa*) are not visible forms (*sanidarśana-rūpa*), all such cases should be analyzed as follows: those bodily and vocal actions (*kāyavākkarman*) subsumed under the meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*) are derived forms that are not visible forms; all others are neither derived forms nor visible forms.

Regarding these four dhyānas, as for how many are derived matter (*upādāya-rūpa*) but not resistant matter (*sapratigha-rūpa*), all should be analyzed as follows: those bodily and vocal actions (*kāya-vāk-karman*) subsumed under the various dhyānas are derived matter but not resistant matter; all others are neither derived matter nor resistant matter.
Regarding the statement "How many are profound because they are difficult to see," etc.: all are profound because they are difficult to see, and they are difficult to see because they are profound.
Regarding the statement "How many are wholesome and have the wholesome as their cause," etc.: all are wholesome and have the wholesome as their cause.
Regarding the question, "How many are unwholesome but do not have the unwholesome as their cause? and so forth: all [of them] are neither unwholesome nor have the unwholesome as their cause.
Regarding the question, "How many are indeterminate but do not have the indeterminate as their cause? and so forth: all [of them] are neither indeterminate nor have the indeterminate as their cause.
Regarding the question of how many are "conditioned by causes" (*hetu-pratyaya*) but not "having a cause" (*sahetu*), all are conditioned by causes and also have a cause.

Regarding the question of how many are "immediately preceding" (*samanantara*) but not "an immediately preceding condition" (*samanantara-pratyaya*), all should be analyzed; that is to say, for the first dhyāna, there are three cases.
Some are equal-and-immediate [conditions] but not equal-and-immediate conditions, namely, future mind and mental factors that are currently arising and manifesting.
Some are both equal-and-immediate and equal-and-immediate conditions, namely, past and present mind and mental factors.

Or [there are those that] are neither equal-immediate [conditions] nor equal-immediate conditions: namely, with the exception of future mind and mental factors that are currently arising and manifesting, all other future mind and mental factors, as well as bodily and vocal actions and formations dissociated from mind.
The second and third dhyānas are likewise.
In the fourth dhyāna, there are three categories.

There are those that are immediate antecedents but not equal-and-immediate conditions; these refer to future mind and mental factors that are currently arising and manifesting, as well as the unconditioned attainment (asaṃjñi-samāpatti) that has already arisen or is currently arising.
Some are both equal-and-immediate [condition] (*samanantara*) and equal-and-immediate condition (*samanantarapratyaya*), namely, past and present mind and mental factors (*cittacaittadharma*).

Some are neither equal-and-immediate nor equal-and-immediate condition, namely, all other future mind and mental factors—excluding those that are currently arising and manifesting—and all other formations dissociated from mind (*cittaviprayuktasaṃskāra*)—excluding the equal-and-immediate formations—as well as bodily and vocal actions (*kāyavākkarman*).

Regarding the question of how many objects of perception (*ālambana-pratyaya*) are not possessed of an object (*sālambana*), all such cases should be analyzed as follows: those bodily and vocal actions (*kāya-vāk-karman*) and formations dissociated from mind (*citta-viprayukta-saṃskāra*) that are included within the meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*) are objects of perception but are not possessed of an object; all others are both objects of perception and possessed of an object.
Regarding the question of how many *adhipatipratyaya* (dominant conditions) are not *sādhipati* (possessing dominance), all are *adhipatipratyaya* and also possess dominance.

Regarding the question of how many *ogha* (floods) are not *anuśrotaugha* (conducive to the floods), all should be analyzed as follows: among the various *dhyānas*, if they are with outflows (*sāsrava*), they are conducive to the floods but are not themselves floods; if they are without outflows (*anāsrava*), they are neither floods nor conducive to the floods.

The four immeasurables (apramāṇa) are: the immeasurable of loving-kindness (maitrī), the immeasurable of compassion (karuṇā), the immeasurable of sympathetic joy (muditā), and the immeasurable of equanimity (upekṣā).

Regarding how many of these four immeasurables possess form (rūpin) and so forth, all should be analyzed as follows: those bodily and vocal actions (kāya-vāk-karman) subsumed under the immeasurables possess form; the remainder are all without form (arūpin).
Regarding how many are with-visibility (*sanidarśana*) and so forth: all are without-visibility.
Regarding how many are with-obstruction (*sapratigha*) and so forth: all are without-obstruction.
Regarding how many are with-outflows (*sāsrava*) and so forth: all are with-outflows.
Regarding how many are conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) and so forth: all are conditioned.
Regarding how many have maturation (*savipāka*) and so forth: all have maturation.
Regarding how many are dependently arisen (*pratītyasamutpanna*) and so forth: all are dependently arisen, produced by causes, and included within the world (*loka*).

Regarding how many [of the] form-aggregates (*rūpa-skandha*) they are subsumed under, all should be analyzed as follows: those bodily and vocal actions (*kāya-vāk-karman*) subsumed under the immeasurables (*apramāṇa*) are subsumed under the form-aggregate; the rest are all subsumed under the name-aggregate (*nāma-skandha*).

Regarding the inclusion within the bases (*āyatana*), all such cases should be analyzed as follows: those comprised by the immeasurables (*apramāṇa*)—namely, the mind, mental consciousness, and internal bases—are included within the internal bases; all others are included within the external bases.
Regarding how many are to be fully known by the thorough knowledge of wisdom (*jñāna-parijñā*): all are to be fully known by the thorough knowledge of wisdom.

Regarding how many of these four immeasurables (*apramāṇa*) are to be fully known by the thorough knowledge of abandonment (*prahāṇa-parijñā*): all are to be fully known by the thorough knowledge of abandonment.
Regarding "how many should be abandoned," all are to be abandoned.
Regarding "how many should be cultivated," all are to be cultivated.
Regarding "how many are defiled," none are defiled.
Regarding the question "How many are results but not possess results," etc.: all are both results and possess results.
Regarding the question "How many are appropriated," etc.: all are non-appropriated.

Regarding the question "How many are derived from the great elements (*mahābhūta*)? etc.: all should be analyzed. That is to say, those bodily and vocal actions subsumed under the immeasurables (*apramāṇa*) are derived from the great elements; the rest are all not derived from the great elements.
Regarding "How many have the superior" (*sottara*): all of them have the superior.
Regarding "How many are with existence" (*bhava-saṃgṛhīta*): all of them are with existence.

Regarding "How many are associated with causes" (*hetu-saṃprayukta*): all should be analyzed as follows. That is to say, the bodily and vocal actions (*kāya-vāk-karman*) subsumed under the immeasurables (*apramāṇa*), as well as the formations dissociated from mind (*citta-viprayukta-saṃskāra*), are not associated with causes; the remainder are all associated with causes.

Regarding the inclusion of these four immeasurables within the six wholesome bases: a portion of the five wholesome bases includes the four immeasurables, and the four immeasurables also include a portion of the five wholesome bases.
Regarding their mutual inclusion with the five unwholesome bases (*akuśalasthāna*), they do not mutually include one another.
Regarding their mutual inclusion with the seven indeterminate bases (*avyākṛtasthāna*), they do not mutually include one another.
Regarding their mutual inclusion with the three outflows bases (*āsravasthāna*), they do not mutually include one another.

Regarding their mutual inclusion with the five contaminated bases (*āsravasthāna*): a portion of the five contaminated bases includes the four immeasurables (*apramāṇa*), and the four immeasurables also include a portion of the five contaminated bases.
Regarding their mutual inclusion with the eight untainted bases (*anāsrava-āyatana*), they do not include one another.
As for how many are past and so forth, all of them are either past, future, or present.
Regarding how many are wholesome and so forth: all are wholesome.
Regarding how many are bound to the desire realm and so forth: all are bound to the form realm.
Regarding how many are of the trainee and so forth: all are neither of the trainee nor of the non-trainee.
Regarding these four immeasurables (*apramāṇa*), as for how many are abandoned by vision (*darśana-heya*) and so forth: all are abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*).

As for how many are not mind (*citta*) and so forth: all should be analyzed. That is to say, the bodily and vocal actions (*kāya-vāk-karman*) and formations dissociated from mind (*citta-viprayukta-saṃskāra*) subsumed under the immeasurables are neither mind, nor mental factors (*caitta*), nor associated with mind;

whereas the aggregate of feeling (*vedanā-skandha*), the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*), and the associated portion of the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) are mental factors that are associated with mind.
Regarding "mind, intellect, and consciousness are only mind":

as for how many [factors] follow the mind in their transformation and are not associated with feeling, and so forth—all such cases should be analyzed, meaning that each has four permutations (catuṣkoṭi).

Or, there are those that follow the mind but are not associated with feeling (*vedanā-samprayukta*), namely: bodily and vocal actions (*kāya-vāk-karman*) subsumed under the immeasurables (*apramāṇa*), as well as the mind-dissociated formations (*citta-viprayukta-saṃskāra*) that follow the mind, together with feeling itself.
Some are associated with feeling but do not follow the mind, namely, the mind, mental consciousness, and mental factors subsumed under the immeasurables (*apramāṇa*).

Some both follow the mind and are associated with feeling, namely, the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*) and the associated aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) subsumed under the immeasurables.

Or those that do not follow the mind and are not associated with feeling, namely: all other formations dissociated from the mind included within the immeasurables (apramāṇa), excluding those formations dissociated from the mind that follow the mind and are included within the immeasurables.

Regarding how many [factors] follow the mind (*cittānuvartin*) and are not associated with perception (*saṃjñā*) or formations (*saṃskāra*), one should understand this as being like the case of feeling (*vedanā*), excluding its own nature.

Regarding how many [factors] follow discursive thought (*vitarkānuvartin*) and are not associated with sustained thought (*vicāra*), all should be analyzed; that is to say, the immeasurable of loving-kindness (*maitrī-apramāṇa*) involves four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*).

Or, there are those that follow vitarka (applied thought) but are not associated with vicāra (sustained thought), namely: bodily and vocal karma, as well as formations dissociated from mind, which are subsumed under the immeasurable state of loving-kindness (*maitrī-apramāṇa*) and follow vitarka; and furthermore, *vicāra* itself when it is associated with *vitarka*.

Or, there are those associated with vicāra but not following vitarka, namely: the vitarka subsumed under the immeasurable of loving-kindness (maitrī-apramāṇa), as well as the mind and mental factors associated with vicāra but dissociated from vitarka.

Some follow the movement of vitarka (applied thought) and are also associated with vicāra (sustained thought), namely, the mental states and mental factors associated with vitarka and vicāra that are subsumed under the immeasurable state of loving-kindness (*maitrī-apramāṇa*).

Others do not follow the movement of vitarka and are not associated with vicāra, namely: excluding those bodily and vocal actions and formations dissociated from mind (*citta-viprayukta-saṃskāra*) that follow the movement of vitarka and are subsumed under the immeasurable state of loving-kindness, all other bodily and vocal actions and formations dissociated from mind subsumed under the immeasurable state of loving-kindness; as well as the vicāra dissociated from vitarka subsumed under the immeasurable state of loving-kindness; and finally, the mental states and mental factors that are neither accompanied by vitarka nor vicāra and are subsumed under the immeasurable state of loving-kindness.
The same applies to the immeasurables of compassion and equanimity.
Regarding the immeasurable of sympathetic joy (*muditā*), there are four propositions.

First, there are those that follow the movement of initial inquiry (*vitarka*) but are not associated with sustained investigation (*vicāra*); these include the bodily and vocal actions, as well as formations dissociated from mind (*citta-viprayukta-saṃskāra*), that are subsumed under the immeasurable of sympathetic joy and follow the movement of initial inquiry, as well as sustained investigation itself.
Or, it may be associated with *vicāra* (sustained thought) but not follow *vitarka* (applied thought), namely, the *vitarka* subsumed under the immeasurable joy (*muditā-apramāṇa*).

Or, it may both follow *vitarka* and be associated with *vicāra*, namely, the mental states and mental factors (*citta-caitta*) associated with both *vitarka* and *vicāra* that are subsumed under the immeasurable joy.

Or [there are those] that neither follow after vitarka nor are associated with vicāra; namely, with the exception of the bodily and vocal karma and the formations dissociated from mind included within the immeasurable joy (*muditā-apramāṇa*) that follow after vitarka, all other bodily and vocal karma and formations dissociated from mind included within the immeasurable joy, as well as the minds and mental factors included within the immeasurable joy that are without vitarka and without vicāra.

Regarding the question of how many views are not bases for views (*na-dṛṣṭi-sthāna*) and so forth, all should be analyzed as follows: among the various immeasurables (*apramāṇa*), some are both views and bases for views, while others are bases for views but not views.
Regarding "this view is also a basis for views": this refers to wisdom (prajñā) subsumed under the immeasurables; all others are bases for views but are not themselves views.

As for how many have the view of a self-identity (satkāyadṛṣṭi) as their cause but are not causes of the view of a self-identity: none of them have the view of a self-identity as their cause, nor are they causes of the view of a self-identity.

Regarding how many karmas are not the maturation of karma (*karmavipāka*) and so forth: all should be analyzed. That is to say, the bodily and vocal actions as well as volition (*cetanā*) included within the immeasurables (*apramāṇa*) are karma but not the maturation of karma; all others are neither karma nor the maturation of karma.
Regarding how many karmas are not "concomitant with karma" (karmānuvartin) and so forth, all should be analyzed; that is, each has four permutations (catuṣkoṭi).
There may be that which is karma but not concomitant with karma, namely, volition (cetanā) subsumed under the immeasurables (apramāṇa).

Some are concomitants of karma but are not karma itself; this refers to the aggregates of perception and consciousness as included within the immeasurables (*apramāṇa*), as well as the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāraskandha*) that are concomitants of karma but are not comprised by volition (*cetanā*).
Some are both karma and concomitants of karma; this refers to bodily and vocal karma as included within the immeasurables.

Or they are neither karma nor concomitants of karma; that is to say, with the exception of those formations dissociated from mind included among the immeasurables that are concomitants of karma, all other formations dissociated from mind included among the immeasurables.

Regarding the question of how many derived forms (*upādāya-rūpa*) are not visible forms (*sanidarśana-rūpa*), all such cases should be analyzed as follows: those comprised within the immeasurable [categories] of bodily and vocal karma are derived forms that are not visible forms; all others are neither derived forms nor visible forms.
*Abhidharmaprakaraṇapādaśāstra*, Fascicle Thirteen.
*Abhidharmaprakaraṇapādaśāstra*, Fascicle Fourteen.
Composed by the Venerable Vasumitra.
