Chapter Seven on the Examination of the Thousand Questions, Part Five. Regarding the question of how many of these four immeasurables (*apramāṇa*) are derived matter (*upādāya-rūpa*) and not resistant matter (*sapratigha-rūpa*), all should be analyzed as follows: those bodily and vocal actions (*kāya-vāk-karman*) subsumed under the immeasurables are derived matter and not resistant matter; all others are neither derived matter nor resistant matter.
Regarding the phrase "difficult to see, therefore profound," etc.: all are profound because they are difficult to see, and they are difficult to see because they are profound.
Regarding the question "how many are wholesome and have wholesomeness as their cause," etc.: all are wholesome and also have wholesomeness as their cause.
Regarding the question of how many are unwholesome and yet not caused by the unwholesome, etc., all are neither unwholesome nor caused by the unwholesome.
Regarding the question of how many are indeterminate and yet not caused by the indeterminate, etc., all are neither indeterminate nor caused by the indeterminate.
Regarding the question of how many are "conditioned by causes" (*hetu-pratyaya*) but not "having a cause" (*sahetu*), all are conditioned by causes and also have a cause.

Regarding the question of how many are "immediately preceding" (*samanantara*) but not "an immediately preceding condition" (*samanantara-pratyaya*), all should be analyzed; that is, each has three propositions (*trikoṭika*).

Or there are those that are equal-and-immediate [conditions] but not equal-and-immediate conditions, namely, the future mind and mental factors currently arising that are subsumed under the immeasurables (*apramāṇa*).
Or there are those that are both equal-and-immediate and equal-and-immediate conditions, namely, the past and present mind and mental factors subsumed under the immeasurables.

Or there are those that are neither equal-and-immediate [conditions] nor equal-and-immediate conditions: namely, with the exception of those future mind and mental factors currently arising and manifesting which are included within the immeasurables, all other future mind and mental factors included within the immeasurables, as well as the bodily and vocal actions and the formations dissociated from mind included within the immeasurables.

Regarding the question of how many conditions as objects (ālambana-pratyaya) are not possessed of an object (sālambana), all such cases should be analyzed as follows: those comprised within the immeasurables (apramāṇa)—namely, bodily and vocal karma and formations dissociated from mind (citta-viprayukta-saṃskāra)—are conditions as objects but are not possessed of an object; all others comprised within the immeasurables are both conditions as objects and possessed of an object.
Regarding the question of how many are dominant conditions (*adhipati-pratyaya*) but do not possess dominance (*ādhipatya*), all are dominant conditions and also possess dominance.
Regarding the question of how many are floods (*ogha*) but are not favorable to the floods (*an-ogha-anukūla*), all are favorable to the floods and yet are not floods.
The four formless [attainments] are: the sphere of infinite space, the sphere of infinite consciousness, the sphere of nothingness, and the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
Regarding how many of these four formless states possess form and so forth: all of them are formless.
Regarding how many are "with visibility" (*sanidarśana*) and so forth: all are "without visibility.
Regarding how many are "with resistance" (*sapratigha*) and so forth: all are "without resistance.
Regarding how many are "with outflows" (*sāsrava*) and so forth: one is "with outflows," while three should be analyzed.
This refers to the sphere of infinite space, which is either contaminated (*sāsrava*) or uncontaminated (*anāsrava*).
What is contaminated?
It refers to the four contaminated aggregates (*skandha*) subsumed within the sphere of infinite space.
What are the untainted [states]?
They are the four untainted aggregates included within the sphere of infinite space.
The same applies to the sphere of infinite consciousness and the sphere of nothingness.
Regarding how many are conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) and so forth: all are conditioned.
Regarding how many have maturation (*savipāka*) and so forth: all should be analyzed.
That is to say, the sphere of infinite space (*ākāśānantyāyatana*) may have maturation, or it may be without maturation.
What is that which has maturation?
It refers to wholesome, out-flowing states of the sphere of infinite space.
What is that which has no maturation?
That is to say, they are neutral (*avyākṛta*) and untainted (*anāsrava*).
The same applies to the sphere of infinite space, the sphere of infinite consciousness, and the sphere of nothingness.
As for the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, it may be subject to karmic maturation (*vipāka*), or it may be without maturation.
What has maturation?
It refers to the wholesome [state] of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
What lacks maturation?
That is to say, the indeterminate sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
As for how many are dependently originated (*pratītyasamutpanna*), etc.: all are dependently originated, produced by causes (*hetuja*), and included within the world (*loka-saṃgṛhīta*).
As for how many are included within form (*rūpa*), etc.: all are included within name (*nāman*).

Regarding the question of how many are included within the internal bases (*ādhyātmikāyatana*) and so forth, all should be analyzed as follows: those comprised of the formless (*ārūpya*)—namely, mind (*citta*), mental faculty (*manas*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*)—are included within the internal bases; all others are included within the external bases (*bāhyāyatana*).

Regarding the question of how many knowledges (*jñāna*) have as their object of thorough knowledge (*parijñeya*) that which is thoroughly known by all-knowledge: it is the object of thorough knowledge for all-knowledge.

Regarding the question of how many of these four formless states (*ārūpya*) have as their object of thorough abandonment (*prahāṇa-parijñeya*) that which is thoroughly abandoned: one has as its object of thorough abandonment that which is thoroughly abandoned [by the path], while three should be analyzed. That is to say, regarding the three formless states: if they are contaminated (*sāsrava*), they have as their object of thorough abandonment that which is thoroughly abandoned; if they are uncontaminated (*anāsrava*), they do not have as their object of thorough abandonment that which is thoroughly abandoned.
Regarding "how many should be abandoned" and so forth: one should be abandoned, and three should be analyzed.
That is to say, among the three formless [aggregates], if they are with outflows (*sāsrava*), they should be abandoned; if they are without outflows (*anāsrava*), they should not be abandoned.
Regarding "how many are to be cultivated" and so forth, all should be analyzed.
That is to say, the sphere of infinite space may be cultivated or may not be cultivated.
How is it to be cultivated?
This refers to the wholesome sphere of infinite space.
What should not be cultivated?
This refers to the indeterminate sphere of infinite space.
The same applies to the sphere of infinite consciousness, the sphere of nothingness, and the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
Regarding how many are defiled and so forth, all [of these] should be analyzed accordingly.
That is to say, the sphere of infinite space is either defiled or undefiled. What is defiled?
It refers to the obscured sphere of infinite space.
What is non-defiled?
It refers to the unobscured [states of] the sphere of infinite space;
the same applies to the sphere of infinite consciousness, the sphere of nothingness, and the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
Regarding the question of how many are results but not possess results, all are both results and possess results.
Regarding the question of how many are appropriated (*upātta*), all are non-appropriated.
Regarding the question of how many are derived from the great elements (*mahābhūta*), all are not derived from the great elements.
Regarding "How many are with superior [objects] (*sottara*)?"—all are with superior objects.
Regarding "How many are existence (*bhava*)?"—one is existence; three should be analyzed.
That is to say, as for the three formless aggregates (*ārūpya*), if they are contaminated (*sāsrava*), they are existence; if they are uncontaminated (*anāsrava*), they are not existence.

Regarding how many causes they are associated with and so forth, all should be analyzed as follows: those formations dissociated from mind (citta-viprayukta-saṃskāra) that are included within the formless realm (ārūpya-dhātu) are not associated with causes; all others are associated with causes.
Regarding the inclusion of these four formless states within the six wholesome bases (*kuśalāyatana*), one should formulate four permutations (*catuṣkoṭi*).

There are cases that are wholesome bases but not formless states; namely, the wholesome aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*), the four aggregates not included among the formless states that are wholesome, and analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyānirodha*).
Alternatively, there are those that are neither formless (*ārūpya*) nor wholesome (*kuśala*), namely: the four formless states that are neutral (*avyākṛta*);
or those that are both wholesome and formless, namely: the four wholesome formless states;

or those that are neither wholesome nor formless, namely: the five unwholesome aggregates (*skandha*), the neutral aggregate of form, the four neutral aggregates not included within the formless realm, as well as space (*ākāśa*) and non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).
Regarding their mutual inclusion with the five unwholesome bases (*akuśala-sthāna*), they do not include one another.
Regarding their mutual inclusion with the seven indeterminate bases (*avyākṛta-sthāna*), four alternatives (*catuṣkoṭi*) should be formulated.

There may be that which is an indeterminate base but not the formless (*ārūpya*): namely, the indeterminate aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*), the four aggregates not included in the formless that are indeterminate, as well as space (*ākāśa*) and non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).
Either there are formless states that are not indeterminate, namely the four wholesome formless attainments;
or there are indeterminate states that are also formless, namely the four indeterminate formless attainments;

or there are states that are neither non-indeterminate nor formless, namely the five unwholesome aggregates, the wholesome aggregate of form, the four wholesome aggregates not included within the formless attainments, and analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).
Regarding the mutual inclusion with the three bases of outflows (*āsravasthāna*), one should formulate four alternatives (*catuṣkoṭi*).
Either they are bases of outflows but not formless (*arūpa*); that is, one base of outflows and a portion of two bases of outflows.
Either they are formless (*arūpa*) but not bases of outflows (*āsravasthāna*), namely the four formless [realms] not included within the bases of outflows;
or they are both bases of outflows and formless, namely a portion of two bases of outflows.

Alternatively, there are those that are neither outflows (*āsrava*) nor formless (*ārūpya*); namely, the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*), the four aggregates not subsumed under the outflows or the formless, and unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛtadharma*).
Regarding their mutual inclusion with the five contaminated bases (*sāsravāyatana*), one should formulate four permutations (*catuṣkoṭi*).
There are cases that are tainted bases but not formless: namely, the tainted aggregate of form and the four tainted aggregates not included within the formless realm.
Or there are cases that are formless but not tainted bases: namely, a portion of the three formless realms.
There are those that are both with outflows (*sāsrava*) and formless (*ārūpya*), namely: one realm of the formless (*ārūpyadhātu*) and a portion of the three realms of the formless.

Or there are those that are neither with outflows nor formless, namely: the untainted aggregate of form (*anāsrava-rūpaskandha*), the four untainted aggregates not subsumed under the formless realms, and unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛtadharma*).
Regarding the mutual inclusion between the eight untainted bases (*anāsrava-āyatana*) and [the aggregates], four permutations (*catuṣkoṭi*) should be established.

First, there are those that are untainted bases but not formless (*ārūpya*): namely, the untainted aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*), the four untainted aggregates not included within the formless realm, and unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*).
Either they are formless but not untainted, which refers to one formless realm and a portion of three formless realms;
or they are both untainted and formless, which refers to a portion of three formless realms.
Or, it is neither an untainted base nor formless; this refers to the tainted aggregate of form and the four tainted aggregates not subsumed under the formless realm.
Regarding how many are past and so forth: all are either past, future, or present.
Regarding how many are wholesome and so forth, all should be analyzed.
That is to say, the sphere of infinite space is either wholesome or indeterminate.
What is wholesome?
This refers to the four virtuous aggregates included within the sphere of infinite space.
What are the indeterminate ones?
They refer to the four indeterminate aggregates included within the sphere of infinite space.
The same applies to the sphere of infinite consciousness, the sphere of nothingness, and the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
Regarding how many are bound to the desire realm and so forth: one is bound to the formless realm, while three should be analyzed.
That is to say, the three formless [attainments] are either associated with the formless realm if they are with-outflow (sāsrava), or unassociated if they are outflow-free (anāsrava).
Regarding how many are "in training" (śaikṣa) and so forth: one is neither-in-training-nor-beyond-training (naivaśaikṣanāśaikṣa), while three should be analyzed.
This refers to the sphere of infinite space, which may be of the learner (*śaikṣa*), the one beyond learning (*aśaikṣa*), or neither of the two (*naivaśaikṣanāśaikṣa*).
What is of the learner?
It refers to the four aggregates (*skandha*) of the learner comprised within the sphere of infinite space.
What is that which is beyond training (*aśaikṣa*)?
It refers to the four aggregates (*skandha*) beyond training included within the sphere of infinite space (*ākāśānantyāyatana*).
What is that which is neither in training nor beyond training (*naivaśaikṣanāśaikṣa*)?
This refers to the four contaminated aggregates (*skandha*) subsumed under the sphere of infinite space (*ākāśānantyāyatana*).
The same applies to the sphere of infinite consciousness (*vijñānānantyāyatana*) and the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*).
Regarding how many of these four formless spheres (*ārūpya*) are abandoned by insight (*darśana-prahātavya*) and so forth, all must be analyzed individually.
That is to say, the sphere of infinite space is either abandoned by insight (*darśana-heya*), abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*), or not abandoned (*aheya*).
What is abandoned by insight?

It refers to that which is abandoned by the patiences at the limit of clear realization (*abhisamaya-antya-kṣānti*) for those who follow by faith (*śraddhānusārin*) or follow by dharma (*dharmānusārin*) regarding the sphere of infinite space.
What, furthermore, is this?

It refers to the twenty-eight latent dispositions (anuśaya) abandoned through seeing, as well as the mind and the formations dissociated from mind that arise in association with them, within the sphere of infinite space (ākāśānantyāyatana).
What is that which is to be abandoned through cultivation?
It refers to the state of the learner (śaikṣa) who has seen the tracks [of the path] and whose [defilements] of the sphere of infinite space are to be abandoned through cultivation.
Furthermore, what is this?

This refers to the three latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) to be abandoned by cultivation, as well as the mental factors dissociated from mind (*citta-viprayukta-saṃskāra*) that are associated with or arise from them, together with the non-defiled, contaminated sphere of infinite space (*ākāśānantyāyatana*).
What is not to be abandoned?
It refers to the untainted (anāsrava) sphere of infinite space;
the spheres of infinite consciousness and nothingness are likewise so.
The sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception is either abandoned by seeing or abandoned by cultivation.
What is abandoned by seeing?
It refers to that which is abandoned by the patiences at the limit of clear realization for those who follow by faith or follow by dharma within the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
What, furthermore, is this?

It refers to the twenty-eight latent dispositions (anuśaya) abandoned through insight, as well as the minds associated with them and the formations dissociated from mind that arise from them, all belonging to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana).
What is that which is to be abandoned through cultivation?
It refers to that which is to be abandoned through cultivation by one in training (śaikṣa) who has seen the path, within the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
Furthermore, what is this?

It refers to the three latent dispositions (anuśaya) abandoned through cultivation, as well as the mental factors dissociated from mind that arise in association with them, and the non-defiled [state] of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.

Regarding "how many are not mind (*citta*) and so forth," all should be analyzed as follows: those conditioned factors dissociated from mind (*cittaviprayuktasaṃskāra*) included within the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) are neither mind, nor mental factors (*caitasika*), nor associated with mind;

the aggregate of feeling (*vedanā-skandha*), the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*), and the associated portion of the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) are mental factors associated with mind;
and mind, thought (*manas*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*) are exclusively mind.

Regarding the question of how many [factors] follow the mind (*cittānuvartin*) but are not associated with feeling (*vedanā-saṃprayukta*), all should be analyzed; that is, each has four permutations (*catuṣkoṭi*).

First, those that follow the mind but are not associated with feeling: these consist of the formations dissociated from mind (*citta-viprayukta-saṃskāra*) that follow the mind and are included within the formless realm (*ārūpya-dhātu*), as well as feeling itself.
Some are associated with feeling but do not follow the mind, namely the mind, mental consciousness, and mental factors subsumed under the formless realm.
Some both follow the mind and are associated with feeling, namely the aggregate of perception and the aggregate of formations associated with [the mind] subsumed under the formless realm.

Or those that do not follow the mind and are not associated with feeling: namely, with the exception of the formations dissociated from mind that are included within the formless realm and which do follow the mind, all other formations dissociated from mind included within the formless realm.

Regarding how many follow the mind (*cittānuvartin*) and are associated with neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatanasamprayukta*), one should understand them as being like feeling (*vedanā*), excluding their own intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).

Regarding how many follow discursive thought (*vitarkānuvartin*) and are not associated with sustained thought (*avicārasamprayukta*), all [of these] do not follow discursive thought and are not associated with sustained thought.
Regarding the question of how many views are not the locus of view (*na-dṛṣṭi-sthāna*) and so forth, all [categories] should be analyzed.
Specifically, regarding the sphere of infinite space (*ākāśānantyāyatana*), four alternatives (*catuṣkoṭi*) should be established.

There may be that which is a view but not the locus of view; this refers to the untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-prajñā*) included within the sphere of infinite space that is not subsumed by the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣaya-jñāna*) and the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpāda-jñāna*).
Or there are cases where it is a station of views but not itself a view; this refers to the contaminated *ākāśānantyāyatana* (sphere of infinite space) that is not subsumed under views.
Or there are cases where it is both a view and a station of views; this refers to the five defiled views and mundane right view (*laukika-samyag-dṛṣṭi*) subsumed within the *ākāśānantyāyatana*.
Or it is that which is neither vision nor the locus of vision; this refers to the uncontaminated (anāsrava) sphere of infinite space that is not subsumed under vision.
The same applies to the spheres of infinite consciousness and nothingness.

Regarding the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*), there are cases where it is both a view (*dṛṣṭi*) and a locus of views (*dṛṣṭisthāna*), and cases where it is a locus of views but not a view.

That which is both a view and a locus of views refers to the five defiled views and mundane right view (*laukikī samyagdṛṣṭi*) subsumed within the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception; all other factors of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception are loci of views but are not views themselves.

Regarding the question of how many [factors] have the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) as their cause but are not themselves causes of the view of a self-identity, all such cases should be analyzed.

That is to say, regarding the sphere of infinite space (*ākāśānantyāyatana*), some have the view of a self-identity as their cause but are not causes of the view of a self-identity; some have the view of a self-identity as their cause and are also causes of the view of a self-identity; and some do not have the view of a self-identity as their cause and are not causes of the view of a self-identity.

Regarding those things that have the view of a self (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) as their cause but are not causes of the view of a self: this refers to all other defiled *ākāśānantyāyatana* (sphere of infinite space), excluding the past and present latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya*), along with their associated and co-existent factors; also excluding the past and present universal latent dispositions abandoned through the vision of origination (*samudaya-darśana-prahātavya*), along with their associated and co-existent *ākāśānantyāyatana*; also excluding the future *ākāśānantyāyatana* associated with the view of a self; and also excluding the future *ākāśānantyāyatana* consisting of the arising, aging, duration, and impermanence of the view of a self and its associated factors. All remaining defiled *ākāśānantyāyatana* fall into this category.
That which has the view of a self (satkāyadṛṣṭi) as its cause and also has the view of a self as its cause refers to the previously excluded sphere of infinite space (ākāśānantyāyatana).
That which does not have the view of a self as its cause and does not have the view of a self as its cause refers to the non-defiled sphere of infinite space.
The same applies to the sphere of infinite consciousness, the sphere of nothingness, and the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
Regarding how many are karma and not the maturation of karma, all should be analyzed accordingly.
Regarding the sphere of infinite space (*ākāśānantyāyatana*), four permutations (*catuṣkoṭi*) should be established: 1.
That which is karma but not the maturation (*vipāka*) of karma: namely, volition (*cetanā*) that is not subsumed under the maturation of the sphere of infinite space.
2. That which is the maturation of karma but not karma: namely, the sphere of infinite space born from the maturation of karma that is not subsumed under volition.
Or, it may be both karma and the maturation of karma (*karmavipāka*), namely, the volition (*cetanā*) born of the maturation of karma in the Sphere of Infinite Space (*ākāśānantyāyatana*).
Or, it may be neither karma nor the maturation of karma, namely, all other states of the Sphere of Infinite Space excluding both karma and the volition born of the maturation of karma in that sphere.
The same applies to the sphere of infinite consciousness, the sphere of nothingness, and the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
Regarding how many [factors] are not concomitant with karma, and so forth, all should be analyzed accordingly.
Regarding the sphere of infinite space, there are three categories: 1.
That which is karma but does not follow along with karma (*karmānuvartin*): namely, volition (*cetanā*) included within the sphere of infinite space.

2. That which follows along with karma but is not karma: namely, the aggregates of feeling, perception, and consciousness included within the sphere of infinite space, as well as the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāraskandha*) that follows along with karma but is not subsumed under volition.

Or they are neither karma nor concomitants of karma; that is to say, with the exception of the formations dissociated from mind that are concomitants of karma and are included within the sphere of infinite space, all other formations dissociated from mind included within the sphere of infinite space.
The same applies to the sphere of infinite consciousness, the sphere of nothingness, and the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
Regarding how many derived forms are not visible forms and so forth: all [of them] are not derived forms and are not visible forms.
Regarding these four formless states (*ārūpya*), as for how many are derived matter (*upādāya-rūpa*) and not resistant matter (*sapratigha-rūpa*), all are neither derived matter nor resistant matter.
Regarding how many are profound because they are difficult to see, all are profound because they are difficult to see, and difficult to see because they are profound.
Regarding the question of how many wholesome states have non-wholesome states as their cause and so forth, all such cases should be analyzed.
Specifically, the sphere of infinite space (*ākāśānantyāyatana*) consists of three propositions.

First, there are those that have wholesome states as their cause but are themselves not wholesome; this refers to the sphere of infinite space that arises as the maturation (*vipāka*) of wholesome karma.
Either it is wholesome and has the wholesome as its cause, namely the wholesome sphere of infinite space;
or it is neither wholesome nor has the wholesome as its cause, namely all other indeterminate spheres of infinite space, excluding those born of the maturation of the wholesome.
The same applies to the latter three formless attainments (*ārūpya*).
Regarding the question of how many are unwholesome (*akuśala*) but not having the unwholesome as their cause, and so forth: all are neither unwholesome nor have the unwholesome as their cause.
Regarding the question of how many are indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) but not having the indeterminate as their cause, and so forth: all should be analyzed accordingly.

This refers to the sphere of infinite space (*ākāśānantyāyatana*), which is either indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) and has an indeterminate cause, or is not indeterminate and does not have an indeterminate cause.
That which is indeterminate and has an indeterminate cause refers to the indeterminate sphere of infinite space.
That which is neither indeterminate nor has indeterminate [factors] as its cause refers to the wholesome sphere of infinite space;
the same applies to the latter three formless spheres.
Regarding how many are object-conditions (ālambana-pratyaya) that are not "having a cause" (sahetu), all are both object-conditions and "having a cause."
Regarding the question of how many are equal-immediate [conditions] but not equal-immediate conditions, all should be analyzed as follows:
the sphere of infinite space (*ākāśānantyāyatana*) consists of three categories.

It may be an equal-immediate condition but not an equal-immediate condition; this refers to the mind and mental factors of the sphere of infinite space that are yet to arise in the future and are currently manifesting, as well as the mind and mental factors of the sphere of infinite space at the moment of the final passing away of an Arhat in the past or present.

Or, it may be both an immediately preceding condition (*samanantara*) and an immediately preceding object-condition (*samanantarālambana-pratyaya*). This refers to all other past and present mind-moments and mental factors of the sphere of infinite space (*ākāśānantyāyatana*), excluding those occurring at the moment of the final death of a past or present Arhat.

Or [there are factors] that are neither equal-and-immediate [factors] nor equal-and-immediate conditions; namely, with the exception of future mind and mental factors of the sphere of infinite space that are currently arising before one, all other future mind and mental factors of the sphere of infinite space, as well as the formations dissociated from mind associated with the sphere of infinite space.
It is the same for the Sphere of Infinite Consciousness and the Sphere of Nothingness.
Regarding the Sphere of Neither-Perception-Nor-Non-Perception, there are three propositions.

It may be an immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*) but not an object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*). This refers to: (1) future mind and mental factors of the Sphere of Neither-Perception-Nor-Non-Perception that are currently arising; (2) past and present mind and mental factors of the Sphere of Neither-Perception-Nor-Non-Perception at the moment an Arhat passes away; and (3) the meditative attainment of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*) that has already arisen and is currently ceasing.

Or, it may be both an equal-and-immediate [condition] and an equal-and-immediate object-condition (*samanantarapratyaya*). This refers to all other past and present minds and mental factors of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*), excluding those at the moment of the final death of an Arhat in the past or present.

Or [there are those] that are neither equal-immediate [condition] nor equal-immediate condition, namely: with the exception of the future mind and mental factors of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception that are currently arising before one, all other future mind and mental factors of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception; and with the exception of the future mental formations dissociated from mind of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception that are equal-immediate [conditions], all other mental formations dissociated from mind of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
Regarding how many object-conditions (ālambana-pratyaya) are not possessed of an object (sālambana), all [categories] should be analyzed as follows:

those formations dissociated from mind (citta-viprayukta-saṃskāra) subsumed under the formless realm (ārūpya-dhātu) are object-conditions but are not possessed of an object; all other [factors] of the formless realm are both object-conditions and possessed of an object.
Regarding the question of how many predominant conditions (*adhipati-pratyaya*) are not "possessing predominance" (*sādhipati*), all predominant conditions are indeed "possessing predominance.
Regarding the question of how many floods (*ogha*) are not "conducive to floods" (*anugata-ogha*), all [of these] should be analyzed.
That is to say, the sphere of infinite space has three categories:
it may be concordant with the floods but not itself a flood, namely, the contaminated sphere of infinite space that is not subsumed under the floods.
Some are both floods (*ogha*) and favorable to the floods, namely a portion of the three floods.
Some are neither floods nor favorable to the floods, namely the untainted (*anāsrava*) sphere of infinite space (*ākāśānantyāyatana*).
The same applies to the sphere of infinite consciousness and the sphere of nothingness.
As for the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, it is either both an outflow and in accordance with the outflows, or in accordance with the outflows but not an outflow itself.
Regarding the floods (*ogha*) and that which is conducive to the floods: this refers to a portion of the three floods; the remainder is all conducive to the floods but is not itself a flood.

There are four types of practitioners of meditative concentration (*dhyāna*): first, there is the practitioner of concentration who, through practice, cultivation, and frequent application, attains dwelling in happiness in the present life (*dṛṣṭadharmasukhavihāra*).
Second, there are those who cultivate concentration; through its practice, cultivation, and frequent application, they attain superior knowledge and vision.
Third, there are those who cultivate concentration; through its practice, cultivation, and frequent application, they attain analytical wisdom.
Regarding the four meditative absorptions (dhyāna) that, when practiced, cultivated, or frequently performed, lead to the exhaustion of all outflows (āsrava):

as for how many of these four cultivated meditative absorptions possess form (rūpin), all should be analyzed. Specifically, the bodily and vocal actions subsumed under these cultivated meditative absorptions possess form; the remainder are all without form (arūpin).
Regarding how many are with-visual-perception (*sadarśana*) and so forth: all are without-visual-perception (*adarśana*).
Regarding how many are with-obstruction (*sapratigha*) and so forth: all are without-obstruction (*apratigha*).
Regarding how many are with-outflows (*sāsrava*) and so forth: one is with-outflows, one is without-outflows (*anāsrava*), and two should be analyzed.
This refers to dwelling in happiness in the present life, which may be either with outflows (*sāsrava*) or without outflows (*anāsrava*).
What is "with outflows"? It refers to the five aggregates with outflows (*pañca-skandhāḥ sāsravāḥ*) that are subsumed under dwelling in happiness in the present life.
What is the untainted (*anāsrava*)?
It refers to the five untainted aggregates (*skandha*) comprised within the dwelling in happiness in the present life (*dṛṣṭadharmasukhavihāra*).
As for discerning wisdom (*prajñā-vibhāga*), it may be either tainted or untainted.
What are the outflows (sāsrava)?
They refer to the five aggregates of clinging (pañca-upādānaskandha) that are comprised within the wisdom of conceptualization.
What are the outflow-free (anāsrava)?
This refers to the five untainted aggregates (*anāsrava-skandha*).
Regarding how many are conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) and so forth: all of them are conditioned.

Regarding how many have maturation (*savipāka*) and so forth: one has maturation, one has no maturation, and two should be analyzed. That is to say, for the sake of dwelling in happiness in the present life (*dṛṣṭadharmasukhavihāra*) and for the sake of analytical wisdom (*pratisaṃkhyā-prajñā*): if they are tainted (*sāsrava*), they have maturation; if they are untainted (*anāsrava*), they have no maturation.
Regarding how many are dependently originated (*pratītyasamutpanna*), and so forth: all are dependently originated, produced by causes, and included within the world (*loka*).

Regarding how many are included within form (*rūpa*), and so forth: all should be analyzed. That is to say, bodily and vocal actions included within meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) are included within form; the rest are all included within the mental (*nāman*).

Regarding the question of which bases (āyatana) they are subsumed under, all such cases should be analyzed as follows: those states of mind, mentation, and consciousness included within meditative concentration are subsumed under the internal bases; all others are subsumed under the external bases.
Regarding the question of how many are fully known by the thorough knowledge of wisdom (*jñāna-parijñā*): all are fully known by the thorough knowledge of wisdom.

Regarding these four meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*), how many are fully known by the thorough knowledge of abandonment (*prahāṇa-parijñā*) and so forth: one is fully known by the thorough knowledge of abandonment, one is not fully known by the thorough knowledge of abandonment, and two should be analyzed.

That is to say, for the sake of dwelling in happiness in the present life and for the sake of analytical wisdom: if it is with outflows (*sāsrava*), it is that which is to be fully known through abandonment; if it is without outflows (*anāsrava*), it is not that which is to be fully known through abandonment.
Regarding "how many should be abandoned" and so forth: one [of the two] should be abandoned, one should not be abandoned, and two should be analyzed.

That is to say, for the sake of dwelling in happiness in the present life and for the sake of analytical wisdom, if they are with outflows (*sāsrava*), they should be abandoned; if they are without outflows (*anāsrava*), they should not be abandoned.
Regarding how many are to be cultivated (*bhāvayitavya*) and so forth: all are to be cultivated.
Regarding how many are defiled (*kliṣṭa*) and so forth: none are defiled.
Regarding how many are fruits (*phala*) but not possessors of fruit (*saphala*) and so forth: all are both fruits and possessors of fruit.
Regarding how many are appropriated (*upātta*) and so forth: all are unappropriated.

Regarding how many are derived from the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) and so forth: all should be analyzed; that is to say, those bodily and vocal actions included within meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) are derived from the primary elements, while the rest are not derived from the primary elements.
Regarding how many are "with superior" (*sottara*): all are with superior.
Regarding how many are "existent" (*sat*) and so forth: one is existent, one is non-existent, and two should be analyzed.

That is to say, for the sake of dwelling in happiness in the present life and for the sake of analytical wisdom, if they are with outflows (*sāsrava*), they exist; if they are without outflows (*anāsrava*), they do not exist.

Regarding how many causes they are associated with and so forth, all should be analyzed as follows: those bodily and vocal actions and formations dissociated from mind (*citta-viprayukta-saṃskāra*) that are comprised within the cultivation of meditative concentration (*dhyāna-bhāvanā*) are not associated with causes; all others are associated with causes.

Regarding the inclusion of these four cultivations of concentration within the six bases of wholesomeness: a portion of the five bases of wholesomeness includes the four cultivations of concentration, and the four cultivations of concentration likewise include a portion of the five bases of wholesomeness.
Regarding their mutual inclusion with the five unwholesome bases, they do not mutually include one another.
Regarding their mutual inclusion with the seven indeterminate bases, they do not mutually include one another.
Regarding their mutual inclusion with the three outflow bases, they do not mutually include one another.
Regarding the mutual inclusion with the five outflow-tainted bases (*āsravasthāna*), one should formulate four alternatives (*catuṣkoṭi*).
There may be outflow-tainted bases that are not meditative cultivation (*samādhi-bhāvanā*), namely, the outflow-tainted five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) not subsumed under meditative cultivation.
Either one cultivates meditative concentration that is not a state of outflows, namely, one type of cultivation of concentration and a portion of two others;
or there are states of outflows that also involve the cultivation of concentration, namely, one type of cultivation of concentration and a portion of two others.
Alternatively, there are cases that are neither impure bases nor the cultivation of meditative concentration, namely: space and the two types of cessation.
Regarding their mutual inclusion with the eight untainted bases (*anāsrava-āyatana*), one should formulate four permutations (*catuṣkoṭi*).
Alternatively, there are cases that are untainted bases but not meditative absorptions, namely: space and the two types of cessation.
Alternatively, there are cases that are meditative absorptions but not untainted bases, namely: one type of meditative absorption and a portion of the other two.

Alternatively, there are cases that are both untainted (*anāsrava*) and cultivated meditative concentration (*bhāvanā-samādhi*), namely: one type of cultivated meditative concentration and a portion of two other types.

Or, there are cases that are neither untainted nor cultivated meditative concentration, namely: the tainted (*sāsrava*) five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) not subsumed under cultivated meditative concentration.
Regarding how many are past and so forth: all are either past, future, or present.
Regarding how many are wholesome and so forth: all are wholesome.
Regarding how many are bound to the desire realm and so forth: one is bound to the form realm, one is unbound, and two should be analyzed.
That is to say, for the sake of dwelling in happiness in the present life, there is that which is with outflows and bound to the form realm, and that which is without outflows and unbound.
For the sake of analytical wisdom, there is that which is bound to the desire realm, or bound to the form realm, or bound to the formless realm, or unbound.
What is that which is bound to the desire realm?
It refers to the five aggregates of the desire realm as apprehended by discriminative wisdom.
What is that which is bound to the form realm?
This refers to the five aggregates of the form realm as apprehended by discerning wisdom.
What is bound to the formless realm?
This refers to the four aggregates of the formless realm as apprehended by discerning wisdom.
What is "unbound" (*aniyata*)?
It refers to the five untainted aggregates (*anāsrava-skandha*).
Regarding how many are "in training" (*śaikṣa*) and so forth: one is "in training," one is "neither in training nor beyond training" (*naiva-śaikṣa-nāśaikṣa*), and two should be analyzed.
This refers to those for the sake of dwelling in happiness in the present life, whether they be trainees (*śaikṣa*), those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), or neither-trainee-nor-beyond-training.
What is the trainee?
It refers to the five aggregates of a trainee comprised within dwelling in happiness in the present life.
What is that which is beyond training (*aśaikṣa*)?
It refers to the five aggregates of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa-skandha*) as comprised within the dwelling in happiness in this very life (*dṛṣṭadharmasukhavihāra*).
What is that which is neither in training nor beyond training (*naivaśaikṣanāśaikṣa*)?
This refers to the contaminated five aggregates comprised within dwelling in happiness in the present life;
they are [the objects] of analytical wisdom, whether it be that of one in training (śaikṣa), one beyond training (aśaikṣa), or neither-in-training-nor-beyond-training (naivaśaikṣanāśaikṣa).
What is the learner (śaikṣa)?
It refers to the five aggregates of the learner.
What is the one beyond learning (aśaikṣa)?
That is to say, the five aggregates of one beyond training (aśaikṣa).
What are those that are neither of training nor beyond training?
That is to say, the five contaminated (sāsrava) aggregates comprised within the wisdom of discrimination.

Regarding these four cultivations of concentration (*dhyāna*), how many are abandoned by vision (*darśana-prahātavya*) and so forth? One is abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-prahātavya*), one is not to be abandoned (*aprahātavya*), and two should be analyzed.

That is to say, for the sake of dwelling in happiness in the present life (*dṛṣṭadharmasukhavihāra*) and for the sake of analytical wisdom (*pratisaṃkhyāna-prajñā*), if they are with outflows (*sāsrava*), they are abandoned by cultivation; if they are without outflows (*anāsrava*), they are not to be abandoned.

Regarding "how many are not mind, etc.," all should be analyzed as follows: all bodily and vocal actions (kāya-vāk-karman) subsumed under meditative concentration (dhyāna-samgṛhīta), as well as formations dissociated from mind (citta-viprayukta-saṃskāra), are neither mind, nor mental factors (caitta), nor associated with mind;

the aggregate of feeling (vedanā-skandha), the aggregate of perception (saṃjñā-skandha), and the associated portion of the aggregate of formations (saṃskāra-skandha) are mental factors associated with mind;
and mind, thought (manas), and consciousness (vijñāna) are exclusively mind.

Regarding how many [factors] follow the mind (*cittānuvartin*) but are not associated with feeling (*vedanā-saṃprayukta*), all should be analyzed as follows: in relation to the dwelling in happiness in the present life (*dṛṣṭadharmasukhavihāra*), one should formulate four permutations (*catuṣkoṭi*).

First, there are those that follow the mind but are not associated with feeling: namely, the bodily and vocal actions (*kāyavākkarma*) subsumed under the dwelling in happiness in the present life, as well as the mind-dissociated formations (*cittaviprayuktasaṃskāra*) that follow the mind, together with feeling itself.
Some are associated with feeling but do not follow the mind; this refers to the mind and mental consciousness comprised within the dwelling in happiness in the present life.

Some both follow the mind and are associated with feeling; this refers to the aggregate of perception and the associated aggregate of formations comprised within the dwelling in happiness in the present life.

Or [those] that do not follow the mind and are not associated with feeling: namely, with the exception of the formations dissociated from mind that follow the mind and are subsumed under dwelling in happiness in the present life, all other formations dissociated from mind that are subsumed under dwelling in happiness in the present life.
It is the same for superior knowledge and vision (*abhiññā*), and likewise for the exhaustion of all taints (*āsava*).
Regarding the wisdom of discernment (*paṭisambhidā-paññā*), one should formulate four permutations (*catuṣkoṭi*).

There are those that follow the mind (*cittānuvartin*) but are not associated with feeling (*vedanā-saṃprayukta*); these refer to bodily and vocal actions that follow the mind, as well as the formations dissociated from mind (*citta-viprayukta-saṃskāra*) and feeling (*vedanā*) included within the wisdom of discernment.
Some are associated with feeling but do not follow the mind, namely, the mind, mental consciousness, and the aggregate of discernment (prajñā) that is included within them.

Some both follow the mind and are associated with feeling, namely, the aggregate of perception (saṃjñā-skandha) and the associated aggregate of formations (saṃskāra-skandha) that are included within discernment.

Or [there are those] that neither follow the mind nor are associated with feeling: namely, all other bodily and vocal actions included within discriminative wisdom, excluding those bodily and vocal actions that follow the mind; and all other formations dissociated from mind included within discriminative wisdom, excluding those formations dissociated from mind that are included within discriminative wisdom.

Regarding how many follow the mind (*cittānuvartin*) and are associated with neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatanasamprayukta*), excluding their own intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), they should be understood as being like feeling (*vedanā*).

Regarding how many follow applied thought (*vitarkānuvartin*) and are not associated with sustained thought (*avicārasamprayukta*), one is without both applied and sustained thought (*avitarkāvicāra*), while three should be analyzed.
Regarding the four propositions concerning dwelling in happiness in the present life (*dṛṣṭadharmasukhavihāra*):

there are those that follow the movement of vitarka (*anuvitarkya*) but are not associated with vicāra (*avicāra-samprayukta*). These include the bodily and vocal karma, the formations dissociated from mind (*citta-viprayukta-saṃskāra*), and vicāra itself, which are subsumed under dwelling in happiness in the present life and follow the movement of vitarka.

Alternatively, there are those associated with investigation (*vicāra*) that do not follow the movement of applied thought (*vitarka*), namely, the applied thoughts subsumed under the dwelling in happiness in the present life (*dṛṣṭadharmasukhavihāra*).

Alternatively, there are those that follow the movement of applied thought and are also associated with investigation, namely, the mental states and mental factors (*citta-caitta-dharma*) associated with both applied thought and investigation that are subsumed under the dwelling in happiness in the present life.

Or, there are those that neither follow after vitarka nor are associated with vicāra; namely, with the exception of the formations dissociated from mind that follow after vitarka and are subsumed under the dwelling in happiness in this very life, all other formations dissociated from mind that are subsumed under the dwelling in happiness in this very life.
Regarding superior knowledge and vision, there are four propositions.

There are those that follow the movement of vitarka (initial inquiry) but are not associated with vicāra (sustained investigation), namely: bodily and vocal karma, formations dissociated from mind, and vicāra itself, which are comprised within superior knowledge and vision and follow the movement of vitarka.

Alternatively, there are those associated with investigation (*vicāra*) but not following after initial inquiry (*vitarka*), namely, the *vitarka* subsumed under superior knowledge and vision (*jñānadarśana*).

Alternatively, there are those that follow after initial inquiry and are also associated with investigation, namely, the mind and mental factors (*citta-caitasika-dharma*) associated with both *vitarka* and *vicāra* that are subsumed under superior knowledge and vision.

Or, there are those that neither follow after vitarka nor are associated with vicāra; namely, with the exception of bodily and vocal actions and formations dissociated from mind that are subsumed under superior knowledge and vision and follow after vitarka, all other bodily and vocal actions and formations dissociated from mind that are subsumed under superior knowledge and vision, as well as the mind and mental factors that are without vitarka and without vicāra and are subsumed under superior knowledge and vision.
Regarding the wisdom of discernment (*vibhāga-prajñā*), there are four propositions.

First, there are those that follow discursive thought (*vitarka*) but are not associated with sustained thought (*vicāra*); these include bodily and vocal actions that follow discursive thought, as well as formations dissociated from mind (*citta-viprayukta-saṃskāra*) that follow discursive thought and are subsumed under the wisdom of discernment, along with the sustained thought that is associated with discursive thought.

Or, there are those associated with investigation (*vicāra*) but not proceeding with initial inquiry (*vitarka*), namely: the *vitarka* subsumed under analytical wisdom (*prajñā*), as well as the mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta-dharma*) that are dissociated from *vitarka* but associated with *vicāra*.

Some are associated with both vitarka (applied thought) and vicāra (sustained thought), namely those mental states and mental factors that are subsumed under discerning wisdom and are associated with both vitarka and vicāra.

Some are neither associated with vitarka nor associated with vicāra, namely: all other bodily and vocal actions subsumed under discerning wisdom, excluding those bodily and vocal actions associated with vitarka; all other formations dissociated from mind subsumed under discerning wisdom, excluding those formations dissociated from mind associated with vitarka; as well as vicāra that is not associated with vitarka, and those mental states and mental factors that are without both vitarka and vicāra.
Regarding the question of how many views are not the locus of views (*na-dṛṣṭi-sthāna*) and so forth, all should be analyzed.
Specifically, concerning the fourfold formulation regarding dwelling in happiness in the present life (*dṛṣṭadharma-sukha-vihāra*):

there may be that which is a view but not the locus of views. This refers to the untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-prajñā*) subsumed under dwelling in happiness in the present life, which is not subsumed under the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣaya-jñāna*) or the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpāda-jñāna*).
Or, there is that which is a basis for views but is not itself a view; this refers to the contaminated states not subsumed under views that serve as abiding in happiness in the present life.
Or, there is that which is both a view and a basis for views; this refers to mundane right view that is subsumed under abiding in happiness in the present life.
Or it is neither view nor the basis for view; this refers to the outflow-free (anāsrava) states not subsumed under view.

[These are] for the sake of dwelling in happiness in the present life and for the sake of superior knowledge and vision. Or it is both view and the basis for view, or it is the basis for view but not view.

"View that is also a basis for view" refers to mundane right view subsumed under superior knowledge and vision; all other [mundane views] subsumed under superior knowledge and vision are bases for view but are not themselves views.
Regarding the wisdom of discrimination (*pratisaṃkhyā-prajñā*), there are four permutations: 1.

That which is vision (*dṛṣṭi*) but not a locus of vision (*dṛṣṭisthāna*): this refers to untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-prajñā*) that is not subsumed under the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣaya-jñāna*) and the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpāda-jñāna*).

2. That which is a locus of vision but not vision: this refers to tainted wisdom (*sāsrava-prajñā*) that is not subsumed under [the aforementioned] vision, yet constitutes the wisdom of discrimination.
Some are both views and bases for views; this refers to mundane right view that is subsumed under analytical wisdom (*prajñā*).

Some are neither views nor bases for views; this refers to the untainted (*anāsrava*) wisdom not subsumed under [mundane] views, as well as the wisdom subsumed under analytical wisdom and the wisdom for the exhaustion of all outflows (*āsravakṣaya*). Wisdom that is a view but not a basis for views exists, while all others are neither views nor bases for views.

Regarding the question of how many [factors] have the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) as their cause but are not themselves causes of the view of a self-identity, and so forth: all [factors] neither have the view of a self-identity as their cause nor are they causes of the view of a self-identity.

Regarding the question of how many [factors] are karma but not the maturation (*vipāka*) of karma, and so forth: all should be analyzed. That is to say, bodily and vocal karma included within meditative concentration (*dhyāna-samgṛhīta*) as well as volition (*cetanā*) are karma but not the maturation of karma; all others are neither karma nor the maturation of karma.
Regarding the question of how many karmas do not follow along with karma (na-anuvartaka-karma), all cases should be analyzed.
Specifically, concerning those that lead to dwelling in happiness in the present life (*dṛṣṭadharma-sukhavihāra*), there are four permutations.
There may be karma that does not follow along with karma, namely: volition (*cetanā*) comprised within that which leads to dwelling in happiness in the present life.

Some are concomitants of karma but are not karma itself; these are the aggregates of feeling, perception, and consciousness as comprised within the dwelling in happiness in the present life, as well as the aggregate of formations concomitant with karma that are not comprised within volition.
Some are both karma and concomitants of karma, namely, the bodily and vocal actions comprised within the dwelling in happiness in the present life (*dṛṣṭadharmasukhavihāra*).

Some are neither karma nor concomitants of karma, namely, all other formations dissociated from mind (*cittaviprayuktasaṃskāra*) comprised within the dwelling in happiness in the present life, excluding those formations dissociated from mind that are concomitants of karma and comprised within the dwelling in happiness in the present life.
The same applies to [actions] for the sake of superior knowledge and vision, as well as for the sake of exhausting all outflows (*āsrava*).
Regarding the four alternatives concerning actions for the sake of analytical wisdom (*pratisaṃkhyāna-prajñā*):

there may be action that is not "concomitant with action" (*anuvartaka*). This refers to all other bodily and vocal actions included within analytical wisdom, as well as volition (*cetanā*), excluding those bodily and vocal actions included within analytical wisdom that are concomitant with action.

Some are concomitants of karma but are not karma itself; these refer to the aggregates of perception and consciousness as encompassed by discerning wisdom, as well as those factors of the aggregate of formations that are concomitants of karma but are not subsumed under volition.
Some are both karma and concomitants of karma; this refers to bodily and vocal karma that is included within the discerning wisdom and follows after karma.

Some are neither karma nor concomitants of karma; this refers to all other formations dissociated from mind (citta-viprayukta-saṃskāra) included within the discerning wisdom, excluding those formations dissociated from mind that follow after karma.

Regarding the question of how many derived forms (*upādāya-rūpa*) are not visible forms (*sanidarśana-rūpa*), all such cases should be analyzed as follows: those bodily and vocal actions (*kāya-vāk-karman*) subsumed under meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) are derived forms that are not visible forms; all others are neither derived forms nor visible forms.

Regarding these four types of cultivated meditative concentration (*dhyāna-bhāvanā*), as to how many are derived matter (*upādāya-rūpa*) and not resistant matter (*sapratigha-rūpa*), all should be analyzed as follows: those bodily and vocal actions (*kāya-vāk-karman*) subsumed under the various cultivated concentrations are derived matter and not resistant matter; all others are neither derived matter nor resistant matter.
Regarding the phrase "difficult to see, therefore profound," etc.: all things are profound because they are difficult to see, and they are difficult to see because they are profound.
Regarding the question "how many are wholesome and have wholesome causes," etc.: all are wholesome and also have wholesome causes.
Regarding the question of how many unwholesome [factors] do not have the unwholesome as their cause, etc., all [of them] are neither unwholesome nor have the unwholesome as their cause.
Regarding the question of how many indeterminate [factors] do not have the indeterminate as their cause, etc., all [of them] are neither indeterminate nor have the indeterminate as their cause.
Regarding the question of how many *hetu-pratyayas* (causal conditions) are not *sahetu* (having a cause), all are both *hetu-pratyaya* and *sahetu*.
Regarding the question of how many *samanantara* [factors] are not *samanantara-pratyaya* (immediately preceding condition), all should be analyzed as having three propositions (*trikoṭika*) each.

Some are equal-immediate [conditions] but not equal-immediate conditions; these refer to the mind and mental factors comprised within the cultivation of meditative concentration that are yet to arise in the future.
Some are both equal-immediate and equal-immediate conditions; these refer to the mind and mental factors comprised within the cultivation of meditative concentration that are past or present.

Or [there are factors] that are neither equal-immediate [factors] nor equal-immediate conditions; namely, with the exception of those future mind and mental factors subsumed under the cultivation of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) that are currently arising before one, all other future mind and mental factors subsumed under the cultivation of meditative concentration, as well as the bodily and vocal actions and the formations dissociated from mind (*citta-viprayukta-saṃskāra*) subsumed under the cultivation of meditative concentration.

Regarding the question of how many objects-of-support conditions (*ālambana-pratyaya*) do not possess an object-of-support (*sālambana*), all such cases should be analyzed as follows: namely, those bodily and vocal actions (*kāya-vāk-karman*) and formations dissociated from mind (*citta-viprayukta-saṃskāra*) that are subsumed under meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) are objects-of-support conditions but do not possess an object-of-support; all others are both objects-of-support conditions and possess an object-of-support.
Regarding the question of how many are dominant conditions (*adhipati-pratyaya*) but do not possess dominance (*ādhipatya*), all are dominant conditions and also possess dominance.

Regarding the question of how many are floods (*ogha*) but are not favorable to the floods (*an-ogha-anukūla*), one is favorable to the floods but is not a flood, one is neither a flood nor favorable to the floods, and two should be analyzed.

That is to say, for the sake of dwelling in happiness in the present life and for the sake of analytical wisdom: if it is with outflows (*sāsrava*), it is favorable to the floods (*ogha-anuloma*) but not a flood; if it is without outflows (*anāsrava*), it is neither a flood nor favorable to the floods.
The seven factors of enlightenment (bodhyaṅga) refer to the factor of enlightenment of mindfulness up to the factor of enlightenment of equanimity.
Regarding how many of these seven factors of enlightenment possess form and so forth: all are formless.
Regarding how many are with visibility (*sanidarśana*) and so forth: all are without visibility.
Regarding how many are with resistance (*sapratigha*) and so forth: all are without resistance.
Regarding how many are with outflows (*sāsrava*) and so forth: all are without outflows.
Regarding how many are conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) and so forth: all are conditioned.
Regarding how many have maturation (*vipāka*) and so forth: none have maturation.
Regarding how many are dependently originated (*pratītyasamutpanna*) and so forth: all are dependently originated, produced by causes, and included within the world (*loka*).
Regarding how many are subsumed under "form" (*rūpa*) and so forth: all are subsumed under "name" (*nāman*).
Regarding how many are subsumed under the internal bases (*adhyātma-āyatana*) and so forth: all are subsumed under the external bases (*bāhya-āyatana*).

Regarding how many are that which is to be fully known through the thorough knowledge of wisdom (*jñāna-parijñā-parijñeya*) and so forth: all are that which is to be fully known through the thorough knowledge of wisdom.
Abhidharmaprakaraṇapādaśāstra, Volume 14 (and Volume 15), composed by the Venerable Vasumitra.

Chapter Seven: Discerning the Thousand Questions, Part Six. Regarding how many of these seven factors of enlightenment are to be fully known through the abandonment of thorough knowledge (*prahāṇa-parijñā*), etc.: none of them are to be fully known through the abandonment of thorough knowledge.
Regarding how many should be abandoned and so forth: none should be abandoned.
Regarding how many should be cultivated and so forth: all are to be cultivated.
Regarding how many are defiled and so forth: none are defiled.
Regarding the question of how many are results but not possess results, all are both results and possess results.
Regarding the question of how many are appropriated (*upātta*), all are non-appropriated.
Regarding the question of how many are derived from the primary elements (*mahābhūta*), all are not derived from the primary elements.
Regarding how many have "superiors": all have superiors.
Regarding how many are "existent" (bhava): none are existent.
Regarding how many are "associated with causes" (hetu-saṃprayukta): all are associated with causes.

Regarding the inclusion of these seven factors of enlightenment within the six bases of wholesomeness: a portion of two bases of wholesomeness includes the seven factors of enlightenment, and the seven factors of enlightenment also include a portion of those two bases of wholesomeness.
Regarding their inclusion within the five unwholesome bases (*akuśalasthāna*), they do not mutually include one another.
Regarding their inclusion within the seven indeterminate bases (*avyākṛtasthāna*), they do not mutually include one another.
Regarding their inclusion within the three outflows bases (*āsravasthāna*), they do not mutually include one another.
Regarding their inclusion within the five contaminated bases (*āsravasthāna*), they do not mutually include one another.

Regarding their inclusion within the eight uncontaminated bases (*anāsravasthāna*), a portion of two uncontaminated bases includes the seven factors of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*), and the seven factors of enlightenment also include a portion of two uncontaminated bases.
Regarding how many are past and so forth: all are either past, future, or present.
Regarding how many are wholesome and so forth: all are wholesome.
Regarding how many are bound to the desire realm and so forth: all are unbound.
Regarding "how many are trainings (*śaikṣa*) and so forth," all should be analyzed.
That is to say, the factor of enlightenment of mindfulness (*smṛti-saṃbodhyaṅga*) is either a training or beyond-training (*aśaikṣa*).
What is a training?
This refers to the awakening factor of mindfulness associated with the attention of one in training.
What is that of one beyond training?
It refers to the awakening factor of mindfulness associated with the attention of one beyond training.
The same applies to the other six factors of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*).
Regarding these seven factors of enlightenment: how many are to be abandoned by vision (*darśana-prahātavya*)? None are to be abandoned.
How many are not mental (*acaitasika*)? All are mental factors (*caitasika*) associated with the mind (*citta-samprayukta*).

Regarding how many [factors] turn according to the mind (*cittānuvartin*) but are not associated with feeling (*vedanā-saṃprayukta*), etc.: one turns according to the mind but is not associated with feeling; six turn according to the mind and are also associated with feeling.

Regarding how many turn according to the mind but are not associated with perception (*saṃjñā*) or formations (*saṃskāra*), etc.: all that turn according to the mind are associated with perception and formations, excluding their own nature (*svabhāva*).
Regarding the question of how many factors follow the movement of vitarka (applied thought) but are not associated with vicāra (sustained thought), all such cases should be analyzed.
That is to say, the mindfulness factor of enlightenment may be accompanied by both vitarka and vicāra, or may be without vitarka and with vicāra only, or may be without both vitarka and vicāra.
What is "with vitarka and vicāra"?
It refers to the awakening factor of mindfulness associated with attention that possesses both vitarka and vicāra.
What is "without vitarka and with only vicāra"?
This refers to the awakening factor of mindfulness associated with attention that is without vitarka and has only vicāra.
What is [the awakening factor] without vitarka and without vicāra?
It refers to the awakening factor of mindfulness associated with attention that is without vitarka and without vicāra.
The enlightenment factors of investigation of phenomena, energy, tranquility, concentration, and equanimity are also like this.
As for the enlightenment factor of joy, it may be accompanied by vitarka and vicāra, or it may be without vitarka and without vicāra.
What is "with vitarka and vicāra"?
It refers to the awakening factor of joy (*prīti-saṃbodhyaṅga*) associated with attention (*manasikāra*) that is accompanied by vitarka and vicāra.
What is "without vitarka and vicāra"?

This refers to the factors of enlightenment such as joy (*prīti*), which are associated with mental attention (*manasikāra*) that is without applied thought (*vitarka*) or sustained thought (*vicāra*).

Regarding how many are "view" (*dṛṣṭi*) and how many are "not the basis of view" (*adṛṣṭisthāna*), six are neither view nor the basis of view; one should be analyzed. Specifically, the wisdom (*prajñā*) included within the factor of enlightenment of the investigation of phenomena (*dharmapravicaya*)—provided it is not subsumed under the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) or the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*)—is "view" and is "the basis of view"; all others are neither view nor the basis of view.

Regarding how many have the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) as their cause but are not causes of the view of a self-identity: all [of these] do not have the view of a self-identity as their cause, nor are they causes of the view of a self-identity.
Regarding how many are karma but not the maturation of karma: all [of these] are neither karma nor the maturation of karma.
Regarding the question of how many karmas do not follow along with karma (*anuvartaka*), all [factors] that follow along with karma are not karma itself.
Regarding the question of how many derived forms (*upādāya-rūpa*) are not visible forms (*sanidarśana-rūpa*), all [factors] are neither derived forms nor visible forms.

Regarding these seven factors of enlightenment: how many are derived matter (upādāya-rūpa) and not resistant matter (sapratigha-rūpa), and so forth? All are neither derived matter nor resistant matter.
How many are profound because they are difficult to see, and so forth? All are profound because they are difficult to see, and difficult to see because they are profound.
Regarding the question of how many are wholesome and have wholesome as their cause, etc.: all are wholesome and have wholesome as their cause.
Regarding the question of how many are unwholesome and have unwholesome as their cause, etc.: none are unwholesome, nor do they have unwholesome as their cause.
Regarding the question of how many are indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) yet not having the indeterminate as their cause, all are neither indeterminate nor have the indeterminate as their cause.
Regarding the question of how many are object-conditions (*ālambana-pratyaya*) yet not having a cause, all are both object-conditions and have a cause.
Regarding the question of how many are immediate [conditions] but not immediate-object conditions (*samanantarapratyaya*), all such cases should be analyzed as follows:

namely, the mindfulness factor of enlightenment (*smṛtisambodhyaṅga*) may be an immediate condition but not an immediate-object condition; or it may be both an immediate condition and an immediate-object condition; or it may be neither an immediate condition nor an immediate-object condition.

Those which are immediate but not an immediately preceding condition (*samanantarapratyaya*) refer to the factors of enlightenment such as mindfulness that are yet to arise in the future and are currently manifesting.
Those which are both immediate and an immediately preceding condition refer to the factors of enlightenment such as mindfulness that belong to the past and the present.

That which is neither an equal-and-immediate [condition] nor an equal-and-immediate condition refers to all other future factors of enlightenment, such as mindfulness, excluding those that are currently arising and present in the future.
The same applies to the other six factors of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*).
Regarding how many are object-conditions (*ālambanapratyaya*) but do not possess an object (*sālambana*), all of them are both object-conditions and possess an object.
Regarding the question of how many are dominant conditions (*adhipati-pratyaya*) but do not possess dominance (*ādhipatya*), all are dominant conditions and also possess dominance.
Regarding the question of how many are floods (*ogha*) but are not conducive to the floods (*anugata-ogha*), none are floods and none are conducive to the floods.
Regarding the twenty-two faculties (*indriya*), they refer to the faculty of the eye up to the faculty of one who has already known (*ājñātāvīndriya*).
Among these twenty-two faculties, how many possess form (*rūpin*)? Seven possess form; fifteen are formless (*arūpin*).
Regarding how many are with-outflow-objects (*sanidarśana*) and so forth: all are without-outflow-objects (*anidarśana*).
Regarding how many are with-obstruction (*sapratigha*) and so forth: seven are with-obstruction, fifteen are without-obstruction (*apratigha*).
Regarding how many are with-outflows (*sāsrava*) and so forth: ten are with-outflows, three are without-outflows (*anāsrava*), and nine should be analyzed.
This refers to the faculty of mind (manas-indriya), which is either with outflows (sāsrava) or without outflows (anāsrava).
What is with outflows?
It is the faculty of mind associated with attention that has outflows.
What is the untainted (*anāsrava*)?
It refers to the faculty of mind (*manendriya*) associated with untainted attention (*manasikāra*).
The same applies to the faculties of pleasure, joy, equanimity, faith, diligence, mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom.
Regarding how many are conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) and so forth: all are conditioned.
Regarding how many have maturation (*savipāka*) and so forth: one has maturation, eleven have no maturation, and ten should be analyzed.
This refers to the faculty of mind (*manendriya*), which may be either with maturation (*savipāka*) or without maturation (*avipāka*).
What is meant by "with maturation"?
It refers to the unwholesome and wholesome contaminated (*sāsrava*) faculties of mind.
What is that which has no maturation?
It refers to the indeterminate and untainted mental faculty (*manas-indriya*).
The same applies to the faculties of pleasure, joy, and equanimity.
The faculty of suffering (duḥkhendriya) is either with maturation (savipāka) or without maturation (avipāka).
What is with maturation? It refers to the faculty of suffering that is wholesome (kuśala) or unwholesome (akuśala).
What is without maturation? It refers to the faculty of suffering that is indeterminate (avyākṛta).

Regarding the faculties of faith, diligence, mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom: if they are with outflows (*sāsrava*), they have maturation (*savipāka*); if they are without outflows (*anāsrava*), they have no maturation (*avipāka*).

As for how many are dependently originated (*pratītyasamutpanna*) and so forth: all of them are dependently originated, produced by causes (*hetuja*), and included within the world (*loka-saṃgṛhīta*).
Regarding how many are comprised within form (*rūpa*) and so forth: seven are comprised within form, and fifteen are comprised within name (*nāman*).

Regarding how many are comprised within internal bases (*ādhyātmikāyatana*) and so forth: eight are comprised within internal bases, eleven are comprised within external bases (*bāhyāyatana*), and three should be analyzed.

That is to say, the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown," the faculty of "knowing," and the faculty of "one who has known" are subsumed under the internal bases of mind, mental consciousness, and the internal sense-sphere; all others are subsumed under the external bases.
Regarding the question of how many of these are fully known by the thorough knowledge of wisdom (*jñāna-parijñā*): all of them are fully known by the thorough knowledge of wisdom.

Regarding the question of how many of these twenty-two faculties (*indriya*) are fully known by the thorough knowledge of abandonment (*prahāṇa-parijñā*): ten are fully known by the thorough knowledge of abandonment, three are not fully known by the thorough knowledge of abandonment, and nine should be analyzed.

That is to say, among the nine faculties beginning with the mind-faculty (*manas*), those that are contaminated (*sāsrava*) are to be fully known through abandonment (*prahāṇa-parijñeya*), while those that are uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) are not to be fully known through abandonment.
Regarding how many are to be abandoned and so forth: ten are to be abandoned, three are not to be abandoned, and nine are to be analyzed.

That is to say, among the nine faculties beginning with the mental faculty (*manas*), those that are with-outflow (*sāsrava*) are to be abandoned, while those that are without-outflow (*anāsrava*) are not to be abandoned.
Regarding how many are to be cultivated (*bhāvayitavya*) and so forth: eight are to be cultivated, eight are not to be cultivated, and six are to be analyzed.
That is to say, the faculty of mind (manendriya) is either to be cultivated or not to be cultivated.
What is to be cultivated?
It is the wholesome faculty of mind.
What is not to be cultivated?
It refers to the unwholesome and indeterminate faculties of mind (*manas-indriya*).
The same applies to the faculties of pleasure, pain, joy, and equanimity.
The faculty of grief (daurmanasyendriya) is either to be cultivated or not to be cultivated.
What is to be cultivated?
It is the wholesome faculty of grief.
What is not to be cultivated?
It refers to the unwholesome faculty of sorrow (*daurmanasyendriya*).
Regarding how many are defiled (*kliṣṭa*) and so forth: sixteen are non-defiled, while six are to be analyzed.
This refers to the mental faculty (*manas*), which is either defiled or non-defiled.
What is defiled? It is the mental faculty that is obscured (*nivṛta*).
What is non-defiled?
It refers to the unobscured mental faculty (*manas-indriya*).
The same applies to the faculties of pleasure, pain, joy, grief, and equanimity.
Regarding how many are results but not possess results, and so forth: all are results and also possess results.
Regarding how many are appropriated (*upātta*) and so forth: fifteen are non-appropriated; seven should be analyzed.
That is to say, the eye-faculty is either appropriated or non-appropriated.
What is appropriated?
It refers to the eye-faculty that is comprised within one's own personal continuity.
What is non-appropriated?
It refers to the eye-faculty that is not comprised within one's own body.
The same applies to the other six material faculties.
Regarding how many are derived from the great elements (*mahābhūta*) and so forth: seven are derived from the great elements, and fifteen are not derived from the great elements.
Regarding how many have something superior (*sottara*): all of them have something superior.
Regarding the question of how many are "existent" (*sat*) and so forth: ten are existent, three are non-existent, and nine should be analyzed.
