That is to say, as for the nine faculties beginning with the mind-faculty (*manas*), if they are with-outflows (*sāsrava*), they are existent; if they are without-outflows (*anāsrava*), they are non-existent.
Regarding how many causes they are associated with and so forth: eight causes are dissociated, and fourteen causes are associated.
As for the inclusion of these twenty-two faculties within the six wholesome bases (*kuśalāyatana*), one should formulate four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*).

Alternatively, there are wholesome bases that are not faculties, namely: the wholesome aggregate of form, the aggregate of perception, the wholesome aggregate of formations not subsumed under the faculties, and analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).
Alternatively, there are faculties that are not wholesome bases, namely: eight faculties and a portion of six faculties.
Some are both wholesome bases (*kuśalāyatana*) and faculties (*indriya*), namely the eight faculties and a portion of the six [sensory] faculties.

Some are neither wholesome bases nor faculties, namely the unwholesome form aggregate (*rūpaskandha*) and formation aggregate (*saṃskāraskandha*), the unwholesome and neutral perception aggregate (*saṃjñāskandha*), as well as the form and formation aggregates not subsumed under the faculties, along with space (*ākāśa*) and non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyānirodha*).
Regarding the mutual inclusion between the five unwholesome bases (*akuśalasthāna*) and the faculties (*indriya*), four permutations (*catuṣkoṭi*) should be established:
1. There are those that are unwholesome bases but not faculties: namely, the aggregates of unwholesome form, perception, and formations (*saṃskāra*).
2. There are those that are faculties but not unwholesome bases: namely, sixteen faculties and a portion of six faculties.
Or it is an unwholesome basis that is also a faculty, namely a portion of the six faculties.

Or it is neither an unwholesome basis nor a faculty, namely the wholesome aggregate of form, the wholesome and neutral aggregate of perception, the wholesome and neutral aggregate of formations not included among the faculties, as well as the neutral aggregate of form not included among the faculties and the unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛtadharma*).
Regarding the mutual inclusion between the seven indeterminate bases (*avyākṛtāyatana*) and the faculties (*indriya*), four permutations (*catuṣkoṭi*) should be established.

There are cases that are indeterminate bases but not faculties: namely, the indeterminate aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*), the indeterminate aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*) and aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) not included among the faculties, as well as space (*ākāśa*) and cessation not through deliberation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).
Either they are faculties but not indeterminate bases, namely the nine faculties and a portion of the five faculties;
or they are both indeterminate bases and faculties, namely eight faculties and a portion of the five faculties.

Or [there are factors] that are neither indeterminate nor faculties: namely, the wholesome and unwholesome aggregates of form and perception, the unwholesome aggregate of formations, as well as the wholesome aggregate of formations not included among the faculties, and analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).
Regarding their inclusion within the three bases of outflows (*āsravasthāna*), they are not mutually inclusive.
Regarding their inclusion within the five bases of outflows (*sāsravasthāna*), one should formulate four alternatives (*catuṣkoṭi*).

There may be a base of outflows that is not a faculty (*indriya*), namely: the outflowing aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*), as well as the outflowing aggregates of form (*rūpa-skandha*) and formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) that are not subsumed under the faculties.
Some faculties are not bases of outflows (*āsrava-sthāna*), namely the three faculties and a portion of nine faculties.
Some are both bases of outflows and faculties, namely ten faculties and a portion of nine faculties.

Or, there are those that are neither outflow-tainted bases nor faculties: namely, the untainted aggregate of form, the aggregate of perception, the untainted aggregate of formations not subsumed under the faculties, and the three unconditioned phenomena.
Regarding the mutual inclusion between the eight untainted bases (*anāsrava-āyatana*) and the faculties (*indriya*), four permutations (*catuṣkoṭi*) should be established.

There may be that which is an untainted base but not an faculty: namely, the untainted form aggregate (*rūpa-skandha*), the perception aggregate (*saṃjñā-skandha*), the untainted formation aggregate (*saṃskāra-skandha*) not included among the faculties, and the three unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*).
Some are faculties but not uncontaminated bases, namely, ten faculties and a portion of nine faculties.
Some are both uncontaminated bases and faculties, namely, three faculties and a portion of nine faculties.
Or, there are those that are neither untainted bases nor faculties: namely, the tainted aggregate of perception, and the tainted aggregates of form and formations not subsumed under the faculties.
Regarding how many are past and so forth: all are either past, future, or present.
Regarding how many are wholesome and so forth: eight are wholesome, eight are indeterminate, and six should be analyzed.
That is to say, the faculty of mind (manas) may be wholesome, unwholesome, or indeterminate.
What is wholesome?
It refers to the mental faculty (manas-indriya) associated with wholesome attention (manasikāra).
What is unwholesome?
This refers to the mental faculty (manas-indriya) associated with unwholesome attention (akuśala-manasikāra).
What is the indeterminate?
It refers to the mental faculty associated with indeterminate attention (avyākṛta-manasikāra).
The same applies to the faculties of pleasure, pain, joy, and equanimity.
As for the faculty of grief, it is either wholesome or unwholesome.
What is wholesome?
This refers to the faculty of sorrow associated with wholesome attention (*manasikāra*).
What is unwholesome?
It refers to the faculty of sorrow associated with unwholesome attention.
Regarding how many are bound to the desire realm and so forth: four are bound to the desire realm, three are unbound, and fifteen should be analyzed.
That is to say, the eye-faculty is either bound to the desire realm or bound to the form realm.
What is bound to the desire realm?
It refers to the eye faculty produced by the primary elements of the desire realm.
What is bound to the form realm?
This refers to the eye faculty derived from the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*).
The same applies to the ear, nose, tongue, and body faculties.
The life faculty (*jīvitendriya*) is either bound to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*), or bound to the form realm, or bound to the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*).
What is bound to the desire realm?
It refers to the life-span of the desire realm.
What is bound to the form realm?
That is to say, the life-span of the form realm.
What is bound to the formless realm?
That is to say, the life-span of the formless realm.
The faculty of mind (manendriya) is either bound to the desire realm, or bound to the form realm, or bound to the formless realm, or unbound. What is bound to the desire realm?
It refers to the faculty of mind associated with mental attention (manasikāra) belonging to the desire realm.
What is that which is bound to the realm of form? It refers to the faculty of mind associated with mental attention belonging to the realm of form.
What is that which is bound to the formless realm? It refers to the faculty of mind associated with mental attention belonging to the formless realm.
What is the unconditioned (*apratisaṃyukta*)? It refers to the faculty of mind (*manendriya*) associated with untainted mental attention (*anāsrava-manasikāra*).
The same applies to the faculty of equanimity (*upekṣendriya*) and the five faculties beginning with faith (*śraddhā*).
As for the faculty of pleasure (*sukhendriya*), it is either bound to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*), or bound to the form realm (*rūpadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*), or unconditioned.
What is bound to the desire realm?
It refers to the faculty of pleasure associated with mental attention belonging to the desire realm.
What is bound to the form realm?
This refers to the faculty of pleasure associated with mental attention belonging to the form realm.
What is unconditioned?
It refers to the faculty of pleasure associated with untainted (anāsrava) mental attention.
The faculty of joy (*saumanasyendriya*) is likewise.
Regarding how many are "in training" (*śaikṣa*) and so forth: two are in training, one is beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), ten are neither in training nor beyond training, and nine should be analyzed.
That is to say, the mental faculty (*manendriya*) is either in training, or beyond training, or neither in training nor beyond training.
What is the faculty of mind of one in training?
It refers to the faculty of mind associated with the mental attention of one in training.
What is that of one beyond training?
This refers to the mental faculty (manas-indriya) associated with the attention (manasikāra) of one beyond training (aśaikṣa).
What is neither-learner-nor-non-learner?
This refers to the mental faculty associated with tainted (sāsrava) attention.
The same applies to the five faculties of pleasure, joy, equanimity, faith, and so forth.

Regarding how many of these twenty-two faculties are abandoned by insight (*darśana-heya*) and so on: nine are abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*), three are not to be abandoned (*aheya*), and ten should be analyzed.
That is to say, the faculty of mind (manendriya) is either abandoned by insight (darśana-heya), abandoned by cultivation (bhāvanā-heya), or not to be abandoned (aheya).
What is abandoned by insight?

It refers to the faculty of mind that is abandoned by the patiences at the limit of clear realization (abhisamaya-antika-kṣānti) for those who follow by faith (śraddhānusārin) or follow by dharma (dharmānusārin).
What, furthermore, is this?
It refers to the mental faculty (*manas*) associated with the eighty-eight latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) abandoned through seeing (*darśana-prahātavya*).
What is abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-prahātavya*)?

This refers to the faculty of mind (*manendriya*) that is to be abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) by one who has seen the tracks (*dṛṣṭiprāpta*) and is still in training (*śaikṣa*). What, then, is this?
It refers to the faculty of mind associated with the ten latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) to be abandoned through cultivation, as well as the non-defiled, out-flowing (*sāsrava*) faculty of mind.
What is not to be abandoned?
It refers to the untainted faculty of mind (*anāsrava-manas-indriya*).
The faculty of equanimity (*upekṣendriya*) is likewise.
The faculty of pleasure (*sukhendriya*) is either abandoned by seeing (*darśana-prahātavya*), abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-prahātavya*), or not to be abandoned (*aprahātavya*).
What is abandoned by seeing?

It refers to the faculty of pleasure that is abandoned by the patiences at the limit of clear realization (*abhisamaya-antika-kṣānti*) for those who follow by faith (*śraddhānusārin*) or follow by dharma (*dharmānusārin*).
What, then, is this? It refers to the faculty of pleasure associated with the twenty-eight latent dispositions (anuśaya) abandoned through seeing.
What is abandoned through cultivation?

This refers to the faculty of pleasure (*sukhendriya*) that is to be abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) by one who has seen the tracks (*dṛṣṭiprāpta*) and is still in training (*śaikṣa*). What, then, is this?

It refers to the faculty of pleasure associated with the five proclivities (*anuśaya*) to be abandoned through cultivation, as well as the undefiled (*akliṣṭa*) impure (*sāsrava*) faculty of pleasure.
What is not to be abandoned? It refers to the untainted faculty of pleasure (*anāsrava-sukhendriya*).
The faculty of joy (*saumanasyendriya*) is either to be abandoned by insight (*darśana-heya*), or to be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*), or not to be abandoned at all.
What is abandoned by insight (*darśana-prahātavya*)?

It refers to the faculty of joy (*saumanasyendriya*) that is abandoned by the patiences (*kṣānti*) at the limit of clear realization (*abhisamaya-anta*) for those who follow by faith (*śraddhānusārin*) or follow by dharma (*dharmānusārin*).
What, moreover, is this?
This refers to the faculty of joy (*somanassindriya*) associated with the fifty-two proclivities (*anuśaya*) to be abandoned by seeing (*darśana-prahātavya*).
What is abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-prahātavya*)?
It refers to the faculty of joy belonging to those who have seen the path (*dṛṣṭapada*) and is abandoned through cultivation.

What, then, is this? It refers to the faculty of joy (*saumanasyendriya*) associated with the six proclivities (*anuśaya*) to be abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*), as well as the undefiled, out-flowing (*sāsrava*) faculty of joy.
What is not to be abandoned (*aheya*)?
This refers to the untainted faculty of joy (*anāsrava-prīti-indriya*).
As for the faculty of grief (*daurmanasya-indriya*), it is either abandoned through seeing (*darśana-heya*) or abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*).
What is abandoned through seeing?

This refers to the faculty of mental distress (*daurmanasyendriya*) that is abandoned by the patiences (*kṣānti*) at the limit of clear observation (*abhisamaya-paryanta*) for those who follow by faith (*śraddhānusārin*) or follow by dharma (*dharmānusārin*). What, then, is this?
It refers to the faculty of mental distress associated with the sixteen underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) to be abandoned through seeing (*darśana-prahātavya*).
What is abandoned through cultivation?
It refers to the faculty of mental distress that is abandoned through cultivation by one who is in training and has seen the tracks [of the path].
What, moreover, is this?
This refers to the faculty of sorrow associated with the two proclivities abandoned through cultivation, as well as the non-defiled faculty of sorrow;
and the five faculties beginning with faith, whether they are contaminated and thus abandoned through cultivation, or uncontaminated and thus not to be abandoned.

Regarding "how many are not mind, etc.": eight are neither mind nor mental factors nor associated with mind; ten are mental factors associated with mind; one is exclusively mind; and three should be analyzed.
The eight faculties subsumed under the three untainted faculties (*anāsrava-indriya*) are mental factors associated with the mind;
one faculty is exclusively the mind itself.

Regarding how many follow the mind (*cittānuvartin*) but are not associated with feeling (*vedanā-saṃprayukta*), and so forth: five follow the mind but are not associated with feeling; one is associated with feeling but does not follow the mind; five both follow the mind and are associated with feeling; eight do not follow the mind and are not associated with feeling; and three should be analyzed individually.

This means that among those subsumed under the three untainted faculties (*anāsrava-indriya*), three faculties follow the mind but are not associated with feeling (*vedanā-saṃprayukta*); one faculty is associated with feeling but does not follow the mind; and five faculties both follow the mind and are associated with feeling.

Regarding how many follow the mind (*cittānuvartin*), are associated with perception (*saṃjñā*), and are associated with formations (*saṃskāra*): one [aggregate] is associated with perception but does not follow the mind; ten follow the mind and are also associated with perception; eight do not follow the mind and are not associated with perception; three should be analyzed.

That is to say, the eight faculties subsumed under the three untainted faculties (anāsrava-indriya) both follow the mind and are associated with perception; one faculty is associated with perception but does not follow the mind; one faculty follows formations (saṃskāra) but does not follow the mind; ten faculties follow the mind and are also associated with formations, excluding their own intrinsic nature; eight faculties neither follow the mind nor are associated with formations; and three [faculties] should be analyzed individually.

That is to say, they are subsumed under the three untainted faculties (*anāsrava-indriya*): one type is associated with mental formations (*cittānuvartin*) but does not follow the mind (*na cittānuparivartin*), while eight types follow the mind and are also associated with mental formations, excluding their own intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).

Regarding how many [factors] follow the movement of vitarka (applied thought) but are not associated with vicāra (sustained thought), and so forth: two are with both vitarka and vicāra; eight are without vitarka and without vicāra; and twelve should be analyzed.
That is to say, the faculty of mind (manas-indriya) is either with both vitarka and vicāra, or without vitarka and with vicāra only, or without both vitarka and vicāra.
What is that which is accompanied by both vitarka and vicāra?
It refers to the faculty of mind associated with attention (manasikāra) that is accompanied by both vitarka and vicāra.
What is that which is without vitarka and with only vicāra?
This refers to the mental faculty (manas) associated with attention that is without vitarka and possesses only vicāra.
What is meant by "without vitarka and without vicāra"?
It refers to the mental faculty associated with attention that is without both vitarka and vicāra.
The faculty of equanimity, the five faculties beginning with faith, and the three untainted faculties are also like this.
As for the faculty of pleasure, it is sometimes accompanied by vitarka and vicāra, and sometimes without vitarka and without vicāra.
What is "with vitarka and vicāra"?
It refers to the faculty of pleasure associated with attention that possesses vitarka and vicāra.
What is "without vitarka and without vicāra"?
This refers to the faculty of pleasure (*sukhendriya*) associated with attention that is without applied thought (*vitarka*) and sustained thought (*vicāra*).
The faculty of joy (*saumanasyendriya*) is likewise.
Regarding how many are views (*dṛṣṭi*) and how many are bases of views (*dṛṣṭisthāna*), one is both a view and a basis of views; nine are bases of views but not views; and twelve should be analyzed.

That is to say, the faculty of mind (manendriya), if it is with outflows (sāsrava), is a locus of views (dṛṣṭisthāna) but is not itself a view; if it is without outflows (anāsrava), it is neither a view nor a locus of views.
The same applies to the faculties of pleasure, joy, and equanimity, as well as the four faculties beginning with faith (śraddhā).
The faculty of wisdom (prajñendriya) has four permutations:
1. It is vision but not a locus of vision; this refers to the untainted faculty of wisdom not subsumed under the knowledge of exhaustion (kṣayajñāna) and the knowledge of non-arising (anutpādajñāna).
2. It is a locus of vision but not vision; this refers to the tainted faculty of wisdom not subsumed under [the category of] vision.
Some are both views and the bases of view, namely, mundane right view.
Some are neither views nor the bases of view, namely, the untainted faculty of wisdom (*anāsrava-prajñendriya*) not included within [the category of] views.

The wisdom included within the faculty of "knowing the unknown" (*anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīndriya*) and the faculty of "having known" (*ājñendriya*) is view but not a basis of view; all others are neither views nor bases of view.

The faculty of wisdom (*prajñendriya*) included within the faculty of one who has final knowledge (*ājñātāvīndriya*), but not included within the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) or the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*), is vision (*dṛṣṭi*) but not a basis for vision (*dṛṣṭisthāna*); the remainder are neither vision nor a basis for vision.

Regarding how many have the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) as their cause but are not causes of the view of a self-identity, sixteen do not have the view of a self-identity as their cause and are not causes of the view of a self-identity; six should be analyzed.

That is to say, regarding the faculty of mind (manas-indriya), there are those that have the view of a self-identity (satkāyadṛṣṭi) as their cause but are not themselves causes of the view of a self-identity; those that have the view of a self-identity as their cause and are also causes of the view of a self-identity; and those that neither have the view of a self-identity as their cause nor are causes of the view of a self-identity.

That which has the view of a self-body (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) as its cause, but is not itself a cause of the view of a self-body, refers to: (1) the mental faculty (*manas-indriya*) associated with the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya*), excluding those belonging to the past and present; (2) the mental faculty associated with the universal latent tendencies (*sarvatraga-anuśaya*) abandoned through the vision of the origin (*samudaya-darśana-prahātavya*), excluding those belonging to the past and present; and (3) the mental faculty associated with the view of a self-body in the future. All other defiled mental faculties [fall into this category].
That which has the view of a self as its cause and also has the view of a self as its cause refers to the mental faculty (manas) previously excluded.
That which neither has the view of a self as its cause nor has the view of a self as its cause refers to the non-defiled mental faculty.
The same applies to the faculties of pleasure, joy, and equanimity. As for the faculty of pain:

if it is defiled, it has the view of a self-identity as its cause but is not itself a cause of the view of a self-identity; if it is undefiled, it neither has the view of a self-identity as its cause nor is it a cause of the view of a self-identity.

The faculty of sorrow (daurmanasyendriya) may have the view of a self-identity (satkāyadṛṣṭi) as its cause but not be a cause of the view of a self-identity; it may have the view of a self-identity as its cause and also be a cause of the view of a self-identity; or it may neither have the view of a self-identity as its cause nor be a cause of the view of a self-identity.

That which has the view of a self-identity as its cause, but is not itself a cause for the view of a self-identity, refers to all other defiled roots of sorrow, excluding those associated with the latent dispositions (anuśaya) abandoned through the vision of suffering in the past and present, and excluding those associated with the universal latent dispositions abandoned through the vision of the origin [of suffering] in the past and present.
That which has the view of a self as its cause and also has the view of a self as its cause refers to the faculty of grief previously excluded.
That which neither has the view of a self as its cause nor has the view of a self as its cause refers to the undefiled faculty of grief.
Regarding how many karmas are not karmic maturation (vipāka) and so forth: one is karmic maturation but not karma; nine are neither karma nor karmic maturation; twelve should be analyzed.
This refers to the eye-faculty (*cakṣur-indriya*), which is either a maturation of karma (*karmavipāka*) but not karma itself, or neither karma nor a maturation of karma.
That which is a maturation of karma but not karma refers to the eye-faculty born of maturation; all other eye-faculties are neither karma nor a maturation of karma.
The same applies to the faculties of ear, nose, tongue, body, female, male, mind, pleasure, pain, joy, and equanimity.
Regarding how many are not karma and do not follow along with karma (*na karmānuvartin*), eight are neither karma nor follow along with karma; fourteen follow along with karma but are not karma.

Regarding how many derived forms (*upādāya-rūpa*) are not visible forms (*sanidarśana-rūpa*), etc.: seven are derived forms that are not visible forms; fifteen are neither derived forms nor visible forms.

Regarding these twenty-two faculties, how many are derived matter and resistant matter, and so forth? Seven are derived matter and also resistant matter; fifteen are neither derived matter nor resistant matter.
Regarding the statement "How many are profound because they are difficult to see," etc.: all are profound because they are difficult to see, and they are difficult to see because they are profound.
Regarding the question "How many are wholesome and have wholesomeness as their cause," etc.: eight are both wholesome and have wholesomeness as their cause; fourteen should be analyzed.
This refers to the eye-faculty (cakṣur-indriya), which either has a wholesome cause but is not itself wholesome, or is neither wholesome nor has a wholesome cause.

That which has a wholesome cause but is not itself wholesome refers to the eye-faculty born of the maturation (vipāka) of wholesome karma; all other eye-faculties are neither wholesome nor have a wholesome cause.
The same applies to the faculties of the ear, nose, tongue, body, femininity, masculinity, and life.

As for the mental faculty (*manas-indriya*), it may have a wholesome cause but not be wholesome itself; or it may be both wholesome and have a wholesome cause; or it may be neither wholesome nor have a wholesome cause.
That which is wholesome as its cause but not itself wholesome refers to the mental faculty (*manas-indriya*) that arises as the maturation (*vipāka*) of wholesome karma.
That which is both wholesome and has the wholesome as its cause refers to the wholesome mental faculty.

That which is neither wholesome nor has the wholesome as its cause refers to all other indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) and unwholesome mental faculties, excluding the mental faculty that arises as the maturation of wholesome karma.
The same applies to the faculties of pleasure, joy, and equanimity.
As for the faculty of pain (*duḥkhendriya*), it is either wholesome and has a wholesome cause, or it is neither wholesome nor has a wholesome cause.
That which is wholesome and has a wholesome cause refers to the wholesome faculty of pain.
That which is neither wholesome nor has a wholesome cause refers to the unwholesome and the indeterminate suffering-faculty (*duḥkhendriya*).
The grief-faculty (*daurmanasyendriya*) is either wholesome and has a wholesome cause, or neither wholesome nor has a wholesome cause.
That which is wholesome and has a wholesome cause refers to the wholesome faculty of grief (*daurmanasyendriya*).
That which is neither wholesome nor has a wholesome cause refers to the unwholesome faculty of grief.
Regarding how many are unwholesome and do not have an unwholesome cause, eight are neither unwholesome nor have an unwholesome cause, while fourteen should be analyzed.
This refers to the eye-faculty (cakṣur-indriya), which is either caused by what is unwholesome (akuśala) but is not itself unwholesome, or is neither unwholesome nor caused by what is unwholesome.

That which is caused by what is unwholesome but is not itself unwholesome is the eye-faculty born of the maturation (vipāka) of unwholesome karma; all other eye-faculties are neither unwholesome nor caused by what is unwholesome.
The same applies to the faculties of the ear, nose, tongue, body, female, male, and life.

As for the mental faculty (*manas-indriya*), it may have what is unwholesome as its cause while not being unwholesome itself; or it may be both unwholesome and have what is unwholesome as its cause; or it may be neither unwholesome nor have what is unwholesome as its cause.

That which has unwholesome causes but is not itself unwholesome refers to the mental faculty (*manas-indriya*) that arises as the maturation (*vipāka*) of the unwholesome, as well as the mental faculty associated with the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and the view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*) bound to the desire realm.
That which is unwholesome and has an unwholesome cause refers to the unwholesome faculty of mind (*manendriya*).

That which is neither unwholesome nor has an unwholesome cause refers to all remaining neutral and wholesome faculties of mind, excluding those that are the maturation of the unwholesome, as well as excluding the faculty of mind associated with the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and the view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*) bound to the desire realm.
The faculty of pleasure (sukhendriya) is either unwholesome and has an unwholesome cause, or it is neither unwholesome nor has an unwholesome cause.
That which is unwholesome and has an unwholesome cause refers to the unwholesome faculty of pleasure.
That which is neither unwholesome nor has an unwholesome cause refers to the wholesome and indeterminate faculties of pleasure (*sukhendriya*).

As for the faculty of pain (*duḥkhendriya*), it may have an unwholesome cause but not be unwholesome itself; or it may be both unwholesome and have an unwholesome cause; or it may be neither unwholesome nor have an unwholesome cause.
That which has unwholesome causes but is not itself unwholesome refers to the faculty of suffering born of maturation (*vipākaja*).
That which is both unwholesome and has unwholesome causes refers to the unwholesome faculty of suffering.

Regarding that which is neither unwholesome nor has an unwholesome cause: this refers to all other indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) and wholesome (*kuśala*) faculties of suffering (*duḥkhendriya*), excluding those born of maturation (*vipākaja*).

As for the faculty of joy (*saumanasyendriya*), it may have an unwholesome cause but not be unwholesome itself; or it may be both unwholesome and have an unwholesome cause; or it may be neither unwholesome nor have an unwholesome cause.

That which has unwholesome as its cause but is not itself unwholesome refers to the faculty of joy (*saumanasyendriya*) associated with the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and the view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*) bound to the desire realm.
That which is both unwholesome and has unwholesome as its cause refers to the unwholesome faculty of joy.

That which is neither unwholesome nor has unwholesomeness as its cause refers to all other indeterminate and wholesome roots of joy, excluding those associated with the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and the view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*) bound to the desire realm.
The faculty of equanimity is also like this.
As for the faculty of grief, it is either unwholesome and has an unwholesome cause, or it is neither unwholesome nor does it have an unwholesome cause.
That which is unwholesome and has an unwholesome cause refers to the unwholesome faculty of grief.
Regarding "neither unwholesome nor having unwholesomeness as its cause," this refers to the wholesome faculty of mental grief (*daurmanasyendriya*).

Regarding "how many are indeterminate and have indeterminacy as their cause, etc.?"—eight are indeterminate and have indeterminacy as their cause; eight are neither indeterminate nor have indeterminacy as their cause; and six are to be analyzed.

That is to say, the mental faculty (manas-indriya) may have an indeterminate (avyākṛta) cause but not itself be indeterminate; or it may be both indeterminate and have an indeterminate cause; or it may be neither indeterminate nor have an indeterminate cause.
That which has an indeterminate cause but is not itself indeterminate refers to the unwholesome faculty of mind.
That which is both indeterminate and has an indeterminate cause refers to the indeterminate faculty of mind.
That which is neither indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) nor has an indeterminate cause refers to the wholesome faculty of mind (*manas-indriya*).
The same applies to the faculties of pleasure, pain, joy, and equanimity.
As for the faculty of grief (*daurmanasya-indriya*), it is either indeterminate with an indeterminate cause, or it is not indeterminate and does not have an indeterminate cause.
That which has an indeterminate cause but is not itself indeterminate refers to the unwholesome faculty of grief (*daurmanasyendriya*).
That which is neither indeterminate nor has an indeterminate cause refers to the wholesome faculty of grief.
Regarding how many are "conditioned by causes" (hetu-pratyaya) but not "having a cause" (sahetu), all are conditioned by causes and also have a cause.

Regarding how many are "immediately preceding" (samanantara) but not "immediately preceding conditions" (samanantara-pratyaya), eight are neither immediately preceding nor immediately preceding conditions, while fourteen should be analyzed.

That is to say, the mind-faculty (manas-indriya) is either an equal-and-immediate [condition] but not an equal-and-immediate object-condition, or it is both an equal-and-immediate [condition] and an equal-and-immediate object-condition, or it is neither an equal-and-immediate [condition] nor an equal-and-immediate object-condition.

Those which are immediate antecedents but not equal-and-immediate conditions refer to the mental faculty (*manas-indriya*) that is about to arise in the future and manifest before one, as well as the mental faculty at the moment of death for an Arhat in the past or present.

Those that are both immediate [condition] and equal-and-immediate condition refer to all past and present mental faculties (manas-indriya), with the exception of the mental faculty at the moment of death of a past or present Arhat.

That which is neither an equal-and-immediate [condition] nor an equal-and-immediate condition refers to all other future mental faculties (manas-indriya), excluding those that are currently arising and manifesting in the future;
the same applies to the faculty of equanimity (upekṣendriya).

The faculty of pleasure (sukhendriya) is either an immediately antecedent condition that is not an equal-and-immediate condition, or it is both an immediately antecedent condition and an equal-and-immediate condition, or it is neither an immediately antecedent condition nor an equal-and-immediate condition.
Those which are equal-immediate but not equal-immediate conditions refer to the faculty of pleasure that is about to arise in the future and is currently manifesting.
Those which are both equal-immediate and equal-immediate conditions refer to the faculty of pleasure in the past and the present.

Those that are neither equal-immediate [condition] nor equal-immediate condition are: with the exception of the faculty of pleasure (*sukhendriya*) that is currently arising in the present, all other future faculties of pleasure;
the same applies to the faculties of pain, joy, and sorrow, the five faculties beginning with faith (*śraddhā*), and the three untainted faculties (*anāsravendriya*).

Regarding the question of how many object-conditions (ālambana-pratyaya) are not possessed of an object (ālambana), eight are object-conditions that are not possessed of an object, while fourteen are both object-conditions and possessed of an object.
Regarding the question "How many adhipatipratyayas (predominant conditions) are also adhipatis (predominant factors)?"—all are adhipatipratyayas and are also adhipatis.
Regarding the question "How many oghas (floods) are not ānuśrotas (conducive to the flood)?"—ten are ānuśrotas but not oghas; three are neither oghas nor ānuśrotas; nine should be analyzed.

This refers to the nine faculties beginning with the mental faculty (*manas*): if they are contaminated (*sāsrava*), they are "conducive to the flood" (*oghānukūla*) but not the flood itself; if they are uncontaminated (*anāsrava*), they are neither the flood nor conducive to the flood.

As for the twelve bases (*āyatana*), these refer to the eye-base (*cakṣur-āyatana*) and the form-base (*rūpa-āyatana*), up to the mental-base (*mana-āyatana*) and the phenomena-base (*dharma-āyatana*).
Regarding these twelve bases (*āyatana*), how many possess form (*rūpin*) and so forth? Ten possess form; one is formless; and one should be analyzed.
That is to say, the base of mental phenomena (*dharmāyatana*) is either with form or without form.
What is that which has form?
It refers to bodily and vocal actions subsumed under the sphere of mental objects (*dharmāyatana*).
What is that which is formless?
This refers to the remaining bases of phenomena (*dharmāyatana*).
Regarding how many are visible (*sanidarśana*) and so forth:
one is visible, and eleven are invisible (*anidarśana*).
Regarding how many possess resistance (*sapratigha*) and so forth: ten possess resistance, and two are without resistance.
Regarding how many are with outflows (*sāsrava*) and so forth: ten are with outflows, and two should be analyzed.
That is to say, the sphere of mind (*manāyatana*) is either with outflows or without outflows.
What is the tainted (*sāsrava*)?
It refers to the sense base of mind (*manāyatana*) associated with tainted attention (*manasikāra*).
What is the untainted (*anāsrava*)?
This refers to the sense base of mind (*manāyatana*) associated with untainted attention (*anāsrava-manasikāra*),
and the sense base of phenomena (*dharmāyatana*), which may be either tainted (*sāsrava*) or untainted (*anāsrava*). What is tainted?

This refers to the contaminated (sāsrava) bodily and vocal actions subsumed under the sphere of mental objects (dharmāyatana), as well as the contaminated aggregates of feeling, perception, and formations.
What is the uncontaminated (anāsrava)?
It refers to the uncontaminated bodily and vocal actions, as well as the uncontaminated aggregates of feeling, perception, and formations, together with unconditioned phenomena (asaṃskṛtadharma).
Regarding "how many are conditioned" and so forth: eleven are conditioned; one should be analyzed, namely the sphere of phenomena (*dharmāyatana*), which may be either conditioned or unconditioned.
What is conditioned?

This refers to bodily and vocal karma included within the sphere of mental objects (*dharmāyatana*), as well as the aggregates of feeling, perception, and formations (*vedanā-saṃjñā-saṃskāra-skandha*).
What is the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*)?
It refers to space (*ākāśa*) and the two types of cessation (*nirodha*).
Regarding how many possess maturation (*vipāka*) and so forth: eight have no maturation; four should be analyzed.
That is to say, the sphere of form (*rūpāyatana*) may either possess maturation or lack maturation.
What has maturation?
It refers to wholesome and unwholesome forms (rūpāyatana).
What lacks maturation?
That is to say, the sphere of form (rūpāyatana) is indeterminate (avyākṛta).
The sphere of sound (śabdāyatana) is likewise.
As for the sphere of mind (manāyatana), it may be either with retribution (savipāka) or without retribution (avipāka).
What possesses maturation?
It refers to the sense base of mind (manāyatana) that is unwholesome or wholesome-with-outflows.
What is that which has no maturation?
It refers to the sense-base of mind (manāyatana) that is indeterminate and untainted (anāsrava).
The same applies to the sense-base of phenomena (dharmāyatana).

Regarding how many are dependently originated (*pratītyasamutpanna*) and so forth: eleven are dependently originated, produced by causes (*hetuja*), and included within the world (*loka-saṃgṛhīta*). One should be analyzed: that is, if the sphere of phenomena (*dharmāyatana*) is conditioned (*saṃskṛta*), it is dependently originated, produced by causes, and included within the world; if it is unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), it is not dependently originated, not produced by causes, and not included within the world.
Regarding how many are comprised by form (*rūpa*) and so forth: ten are comprised by form; one is comprised by name (*nāman*); and one should be analyzed.
That is to say, the bodily and vocal actions included within the sphere of phenomena (*dharmāyatana*) are comprised by form, while the remainder are all comprised by name.
Regarding how many are included within the internal bases (*ādhyātmikāyatana*), etc.: six are included within the internal bases, and six are included within the external bases (*bāhyāyatana*).
Regarding how many are to be fully known through the thorough knowledge of wisdom (*jñānaparijñāparijñeya*), etc.: all are to be fully known through the thorough knowledge of wisdom.

Regarding the question of how many among these twelve bases (*āyatana*) are to be fully known through the complete knowledge of abandonment (*prahāṇa-parijñā*), ten are to be fully known through the complete knowledge of abandonment, while two should be analyzed.

That is to say, as for the mind base (*mana-āyatana*) and the mental-object base (*dharma-āyatana*): if they are with outflows (*sāsrava*), they are to be fully known through the complete knowledge of abandonment; if they are without outflows (*anāsrava*), they are not to be fully known through the complete knowledge of abandonment.
Regarding "how many should be abandoned" and so forth: ten [bases] should be abandoned, while two should be analyzed.

That is to say, regarding the mind base (*manāyatana*) and the mental-object base (*dharmāyatana*), if they are with outflows (*sāsrava*), they should be abandoned; if they are without outflows (*anāsrava*), they should not be abandoned.
Regarding "how many should be cultivated" and so forth: eight are not to be cultivated, and four should be analyzed.
That is to say, the sphere of form (*rūpāyatana*) may be either to be cultivated or not to be cultivated.
How is it to be cultivated?
This refers to the wholesome sphere of form (*rūpāyatana*). What is not to be cultivated?
This refers to the unwholesome and neutral spheres of form.
The sphere of sound and the sphere of mind are also like this.
As for the sphere of mental objects (*dharmāyatana*), it is either to be cultivated or not to be cultivated.
What is to be cultivated?
This refers to the sphere of wholesome conditioned phenomena.
What is not to be cultivated?
This refers to the spheres of unwholesome and indeterminate phenomena, as well as analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).
Regarding "how many are defiled" and so forth: eight are non-defiled, and four should be analyzed.
That is to say, the sphere of form (*rūpāyatana*) is either defiled or non-defiled. What is defiled?
This refers to the obscured form-base (*rūpāyatana*). What is non-defiled?
This refers to the unobscured form-base.
The same applies to the sense bases of sound, mind, and mental objects (*dharmāyatana*).
Regarding how many are results (*phala*) but not possessors of results (*saphala*), etc.: eleven are both results and possessors of results; one should be analyzed.
That is to say, the base of mental objects may be a result but not a possessor of results, or it may be both a result and a possessor of results, or neither a result nor a possessor of results.
That which is a fruit but does not possess a fruit refers to analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).
That which is both a fruit and possesses a fruit refers to the sphere of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*).
That which is neither a fruit nor possesses a fruit refers to space (*ākāśa*) and non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).
Regarding how many are appropriated (*upātta*) and so forth:
three are unappropriated, while nine should be analyzed.
That is to say, the sense-base of the eye is either appropriated or unappropriated.
What is appropriated?
It refers to the sense base of the eye that is comprised within one's own body.
What is non-appropriated?
This refers to the sense base of the eye that is not comprised within its own substance;
the same applies to the sense bases of visible form, ear, nose, odor, tongue, taste, body, and tangibles.
Regarding how many are derived from the great elements (*mahābhūta*) and so forth: nine are derived from the great elements, one is not derived from the great elements, and two should be analyzed.

That is to say, among the sense bases, the tangible base (*spraṣṭavyāyatana*) consists of solidity, moisture, heat, and motion, which are not derived from the primary elements (*mahābhūta*); the others are derived from the primary elements.
Within the sense base of mental objects (*dharmāyatana*), bodily and vocal actions are derived from the primary elements; the rest are not derived from the primary elements.

Regarding the phrase "how many are with superior" (*sottara*): eleven are with superior; one should be analyzed. That is to say, the sphere of phenomena (*dharmāyatana*) that is cessation through deliberation (*pratisaṃkhyānirodha*) is without superior (*anuttara*); all others are with superior.
Regarding the statement "how many are 'existent' (*bhava*) and so forth": ten are existent; two should be analyzed.

That is to say, the sense-sphere of mind (*manāyatana*) and the sense-sphere of phenomena (*dharmāyatana*) are existent if they are with outflows (*sāsrava*), and non-existent if they are without outflows (*anāsrava*).

Regarding how many causes they are associated with and so forth: ten causes are not associated; one cause is associated; and one [category] should be analyzed. That is to say, among the dharmas of the sphere of mental objects (*dharmāyatana*), those that are mental concomitants (*caitta*) are associated with causes, while the remainder are not associated with causes.
*Abhidharmaprakaraṇapādaśāstra*, Fascicle Fifteen.
*Abhidharmaprakaraṇapādaśāstra*, Fascicle Sixteen.
Composed by the Venerable Vasumitra.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang by Imperial Decree.

Chapter Seven: Discerning the Thousand Questions, Part Seven. Regarding the inclusion of these twelve bases (*āyatana*) within the six wholesome bases (*kuśalāyatana*): the six wholesome bases include a portion of four bases, and a portion of those four bases also includes the six wholesome bases.

Regarding their mutual inclusion with the five unwholesome bases (*pañca-akuśala-sthānāni*): the five unwholesome bases include a portion of the four bases, and a portion of the four bases also includes the five unwholesome bases.

Regarding the mutual inclusion with the seven indeterminate bases (*avyākṛtāyatana*): the seven indeterminate bases include a portion of the eight bases and a portion of the four bases; likewise, a portion of the eight bases and a portion of the four bases also include the seven indeterminate bases.

Regarding their mutual inclusion with the three bases of outflows (*āsrava-sthāna*): the three bases of outflows include a portion of one base, and that portion of one base also includes the three bases of outflows.

Regarding their mutual inclusion with the five bases of outflows (*sāsrava-sthāna*): the five bases of outflows include ten bases and a portion of two bases, and those ten bases and portion of two bases also include the five bases of outflows.

Regarding the mutual inclusion with the eight untainted bases (*anāsrava-āyatana*): the eight untainted bases include a portion of two bases, and a portion of those two bases also includes the eight untainted bases.

Regarding "how many are past," etc.: eleven are either past, future, or present; one should be analyzed. That is to say, if the sphere of phenomena (*dharmāyatana*) is conditioned (*saṃskṛta*), it is either past, future, or present; if it is unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), it is neither past, nor future, nor present.
Regarding how many are wholesome and so forth: eight are indeterminate, and four should be analyzed.
That is to say, the sphere of form (rūpāyatana) may be wholesome, unwholesome, or indeterminate.
What is wholesome?
This refers to wholesome bodily intimation.
What is unwholesome?
It refers to unwholesome bodily intimation.
What is the indeterminate?
It refers to all other bases of form (*rūpāyatana*) apart from wholesome and unwholesome bodily intimation (*kāyavijñapti*).
As for the base of sound (*śabdāyatana*), it may be wholesome, unwholesome, or indeterminate.
What is wholesome?
It refers to wholesome vocal intimation.
What is unwholesome?
This refers to unwholesome vocal intimation.
What is the indeterminate?
It refers to all other spheres of sound, excluding wholesome and unwholesome vocal intimations.
The sense base of mind (manāyatana) is either wholesome, unwholesome, or indeterminate.
What is wholesome?
It refers to the sense base of mind associated with wholesome attention (manasikāra).
What is unwholesome?
It refers to the sense base of mind associated with unwholesome attention.
What is indeterminate?
This refers to the sense base of mind (manāyatana) associated with indeterminate attention (avyākṛta-manasikāra),
and the sense base of mental objects (dharmāyatana), which may be wholesome, unwholesome,
or indeterminate. What is wholesome?

This refers to wholesome bodily and vocal actions subsumed under the sphere of mental objects (*dharmāyatana*), as well as the wholesome aggregates of feeling, perception, and formations, together with analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyānirodha*).
What is unwholesome?
It refers to unwholesome bodily and vocal actions subsumed under the sphere of mental objects, as well as the unwholesome aggregates of feeling, perception, and formations.
What is the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*)?
It refers to the aggregates of feeling, perception, and formations that are indeterminate, as well as space (*ākāśa*) and non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).
Regarding how many are bound to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*) and so forth: two are bound to the desire realm, while ten should be analyzed.
That is to say, the sense-base of the eye is either bound to the desire realm or bound to the form realm.
What is meant by being bound to the desire realm?
It refers to the sense-base of the eye produced from the primary elements of the desire realm.
What is that which is bound to the realm of form (*rūpadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*)?
It refers to the sense-base of the eye (*cakṣur-āyatana*) produced by the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) of the realm of form.
The same applies to the sense-bases of visible forms, the ear, sounds, the nose, the tongue, and the body.
The sense base of tangibles is either bound to the desire realm or bound to the form realm.
What is bound to the desire realm?
It refers to the four great elements of the desire realm and the sense base of tangibles derived from those great elements of the desire realm.
What is bound to the realm of form (*rūpadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*)?
It refers to the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) of the realm of form and the sphere of tangibles (*spraṣṭavyāyatana*) derived from those great elements of the realm of form.
As for the sphere of mind (*manāyatana*), it is either bound to the desire realm, or bound to the realm of form, or bound to the formless realm, or unbound.
What is bound to the desire realm?
It refers to the sense base of mind associated with mental attention belonging to the desire realm.
What is bound to the form realm?
This refers to the sense base of mind associated with mental attention belonging to the form realm.
What is that which is bound to the formless realm?
It refers to the sense base of mind associated with mental attention belonging to the formless realm.
What is non-bound (*apratisaṃyukta*)?
It refers to the sense-base of mind (*manāyatana*) associated with outflow-free attention (*anāsrava-manasikāra*).
As for the sense-base of phenomena (*dharmāyatana*), it may be bound to the desire realm, the form realm, the formless realm, or it may be non-bound.
What is bound to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*)?

It refers to the bodily and vocal actions included within the sphere of phenomena (*dharmāyatana*) that belong to the desire realm, as well as the aggregates of feeling, perception, and formations belonging to the desire realm.
What is bound to the form realm (*rūpadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*)?

This refers to the form included within the sphere of phenomena (*dharmāyatana*), namely the bodily and vocal actions of the form realm, as well as the aggregates of feeling, perception, and formations of the form realm.
What is bound to the formless realm?
This refers to the aggregates of feeling, perception, and formations of the formless realm.
What is "unbound" (*apratisaṃyukta*)?

It refers to untainted (*anāsrava*) bodily and vocal actions, as well as the untainted aggregates of feeling, perception, and formations, together with the three unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) phenomena.
Regarding how many are "in training" (*śaikṣa*) and so forth: ten are neither in training nor beyond training (*naivaśaikṣanāśaikṣa*); two are to be analyzed.

That is to say, the sense base of mind (manāyatana) is either that of one in training (śaikṣa), or that of one beyond training (aśaikṣa), or that of one who is neither in training nor beyond training.
What is that of one in training?
It refers to the sense base of mind associated with the mental attention of one in training.
What is that which is beyond training (*aśaikṣa*)?
It refers to the sense base of mind (*manāyatana*) associated with mental attention (*manasikāra*) of one beyond training.
What is that which is neither in training nor beyond training (*naivaśaikṣanāśaikṣa*)?
This refers to the sense-sphere of mind (*manāyatana*) and the sense-sphere of phenomena (*dharmāyatana*) associated with tainted attention (*sāsrava-manasikāra*).
These may be of the type of training (*śaikṣa*), beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), or neither of training nor beyond training (*naivaśaikṣanāśaikṣa*).
What is of the type of training?
This refers to the bodily and vocal actions of one in training (*śaikṣa*), as well as the aggregates of feeling, perception, and formations of one in training.
What is that which is beyond training (*aśaikṣa*)?
It refers to the bodily and vocal actions of one beyond training, as well as the aggregates of feeling, perception, and formations of one beyond training.
What is that which is neither-trainee-nor-non-trainee?

It refers to the contaminated bodily and vocal actions subsumed under the sphere of phenomena (*dharmāyatana*), as well as the contaminated aggregates of feeling, perception, and formations, together with space and the two types of cessation.
Regarding how many of these twelve bases (āyatana) are abandoned by insight (darśana-heya), etc.: ten are abandoned by cultivation (bhāvanā-heya), and two should be analyzed.
That is to say, the mind base (manāyatana) is either abandoned by insight, abandoned by cultivation, or not abandoned at all.
What is abandoned by insight?
It refers to that which is abandoned by the patiences at the limit of clear realization for those who practice through faith or through the Dharma within the sphere of the mind.
Furthermore, what is this?
This refers to the mind-base (*manāyatana*) associated with the eighty-eight proclivities (*anuśaya*) abandoned through seeing (*darśana-prahātavya*).
What is abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-prahātavya*)?
It refers to the mind-base belonging to those who have seen the path (*dṛṣṭapada*) and is abandoned through cultivation.
What, then, is this? It refers to the sphere of mind (manāyatana) associated with the ten proclivities (anuśaya) to be abandoned through cultivation, as well as the undefiled impure sphere of mind.
What is not to be abandoned?
This refers to the untainted (anāsrava) sense-base of mind (manāyatana) and the sense-base of phenomena (dharmāyatana),
which are either to be abandoned by insight (darśana-heya), to be abandoned by cultivation (bhāvanā-heya), or not to be abandoned (aheya).
What is to be abandoned by insight?
This refers to that which is abandoned by the patiences at the limit of clear realization (*abhisamaya*) for those who follow by faith (*śraddhānusārin*) or follow by dharma (*dharmānusārin*).
Furthermore, what is this?

It refers to the eighty-eight latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) to be abandoned through seeing, along with their associated factors of the sphere of mental objects (*dharmāyatana*), as well as the non-associated formations (*cittaviprayuktasaṃskāra*) arising together with them.
What is abandoned through cultivation?

It refers to those factors within the sphere of mental objects (*dharmāyatana*) that are abandoned through cultivation by one who has attained the vision of the tracks of training (*śaikṣa-dṛṣṭiprāpta*).
What, furthermore, are these?

This refers to the ten latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) and their associated factors within the sphere of mental objects (*dharmāyatana*), as well as the non-informative (*avijñapti*) bodily and vocal actions arising from them, the formations dissociated from mind (*cittaviprayukta-saṃskāra*), and the non-defiled contaminated (*sāsrava*) factors within the sphere of mental objects.
What is not to be abandoned? It refers to the sphere of untainted phenomena (*anāsrava-dharmāyatana*).

Regarding how many are neither mind (*citta*), nor mental factors (*caitta*), nor associated with mind (*cittasaṃprayukta*): ten are neither mind, nor mental factors, nor associated with mind; one is exclusively mind; and one should be analyzed. That is to say, regarding the sphere of phenomena (*dharmāyatana*), if it has an object of cognition (*sālambana*), it is a mental factor and is associated with mind; if it lacks an object of cognition (*anālambana*), it is neither mind, nor a mental factor, nor associated with mind.

Regarding how many turn according to the mind (*cittānuvartin*) but are not associated with feeling (*vedanā-saṃprayukta*), and so forth: ten do not turn according to the mind and are not associated with feeling; one is associated with feeling but does not turn according to the mind; one should be analyzed—namely, the sphere of phenomena (*dharmāyatana*)—as either turning according to the mind but not associated with feeling, or turning according to the mind and also associated with feeling, or not turning according to the mind and not associated with feeling.

Those that follow the mind but are not associated with feeling (*vedanā*) refer to bodily and vocal actions that follow the mind, the formations dissociated from mind (*citta-viprayukta-saṃskāra*), and feeling itself.
Those that both follow the mind and are associated with feeling refer to the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*) and the associated aggregate of formations (*saṃprayukta-saṃskāra-skandha*).

Those that do not follow the mind and are not associated with feeling are: with the exception of bodily and vocal actions that follow the mind and the formations dissociated from mind, all other bodily and vocal actions, formations dissociated from mind, and unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛtadharma*).

Regarding how many follow the mind (*cittānuvartin*), are not associated with perception (*saṃjñā*) or formations (*saṃskāra*), and so forth: excluding their own intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), they should be understood in the same manner as feeling (*vedanā*).

Regarding how many follow discursive thought (*vitarkānuvartin*), are not associated with sustained thought (*vicāra*), and so forth: ten do not follow discursive thought and are not associated with sustained thought; two should be analyzed.
That is to say, the sense-base of mind (manāyatana) is either with vitarka and vicāra, or without vitarka and with vicāra only, or without vitarka and without vicāra.
What is "with vitarka and with vicāra"?
It refers to the sense-base of mind associated with attention (manasikāra) that possesses both vitarka and vicāra.
What is "without vitarka and with vicāra"?
It refers to the sphere of mind (manāyatana) associated with attention that is without vitarka and with only vicāra.
What is "without vitarka and without vicāra"?

This refers to the sense-sphere of mind (*manāyatana*) associated with attention that is without applied thought (*vitarka*) and sustained thought (*vicāra*). Regarding the sense-sphere of mental objects (*dharmāyatana*), there are four possibilities:

some follow the movement of applied thought but are not associated with sustained thought; these include bodily and vocal actions that follow the movement of applied thought, formations dissociated from mind (*cittaviprayuktasaṃskāra*), and sustained thought itself when it is associated with applied thought.

Alternatively, there are those associated with investigation (*vicāra*) but not following after initial inquiry (*vitarka*), namely: the mental factors associated with investigation that are themselves *vitarka* or are dissociated from *vitarka*.
Alternatively, there are those that follow after initial inquiry and are also associated with investigation, namely: the mental factors associated with both *vitarka* and *vicāra*.

Or [those factors] that neither follow after vitarka nor are associated with vicāra: namely, with the exception of the bodily and vocal actions and the formations dissociated from mind that follow after vitarka, all other bodily and vocal actions and formations dissociated from mind, as well as vicāra not associated with vitarka, and furthermore, those mental factors that are neither accompanied by vitarka nor vicāra, and unconditioned phenomena (asaṃskṛta-dharma).

Regarding the question of how many are "views" (dṛṣṭi) and how many are "bases of views" (dṛṣṭisthāna): one [base] is both a view and a base of views; nine are bases of views but not views; and two should be analyzed.

That is to say, as for the mind-base (manāyatana), if it is with outflows (sāsrava), it is a base of views but not a view; if it is without outflows (anāsrava), it is neither a base of views nor a view.
The sphere of phenomena (dharmāyatana) consists of four propositions.

First, there is that which is vision but not the sphere of vision: this refers to untainted wisdom (anāsravaprajñā) not subsumed under the knowledge of exhaustion (kṣayajñāna) and the knowledge of non-arising (anutpādajñāna).
Second, there is that which is the sphere of vision but not vision: this refers to the tainted sphere of phenomena (sāsravadharmāyatana) not subsumed under vision.
Some are views and also the basis for views, namely the five defiled views and mundane right view.
Some are neither views nor the basis for views, namely the uncontaminated dharma-bases not included within views.

Regarding how many [factors] have the view of a self-identity (satkāyadṛṣṭi) as their cause but are not themselves causes of the view of a self-identity: eight do not have the view of a self-identity as their cause and are not causes of the view of a self-identity; four should be analyzed.

That is to say, regarding the sphere of form (*rūpāyatana*): if it is defiled, it has the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) as its cause but is not itself a cause of the view of a self-identity; if it is non-defiled, it neither has the view of a self-identity as its cause nor is it a cause of the view of a self-identity.
The sphere of sound is also like this.

Regarding the sphere of mind, some have the view of a self-body (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) as their cause but are not themselves causes of the view of a self-body; some have the view of a self-body as their cause and are also causes of the view of a self-body; and some neither have the view of a self-body as their cause nor are they causes of the view of a self-body.

That which has the view of a self (satkāyadṛṣṭi) as its cause but is not itself the view of a self refers to: the mental bases (manāyatana) associated with the proclivities (anuśaya) to be abandoned by the vision of suffering (duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya), excluding those of the past and present; the mental bases associated with the universal proclivities (sarvatraga-anuśaya) to be abandoned by the vision of the origin (samudaya-darśana-prahātavya), excluding those of the past and present; and the mental bases associated with the view of a self in the future; as well as all other defiled (kliṣṭa) mental bases.
That which has the view of a self as its cause and is also a cause for the view of a self refers to the sense-sphere of mind (manāyatana) previously excluded.
That which neither has the view of a self as its cause nor is a cause for the view of a self refers to the non-defiled sense-sphere of mind.

Regarding the sphere of mental objects (dharmāyatana), some have the view of a self-identity (satkāyadṛṣṭi) as their cause but are not themselves causes for the view of a self-identity; some have the view of a self-identity as their cause and are also causes for the view of a self-identity; and some neither have the view of a self-identity as their cause nor are they causes for the view of a self-identity.

Regarding those things that have the view of a self (satkāyadṛṣṭi) as their cause but are not causes of the view of a self: this refers to all other defiled dharma-bases, excluding the following: (1) the past and present latent dispositions (anuśaya) abandoned through the vision of suffering, along with their associated and co-existent dharmas; (2) the past and present universal latent dispositions abandoned through the vision of the origin [of suffering], along with their associated and co-existent dharmas; (3) future dharmas associated with the view of a self; and (4) the future birth, aging, duration, and impermanence of the view of a self and its associated dharmas. All remaining defiled dharma-bases constitute this category.

That which has the view of a self (satkāyadṛṣṭi) as its cause and also has the view of a self as its cause refers to the sphere of mental objects (dharmāyatana), excluding what was previously mentioned.
That which neither has the view of a self as its cause nor has the view of a self as its cause refers to the undefiled sphere of mental objects.
Regarding the question of how many *karmas* are not *karmavipākas*, all [bases] should be analyzed.
That is to say, the eye-base (*cakṣur-āyatana*) is either a *karmavipāka* that is not a *karman*, or it is neither a *karman* nor a *karmavipāka*.

That which is the maturation of karma but not karma itself refers to the sense base of the eye that arises as maturation; all other instances of the sense base of the eye are neither karma nor the maturation of karma.
The same applies to the sense bases of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind, as well as to odors, tastes, tangibles, and mental objects.
The sphere of visible form may be karma but not the maturation of karma, or the maturation of karma but not karma, or neither karma nor the maturation of karma.
That which is karma but not the maturation of karma refers to bodily intimation (*kāyavijñapti*).
That which is the maturation of karma but not karma refers to the sphere of form (*rūpāyatana*) born from the maturation of karma.

That which is neither karma nor the maturation of karma refers to all other spheres of form, excluding the sphere of form that is either karma or the maturation of karma, as well as the sphere of sound (*śabdāyatana*), which may be either karma but not the maturation of karma, or neither karma nor the maturation of karma.

That which is karma but not the maturation of karma refers to vocal intimation (*vāgvijñapti*). All other instances of the sphere of sound (*śabdāyatana*) are neither karma nor the maturation of karma.
Regarding the sphere of mental objects (*dharmāyatana*), there are four permutations.
Some are karma but not the maturation of karma, namely: bodily and vocal karma subsumed under the sphere of mental objects, as well as volition (*cetanā*) that is not subsumed under maturation.

Either it is the maturation of karma but not karma itself, namely, those phenomena included within the sphere of mental objects (*dharmāyatana*) that arise from the maturation of karma and are not subsumed under volition (*cetanā*);
or it is both karma and the maturation of karma, namely, volition that arises from maturation.

Or [there are those] that are neither karma nor the maturation of karma; this refers to all other bases of phenomena (*dharmāyatana*) excluding the base of phenomena that constitutes karma and the base of phenomena that constitutes the maturation of karma.
Regarding how many are karma but do not follow from karma, and so forth: eight are neither karma nor follow from karma; one follows from karma but is not karma; three should be analyzed.
That is to say, the sphere of form (rūpāyatana) is either karma that does not follow from karma, or neither karma nor following from karma.
That which is karma but does not follow from karma refers to bodily intimation (kāyavijñapti); all other spheres of form are neither karma nor following from karma.
The sphere of sound (śabdāyatana) is either karma that does not follow along with karma (na-anuvartaka), or neither karma nor following along with karma.
That which is karma but does not follow along with karma refers to vocal intimation (vāgvijñapti); all other spheres of sound are neither karma nor following along with karma.
The sphere of mental objects (dharmāyatana) consists of four propositions.

There are those that are karma but do not follow along with karma (na-anuvartaka), namely: all bodily and vocal karma included within the sphere of mental objects—excluding the bodily and vocal karma that follows along with karma—as well as volition (cetanā).

Some are concomitants of karma but are not karma itself; this refers to the aggregate of feeling, the aggregate of perception, and those factors within the aggregate of formations that are concomitants of karma but are not themselves subsumed under volition (*cetanā*).
Some are both karma and concomitants of karma; this refers to bodily and vocal karma that are concomitants of karma.
Or [there are those] that are neither karma nor concomitants of karma, namely, all other bases of phenomena (dharmāyatana) excluding karma and the dharmas that are concomitants of karma.
Regarding how many are derived matter (upādāyarūpa) but not visible matter (sanidarśana-rūpa), there are three propositions.
Some derived matter is not visible matter, namely the eight bases and a portion of two bases;
some derived matter is also visible matter, namely one base.
Or, there are those which are neither derived matter nor visible matter; these refer to one entire base and a portion of two bases.
Regarding how many of these twelve bases are derived matter but not resistant matter, and so forth, there are four permutations.
Alternatively, there are derived forms that are not resistant forms, namely a small portion of one base.
Or there are resistant forms that are not derived forms, namely a small portion of one base.
Or, there are derived forms that are also resistant forms, namely the nine bases and a portion of one base;
or, there are forms that are neither derived nor resistant forms, namely one base and a portion of one base.
Regarding the statement "How many are profound because they are difficult to see," etc.: all are profound because they are difficult to see, and they are difficult to see because they are profound.
Regarding the statement "How many are wholesome or have non-wholesome as their cause," etc.: all should be analyzed accordingly.
That is to say, the eye-base is either caused by what is wholesome but is itself not wholesome, or is neither wholesome nor caused by what is wholesome.

That which is caused by what is wholesome but is itself not wholesome refers to the eye-base born of the maturation of wholesome karma; all other eye-bases are neither wholesome nor caused by what is wholesome.
The same applies to the sense bases of the ear, nose, odor, tongue, taste, body, and tangible objects.

As for the sense base of visible forms, it may have a wholesome cause but not be wholesome itself; or it may be both wholesome and have a wholesome cause; or it may be neither wholesome nor have a wholesome cause.
That which is wholesome as its cause but not itself wholesome refers to the form base (*rūpāyatana*) born from the maturation (*vipāka*) of the wholesome.
That which is both wholesome and has the wholesome as its cause refers to the wholesome form base.

That which is neither wholesome nor has the wholesome as its cause refers to all other indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) and unwholesome form bases, excluding the form base born from the maturation of the wholesome.
The sphere of mind (*manāyatana*) is likewise.
As for the sphere of sound (*śabdāyatana*), it is either wholesome and has a wholesome cause, or it is neither-wholesome-nor-unwholesome and has a neither-wholesome-nor-unwholesome cause.
That which is wholesome and has a wholesome cause refers to the wholesome sphere of sound; all other spheres of sound have a neither-wholesome-nor-unwholesome cause.
The sphere of phenomena (dharmāyatana) consists of four possibilities.
It may be wholesome but not have wholesomeness as its cause, namely, analytical cessation (pratisaṃkhyānirodha).
Or it may have wholesomeness as its cause but not be wholesome itself, namely, those phenomena belonging to the sphere of phenomena that arise as the maturation (vipākaja) of wholesome [karma].
Either it is wholesome and has the wholesome as its cause, namely, the sphere of wholesome conditioned phenomena;

or it is neither wholesome nor has the wholesome as its cause, namely, all other indeterminate and unwholesome phenomena, excluding the sphere of phenomena produced by the maturation of the wholesome.
Regarding the categories such as "how many are unwholesome but not caused by the unwholesome," all should be analyzed.
That is to say, the sense-base of the eye is either unwholesome but not caused by the unwholesome, or neither unwholesome nor caused by the unwholesome.

That which has unwholesome as its cause but is not itself unwholesome refers to the eye-base produced from the maturation of the unwholesome; all other eye-bases are neither unwholesome nor have unwholesome as their cause.
The same applies to the ear, nose, odors, tongue, tastes, body, and tangibles.

As for the sense-base of visible forms (*rūpāyatana*), it may have an unwholesome cause but not itself be unwholesome; or it may be both unwholesome and have an unwholesome cause; or it may be neither unwholesome nor have an unwholesome cause.
That which has unwholesome as its cause but is not itself unwholesome refers to the form base (*rūpāyatana*) born of the maturation (*vipāka*) of the unwholesome.
That which is both unwholesome and has unwholesome as its cause refers to the unwholesome form base.

Regarding that which is neither unwholesome nor has an unwholesome cause: this refers to all other indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) and wholesome (*kuśala*) bases of form (*rūpāyatana*), excluding those bases of form produced as the maturation (*vipākaja*) of the unwholesome.
As for the base of sound (*śabdāyatana*), it is either unwholesome and has an unwholesome cause, or it is neither unwholesome nor has an unwholesome cause.
That which is unwholesome and has an unwholesome cause refers to the sphere of sound that is unwholesome; all other spheres of sound are neither unwholesome nor have an unwholesome cause.

As for the sphere of mind (*manāyatana*), it may have an unwholesome cause but not be unwholesome itself, or it may be both unwholesome and have an unwholesome cause, or it may be neither unwholesome nor have an unwholesome cause.

That which has unwholesome causes but is not itself unwholesome refers to the sense-sphere of mind that arises as the maturation of the unwholesome, as well as the sense-sphere of mind associated with the view of a self-identity and the view of extreme attachment within the desire realm.
That which is unwholesome and also has the unwholesome as its cause refers to the unwholesome sphere of mind (*manāyatana*).

That which is neither unwholesome nor has the unwholesome as its cause refers to all remaining indeterminate and wholesome spheres of mind, excluding the unwholesome spheres of mind that are the maturation of karma, and excluding the spheres of mind associated with the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and the view of extreme attachment (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*) within the desire realm.

The sphere of mental objects (dharmāyatana) is either caused by that which is unwholesome but is not itself unwholesome, or it is both unwholesome and caused by that which is unwholesome, or it is neither unwholesome nor caused by that which is unwholesome.

That which has unwholesome causes but is not itself unwholesome refers to: the sphere of phenomena (*dharmāyatana*) consisting of factors born of the maturation (*vipāka*) of the unwholesome; the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and the view of extreme adherence (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*) within the desire realm, together with their associated factors in the sphere of phenomena; and those formations dissociated from mind (*cittaviprayuktasaṃskāra*) that arise simultaneously with them.
That which is unwholesome and has an unwholesome cause refers to the sphere of phenomena (*dharmāyatana*) consisting of those factors that originate from the unwholesome.

That which is neither unwholesome nor has an unwholesome cause refers to all remaining indeterminate and wholesome spheres of phenomena, excluding the spheres of phenomena consisting of factors born of the maturation (*vipākaja*) of the unwholesome, as well as excluding the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), the view of extreme adherence (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*), their associated factors, and the formations dissociated from mind (*cittaviprayuktasaṃskāra*) that originate from them within the desire realm.

Regarding the question of how many indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) factors do not have the indeterminate as their cause, etc.: eight indeterminate factors have the indeterminate as their cause; four require further analysis.

That is to say, the sphere of form (*rūpāyatana*) may have the indeterminate as its cause but not be indeterminate itself; or it may be indeterminate and also have the indeterminate as its cause; or it may neither be indeterminate nor have the indeterminate as its cause.
That which has an indeterminate cause but is not itself indeterminate refers to unwholesome form-bases (*rūpāyatana*).
That which is both indeterminate and has an indeterminate cause refers to indeterminate form-bases.
That which is neither indeterminate nor has indeterminate [factors] as its cause refers to wholesome form-bases (*rūpāyatana*).
The same applies to the sound-base and the mind-base (*manāyatana*).
Regarding the dharma-base (*dharmāyatana*), there are four propositions.
Some are neutral (avyākṛta) but do not have neutrality as their cause, namely space (ākāśa) and cessation not through deliberation (apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha).
Some have neutrality as their cause but are not neutral themselves, namely the sphere of unwholesome dharmas (akuśala-dharmāyatana).
Either they are indeterminate and have the indeterminate as their cause, namely, the category of indeterminate conditioned phenomena;
or they are neither indeterminate nor have the indeterminate as their cause, namely, the category of wholesome phenomena.

Regarding the statement "how many conditions are not 'having a cause' (sahetu)," eleven [bases] are both conditions (*pratyaya*) and have a cause; one should be analyzed: namely, the sphere of phenomena (*dharmāyatana*). If it is conditioned (*saṃskṛta*), it is both a condition and has a cause; if it is unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), it is neither a condition nor does it have a cause.
