Regarding the question of how many are immediate [condition] but not immediate condition, and so forth: ten are neither immediate nor immediate condition; two should be analyzed.

That is to say, the sphere of mind (manāyatana) is either an immediate [condition] but not an immediate condition, or both an immediate [condition] and an immediate condition, or neither an immediate [condition] nor an immediate condition.

Those that are immediate but not the condition as an immediate antecedent (samanantara-pratyaya) refer to the sphere of mind (manāyatana) that is about to arise in the future and manifest before one, as well as the sphere of mind at the moment of death for an Arhat in the past or present.

Those that are both equal-immediate [conditions] and equal-immediate conditions refer to all other past and present mental bases (*manāyatana*), excluding the mental base at the moment of death of an Arhat in the past or present.

Regarding those that are neither equal-and-immediate nor equal-and-immediate conditions: this refers to all other future mental bases (*manāyatana*), with the exception of the future mental base that is currently arising and present before one.

As for the mental-object base (*dharmāyatana*), it may be an equal-and-immediate [condition] but not an equal-and-immediate condition, or both an equal-and-immediate [condition] and an equal-and-immediate condition, or neither an equal-and-immediate [condition] nor an equal-and-immediate condition.

Those that are immediate antecedents but not equal-and-immediate conditions refer to: all mental factors (*caitasika-dharma*) that are about to arise in the future; all mental factors at the moment of death for an Arhat in the past or present; and the states of non-conceptualization (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*) and cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*) when they have already arisen or are currently arising.

Those which are both equal-immediate [conditions] and equal-immediate conditions refer to all other past and present mental factors, excluding those mental factors at the moment of the final death of an Arhat in the past or present.

Those that are neither equal-and-immediate [conditions] nor equal-and-immediate conditions refer to: all other future mental factors (caitta-dharma) excluding those future mental factors that are currently arising and manifesting; all other formations dissociated from mind (cittaviprayukta-saṃskāra) excluding the equal-and-immediate formations dissociated from mind; as well as bodily and vocal actions, space, and the two types of cessation (nirodha).

Regarding how many object-conditions (ālambana-pratyaya) do not possess an object (ālambana), and so forth: ten object-conditions do not possess an object; one object-condition also possesses an object; and one [condition] should be analyzed.

This refers to the sphere of mental objects (dharmāyatana): if they are mental concomitants (caitta), they are both objective conditions (ālambanapratyaya) and possess an object; if they are not mental concomitants, they are objective conditions but do not possess an object.

Regarding the question of how many are dominant conditions (*adhipati-pratyaya*) but do not possess dominance (*adhipatitva*), eleven are both dominant conditions and possess dominance; one should be analyzed: namely, the sphere of phenomena (*dharmāyatana*). If it is conditioned (*saṃskṛta*), it is both a dominant condition and possesses dominance; if it is unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), it is a dominant condition but does not possess dominance.
Regarding how many are floods (*ogha*) but not favorable to the floods (*anugata-ogha*), and so forth: ten are favorable to the floods but are not floods; two should be analyzed.

That is to say, as for the sphere of mind (*manāyatana*): if it is with outflows (*sāsrava*), it is favorable to the floods but not a flood; if it is without outflows (*anāsrava*), it is neither a flood nor favorable to the floods.
The sphere of phenomena (*dharmāyatana*) is either conducive to the flood but not the flood itself, or both the flood and conducive to the flood, or neither the flood nor conducive to the flood.
That which is conducive to the flood but not the flood refers to the contaminated (*sāsrava*) sphere of phenomena not subsumed under the floods.
"Floods and also those conforming to floods" refers to the four floods.
"Neither floods nor conforming to floods" refers to the uncontaminated sphere of phenomena (*dharmāyatana*).
The five aggregates refer to the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*) up to the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñānaskandha*).
Regarding how many of these five aggregates possess form and so forth: one has form, and four are formless.
Regarding how many are visible and so forth: four are invisible; one should be analyzed—namely, the aggregate of form—which is either visible or invisible.
What is that which is with visibility?
It refers to one location.
What is that which is without visibility?
This refers to nine bases (*āyatana*) and a portion of one base.

Regarding how many are resistant (*sapratigha*) and so forth: four are non-resistant (*apratigha*), and one should be analyzed—namely, the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*), which is either resistant or non-resistant.
What is the resistant?
It refers to the ten bases.
What is the non-resistant?
This refers to a small portion of one location.
Regarding how many are with outflows (*sāsrava*) and so forth, all should be analyzed as follows:
the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*) is either with outflows or without outflows (*anāsrava*).
What are the outflows (sāsrava)?
They are ten bases (āyatana) and a portion of one base.
What are the outflow-free (anāsrava)?
This refers to a small portion of one location:
the aggregate of feeling (vedanā-skandha), which may be either with outflows (sāsrava) or without outflows (anāsrava).
What is with outflows?
It refers to the aggregate of feeling associated with tainted attention (*sāsrava-manasikāra*).
What is untainted?
It refers to the aggregate of feeling associated with untainted attention (*anāsrava-manasikāra*).
The aggregates of perception and consciousness are likewise.
As for the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*), it is either with outflows (*sāsrava*) or without outflows (*anāsrava*).
What is with outflows?
This refers to the formations aggregate (saṃskāra-skandha) associated with outflowing consciousness (sāsrava-citta) and those dissociated from consciousness.
What is the untainted (anāsrava)?
It refers to the formations aggregate associated with untainted consciousness and those dissociated from consciousness.
Regarding how many are conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) and so forth: all are conditioned.
Regarding how many have maturation (*vipāka*) and so forth: all should be analyzed.
That is to say, the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*) may either have maturation or be without maturation.
What is that which has maturation?
It refers to the unwholesome and the wholesome-with-outflows (sāsrava) aggregate of form (rūpaskandha).
What is that which lacks maturation?
This refers to the indeterminate and untainted (*anāsrava*) aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*).
The same applies to the other four aggregates.

As for how many are dependently originated (*pratītyasamutpanna*), etc.: all are dependently originated, produced by causes (*hetusamutpanna*), and included within the temporal world (*adhvasaṃgṛhīta*).
Regarding how many are included within form (*rūpa*) and so forth: one is included within form, and four are included within name (*nāman*).

Regarding how many are included within internal bases (*ādhyātmika-āyatana*) and so forth: one is included within an internal base, three are included within external bases (*bāhya-āyatana*), and one should be analyzed.
That is to say, the aggregate of form is either included within the internal bases or included within the external bases.
What is included within the internal bases?
It refers to the five internal bases.
What is included within the external bases (*bāhyāyatana*)?
It refers to the five external bases and a portion of one external base.
Regarding how many are to be fully known through the thorough knowledge of wisdom (*jñānaparijñā*), all of them are to be fully known through the thorough knowledge of wisdom.

Regarding the question of how many of these five aggregates are to be fully known through the complete knowledge of abandonment (*prahāṇa-parijñā*), all should be analyzed as follows: those aggregates that are with outflows (*sāsrava*) are to be fully known through the complete knowledge of abandonment; those that are without outflows (*anāsrava*) are not to be fully known through the complete knowledge of abandonment.

Regarding "how many are to be abandoned," all [the aggregates] must be analyzed: that is, those aggregates which are with outflows (*sāsrava*) are to be abandoned, while those which are without outflows (*anāsrava*) are not to be abandoned.

Regarding "how many are to be cultivated," all [the aggregates] must be analyzed: that is, those aggregates which are wholesome (*kuśala*) are to be cultivated, while those which are not wholesome are not to be cultivated.
Regarding how many are defiled and so forth: all should be analyzed. That is to say, among the aggregates, those that are obscured are defiled, while those that are unobscured are not defiled.
Regarding how many are results and possess results and so forth: all are results and also possess results.

Regarding how many are appropriated (*upātta*) and so forth: four are unappropriated; one should be analyzed. That is, the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*) may be either appropriated or unappropriated.
What is appropriated?
It refers to the aggregate of form that is comprised within one's own personal continuum.
What is non-appropriated?

Regarding the question of how many of the form aggregates not included within their own substance are derived from the great elements (*mahābhūta*), four are not derived from the great elements, while one should be analyzed. That is to say, the aggregate of form may be derived from the great elements, or it may not be derived from the great elements.
What are those derived from the great elements?
They are nine bases and a portion of two bases.
What are those not derived from the great elements?
Regarding the question "How many are *sopadhiśeṣa* (with remainder)?
and so forth: all are *sopadhiśeṣa*. Regarding the question "How many are *bhava* (existence)?

and so forth: all should be analyzed; that is to say, those aggregates (*skandha*) which are with outflows (*āsrava*) are *bhava*, whereas those which are without outflows (*anāsrava*) are not *bhava*.
Regarding how many causes they are associated with and so forth: one is not associated with any cause, three are associated with causes, and one should be analyzed.

That is to say, as for the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*): if they are mental factors (*caitta*), they are associated with causes; if they are not mental factors, they are not associated with causes.
Regarding the inclusion of these five aggregates within the six wholesome bases (*kuśalāyatana*), there are four permutations (*catuṣkoṭi*).
First, there are wholesome bases that are not aggregates, namely, analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyānirodha*).
Second, there are aggregates that are not wholesome bases, namely, the unwholesome and neutral five aggregates.
Some wholesome bases (*kuśalāyatana*) are also aggregates (*skandha*), namely the wholesome five aggregates.
Some are neither wholesome bases nor aggregates, namely space (*ākāśa*) and cessation not through deliberation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).

Regarding their mutual inclusion with the five unwholesome bases (*akuśalāyatana*): the five unwholesome bases include a portion of the five aggregates, and a portion of the five aggregates also includes the five unwholesome bases.
Regarding the mutual inclusion between the seven neutral bases (*avyākṛtāyatana*) and the aggregates (*skandha*), there are four permutations (*catuṣkoṭi*).
First, there are those that are neutral bases but not aggregates, namely: space (*ākāśa*) and cessation not through deliberation (*apratisaṃkhyānirodha*).
Second, there are those that are aggregates but not neutral bases, namely: the five aggregates that are wholesome (*kuśala*) or unwholesome (*akuśala*).
Alternatively, there are those that are both indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) and bases (*āyatana*), namely the five indeterminate aggregates (*skandha*).
Or there are those that are neither indeterminate bases nor aggregates, namely cessation through deliberation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).

Regarding their mutual inclusion with the three bases of outflows (*āsrava-āyatana*): the three bases of outflows include a portion of one aggregate, and a portion of that one aggregate also includes the three bases of outflows.

Regarding their mutual inclusion with the five bases of outflows (*pañca sāsravāyatana*): the five bases of outflows include a portion of the five aggregates (*pañca skandha*), and a portion of the five aggregates also includes the five bases of outflows.
Regarding the mutual inclusion between the eight untainted bases (*anāsrava-āyatana*) and the aggregates (*skandha*), four permutations (*catuṣkoṭi*) should be established:
1. There are untainted bases that are not aggregates, namely: space (*ākāśa*) and the two types of cessation (*nirodha*). 2.
There are aggregates that are not untainted bases, namely: the five tainted aggregates (*sāsrava-skandha*).
Some are both untainted bases (*anāsrava-āyatana*) and aggregates (*skandha*), namely the five untainted aggregates.
Some are neither untainted bases nor aggregates; such a thing cannot be found.
As for how many are past and so forth: all are either past, future, or present.
Regarding "how many are wholesome," etc., all should be analyzed: that is, the aggregates are either wholesome, unwholesome, or indeterminate.
What is wholesome?
It refers to the five wholesome aggregates.
What is unwholesome?
It refers to the five unwholesome aggregates.
What is indeterminate?
This refers to the five aggregates that are indeterminate (*avyākṛta*).
Regarding the question of how many are bound to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*) and so forth, all should be analyzed as follows:

namely, the aggregates are either bound to the desire realm, or bound to the form realm (*rūpadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*), or bound to the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*), or unbound (*apratisaṃyukta*).
What is bound to the desire realm?
It refers to the five aggregates of the desire realm.
What is bound to the form realm?
This refers to the five aggregates of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*).
What is bound to the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*)?
This refers to the four aggregates of the formless realm.
What is "unbound"?
It refers to the five untainted aggregates (*anāsrava-skandha*).
Regarding how many are "in training" (*śaikṣa*) and so forth, all [categories] should be analyzed accordingly.
That is to say, the aggregates are either those of one in training (*śaikṣa*), those of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), or those of neither training nor beyond training (*naivaśaikṣanāśaikṣa*).
What are those of one in training?
They are the five aggregates of one in training.
What is that which is beyond training (*aśaikṣa*)?
It refers to the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*) of one beyond training.
What is that which is neither in training nor beyond training (*naivaśaikṣanāśaikṣa*)?
This refers to the five contaminated aggregates (*sāsrava-skandha*).
Regarding how many of these five aggregates are abandoned by insight (*darśana-prahātavya*) and so forth, all must be analyzed as follows:
the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*), if contaminated, is abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-prahātavya*); if uncontaminated (*anāsrava*), it is not to be abandoned.
The aggregate of feeling (vedanā-skandha) is either abandoned by seeing (darśana-heya), abandoned by cultivation (bhāvanā-heya), or not to be abandoned (aheya).
What is abandoned by seeing?

It refers to that portion of the aggregate of feeling which is abandoned by the patiences (kṣānti) at the limit of clear realization (abhisamaya-anta) for those who practice in accordance with faith (śraddhānusārin) or in accordance with the Dharma (dharmānusārin).
What, furthermore, is this?
It refers to the aggregate of feeling associated with the eighty-eight underlying tendencies (anuśaya) abandoned through seeing.
What is abandoned through cultivation (bhāvanā)?
This refers to the aggregate of feeling that is to be abandoned through cultivation by one who has seen the tracks of the training. What, then, is this?
It refers to the aggregate of feeling associated with the ten latent dispositions to be abandoned through cultivation, as well as the non-defiled, out-flowing (sāsrava) aggregate of feeling.
What is not to be abandoned?
It refers to the untainted aggregate of feeling.
The aggregates of perception and consciousness are likewise.
The aggregate of formations (saṃskāra-skandha) is either abandoned by insight (darśana-heya), abandoned by cultivation (bhāvanā-heya), or not to be abandoned (aheya).
What is abandoned by insight?

It refers to those formations within the aggregate of formations that are abandoned by the patiences (kṣānti) at the limit of clear realization (abhisamaya-anta) for those who follow by faith (śraddhānusārin) or follow by dharma (dharmānusārin).

What, then, is this? It refers to the eighty-eight latent dispositions (anuśaya) abandoned through insight, along with the aggregate of formations (saṃskāra-skandha) associated with them, as well as the formations dissociated from mind (citta-viprayukta-saṃskāra) that arise together with them.
What is abandoned through cultivation?
It refers to that which belongs to the aggregate of formations (saṃskāra-skandha) for those in training who have seen the path and are abandoned through cultivation.
Furthermore, what is this?

This refers to the ten latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) abandoned through cultivation, along with their associated aggregates of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*), as well as the non-associated formations (*citta-viprayukta-saṃskāra*) arising from them, and any non-defiled, contaminated aggregates of formations.
What is not to be abandoned? It refers to the untainted aggregate of formations (*anāsrava-saṃskāra-skandha*).

Regarding how many are not mind, etc.: one is neither mind, nor mental factor, nor associated with mind; two are mental factors associated with mind; one is exclusively mind; and one should be analyzed.

That is to say, regarding the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*): if it has an object of perception, it is a mental factor (*caitta*) associated with the mind; if it lacks an object of perception, it is neither mind nor mental factor, nor is it associated with the mind.

Regarding how many follow the mind (*cittānuvartin*) but are not associated with feeling (*vedanā-saṃprayukta*), and so forth: one follows the mind but is not associated with feeling; one is associated with feeling but does not follow the mind; one both follows the mind and is associated with feeling; and two should be analyzed.

This refers to the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*), which is either concomitant with the mind but not associated with feeling (*vedanā-samprayukta*), or not concomitant with the mind and not associated with feeling.

That which is concomitant with the mind but not associated with feeling refers to bodily and vocal actions (*kāya-vāk-karman*) that follow the mind; all other aggregates of form are not concomitant with the mind and are not associated with feeling.
The aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) consists of three categories:
(1) those that follow the mind but are not associated with feeling (*vedanā*), namely the formations dissociated from mind (*citta-viprayukta-saṃskāra*) that follow the mind;
(2) those that follow the mind and are also associated with feeling, namely the mental factors (*caitasika*) within the aggregate of formations.

Or, there are those that do not follow the mind and are not associated with feeling; these refer to all other formations dissociated from mind, excluding those formations dissociated from mind that do follow the mind.

Regarding how many follow the mind but are not associated with perception and formations, one should understand this as being like [the case of] feeling, with the exception of the intrinsic nature of perception itself.

Two [categories] are both concomitants of mind (*cittānuvartin*) and associated with formations (*saṃprayukta-saṃskāra*); one is associated with formations but not a concomitant of mind; two others should be analyzed.
That is to say, the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*) is either a concomitant of mind but not associated with formations, or neither a concomitant of mind nor associated with formations.

That which follows the mind but is not associated with formations refers to the bodily and vocal actions that follow the mind; all other aggregates of form (rūpa-skandha) neither follow the mind nor are associated with formations.
The aggregate of formations (saṃskāra-skandha) consists of three categories.
Some are concomitant with the mind but are not associated with formations, namely, the formations dissociated from the mind that are concomitant with the mind.
Some are both concomitant with the mind and associated with formations, namely, the aggregate of formations that are mental factors, excluding their own intrinsic nature.

Or, there are those that do not follow the mind and are not associated with vitarka, namely: all other mental non-concomitants (citta-viprayukta-saṃskāra), excluding those mental non-concomitants that do follow the mind.
Regarding how many follow vitarka and are not associated with vicāra, and so forth—all such cases should be analyzed accordingly.

This refers to the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*), which either follows the movement of vitarka (*anuvartaka*) and is not associated with vicāra (*asamprayukta*), or does not follow the movement of vitarka and is not associated with vicāra.

That which follows the movement of vitarka and is not associated with vicāra refers to bodily and vocal actions that follow the movement of vitarka; all other aggregates of form do not follow the movement of vitarka and are not associated with vicāra.
The aggregate of feeling is either with vitarka and vicāra, or without vitarka and with vicāra only, or without vitarka and without vicāra.
What is with vitarka and vicāra?
It refers to the aggregate of feeling associated with attention (manasikāra) that is accompanied by vitarka and vicāra.
What is "without vitarka and with vicāra"?
It refers to the aggregate of feeling associated with attention that is without vitarka and with vicāra.
What is "without vitarka and without vicāra"?
This refers to the aggregate of feeling associated with attention that is without vitarka and without vicāra.
The same applies to the aggregates of perception and consciousness.
Regarding the aggregate of formations, there are four propositions.

Either it follows the movement of vitarka but is not associated with vicāra—namely, the formations dissociated from mind that follow the movement of vitarka, as well as the vicāra associated with vitarka;

or it is associated with vicāra but does not follow the movement of vitarka—namely, vitarka itself and those mental factors of the saṃskāra-skandha associated with vicāra that are dissociated from vitarka.
Some follow vitarka and are also associated with vicāra; this refers to the aggregate of formations (saṃskāraskandha) consisting of mental factors that are associated with both vitarka and vicāra.

Some do not follow vitarka and are not associated with vicāra; this refers to all other formations dissociated from mind (cittaviprayuktasaṃskāra), excluding those formations dissociated from mind that follow vitarka, as well as vicāra that is not associated with vitarka, and the aggregate of formations consisting of mental factors that are neither accompanied by vitarka nor vicāra.
Regarding the question of how many are "views" (*dṛṣṭi*) and how many are "bases of views" (*dṛṣṭisthāna*), all [categories] should be analyzed.
That is to say, the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*) consists of three propositions.
Some are bases of views but are not views themselves; these are nine bases (*āyatana*) and a portion of one base.
Some are both views and the bases of views, namely one base (the eye-faculty).
Some are neither views nor bases of views, namely a portion of one base (the mind-faculty).

As for the aggregates of feeling, perception, and consciousness: if they are with outflows (*sāsrava*), they are bases of views but not views; if they are without outflows (*anāsrava*), they are neither views nor bases of views.
The aggregate of formations (saṃskāra-skandha) consists of four propositions:

either it is vision but not a sphere of vision, namely untainted wisdom (anāsravā prajñā) not included within the knowledge of exhaustion (kṣaya-jñāna) and the knowledge of non-arising (anutpāda-jñāna);
or it is a sphere of vision but not vision, namely the tainted aggregate of formations not included within vision.
Some are views and also bases for views; these are the five defiled views and mundane right view.
Some are neither views nor bases for views; these are the untainted aggregate of formations not included within the category of views.
*Abhidharmaprakaraṇapāda-śāstra*, Chapter Sixteen: Section on the Sarvāstivādins.
*Abhidharmaprakaraṇapāda-śāstra*, Volume Seventeen.
Composed by the Venerable Vasumitra.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang by Imperial Decree.

Chapter Seven: Discerning the Thousand Questions, Part Eight. Regarding the question of how many [factors] have the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) as their cause but do not themselves have the view of a self-identity as their cause, and so forth—all such cases should be analyzed accordingly.

That is to say, the aggregate of form (rūpaskandha) which, if defiled, has the view of a self-identity (satkāyadṛṣṭi) as its cause but is not itself the cause of the view of a self-identity; or, if undefiled, is neither the cause of the view of a self-identity nor has the view of a self-identity as its cause.
The aggregate of feeling (vedanā-skandha) has three propositions.

There are those that have the view of a self-identity (satkāya-dṛṣṭi) as their cause but are not themselves causes of the view of a self-identity; namely, with the exception of the aggregate of feeling associated with the proclivities (anuśaya) to be abandoned through the vision of suffering (duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya) in the past and present, and with the exception of the aggregate of feeling associated with the universal proclivities (sarvatraga-anuśaya) to be abandoned through the vision of origin (samudaya-darśana-prahātavya) in the past and present, as well as excluding the future aggregate of feeling associated with the view of a self-identity, all other defiled aggregates of feeling.

There are those which have the view of a self as their cause and also have the view of a self as their cause, namely, the aggregate of feeling (vedanā-skandha) excluding what was previously set aside.
There are those which neither have the view of a self as their cause nor have the view of a self as their cause, namely, the undefiled aggregate of feeling.

The same applies to the aggregates of perception (*saṃjñā*) and consciousness (*vijñāna*). The aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) consists of three propositions: 1. There are formations that have the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) as their cause, but are not themselves causes of the view of a self-identity. These include:

all formations other than the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya*) in the past and present, along with their associated and co-existent factors; all formations other than the universal latent dispositions abandoned through the vision of the origin (*samudaya-darśana-prahātavya*) in the past and present, along with their associated and co-existent factors; all formations associated with the future view of a self-identity; and the arising, aging, duration, and impermanence of the future view of a self-identity and its associated factors. All remaining defiled (*kliṣṭa*) formations belong to this category. 2. [There are formations that are both causes of the view of a self-identity and have it as their cause. 3. [There are formations that are neither causes of the view of a self-identity nor have it as their cause. (Note: The second and third propositions are implied by the structure of the three-fold classification, though the text explicitly details only the first.)

There are those that have the view of a self as their cause and also have the view of a self as their cause, namely, the aggregate of formations (saṃskāra-skandha) excluding what was previously set aside.
There are those that neither have the view of a self as their cause nor have the view of a self as their cause, namely, the undefiled aggregate of formations.
Regarding the question of how many *karmas* are not *karma-vipāka* (the maturation of karma) and so forth, all [categories] should be analyzed.
That is to say, the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*) consists of three propositions.
Some are *karma* but not *karma-vipāka*, namely, bodily and vocal *karma*.
Or, it may be the maturation of karma but not karma itself; this refers to the aggregate of form born from the maturation of karma.
Or, it may be neither karma nor the maturation of karma; this refers to all other aggregates of form, excluding both karma and the aggregate of form that is the maturation of karma.
The aggregate of feeling (vedanā-skandha) is either the maturation of karma that is not karma itself, or neither karma nor the maturation of karma.

That which is the maturation of karma but not karma refers to the aggregate of feeling born from the maturation of karma; all other aggregates of feeling are neither karma nor the maturation of karma.
The same applies to the aggregates of perception (*saṃjñā*) and consciousness (*vijñāna*).
Regarding the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra*), there are four possibilities:
there may be that which is karma but not the maturation of karma, namely, volition (*cetanā*) that is not subsumed under karmic maturation.
Either it is the maturation of karma but not karma itself— namely, the formations aggregate produced from the maturation of karma that are not subsumed under volition—
or it is both karma and the maturation of karma— namely, volition produced from the maturation of karma.

Or [there are those] which are neither karma nor the maturation of karma; that is to say, with the exception of the aggregate of formations that are karma and those that are the maturation of karma, all other remaining aggregates of formations.
Regarding how many are karma but do not follow along with karma, etc.: three follow along with karma but are not karma, while two should be analyzed.
The aggregate of form (rūpaskandha) consists of three categories: 1.
Karma that is not concomitant with karma (na karmānuvartin), which refers to all other bodily and vocal actions except for those bodily and vocal actions that are concomitant with karma;
2. Karma that is also concomitant with karma, which refers to those bodily and vocal actions that are concomitant with karma.
Or it is neither karma nor concomitant with karma; this refers to all other aggregates of form (rūpa-skandha) excluding karma and that which is concomitant with karma.
Regarding the aggregate of formations (saṃskāra-skandha), there are three cases:
first, it is karma but not concomitant with karma, namely volition (cetanā).
Some are concomitants of karma but are not karma itself; this refers to the formations aggregate (saṃskāra-skandha) that are concomitants of karma but are not subsumed under volition (cetanā).

Some are neither karma nor concomitants of karma; this refers to all other formations dissociated from mind (citta-viprayukta-saṃskāra), excluding those formations dissociated from mind that are concomitants of karma.

Regarding the question of how many derived forms (*upādāya-rūpa*) are not visible forms (*sanidarśana-rūpa*), four are derived forms that are not visible forms; one should be analyzed, namely, the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*) consists of three propositions.
Some derived matter is not visible matter, namely the eight bases and a portion of two bases;
some derived matter is also visible matter, namely one base.
Or, it is neither derived matter nor visible matter; this refers to a small portion of one base (*āyatana*).
Regarding these five aggregates, how many are derived matter but not resistant matter (*sapratigha*)? Four are neither derived matter nor resistant matter; one should be analyzed.
That is to say, the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*) should be analyzed according to four alternatives (*catuṣkoṭi*).
Either it is derived matter (*bhautika-rūpa*) but not resistant matter (*sapratigha-rūpa*), which refers to a portion of one base (*āyatana*);
or it is resistant matter but not derived matter, which refers to a portion of one base.
Alternatively, there may be derived matter that is also resistant matter, namely the nine bases and a portion of one base;
or there may be neither derived matter nor resistant matter—such matter is not to be found.
Regarding the phrase "difficult to see, therefore profound," etc.: because all things are difficult to see, they are profound; because they are profound, they are difficult to see.
Regarding the question "how many are wholesome, and how many have the unwholesome as their cause," etc.: all [of these] should be analyzed.
That is to say, each has three propositions.
First, that which has wholesome as its cause but is not itself wholesome: namely, the five aggregates born of the maturation of the wholesome.
Second, that which is both wholesome and has wholesome as its cause: namely, the wholesome five aggregates.

Or [there are those] that are neither wholesome nor have the wholesome as their cause; this refers to all other indeterminate and unwholesome five aggregates, excluding the five aggregates born of the maturation of the wholesome.
Regarding how many are unwholesome but do not have the unwholesome as their cause, and so forth—all such cases should be analyzed accordingly.
That is to say, the aggregate of form (rūpaskandha) consists of three categories:
first, that which has unwholesome causes but is not itself unwholesome, namely, the aggregate of form born from the maturation (vipākaja) of unwholesomeness;
second, that which is both unwholesome and has unwholesome causes, namely, the unwholesome aggregate of form.

Or [there are those] that are neither unwholesome nor have unwholesomeness as their cause; this refers to all other indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) form-aggregates, excluding those that are the maturation (*vipāka*) of unwholesome karma, as well as wholesome form-aggregates.
Regarding the feeling-aggregate (*vedanā-skandha*), there are three propositions.

Or, there are those that have unwholesome causes but are not themselves unwholesome; namely, the aggregate of feeling born of the maturation of the unwholesome, as well as the aggregate of feeling associated with the view of a self-identity (satkāyadṛṣṭi) and the view of extreme adherence (antagrāhadṛṣṭi) bound to the desire realm.
Or it is unwholesome and has the unwholesome as its cause, namely, the aggregate of feeling that is unwholesome.

Or it is neither unwholesome nor has the unwholesome as its cause, namely, with the exception of the aggregate of feeling born of the maturation of the unwholesome, and with the exception of the aggregate of feeling associated with the view of a self-identity and the view of extremes bound to the desire realm, all other indeterminate [feelings], as well as the wholesome aggregate of feeling.
The same applies to the aggregates of perception (*saṃjñā*) and consciousness (*vijñāna*). The aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) consists of three propositions.

First, there are those that have unwholesome causes but are not themselves unwholesome; namely, the aggregate of formations born of the maturation (*vipākaja*) of the unwholesome, as well as the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and the view of extreme adherence (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*) bound to the desire realm, along with their associated and co-arising aggregates of formations.
Or [it is] unwholesome and has the unwholesome as its cause, namely, the unwholesome aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*).

Or it is neither unwholesome nor has the unwholesome as its cause, namely, with the exception of the resultant unwholesome aggregate of formations, and with the exception of the view of a self-identity (*satkāya-dṛṣṭi*) and the view of extremes (*antagrāha-dṛṣṭi*) bound to the desire realm, along with their associated and co-arisen aggregates of formations; all other indeterminate and wholesome aggregates of formations.
Regarding the question of how many indeterminate (avyākṛta) phenomena do not have the indeterminate as their cause, all such cases should be analyzed, meaning there are three propositions for each.
For instance, there are those that have the indeterminate as their cause but are not themselves indeterminate, namely, the five aggregates (skandha) of unwholesome (akuśala) nature.
Some are indeterminate and have indeterminate factors as their cause, namely the five aggregates that are indeterminate.
Some are neither indeterminate nor have indeterminate factors as their cause, namely the five aggregates that are wholesome.
Regarding the question of how many are "conditioned by causes" (*hetu-pratyaya*) but not "having a cause" (*sahetu*), all are conditioned by causes and also have a cause.

Regarding the question of how many are "immediately preceding" (*samanantara*) but not "immediately preceding conditions" (*samanantara-pratyaya*), one is neither immediately preceding nor an immediately preceding condition, while four should be analyzed.
The aggregate of feeling (vedanā-skandha) consists of three categories:

those that are equal-and-immediate (samanantara) but not equal-and-immediate conditions (samanantara-pratyaya); namely, the aggregate of feeling that is about to arise in the future, as well as the aggregate of feeling at the moment of death for an Arhat in the past or present.

Or it is both an equal-and-immediate [condition] and an equal-and-immediate object-condition (*samanantarālambana-pratyaya*); that is to say, with the exception of the aggregate of feeling at the moment of death for an Arhat in the past or present, all other past and present aggregates of feeling.

Or [there are cases that] are neither equal-and-immediate [condition] nor equal-and-immediate condition: namely, with the exception of the aggregate of feeling that is currently arising in the present within the future, all other remaining aggregates of feeling in the future;
the same applies to the aggregates of perception and consciousness.
The aggregate of formations (saṃskāra-skandha) consists of three categories.

It may be an immediately preceding condition (samanantara-pratyaya) but not an object-condition (ālambana-pratyaya). This refers to: (1) mental factors of the aggregate of formations that are future and currently arising; (2) the mental factors of the aggregate of formations at the moment of death of an Arhat in the past or present; and (3) the state of non-conceptualization (asaṃjñi-samāpatti) and the cessation attainment (nirodha-samāpatti), when they have already arisen or are currently arising.

Or those which are both equal-immediate [conditions] and equal-immediate conditions: namely, with the exception of the past and present mental aggregates and mental concomitants at the moment of the final death of an Arhat, all other past and present mental aggregates and mental concomitants.

Or [there are those] that are neither immediate antecedents nor immediate conditions: namely, with the exception of the future aggregates of mental concomitants (caitta-saṃskāra-skandha) that are currently arising and manifesting, all other remaining future aggregates of mental concomitants; and with the exception of the mind-dissociated formations (citta-viprayukta-saṃskāra) that are immediate antecedents, all other remaining mind-dissociated formations.

Regarding the question of how many object-conditions (ālambana-pratyaya) do not possess an object (ālambana), one is an object-condition that does not possess an object; three are both object-conditions and possess objects; and one should be analyzed.

This refers to the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*): if they are mental factors (*caitta*), they are both object-conditions (*ālambana-pratyaya*) and possess objects; if they are not mental factors, they are object-conditions but do not possess objects.
Regarding the question of how many *adhipati-pratyaya* (dominant conditions) are not *sādhipati* (possessing dominance), all are *adhipati-pratyaya* and also possess dominance.
Regarding the question of how many *ogha* (floods) are not *anu-ogha* (conducive to floods), all should be analyzed accordingly.

That is to say, the aggregate of form (rūpaskandha) is, if it is with outflows (sāsrava), a flood-conducive but not a flood; if it is without outflows (anāsrava), it is neither a flood nor flood-conducive.
The aggregates of feeling (vedanā), perception (saṃjñā), and consciousness (vijñāna) are also thus.
The aggregate of formations (saṃskāraskandha) consists of three categories:
either conforming to the floods (ogha) but not being a flood itself, which refers to the outflow-tainted (sāsrava) aggregate of formations not subsumed under the floods;
or being both a flood and conforming to the floods, which refers to the four floods themselves.
Or that which is neither a flood nor favorable to the floods, namely the untainted aggregate of formations (*anāsrava-saṃskāra-skandha*).

As for the eighteen elements (*dhātu*), they are the eye element, the form element, the eye-consciousness element, and so forth, up to the mind element, the mental-object element, and the mind-consciousness element.
Regarding these eighteen elements (*dhātus*), how many possess form (*rūpin*) and so forth? Ten possess form; seven are formless; one should be analyzed.
That is to say, the element of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*) may either possess form or be formless.
What is that which possesses form?
It refers to the bodily and vocal actions subsumed within the dharma-element; all other elements of the dharma-realm are formless.
Regarding how many are visible and so forth: one is visible, and seventeen are invisible.
Regarding how many are with resistance (*sapratigha*) and so forth: ten are with resistance, and eight are without resistance.
Regarding how many are with outflows (*sāsrava*) and so forth: fifteen are with outflows, and three should be analyzed.
That is to say, the mind-element (manodhātu) is either with-outflows (sāsrava) or without-outflows (anāsrava).
What is with-outflows?
It refers to the mind-element associated with outflowing mental attention (manasikāra).
What is the untainted (*anāsrava*)?
It refers to the mind-element (*manodhātu*) associated with untainted attention (*manasikāra*).
The same applies to the mental-consciousness-element (*manovijñānadhātu*).
The dharma-realm (dharmadhātu) is either with outflows (sāsrava) or without outflows (anāsrava).
What is with outflows?
It refers to the outflowing bodily and vocal actions subsumed within the dharma-realm, as well as the outflowing aggregates of feeling, perception, and formations.
What is the untainted (*anāsrava*)?

It refers to untainted bodily and vocal karma, as well as the untainted aggregates of feeling, perception, and formations (*vedanā-saṃjñā-saṃskāra-skandha*), together with unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*).
Regarding how many are conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) and so forth: seventeen are conditioned; one should be analyzed.
That is to say, the dharma-realm is either conditioned or unconditioned.
What is conditioned?
It refers to the bodily and vocal actions subsumed within the dharma-realm, as well as the aggregates of feeling, perception, and formations.
What is the unconditioned?
It refers to space and the two types of cessation.
Regarding how many have maturation and so forth: eight have no maturation; ten should be analyzed.
This refers to the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), which may have maturation (*vipāka*) or may be without maturation.
What is that which has maturation?
It refers to the wholesome and unwholesome [karma] of the form realm.
What is that which has no maturation?
It refers to neutral [dharmas] of the form realm and sound, as well as the five consciousness realms; it is the same for these.
The mind-element (*manodhātu*) is either with maturation (*savipāka*) or without maturation (*avipāka*).
What is with maturation?
It refers to the unwholesome and wholesome contaminated mind-elements.
What is that which is without maturation?
It refers to the indeterminate and untainted mental element (*manodhātu*).
The same applies to the dharma-element (*dharmadhātu*) and the mental-consciousness-element (*manovijñānadhātu*).

Regarding the question of how many are dependently originated (*pratītyasamutpanna*) and so forth: seventeen are dependently originated, produced by causes (*hetusamutpanna*), and included within the worldly (*loka-saṃgṛhīta*); one should be analyzed.

That is to say, as for the dharma-element (*dharmadhātu*), if it is conditioned (*saṃskṛta*), it is dependently originated, produced by causes, and included within the worldly; if it is unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), it is not dependently originated, not produced by causes, and not included within the worldly.
Regarding how many are comprised within form (*rūpa*) and so forth: ten are comprised within form, seven are comprised within name (*nāman*), and one should be analyzed.
That is to say, those bodily and vocal actions comprised within the dharma-element (*dharmadhātu*) are comprised within form; all others are comprised within name.
Regarding how many are included within the internal bases (*āyatana*), twelve are included within the internal bases and six are included within the external bases.
Regarding how many are to be fully known through the thorough knowledge of wisdom (*jñāna-parijñā*), all are to be fully known through the thorough knowledge of wisdom.

Regarding the question of how many among these eighteen elements (*dhātu*) are to be fully known through the knowledge of abandonment (*prahāṇa-parijñā*), fifteen are to be fully known through the knowledge of abandonment, while three should be analyzed.

That is to say, regarding the mind-element (*manodhātu*), the phenomena-element (*dharmadhātu*), and the mind-consciousness-element (*manovijñānadhātu*): if they are with outflows (*sāsrava*), they are to be fully known through abandonment; if they are without outflows (*anāsrava*), they are not to be fully known through abandonment.
As for how many are to be abandoned and so forth: fifteen are to be abandoned, while three are to be analyzed.

That is to say, the mind-element (manodhātu), the phenomena-element (dharmadhātu), and the mind-consciousness-element (manovijñānadhātu): if they are with outflows (sāsrava), they are to be abandoned; if they are without outflows (anāsrava), they are not to be abandoned.
Regarding how many are to be cultivated (bhāvayitavya) and so forth: eight are not to be cultivated, while ten are to be analyzed.
That is to say, the form realm (rūpadhātu) is either to be cultivated or not to be cultivated.
What is to be cultivated?
It refers to wholesome states of the form realm.
What is it that should not be cultivated?
It refers to the unwholesome and the indeterminate [factors] of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*).
The same applies to the sound element (*śabdadhātu*), the six consciousness elements (*ṣaḍvijñānadhātu*), and the mind element (*manodhātu*).
The dharma-realm (dharmadhātu) is either to be cultivated or not to be cultivated.
What is to be cultivated?
It refers to the wholesome conditioned dharma-realm.
What is not to be cultivated?
It refers to the unwholesome, the indeterminate dharma-realm, and analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).
Regarding how many are defiled and so forth: eight are non-defiled; ten are to be analyzed.
This refers to the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), which is either afflicted (*kliṣṭa*) or non-afflicted (*akliṣṭa*).
What is afflicted?
It is the obscured form realm (*nivṛta-rūpadhātu*).
What is non-defiled?
It refers to the unobscured [dharmas] of the form realm.
The same applies to the sound element, the six consciousness elements, and the mind and mental-object elements.
Regarding the question of how many are results but not possess results, and so forth: seventeen are both results and possess results; one should be analyzed.
That is to say, the dharma-element (dharmadhātu) consists of three propositions.
There are those that are results but do not possess results, namely, analytical cessation (pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha).
Alternatively, some are results and also possess results, namely the conditioned dharma-realm (*saṃskṛtadharmadhātu*).
Some are neither results nor possess results, namely space (*ākāśa*) and cessation not through deliberation (*apratisaṃkhyānirodha*).
Regarding how many are appropriated (*upātta*) and so forth: nine are unappropriated; nine should be analyzed.
That is to say, the eye-element is either appropriated or non-appropriated. What is appropriated?
It refers to the eye-element that is comprised within one's own personal continuum.
What is non-appropriated?
It refers to the eye-element that is not comprised within one's own personal continuum.
The same applies to the elements of visible form, ear, nose, odor, tongue, taste, body, and tangibles.

Regarding how many are derived from the great elements (*mahābhūta*) and so forth: nine and a portion of two are derived from the great elements; seven and a portion of two are not derived from the great elements.
Regarding the phrase "how many have a superior": seventeen have a superior; one should be analyzed.
That is, the dharma-element (dharmadhātu) may either have a superior or be without a superior.
What is meant by "having a superior"?
This refers to the conditioned realm (*saṃskṛtadhātu*), as well as space (*ākāśa*) and cessation not through deliberation (*apratisaṃkhyānirodha*).
What is the unsurpassed? It is cessation through deliberation (*pratisaṃkhyānirodha*).
Regarding the question "How many are 'existent' (*sat*) and so forth": fifteen are existent; three should be analyzed.

That is to say, as for the mind (*manas*), mental objects (*dharma*), and mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) elements: if they are with outflows (*sāsrava*), they are existent; if they are without outflows (*anāsrava*), they are not existent.
Regarding how many causes they are associated with and so forth: seven causes they are associated with, ten causes they are not associated with, and one [cause] should be analyzed.

That is to say, regarding the dharma-element (*dharmadhātu*): if it consists of mental factors (*caitta*), it is associated with causes; if it does not consist of mental factors, it is not associated with causes.

Regarding the inclusion of these eighteen elements within the six wholesome bases: the six wholesome bases include a portion of ten elements, and a portion of those ten elements also includes the six wholesome bases.

Regarding their mutual inclusion with the five unwholesome bases (*pañcākuśalasthānāni*): the five unwholesome bases include a portion of ten elements (*daśadhātu*), and a portion of those ten elements also includes the five unwholesome bases.

Regarding the inclusion of the seven neutral bases (*avyākṛta-sthāna*): the seven neutral bases include a portion of eight elements (*dhātu*) and ten elements, and a portion of those eight and ten elements also includes the seven neutral bases.

Regarding their mutual inclusion with the three bases of outflows (*āsrava-sthāna*): the three bases of outflows include a portion of one element, and a portion of that one element also includes the three bases of outflows.

Regarding their mutual inclusion with the five bases of outflows (*sāsrava-sthāna*): the five bases of outflows include fifteen elements and a portion of three elements, and those fifteen elements and a portion of three elements also include the five bases of outflows.

Regarding the mutual inclusion with the eight untainted bases (*anāsrava-āyatana*): the eight untainted bases include a portion of the three realms, and a portion of the three realms also includes the eight untainted bases.
Regarding how many are past and so forth: seventeen are either past, future, or present; one should be analyzed.
That is to say, the dharma-element (dharmadhātu), if conditioned, is either past, future, or present; if unconditioned, it is neither past, nor future, nor present.
Regarding how many are wholesome and so forth: eight are indeterminate, while ten should be analyzed.
That is to say, the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*) may be wholesome, unwholesome, or indeterminate.
What is wholesome?
This refers to wholesome bodily intimation.
What is unwholesome?
It refers to unwholesome bodily intimation.
What is the indeterminate?
It refers to all other instances of the form element (rūpadhātu) excluding wholesome and unwholesome bodily intimation (kāyavijñapti),
as well as the sound element (śabdadhātu), which may be wholesome, unwholesome, or indeterminate.
What is wholesome?
It refers to wholesome vocal intimation (*vāgvijñapti*). What is unwholesome?
This refers to unwholesome vocal intimation (*vāgvijñapti*).
What is the indeterminate?
It refers to all other elements of sound (*śabdadhātu*) excluding wholesome and unwholesome vocal intimations.
The visual consciousness element is either wholesome, unwholesome, or indeterminate.
What is wholesome?
It refers to visual consciousness associated with wholesome attention (*manasikāra*).
What is unwholesome?
It refers to eye-consciousness associated with unwholesome attention (*manasikāra*).
What is neutral (*avyākṛta*)?
This refers to visual consciousness associated with indeterminate attention (*avyākṛta-manasikāra*).
The same applies to the remaining five consciousness elements and the mind element (*manodhātu*).
As for the mental-object element (*dharmadhātu*), it may be wholesome, unwholesome, or indeterminate.
What is wholesome?

It refers to wholesome bodily and vocal actions subsumed within the dharma-element, as well as the wholesome aggregates of feeling, perception, and formations, and analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).
What is unwholesome?
This refers to unwholesome bodily and vocal actions subsumed within the dharma-dhātu, as well as the unwholesome aggregates of feeling, perception, and formations.
What is the indeterminate?
It refers to the indeterminate aggregates of feeling, perception, and formations, as well as space and non-analytical cessation.
Regarding how many are bound to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*) and so forth: four are bound to the desire realm; fourteen should be analyzed.
That is to say, the eye-element (*cakṣurdhātu*) is either bound to the desire realm or bound to the form realm (*rūpadhātu*).
What is bound to the desire realm?
It refers to the eye element produced by the primary elements of the desire realm.
What is bound to the form realm?
This refers to the eye-element derived from the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*).
The same applies to the elements of visible form, ear, sound, nose, tongue, and body.
As for the element of tangibles (*spraṣṭavyadhātu*), it is either bound to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*) or bound to the form realm.
What is bound to the desire realm?
It refers to the four great elements of the desire realm and the derived tangible element.
What is bound to the form realm?
This refers to the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) and the derived tangible object (*spraṣṭavyadhātu*),
as well as the eye-consciousness element (*cakṣurvijñānadhātu*), which are either bound to the desire realm (*kāmadhātupratisaṃyukta*) or bound to the form realm.
What is bound to the desire realm?
This refers to eye-consciousness associated with mental attention belonging to the desire realm.
What is [eye-consciousness] bound to the form realm?
It refers to eye-consciousness associated with mental attention belonging to the form realm.
The ear, body, and consciousness elements are also thus.
The mind element is either bound to the desire realm, or bound to the form realm, or bound to the formless realm, or unbound.
What is bound to the desire realm?
It refers to the mental faculty (*manodhātu*) associated with attention (*manasikāra*) belonging to the desire realm.
What is bound to the form realm?
That is to say, the mental element (manodhātu) associated with attention belonging to the form realm (rūpadhātu).
What is that which is bound to the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu)?
That is to say, the mental element associated with attention belonging to the formless realm.
What is the unconditioned (*asaṃyukta*)?
It refers to the mind-element (*manodhātu*) associated with untainted attention (*anāsravamanasikāra*).
The same applies to the mental-consciousness-element (*manovijñānadhātu*).
The dharma-realm (dharmadhātu) is either bound to the desire realm, bound to the form realm, bound to the formless realm, or unbound.
What is bound to the desire realm?

It refers to the bodily and vocal actions included within the dharma-realm that belong to the desire realm, as well as the aggregates of feeling, perception, and formations belonging to the desire realm.
What is that which is bound to the realm of form (*rūpadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*)?
It refers to the bodily and vocal actions subsumed under the dharma-element (*dharmadhātu*), as well as the aggregates of feeling, perception, and formations belonging to the realm of form.
What is that which is bound to the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*)?
This refers to the aggregates of feeling, perception, and formations belonging to the formless realm. What is "unbound"?
This refers to untainted (anāsrava) bodily and vocal actions, as well as the untainted aggregates of feeling, perception, and formations, together with unconditioned phenomena (asaṃskṛtadharma).
Regarding how many are "in training" (*śaikṣa*) and so forth: fifteen are neither-in-training-nor-beyond-training (*naiva-śaikṣa-naivāśaikṣa*); three should be analyzed.
That is to say, the mind-element (*manodhātu*) is either in training, or beyond training, or neither-in-training-nor-beyond-training.
What is the learner (śaikṣa)?
It refers to the mind-element (manodhātu) associated with the attention of a learner.
What is the one beyond learning (aśaikṣa)?
That is to say, the mind-element associated with the mental attention of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*).
What is neither-learner-nor-non-learner?
That is to say, the mind-element associated with tainted (*sāsrava*) mental attention.
The consciousness element is also thus.
The dharma element is either trainee (*śaikṣa*), or non-trainee (*aśaikṣa*), or neither-trainee-nor-non-trainee (*naivaśaikṣanāśaikṣa*).
What is trainee?
This refers to the bodily and vocal actions of one in training, as well as the aggregates of feeling, perception, and formations of one in training.
What is "beyond training" (aśaikṣa)?
It refers to the bodily and vocal actions of one beyond training, as well as the aggregates of feeling, perception, and formations of one beyond training.
What is that which is neither-learner-nor-non-learner?

It refers to the contaminated bodily and vocal actions included within the dharma-realm, as well as the contaminated aggregates of feeling, perception, and formations, together with unconditioned phenomena.
Regarding how many of these eighteen elements (*dhātu*) are abandoned by insight (*darśana-heya*), etc.: fifteen are abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*); three should be analyzed.
That is to say, the mind element (*manodhātu*) is either abandoned by insight, abandoned by cultivation, or not abandoned at all (*aheya*).
What is abandoned through vision?

It refers to the mental element (*manodhātu*) that is abandoned by the patiences (*kṣānti*) at the limit of clear realization for those who follow by faith (*śraddhānusārin*) or follow by dharma (*dharmānusārin*).
Furthermore, what is this?
This refers to the mental faculty (*manodhātu*) associated with the eighty-eight proclivities (*anuśaya*) to be abandoned through seeing.
What is abandoned through cultivation?
It refers to the mental faculty of those in training (*śaikṣa*) who have seen the path and is to be abandoned through cultivation.

What, then, is this? It refers to the mental element (*manodhātu*) associated with the ten proclivities (*anuśaya*) to be abandoned through cultivation, as well as the non-defiled, out-flowing (*āsrava*) mental element.
What is not to be abandoned?
That is to say, the uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) mind-element (*manodhātu*).
The same applies to the mind-consciousness-element (*manovijñānadhātu*).
As for the dharma-element (*dharmadhātu*), it is either abandoned by seeing (*darśana-prahātavya*), abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-prahātavya*), or not to be abandoned (*aprahātavya*).
What is abandoned by insight (*darśana-prahātavya*)?

It refers to those factors within the dharma-element (*dharmadhātu*) that are abandoned by the patiences (*kṣānti*) at the limit of clear realization (*abhisamaya-antya-kṣānti*) for those who practice in accordance with faith (*śraddhānusārin*) or in accordance with the Dharma (*dharmānusārin*).
Furthermore, what are these?

This refers to the eighty-eight latent dispositions (anuśaya) abandoned through seeing, along with their associated factors in the dharma-element and the non-associated formations arising together with them.
What is abandoned through cultivation?
This refers to the dharma-element (dharmadhātu) that is abandoned through cultivation (bhāvanā-heya), which has been seen by one training on the path (śaikṣa-dṛṣṭa-mārga). What, then, is this?

It refers to the ten latent dispositions (anuśaya) abandoned through cultivation and their associated dharmas within the dharma-element, as well as the bodily and vocal actions arising from them, the formations dissociated from mind (citta-viprayukta-saṃskāra), and non-defiled impure (sāsrava) dharmas within the dharma-element.
What is not to be abandoned?
It refers to the untainted dharma-realm (*anāsrava-dharmadhātu*).

Regarding how many are neither mind (*citta*), nor mental factors (*caitta*), nor associated with mind (*cittasaṃprayukta*): ten are neither mind, nor mental factors, nor associated with mind; seven are exclusively mind; one should be analyzed.

That is to say, regarding the dharma-realm (dharmadhātu): if it has an object of cognition, it is a mental factor associated with the mind; if it lacks an object of cognition, it is neither mind nor mental factor, nor is it associated with the mind.

Regarding how many follow the mind (*cittānuvartin*) but are not associated with feeling (*vedanā-samprayukta*), and so forth: ten do not follow the mind and are not associated with feeling; seven are associated with feeling but do not follow the mind; one should be analyzed.
That is to say, the dharma-dhātu consists of three categories:
those that follow the mind but are not associated with feeling; these are bodily and vocal actions that follow the mind, the formations dissociated from mind, and feeling itself.
Some are both concomitant with the mind and associated with feeling, namely, the aggregate of perception and the associated aggregate of formations.

Others are neither concomitant with the mind nor associated with feeling, namely, all other bodily and vocal actions and formations dissociated from the mind, excluding those bodily and vocal actions and formations dissociated from the mind that are concomitant with the mind, as well as unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛtadharma*).

Regarding how many [factors] follow the mind (*cittānuvartin*), are not associated with perception (*saṃjñā*) or formations (*saṃskāra*), and so forth: excluding their own nature (*svabhāva*), they should be understood as being like feeling (*vedanā*).

Regarding how many [factors] follow vitarka (*vitarkānuvartin*), are not associated with vicāra, and so forth: ten do not follow vitarka and are not associated with vicāra; five possess both vitarka and vicāra; and three should be analyzed.
That is to say, the mind-element (manodhātu) is either with vitarka and vicāra, or without vitarka and with vicāra only, or without vitarka and without vicāra.
What is "with vitarka and with vicāra"?
It refers to the mind-element associated with mental attention (manasikāra) that possesses both vitarka and vicāra.
What is that which is without vitarka and with only vicāra?
It refers to the mental element (manodhātu) associated with attention (manasikāra) that is without vitarka and with only vicāra.
What is that which is without vitarka and without vicāra?
This refers to the mental element (manodhātu) associated with attention that is without applied thought or sustained thought;
the mental consciousness element (manovijñānadhātu) is likewise.
Regarding the dharma-element (dharmadhātu), there are four alternatives.

Some follow the movement of vitarka but are not associated with vicāra; these are bodily and vocal karma following the movement of vitarka, the formations dissociated from mind (citta-viprayukta-saṃskāra), and vicāra that is associated with vitarka.

Some are associated with vicāra but do not follow the movement of vitarka; these are vitarka itself and those mental factors (caitta-dharma) associated with vicāra that are not themselves associated with vitarka.

Some follow the movement of vitarka (*vitarkānuparivartin*) and are also associated with vicāra (*vicārasamprayukta*), namely, those mental factors (*caitasika-dharma*) associated with both vitarka and vicāra.

Others do not follow the movement of vitarka and are not associated with vicāra, namely, with the exception of bodily and vocal actions (*kāya-vāk-karman*) following vicāra and the formations dissociated from mind (*citta-viprayukta-saṃskāra*), all other bodily and vocal actions and formations dissociated from mind, as well as vicāra that is not associated with vitarka, and furthermore, those mental factors that are without both vitarka and vicāra, and unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*).

Regarding the question of how many are views (*dṛṣṭi*) and how many are bases of view (*dṛṣṭisthāna*): one is both a view and a base of view; fourteen are bases of view but not views; and three should be analyzed.

That is to say, as for the mind-element (*manodhātu*): if it is with outflows (*sāsrava*), it is a base of view but not a view; if it is without outflows (*anāsrava*), it is neither a view nor a base of view.
The consciousness element is also like this.
Regarding the dharma-element, there are four propositions.

First, that which is vision but not a locus of vision: this refers to untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-prajñā*) not subsumed under the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) or the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*).
Some are views but not bases of view, namely the contaminated *dharmadhātu* not subsumed under view.
Some are both views and bases of view, namely the five defiled views and mundane right view.
Or that which is neither seeing nor the locus of seeing, namely the untainted dharma-realm (anāsrava-dharmadhātu) not subsumed under seeing.

Regarding how many have the view of a self-identity (satkāyadṛṣṭi) as their cause but are not themselves the cause of the view of a self-identity: eight do not have the view of a self-identity as their cause and are not the cause of the view of a self-identity; ten should be analyzed.

That is to say, regarding the form realm (*rūpadhātu*): if it is defiled, it has the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) as its cause, but is not itself the cause of the view of a self-identity; if it is non-defiled, it neither has the view of a self-identity as its cause nor is it the cause of the view of a self-identity.
The same applies to the sound-element and the five consciousness-elements.

As for the mental-consciousness-element, it may have the view of a self-body (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) as its cause but not be a cause of the view of a self-body; or it may have the view of a self-body as its cause and also be a cause of the view of a self-body; or it may neither have the view of a self-body as its cause nor be a cause of the view of a self-body.

That which has the view of a self (satkāyadṛṣṭi) as its cause, but is not itself a cause of the view of a self, refers to: all other defiled mental spheres (manodhātu), excluding the mental sphere associated with the proclivities (anuśaya) to be abandoned by the vision of suffering (duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya) in the past and present; excluding the mental sphere associated with the universal proclivities (sarvatraga-anuśaya) to be abandoned by the vision of origination (samudaya-darśana-prahātavya) in the past and present; and excluding the mental sphere associated with the view of a self in the future.
That which has the view of a self as its cause and for which the view of a self is also the cause refers to the mental element (manodhātu) previously excluded.
That which does not have the view of a self as its cause and for which the view of a self is not the cause refers to the non-defiled mental element.
The consciousness-element (*vijñāna-dhātu*) is also like this. The dharma-element (*dharma-dhātu*) consists of three propositions.

There are those that have the view of a self-identity (*satkāya-dṛṣṭi*) as their cause, but are not causes for the view of a self-identity. These include: (1) all other defiled dharma-elements, excluding the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya*) in the past and present, along with their associated and co-existent dharmas; (2) excluding the universal latent dispositions abandoned through the vision of the origin (*samudaya-darśana-prahātavya*) in the past and present, along with their associated and co-existent dharma-elements; (3) excluding the future dharma-elements associated with the view of a self-identity; and (4) excluding the future birth, aging, duration, and impermanence of the view of a self-identity and its associated dharmas. All remaining defiled dharma-elements fall into this category.
There are those that have the view of a self as their cause and also have the view of a self as their cause, namely, the dharma-element excluding what was previously mentioned.
There are those that neither have the view of a self as their cause nor have the view of a self as their cause, namely, the non-defiled dharma-element.
Regarding the question of how many *karmas* are not *karma-vipāka* (the maturation of karma) and so forth, all [categories] should be analyzed.
That is to say, the eye-element (*cakṣur-dhātu*) is either *karma-vipāka* that is not *karman*, or neither *karman* nor *karma-vipāka*.
That which is the maturation of karma but not karma itself refers to the eye-element born of maturation.
That which is neither karma nor the maturation of karma refers to the remaining eye-elements.
The same applies to the ear, nose, tongue, body, odor, flavor, and tangible-object elements, as well as the seven mind-elements.
The realm of form (rūpadhātu) consists of three propositions.
First, there are those that are karma but not karmic maturation (vipāka), namely, bodily intimation (kāyavijñapti).

Second, there are those that are karmic maturation but not karma, namely, the matter of the realm of form produced by karmic maturation. Third, there are those that are both karma and karmic maturation. Third, there are those that are neither karma nor karmic maturation. [Note: The third category is implied by the structure of the three propositions.]
Or it is neither karma nor the maturation of karma; that is to say, with the exception of karma and the matter that is the maturation of karma, all other matter within the realm of form.
The element of sound has two categories:
it is either karma but not the maturation of karma, namely vocal intimation (*vāgvijñapti*).
Or it is neither karma nor the maturation of karma; this refers to the remaining elements of the sound-sphere (*śabdadhātu*).
Regarding the dharma-sphere (*dharmadhātu*), there are four propositions.

It may be karma but not the maturation of karma; this refers to bodily and vocal actions included within the dharma-sphere, as well as volition (*cetanā*) that is not subsumed under the maturation of karma.
Either it is the maturation of karma but not karma itself, namely, those factors within the dharma-element that are the maturation of karma and are not subsumed under volition;
or it is both karma and the maturation of karma, namely, volition born of the maturation of karma.

Or, there are those that are neither karma nor the maturation of karma; this refers to all other elements of the dharma-realm (dharmadhātu) excluding both karma and the dharmas that are the maturation of karma.

Regarding how many are karma but do not follow from karma, and so forth: seven follow from karma but are not karma; eight are neither karma nor follow from karma; three should be analyzed individually.
This refers to the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), which may be karma that does not follow from karma, or neither karma nor that which follows from karma.
That which is karma but does not follow from karma refers to bodily intimation (*kāyavijñapti*).
That which is neither karma nor concomitant with karma refers to the remaining [elements] of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) and the sound element (*śabdadhātu*);
these are either karma that is not concomitant with karma, or neither karma nor concomitant with karma.
That which is karma but does not follow along with karma is vocal intimation (*vāgvijñapti*).
That which is neither karma nor follows along with karma refers to the remaining elements of the sound-sphere (*śabdadhātu*).
Regarding the dharma-sphere (*dharmadhātu*), there are four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*).

Alternatively, there are those that are not concomitant with karma (*na karmānuvartin*), namely: excluding those bodily and vocal actions that are concomitant with karma, all other bodily and vocal actions as well as volition (*cetanā*) included within the element of mental objects (*dharmadhātu*).

Alternatively, there are those that are concomitant with karma but are not karma itself, namely: the aggregate of feeling (*vedanā-skandha*), the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*), and those factors of the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) that are concomitant with karma but are not subsumed under volition.
Some are both karma and follow along with karma, namely, bodily and vocal karma that follow along with karma.
Some are neither karma nor follow along with karma, namely, all other elements of the dharma-realm (dharmadhātu) excluding karma and those factors that follow along with karma.
Regarding the question of how many derived forms (*upādāya-rūpa*) are not visible forms (*sanidarśana-rūpa*), one should formulate three propositions.
First, there are derived forms that are not visible forms; these refer to the eight elements (*dhātu*) and a portion of two other elements.
Alternatively, there are derived forms that are also visible forms, namely one element;
or there are neither derived forms nor visible forms, namely seven elements and a portion of two elements.
Regarding these eighteen elements, as to how many are derived matter but not obstructive matter and so forth, one should formulate four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*).
Or, there may be derived matter that is not obstructive matter; this refers to a small portion of one element.
There are instances where there is resistance but no derived matter, namely, a small portion of one element.
There are also instances where there is both derived matter and resistance, namely, nine elements and a small portion of one element.
Or, there are those that are neither derived matter nor obstructive matter; these refer to the seven elements and a portion of one element.
Regarding how many are profound because they are difficult to see, and so forth: all are profound because they are difficult to see, and they are difficult to see because they are profound.
Regarding the question of how many are wholesome with non-wholesome as their cause and so forth, all should be analyzed.
That is to say, the eye-element is either wholesome with a non-wholesome cause, or neither-wholesome-nor-non-wholesome with a non-wholesome cause.
That which is wholesome as its cause but not itself wholesome refers to the eye-element produced from the maturation of wholesome karma.
That which is neither wholesome nor has wholesome as its cause refers to the remaining eye-elements.
The same applies to the ear, nose, odor, tongue, taste, body, and tangible-object elements.
The realm of form (rūpadhātu) has three categories.
First, that which is caused by the wholesome but is not itself wholesome; this refers to the form born of the maturation of the wholesome within the realm of form.
Second, that which is both wholesome and caused by the wholesome; this refers to the wholesome [form] within the realm of form.

Or [there are those] that are neither wholesome nor have the wholesome as their cause; this refers to all remaining indeterminate and unwholesome [dharmas] of the form realm, excluding the wholesome [dharmas] born of maturation in the form realm.
The same applies to the six consciousnesses and the mind-element (*manodhātu*).
The sound element has two categories:
either it is wholesome and also has wholesome causes, namely the wholesome sound element;
or it is neither wholesome nor has wholesome causes, namely the unwholesome and indeterminate sound elements.
The dharma-realm (dharmadhātu) has four permutations.
First, that which is wholesome but does not have the wholesome as its cause, namely, analytical cessation (pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha).
Second, that which has the wholesome as its cause but is not itself wholesome, namely, the dharma-realm consisting of dharmas born of the maturation of the wholesome.
Either it is wholesome and has the wholesome as its cause, namely, the wholesome conditioned *dharmadhātu*;

or it is neither wholesome nor has the wholesome as its cause, namely, all remaining indeterminate and unwholesome *dharmadhātus*, excluding those that are wholesome and produced by maturation (*vipākaja*).
Regarding the categories such as "how many are unwholesome but not having the unwholesome as their cause," all should be analyzed.
That is to say, the eye-element is either unwholesome but not having the unwholesome as its cause, or it is neither unwholesome nor having the unwholesome as its cause.
That which has unwholesome causes but is not itself unwholesome refers to the eye-element born of the maturation of unwholesome karma.
That which is neither unwholesome nor has unwholesome causes refers to the remaining eye-elements.
