The same applies to the ear, nose, odor, tongue, taste, body, and tangible-object elements.
Regarding the form element (*rūpa-dhātu*), there are three categories:
some are caused by the unwholesome (*akuśala-hetuka*) but are not themselves unwholesome; this refers to the form element born as the maturation (*vipāka*) of the unwholesome within the form realm.
Or it is unwholesome and has the unwholesome as its cause, namely, unwholesome [matter] of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*).

Or it is neither unwholesome nor has the unwholesome as its cause, namely, all other neutral (*avyākṛta*) and wholesome [matters] of the form realm, excluding those born of the maturation (*vipākaja*) of the unwholesome.
The same applies to the elements of eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and consciousness.
The sound element has two categories:
either it is unwholesome and has an unwholesome cause, namely, the unwholesome sound element; [or it is indeterminate and has an indeterminate cause].
Or [it is] neither unwholesome nor has unwholesomeness as its cause; this refers to the wholesome and indeterminate sound-element (*śabdadhātu*).
The mind-element (*manodhātu*) consists of three propositions.

Or [it is] that which has unwholesomeness as its cause but is not itself unwholesome; this refers to the mind-element arising from the maturation of the unwholesome, as well as the mind-element associated with the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and the view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*) bound to the desire realm.
Either it is unwholesome and has the unwholesome as its cause, namely, the unwholesome mind-element (*manodhātu*);

or it is neither unwholesome nor has the unwholesome as its cause, namely, all other indeterminate and wholesome mind-elements, excluding the mind-element that arises as the maturation of the unwholesome, and excluding the mind-element associated with the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and the view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*) bound to the desire realm.
The same applies to the consciousness element (*vijñānadhātu*).
The dharma element (*dharmadhātu*) has three categories:

there are those that have unwholesome causes but are not themselves unwholesome. These include the dharma element born of the maturation (*vipākaja*) of the unwholesome, as well as the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and the view of extreme adherence (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*) bound to the desire realm, along with the dharmas associated with and arising from them.
Either it is unwholesome and has the unwholesome as its cause, namely, the unwholesome dharma-element;

or it is neither unwholesome nor has the unwholesome as its cause, namely, with the exception of the dharma-element produced by the maturation of the unwholesome, and with the exception of the dharma-element associated with and arising from the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and the view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*) in the desire realm, all other remaining indeterminate and wholesome dharma-elements.

Regarding the question of how many are indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) but not having the indeterminate as their cause, and so forth: eight are indeterminate and have the indeterminate as their cause; ten should be analyzed.
That is to say, for the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), there are three propositions.
Either that which has an indeterminate cause but is not itself indeterminate— namely, unwholesome [dharmas] of the form realm—
or that which is both indeterminate and has an indeterminate cause— namely, indeterminate [dharmas] of the form realm.
Or [there are cases that] are neither indeterminate nor have indeterminacy as their cause; this refers to wholesome [factors] of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*).

The same applies to the sound element (*śabdadhātu*), the six consciousness elements (*ṣadvijñānadhātu*), and the mind element (*manodhātu*). Regarding the dharma element (*dharmadhātu*), there are four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*).
Some are indeterminate but do not have the indeterminate as their cause, namely space and non-analytical cessation.
Some have the indeterminate as their cause but are not themselves indeterminate, namely the unwholesome dharma-realm.
Either it is indeterminate and has an indeterminate cause, namely the indeterminate conditioned dharma-realm;
or it is neither indeterminate nor has an indeterminate cause, namely the wholesome dharma-realm.
Regarding the statement "how many conditions are not 'having a cause' (*sahetuka*) and so forth": seventeen are both conditions (*pratyaya*) and have a cause;

one should be analyzed. That is to say, as for the dharma-element (*dharmadhātu*): if it is conditioned (*saṃskṛta*), it is both a condition and has a cause; if it is unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), it is neither a condition nor does it have a cause.

Regarding the question of how many are immediate antecedents (*samanantara*) but not immediate conditions (*samanantarapratyaya*), ten are neither immediate antecedents nor immediate conditions; eight should be analyzed.
Specifically, the visual consciousness element (*cakṣurvijñānadhātu*) consists of three cases.
Or it may be an equal-and-immediate [condition] but not an equal-and-immediate condition, namely, a future visual consciousness that is currently arising before one.
Or it may be both an equal-and-immediate [condition] and an equal-and-immediate condition, namely, past and present visual consciousnesses.

Or [there are cases that] are neither equal-immediate [condition] nor equal-immediate condition: namely, with the exception of the eye-consciousness that is currently arising in the present, all other future eye-consciousnesses.
The same applies to the consciousness-elements of the ear, nose, tongue, and body.
The mind-element (manodhātu) consists of three categories:

it may be an equal-and-immediate antecedent (samanantara) that is not an equal-and-immediate condition (samanantarapratyaya). This refers to the mind-element of the future that is currently arising before one, as well as the mind-element at the moment of death for an Arhat in the past or present.

Or it is both an immediately preceding condition (*samanantara*) and an immediately preceding object-condition (*samanantarālambana-pratyaya*); that is to say, with the exception of the mental element (*manodhātu*) at the moment of death for past and present Arhats, all other past and present mental elements [are such].

Or there are those that are neither immediate nor immediate conditions: namely, with the exception of the mental element (*manodhātu*) that is presently arising in the future, all other remaining future mental elements.
The same applies to the mental-consciousness element (*manovijñānadhātu*).
The dharma-realm consists of three categories.

Some are equal-and-immediate [conditions] but not equal-and-immediate causes (*samanantarapratyaya*). These include: all mental factors (*caitasika-dharma*) that are future and currently arising; all mental factors at the moment of the final death of an Arhat in the past or present; and the states of non-conceptualization (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*) and the cessation-attainment (*nirodha-samāpatti*) once they have arisen and are currently occurring.

Or those that are both equal-immediate [conditions] and equal-immediate conditions: namely, with the exception of all mental factors at the moment of the final death of an Arhat in the past or present, all other past and present mental factors.

Or [there are factors] that are neither equal-immediate [factors] nor equal-immediate conditions: namely, with the exception of all future mental factors that are currently arising before one, all other future mental factors; and with the exception of the mind-dissociated formations that are equal-immediate [conditions], all other mind-dissociated formations; as well as bodily and vocal actions, together with unconditioned phenomena.

Regarding how many are object-conditions (ālambana-pratyaya) but do not possess an object (ālambana), and so forth: ten are object-conditions but do not possess an object; seven are both object-conditions and possess an object; one should be analyzed.

That is to say, regarding the dharma-realm: if they are mental factors (*caitta*), they are both objective conditions (*ālambana-pratyaya*) and possess objects; if they are not mental factors, they are objective conditions but do not possess objects.

Regarding the question of how many predominant conditions (*adhipati-pratyaya*) are not accompanied by predominance (*ādhipatya*), seventeen are both predominant conditions and possess predominance; one should be analyzed.

That is to say, regarding the dharma-element (*dharmadhātu*): if it is conditioned (*saṃskṛta*), it is both a predominant condition and possesses predominance; if it is unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), it is a predominant condition but does not possess predominance.
Regarding how many *oghāḥ* (floods) are not *ānugāmin-oghāḥ* (conducive to floods), fifteen are *ānugāmin-oghāḥ* but not *oghāḥ*; three should be analyzed.

That is to say, as for the mind-element (*manodhātu*): if it is with outflows (*sāsrava*), it is conducive to floods but not a flood; if it is without outflows (*anāsrava*), it is neither a flood nor conducive to floods.
The consciousness element is also like this.
The dharma-element consists of three categories:
it may be concordant with the flood but not itself a flood, namely, the contaminated dharma-element that is not subsumed within the floods.
Some are both floods (*ogha*) and favorable to the floods; these are the four floods.
Some are neither floods nor favorable to the floods; these are the untainted dharma-realm (*anāsrava-dharmadhātu*).
*Sarvāstivādavinayavibhāṣā-śāstra*, Fascicle Seventeen.
Abhidharma-prakaraṇa-pāda-śāstra, Fascicle 18.
Composed by the Venerable Vasumitra;
translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang by Imperial Decree.

Chapter Eight: Determination of the Distinctions Dharmas possessing form are subsumed under eleven elements (dhātus), eleven bases (āyatanas), and one aggregate (skandha). They are known by eight cognitions—excluding the cognition of others' minds and the cognition of cessation—and are cognized by the six consciousnesses. The latent dispositions (anuśayas) that are universal in the desire and form realms, as well as those to be abandoned through cultivation, increase in association with them.

Only material phenomena (rūpadharma) are subsumed under ten elements (dhātu), ten bases (āyatana), and one aggregate (skandha); they are not known by [supramundane] knowledge, are cognized by the five consciousnesses, and are not the locus where latent dispositions (anuśaya) increase.

Non-material phenomena (arūpadharma) are subsumed under eight elements, two bases, and four aggregates; they are known by ten types of knowledge, are cognized by one consciousness, and are the locus where all latent dispositions increase.

Only formless phenomena (*arūpadharma*) are subsumed under seven elements (*dhātu*), one base (*āyatana*), and four aggregates (*skandha*). They are known by two knowledges (*jñāna*), namely the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*) and the knowledge of cessation (*nirodhajñāna*); they are not cognized by consciousness (*vijñāna*). All [defilements] of the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), the two categories of the desire and form realms (*kāmadhātu* and *rūpadhātu*), and the non-universal latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) to be abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkha*) and origin (*samudaya*) increase therein.

The phenomena that are objects of vision (dṛṣṭa-dharma) are subsumed under one element (dhātu), one base (āyatana), and one aggregate (skandha). They are known by seven cognitions—excluding the cognition of others' minds, the cognition of cessation, and the cognition of the path—and are cognized by two consciousnesses. The latent dispositions (anuśaya) that are universal in the desire and form realms, as well as those to be abandoned through cultivation, increase in relation to them.

Only those phenomena that are with-outflow (*sāsrava*) are comprised within one element, one base, and are not included among the aggregates; they are not known by [the supramundane] knowledge, are cognized by one consciousness, and are not the locus where latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) increase.

Those phenomena that are without-outflow (*anāsrava*) are comprised within seventeen elements, eleven bases, and five aggregates; they are known by ten knowledges, cognized by five consciousnesses, and are the locus where all latent dispositions increase.

Only those phenomena that are not objects of the view [of self and what belongs to self] are subsumed under seventeen elements (dhātu), eleven bases (āyatana), and four aggregates (skandha). They are known by three types of knowledge—namely, the knowledge of others' minds, the knowledge of cessation, and the knowledge of the path—and are cognized by four types of consciousness. Regarding the latent dispositions (anuśaya) that increase therein: they include all [dispositions] of the formless realm, two categories of the desire realm, and the non-universal latent dispositions abandoned through the vision of suffering and the origin.

Opposable phenomena (*sapratigha-dharma*) are subsumed under ten elements (*dhātu*), ten bases (*āyatana*), and one aggregate (*skandha*). They are known by seven cognitions—excluding the cognition of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*), the cognition of cessation (*nirodhajñāna*), and the cognition of the path (*mārgajñāna*)—and are cognized by the six consciousnesses (*ṣadvijñāna*). The pervasive latent dispositions (*sarvatragānuśaya*) of the desire and form realms, as well as those to be abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*), increase in association with them.

Only those phenomena that are with resistance (*sapratigha*) are not subsumed under ten elements (*dhātu*), ten bases (*āyatana*), or any aggregate (*skandha*); they are not known by any cognition (*jñāna*), are cognized by the five consciousnesses (*vijñāna*), and are not the locus for the increase of latent dispositions (*anuśaya*).

Those phenomena that are without resistance (*apratigha*) are subsumed under eight elements, two bases, and five aggregates; they are known by ten cognitions, cognized by one consciousness, and are the locus for the increase of all latent dispositions.

Only non-obstructive (*apratigha*) dharmas are subsumed under eight elements (*dhātu*), two bases (*āyatana*), and four aggregates (*skandha*). They are known by three knowledges (*jñāna*), namely the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*), the knowledge of cessation (*nirodhajñāna*), and the knowledge of the path (*mārgajñāna*). They are not cognized by consciousness (*vijñāna*). All latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) of the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), all [latent dispositions] of the two categories of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) and the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), as well as the non-universal (*asarvatraga*) latent dispositions abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkha*) and origin (*samudaya*), increase in association with them.

Conditioned phenomena with outflows (*sāsrava-dharma*) are subsumed within the eighteen elements (*dhātu*), the twelve bases (*āyatana*), and the five aggregates (*skandha*). They are known by eight cognitions (*jñāna*), excluding the cognition of cessation (*nirodha-jñāna*) and the cognition of the path (*mārga-jñāna*); they are cognized by the six consciousnesses (*vijñāna*), and all latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) increase in accordance with them.

Only the contaminated (*sāsrava*) phenomena are comprised of fifteen elements (*dhātu*), ten bases (*āyatana*), and are not included within the aggregates (*skandha*). They are known by two types of knowledge—namely, the knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-jñāna*) and the knowledge of origin (*samudaya-jñāna*)—and are cognized by the five sensory consciousnesses (*vijñāna*). All latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) increase in accordance with them.

The untainted dharmas (*anāsrava-dharma*) are subsumed within the three realms, two bases, and five aggregates; they are known by eight knowledges, excluding the knowledge of suffering and the knowledge of origin; they are cognized by one consciousness, and the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) do not increase therein.

Only untainted phenomena (*anāsrava-dharma*) are not subsumed under the elements (*dhātu*), the bases (*āyatana*), or the aggregates (*skandha*). They are known by two types of knowledge—namely, the knowledge of cessation (*nirodha-jñāna*) and the knowledge of the path (*mārga-jñāna*)—but are not cognized by consciousness (*vijñāna*), nor do latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) increase therein.

Conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*) are subsumed within the eighteen elements (*dhātu*), the twelve bases (*āyatana*), and the five aggregates (*skandha*). They are known by nine cognitions, excluding the cognition of cessation (*nirodhajñāna*); they are cognized by the six consciousnesses; and all latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) increase in accordance with them.

Only conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*) are subsumed within seventeen elements (*dhātu*), eleven bases (*āyatana*), and five aggregates (*skandha*). They are known by four knowledges (*jñāna*), namely: the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*), the knowledge of suffering (*duḥkhajñāna*), the knowledge of origin (*samudayajñāna*), and the knowledge of the path (*mārgajñāna*). They are cognized by the five consciousnesses (*vijñāna*), and all latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) increase therein.

Unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*) are comprised of one element (*dhātu*), one base (*āyatana*), and are not included within the aggregates (*skandha*). They are known by six types of knowledge—excluding the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*), the knowledge of suffering (*duḥkhajñāna*), the knowledge of origin (*samudayajñāna*), and the knowledge of the path (*mārgajñāna*)—and are cognized by one consciousness. Latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) do not increase therein.

Only unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛtadharma*) are not subsumed under the elements (*dhātu*), the bases (*āyatana*), or the aggregates (*skandha*); they are known by a single cognition, namely the cognition of cessation (*nirodhajñāna*); they are not cognized by consciousness (*vijñāna*), and no latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) increase therein.

The dharmas with conflict and without conflict; worldly and supramundane dharmas; dharmas that fall within the realms and those that do not; dharmas with attachment and those without attachment; dharmas based on indulgence and those based on renunciation; dharmas conducive to fetters and those not conducive to fetters; dharmas conducive to grasping and those not conducive to grasping; and dharmas conducive to entanglements and those not conducive to entanglements—these should be understood in the same manner as the dharmas with outflows and without outflows.

Conditioned phenomena (saṃskṛta-dharma) are subsumed within ten elements (dhātu), four bases (āyatana), and five aggregates (skandha); they are known by ten cognitions (jñāna) and cognized by three consciousnesses (vijñāna). They are associated with the increase of all latent dispositions (anuśaya) in the desire realm, as well as the pervasive (sarvatraga) and those to be abandoned through cultivation (bhāvanā-heya) in the form and formless realms.

Only the *avyākṛta-dharma* (unspecified phenomena) is not subsumed under the elements (*dhātu*), bases (*āyatana*), or aggregates (*skandha*). It is known by two types of knowledge, namely the knowledge of cessation (*nirodha-jñāna*) and the knowledge of the path (*mārga-jñāna*). It is not cognized by consciousness (*vijñāna*). The latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) belonging to the two categories of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) and those abandoned through the vision of origin (*samudaya-darśana-prahātavya*)—provided they are not universal (*asarvatraga*)—increase in association with it.

The indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) dharmas are subsumed within the eighteen elements (*dhātu*), the twelve bases (*āyatana*), and the five aggregates (*skandha*). They are known by eight cognitions, excluding the cognition of cessation (*nirodhajñāna*) and the cognition of the path (*mārgajñāna*). They are cognized by the six consciousnesses. They include all [defilements] of the form and formless realms, as well as the two categories of the desire realm and the pervasive latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) to be abandoned through the vision of origin (*samudayadarśana-prahātavya*). These [latent dispositions] increase in association with them.

Only indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) dharmas: eight elements (*dhātu*), eight bases (*āyatana*), and [the remainder] are not included within the aggregates (*skandha*). They are not known by the knowledges (*jñāna*), but are cognized by three consciousnesses (*vijñāna*). The latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) belonging to the two categories of the form and formless realms, as well as those non-universal (*asarvatraga*) dispositions abandoned through the vision of suffering and its origin, increase in association with them.

Dharmas that are obscured (nivṛta) are comprised within ten elements (dhātu), four bases (āyatana), and five aggregates (skandha). They are known by eight cognitions (jñāna), excluding the cognition of cessation (nirodha-jñāna) and the cognition of the path (mārga-jñāna); they are cognized by three consciousnesses (vijñāna), and all latent dispositions (anuśaya) increase in accordance with them.

Only the obscured-unwholesome (*nivṛtāvyākṛta*) dharmas are not subsumed under the elements (*dhātu*), the bases (*āyatana*), or the aggregates (*skandha*); they are not known by the [supramundane] knowledges (*jñāna*), nor cognized by consciousness (*vijñāna*). The latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) belonging to the two categories of the three realms and those abandoned through the vision of suffering and origin (*duḥkha-samudaya-darśana-prahātavya*) that are non-universal (*asarvatraga*) increase therein.

Unobscured phenomena are subsumed within the eighteen elements, the twelve bases, and the five aggregates; they are known by ten cognitions and cognized by the six consciousnesses; and the latent dispositions (anuśaya) that are universal throughout the three realms and those to be abandoned through cultivation increase therein.

Only unobscured-neutral dharmas are not subsumed under the eight elements (dhātu), the eight bases (āyatana), or the aggregates (skandha). They are known by two knowledges—namely, the knowledge of cessation (nirodhajñāna) and the knowledge of the path (mārgajñāna)—and are cognized by three consciousnesses; furthermore, latent dispositions (anuśaya) do not increase therein.

The dharmas to be cultivated (*bhāvanīya*) are subsumed under ten bases (*dhātu*), four spheres (*āyatana*), and five aggregates (*skandha*). They are known by nine knowledges (*jñāna*), excluding the knowledge of cessation (*nirodhajñāna*); they are cognized by three consciousnesses (*vijñāna*). The latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) that are universal throughout the three realms (*tridhātupervāsin*) and those to be abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanāheya*) increase in association with them.

It is exclusively a dharma to be cultivated; it is not subsumed under the elements (dhātu), the bases (āyatana), or the aggregates (skandha). It is known by a single knowledge, namely the knowledge of the path (mārgajñāna); it is not cognized by consciousness, and latent dispositions (anuśaya) do not increase therein.

That which is not to be cultivated is subsumed within the eighteen elements (*dhātu*), the twelve bases (*āyatana*), and the five aggregates (*skandha*). It is known by nine knowledges (*jñāna*), excluding the knowledge of the path (*mārgajñāna*), and is cognized by the six consciousnesses (*vijñāna*). All latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) increase in association with it.

Only those factors that should not be cultivated are the eight elements (*dhātu*) and eight bases (*āyatana*) not subsumed under the aggregates (*skandha*). They are known by a single type of knowledge, namely the knowledge of cessation (*nirodhajñāna*), and are cognized by three types of consciousness. Regarding the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*), they are increased by the two categories of the three realms, as well as by the non-universal (*asarvatraga*) dispositions abandoned through the vision of suffering and origin.

Defiled phenomena (*kliṣṭa-dharma*) are subsumed under ten elements (*dhātu*), four bases (*āyatana*), and five aggregates (*skandha*). They are known by eight cognitions (*jñāna*), excluding the cognition of cessation (*nirodha-jñāna*) and the cognition of the path (*mārga-jñāna*), and are cognized by three consciousnesses (*vijñāna*). All latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) increase in accordance with them.

Only defiled phenomena (*kliṣṭa-dharma*) are not subsumed under the elements (*dhātu*), bases (*āyatana*), or aggregates (*skandha*); they are not known by the knowledges (*jñāna*), nor cognized by consciousness (*vijñāna*); and the non-universal (*asarvatraga*) latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) belonging to the two categories of the three realms, as well as those abandoned through the vision of suffering and origin, increase in association with them.

Non-defiled phenomena (akliṣṭa-dharma) are subsumed within the eighteen elements (dhātu), the twelve bases (āyatana), and the five aggregates (skandha). They are known by ten types of knowledge (jñāna) and cognized by the six consciousnesses (vijñāna). The latent dispositions (anuśaya) that are universal throughout the three realms and those to be abandoned through cultivation (bhāvanā-heya) increase in relation to them.

Only non-defiled phenomena are comprised within eight elements (dhātu), eight bases (āyatana), and not within the aggregates (skandha). They are known by two types of knowledge—namely, the knowledge of cessation (nirodhajñāna) and the knowledge of the path (mārgajñāna)—and are cognized by three consciousnesses (vijñāna). Latent dispositions (anuśaya) do not increase therein.
The same applies to dharmas that are with-outflow (sāsrava) and without-outflow (anāsrava).

Dharmas that have maturation (savipāka) are comprised within ten elements (dhātu), four bases (āyatana), and five aggregates (skandha). They are known by eight knowledges (jñāna), excluding the knowledge of cessation (nirodhajñāna) and the knowledge of the path (mārgajñāna), and are cognized by three consciousnesses (vijñāna). They include all [defilements] of the desire realm (kāmadhātu), the universal [defilements] of the form and formless realms (rūpadhātu and ārūpyadhātu), and the latent tendencies (anuśaya) abandoned through cultivation (bhāvanā-heya) which increase therein.

Only the dharma of maturation (vipāka) is not subsumed under the elements (dhātu), the bases (āyatana), or the aggregates (skandha); it is not known by the knowledges (jñāna), nor cognized by consciousness (vijñāna); and it is accompanied by the increase of the two classes [of afflictions] of the desire realm and the non-universal proclivities (anuśaya) to be abandoned through the vision of the origin (samudaya).

Dharmas that are non-resultant (avipāka) are subsumed within the eighteen elements (dhātu), the twelve bases (āyatana), and the five aggregates (skandha). They are known by ten cognitions (jñāna) and cognized by six consciousnesses (vijñāna). They include all [dharmas] of the form and formless realms, as well as two categories of the desire realm; furthermore, the pervasive latent dispositions (anuśaya) to be abandoned through the vision of suffering and origin increase therein.

Only those dharmas that are without maturation (avipāka)—namely, the eight elements (dhātu), the eight bases (āyatana), and those not included within the aggregates (skandha)—are known by two knowledges, namely the knowledge of cessation (nirodhajñāna) and the knowledge of the path (mārgajñāna), and are cognized by three consciousnesses. They are subject to the increase of the latent dispositions (anuśaya) belonging to the two categories of the form and formless realms, as well as those abandoned through the vision of suffering and origin that are non-universal (aprakaraṇa).

The view of phenomena (*dṛṣṭi-dharma*) is subsumed under two elements (*dhātu*), two bases (*āyatana*), and two aggregates (*skandha*). It is known by nine knowledges (*jñāna*), excluding the knowledge of cessation (*nirodha-jñāna*); it is cognized by one consciousness (*vijñāna*). Regarding its latent tendencies (*anuśaya*), the outflow-tainted objects of the three realms (*sāsrava-ālambana*) and the untainted objects associated with views (*anāsrava-ālambana*)—namely, ignorance (*avidyā-anuśaya*)—increase therein.

Only those phenomena that are not objects of vision (adṛṣṭa-dharma) comprise one element (dhātu), one base (āyatana), and are not included within the aggregates (skandha); they are not known by the knowledges (jñāna), not cognized by consciousness (vijñāna), and in them no latent dispositions (anuśaya) increase.

Those phenomena that are objects of vision (dṛṣṭa-dharma) comprise seventeen elements, eleven bases, and five aggregates; they are known by ten knowledges, cognized by six consciousnesses, and all latent dispositions increase therein.

Exclusively non-view phenomena (*adṛṣṭi-dharma*), they are subsumed under sixteen elements (*dhātu*), ten bases (*āyatana*), and three aggregates (*skandha*). They are known by one knowledge, namely the knowledge of cessation (*nirodha-jñāna*), and are cognized by five consciousnesses (*vijñāna*). With the exception of the untainted objects associated with views and ignorance (*avidyā*), all other untainted-object latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) increase therein.

Internal phenomena (ādhyātmika-dharma) are subsumed under twelve bases (āyatana), six sense-fields (āyatana), and two aggregates (skandha). They are known by nine knowledges (jñāna), excluding the knowledge of cessation (nirodha-jñāna), and are cognized by one consciousness (vijñāna). All latent dispositions (anuśaya) increase in relation to them.

Internal phenomena (*adhyātma-dharma*) are subsumed within twelve bases (*āyatana*), six sense-fields (*āyatana*), and one aggregate (*skandha*); they are not known by [supramundane] knowledge (*jñāna*), are not cognized by consciousness (*vijñāna*), and are not the locus where latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) increase.

External phenomena (*bāhya-dharma*) are subsumed within six elements (*dhātu*), six sense-fields (*āyatana*), and four aggregates (*skandha*); they are known by ten types of knowledge, cognized by six types of consciousness, and are the locus where all latent dispositions increase.

Only external phenomena (*bāhyadharma*) are subsumed under six elements (*dhātu*), six bases (*āyatana*), and three aggregates (*skandha*). They are known by one cognition, namely the cognition of cessation (*nirodhajñāna*); they are cognized by the five consciousnesses (*vijñāna*), and the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) do not increase therein.

Appropriated phenomena (*upātta-dharma*) are subsumed under nine elements, nine bases, and one aggregate. They are known by seven cognitions—excluding the cognition of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*) and the cognitions of cessation and the path—and are cognized by the five consciousnesses. The latent dispositions that are universal (*sarvatraga*) in the desire and form realms, as well as those to be abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*), increase therein.

Only appropriated phenomena (*upātta-dharma*) are not subsumed under the elements (*dhātu*), bases (*āyatana*), or aggregates (*skandha*); they are not known by the knowledges (*jñāna*), not cognized by the consciousnesses (*vijñāna*), and the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) do not increase therein.

Non-appropriated phenomena (*anupātta-dharma*) are subsumed under the eighteen elements, twelve bases, and five aggregates; they are known by ten knowledges, cognized by six consciousnesses, and all latent dispositions increase therein.

Only those phenomena that are not appropriated (anupātta) are subsumed under nine elements (dhātu), three bases (āyatana), and four aggregates (skandha). They are known by three knowledges (jñāna)—namely, the knowledge of others' minds (paracittajñāna), the knowledge of cessation (nirodhajñāna), and the knowledge of the path (mārgajñāna)—and cognized by one consciousness (vijñāna). All latent dispositions (anuśaya) belonging to the entire formless realm (ārūpyadhātu), two categories of the desire and form realms (kāmadhātu and rūpadhātu), and the non-universal (asarvatraga) dispositions abandoned through the vision of suffering (duḥkha) and origin (samudaya) increase therein.

Mental factors (*cittadharma*) are subsumed under seven elements (*dhātu*), one base (*āyatana*), and one aggregate (*skandha*); they are known by nine knowledges (*jñāna*), excluding the knowledge of cessation (*nirodhajñāna*); they are cognized by one consciousness (*vijñāna*); and all latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) increase therein.

Mental factors alone are subsumed under seven elements, one base, and one aggregate; they are not known by [the aforementioned] knowledges, are not cognized by consciousness, and are not subject to the increase of latent dispositions.

Non-mental phenomena are subsumed within eleven elements, eleven bases, and four aggregates; they are known by ten knowledges and cognized by six consciousnesses, with all latent dispositions (anuśaya) increasing therein.

Non-mental phenomena alone are subsumed within eleven elements, eleven bases, and four aggregates; they are known by one knowledge, namely the knowledge of cessation (nirodha-jñāna), and cognized by five consciousnesses, with no latent dispositions increasing therein.

Dharmas that possess an object (sālambana) are subsumed under eight elements (dhātu), two bases (āyatana), and four aggregates (skandha). They are known by nine knowledges (jñāna), excluding the knowledge of cessation (nirodhajñāna), and are cognized by one consciousness (vijñāna). All latent proclivities (anuśaya) increase in accordance with them.

There is only the dharma that serves as an object; it is subsumed under seven elements (dhātus), one base (āyatana), and three aggregates (skandhas). It is known by a single type of knowledge, namely the knowledge of others' minds (paracittajñāna); it is not cognized by consciousness (vijñāna). The latent dispositions (anuśaya) belonging to the three realms and those that are outflow-free (anāsrava) increase in relation to it as their objects.

Dharmas that lack an object of cognition are subsumed under eleven elements (dhātus), eleven bases (āyatanas), and two aggregates (skandhas). They are known by nine types of knowledge, excluding the knowledge of others' minds, and are cognized by the six consciousnesses. Regarding them, the latent dispositions (anuśayas) with outflow that take the three realms as their objects increase in accordance with those objects.

Only those phenomena that lack an object of cognition (anālambana-dharma) are subsumed within ten elements (dhātu), ten bases (āyatana), and one aggregate (skandha). They are known by a single type of knowledge, namely the knowledge of cessation (nirodha-jñāna); they are cognized by the five sensory consciousnesses (pañca-vijñāna), and no latent dispositions (anuśaya) increase therein.

Mental factors (caitta-dharma) are subsumed under one element, one base, and three aggregates; they are known by nine knowledges, excluding the knowledge of cessation; they are cognized by one consciousness; and all latent dispositions (anuśaya) increase in accordance with them.

Mental factors (*caitta*) are not subsumed under the [eighteen] elements (*dhātu*), the [twelve] bases (*āyatana*), or two of the aggregates (*skandha*); they are not known by the [ten] knowledges (*jñāna*), nor cognized by the [six] consciousnesses (*vijñāna*), and the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) do not increase therein.

Non-mental factors are subsumed under the eighteen elements, the twelve bases, and three of the aggregates; they are known by the ten knowledges, cognized by the six consciousnesses, and all latent dispositions increase therein.

It is exclusively a non-mental-factor dharma (cittaviprayuktadharma), subsumed under seventeen elements (dhātu), eleven bases (āyatana), and two aggregates (skandha). It is known by one type of knowledge, namely the knowledge of cessation (nirodhajñāna); it is cognized by the five consciousnesses; and it is not the locus for the increase of latent dispositions (anuśaya).

The category of karma (*karmadharma*) is subsumed under the three realms, three bases, and two aggregates; it is known by nine knowledges, excluding the knowledge of cessation (*nirodhajñāna*); it is cognized by the three consciousnesses; and all latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) increase in accordance with it.

The category of "only karma" (*kevalakarmadharma*) is not subsumed under any realm, base, or aggregate; it is not known by any knowledge, not cognized by any consciousness, and no latent dispositions increase in accordance with it.

Non-karmic phenomena (*akarmadharma*) are subsumed within the eighteen elements (*dhātu*), twelve bases (*āyatana*), and five aggregates (*skandha*); they are known by ten knowledges (*jñāna*) and cognized by six consciousnesses (*vijñāna*), with all latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) increasing therein.

Non-karmic phenomena alone are subsumed within fifteen elements, nine bases, and three aggregates; they are known by one knowledge, namely the knowledge of cessation (*nirodhajñāna*), and are cognized by three consciousnesses, wherein no latent dispositions increase.

Wholesome phenomena (*kuśala-dharma*) are subsumed within ten bases (*dhātu*), four spheres (*āyatana*), and five aggregates (*skandha*); they are known by ten cognitions (*jñāna*) and cognized by three consciousnesses (*vijñāna*); and the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) that are universal throughout the three realms as well as those to be abandoned through cultivation increase therein.

Exclusively wholesome phenomena (*kuśala-dharma*) are not subsumed under the elements (*dhātu*), the bases (*āyatana*), or the aggregates (*skandha*). They are known by two types of knowledge, namely the knowledge of cessation (*nirodha-jñāna*) and the knowledge of the path (*mārga-jñāna*); they are not cognized by consciousness (*vijñāna*), and latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) do not increase therein.

Unwholesome phenomena (*akuśala-dharma*) are subsumed within ten elements (*dhātu*), four bases (*āyatana*), and five aggregates (*skandha*). They are known by seven cognitions (*jñāna*), excluding the cognition of subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*), the cognition of cessation (*nirodha-jñāna*), and the cognition of the path (*mārga-jñāna*); they are cognized by three consciousnesses (*vijñāna*). All latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) increase in association with them.

Only unwholesome dharmas are not subsumed under the elements (dhātu), the bases (āyatana), or the aggregates (skandha); they are not known by the knowledges (jñāna) and are not cognized by consciousness (vijñāna). The two classes [of afflictions] of the desire realm and the non-universal latent dispositions (anuśaya) abandoned through the vision of the origin of suffering increase therein.

The indeterminate (avyākṛta) dharmas are subsumed within the eighteen elements (dhātu), the twelve bases (āyatana), and the five aggregates (skandha). They are known by eight cognitions, excluding the cognition of cessation (nirodhajñāna) and the cognition of the path (mārgajñāna); they are cognized by the six consciousnesses. They include all [defilements] of the form and formless realms, as well as those of two categories in the desire realm, and the pervasive latent dispositions (anuśaya) to be abandoned through the vision of origin (samudaya-darśana-prahātavya). These [indeterminate dharmas] are increased by these [latent dispositions].

Only indeterminate dharmas are comprised within eight elements and eight bases, but not within the aggregates; they are not known by the knowledges, but are cognized by three consciousnesses; and the two categories [of defilements] belonging to the form and formless realms, as well as the non-universal latent dispositions abandoned through the vision of suffering and the origin, increase in association with them.

The factors abandoned by insight (*darśana-prahātavya-dharma*) are subsumed under the three realms, two bases, and four aggregates; they are known by eight knowledges, excluding the knowledge of cessation and the knowledge of the path, and are cognized by one consciousness; all latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) abandoned by insight increase in relation to them.

Only those phenomena abandoned by insight (darśana-prahātavya) are not subsumed under the elements (dhātu), the bases (āyatana), or the aggregates (skandha); they are not known by knowledge (jñāna) and are not cognized by consciousness (vijñāna). The non-universal (asarvatraga) latent dispositions (anuśaya) belonging to the two categories of the three realms and those to be abandoned by the vision of suffering and origination increase in association with them.

The dharmas to be abandoned by cultivation (bhāvanā-heya) are subsumed within the eighteen elements (dhātu), the twelve bases (āyatana), and the five aggregates (skandha). They are known by eight cognitions, excluding the cognition of cessation (nirodha-jñāna) and the cognition of the path (mārga-jñāna), and are cognized by the six consciousnesses (vijñāna). The latent dispositions (anuśaya) that are universal throughout the three realms (traidhātuka-sarvatraga) and those to be abandoned by cultivation increase in relation to them.

Only those phenomena abandoned through cultivation (bhāvanā-heya) are comprised of fifteen elements (dhātu), ten bases (āyatana), and are not included within the aggregates (skandha). They are not known by the [supramundane] knowledges, are cognized by the five consciousnesses, and all latent dispositions (anuśaya) to be abandoned through cultivation increase therein.

Dharmas not to be abandoned (*apraheya*) are subsumed within the three realms, two bases, and five aggregates; they are known by eight knowledges—excluding the knowledges of suffering and origin—and cognized by one consciousness; they are not increased by latent dispositions (*anuśaya*).

Only those dharmas that are not to be abandoned (aheya) are not subsumed under the elements (dhātu), the bases (āyatana), or the aggregates (skandha). They are known by two knowledges, namely the knowledge of cessation (nirodhajñāna) and the knowledge of the path (mārgajñāna); they are not cognized by consciousness, and no latent dispositions (anuśaya) increase therein.

The training factors (*śikṣā-dharma*) are subsumed under the three realms, two bases, and five aggregates; they are known by seven knowledges—excluding the knowledges of suffering, origin, and cessation—and are cognized by one consciousness; the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) do not increase therein.

Only the dharmas of training (śaikṣa) are not subsumed under the elements (dhātu), the bases (āyatana), or the aggregates (skandha); they are not known by cognition (jñāna), not cognized by consciousness (vijñāna), and in them latent dispositions (anuśaya) do not increase.
The same applies to the dharmas beyond training (aśaikṣa).

Dharmas that are neither-learner-nor-non-learner are subsumed within the eighteen elements, the twelve bases, and the five aggregates; they are known by nine knowledges, excluding the knowledge of the path, and are cognized by the six consciousnesses; all latent dispositions increase in relation to them.

Only those phenomena that are neither-learner-nor-non-learner (naivaśaikṣanāśaikṣa) are comprised of fifteen elements (dhātu), ten bases (āyatana), and are not included within the aggregates (skandha). They are known by three types of knowledge—namely, the knowledge of suffering, the knowledge of origin, and the knowledge of cessation—and are cognized by the five sensory consciousnesses. All latent dispositions (anuśaya) increase in accordance with them.

Dharmas bound to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*) are subsumed within the eighteen elements (*dhātu*), the twelve bases (*āyatana*), and the five aggregates (*skandha*). They are known by seven cognitions—excluding the cognition of subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*), the cognition of cessation (*nirodha-jñāna*), and the cognition of the path (*mārga-jñāna*)—and are cognized by the six consciousnesses (*vijñāna*). All latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) of the desire realm increase in relation to them.

Only those phenomena bound to the desire realm (kāmadhātu-pratisaṃyukta-dharma) are not subsumed under four elements (dhātu), two bases (āyatana), or any aggregates (skandha); they are not known by any [supramundane] knowledge (jñāna), but are cognized by two consciousnesses (vijñāna), and all latent dispositions (anuśaya) of the desire realm increase in association with them.

Dharmas bound to the realm of form (rūpadhātu-pratisaṃyukta) are subsumed within fourteen elements (dhātu), ten bases (āyatana), and five aggregates (skandha). They are known by seven cognitions (jñāna), excluding the cognition of cessation (nirodhajñāna) and the cognition of the path (mārgajñāna); they are cognized by four consciousnesses (vijñāna), and all latent dispositions (anuśaya) of the realm of form increase therein.

Only those phenomena bound to the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) are not subsumed under any element (*dhātu*), sense-field (*āyatana*), or aggregate (*skandha*); they are not known by any cognition (*jñāna*) and are not cognized by any consciousness (*vijñāna*); yet all latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) belonging to the form realm increase in relation to them.

Dharmas associated with the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu-pratisaṃyukta) are subsumed under three realms, two bases, and four aggregates; they are known by six knowledges—excluding the knowledge of others' minds, the knowledge of cessation, and the knowledge of the path—and are cognized by one consciousness; all latent dispositions (anuśaya) of the formless realm increase in relation to them.

Only those phenomena bound to the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu-pratisaṃyukta-dharma) are not subsumed under the elements (dhātu), the bases (āyatana), or the aggregates (skandha); they are not known by knowledge (jñāna), nor cognized by consciousness (vijñāna), yet all latent dispositions (anuśaya) belonging to the formless realm increase in relation to them.

The unconditioned (apratisaṃyukta) dharmas are subsumed under two bases (āyatana), five aggregates (skandha), and three realms (dhātu). They are known by eight knowledges (jñāna), excluding the knowledge of suffering (duḥkha-jñāna) and the knowledge of origin (samudaya-jñāna); they are cognized by one consciousness (vijñāna), and no underlying tendencies (anuśaya) increase therein.

Only those dharmas that are unconditioned (apratisaṃyukta) are not subsumed under the elements (dhātu), the bases (āyatana), or the aggregates (skandha). They are known by two types of knowledge, namely the knowledge of cessation (nirodhajñāna) and the knowledge of the path (mārgajñāna); they are not cognized by consciousness, and no latent dispositions (anuśaya) increase therein.

Past phenomena are subsumed within the eighteen elements, the twelve bases, and the five aggregates; they are known by nine types of knowledge—excluding the knowledge of cessation—and are cognized by the six consciousnesses; all latent dispositions increase in relation to them.

Only past phenomena are not subsumed under the elements (*dhātu*), the bases (*āyatana*), or the aggregates (*skandha*); they are not known by cognition (*jñāna*), not cognized by consciousness (*vijñāna*), and do not serve as the basis for the increase of latent tendencies (*anuśaya*).
The same applies to future and present phenomena.

Dharmas that are neither past, nor future, nor present are comprised within one element, one base, and are not included in the aggregates. They are known by six types of knowledge—excluding the knowledge of others' minds, the knowledge of suffering, the knowledge of origin, and the knowledge of the path—and are cognized by one consciousness. Latent dispositions do not increase with respect to them.

Only those phenomena that are neither past, nor future, nor present; which are not subsumed under the elements (*dhātu*), the bases (*āyatana*), or the aggregates (*skandha*); which are known by a single cognition, namely the cognition of cessation (*nirodha-jñāna*); which are not cognized by consciousness (*vijñāna*); and in which no latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) increase.

The phenomena subsumed under the Noble Truth of Suffering are comprised within the eighteen elements, the twelve bases, and the five aggregates; they are known by seven cognitions—excluding the cognitions of origin, cessation, and the path—and are cognized by the six consciousnesses; all latent dispositions increase in relation to them.

Only those phenomena subsumed under the Noble Truth of Suffering are not subsumed under the elements (*dhātu*), the bases (*āyatana*), or the aggregates (*skandha*). They are known by a single type of knowledge, namely the knowledge of suffering; they are not cognized by consciousness, and latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) do not increase therein.

The phenomena subsumed under the noble truth of the origin are comprised within the eighteen elements, the twelve bases, and the five aggregates; they are known by seven cognitions—excluding the cognitions of suffering, cessation, and the path—and are cognized by the six consciousnesses; all latent dispositions increase in relation to them.

The phenomena subsumed under the noble truth of the origin alone are not subsumed under the elements (*dhātu*), the bases (*āyatana*), or the aggregates (*skandha*). They are known by a single cognition, namely the cognition of the origin; they are not cognized by consciousness, nor do latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) increase therein.

The phenomena subsumed under the Noble Truth of Cessation are comprised of one element (dhātu), one base (āyatana), and are not comprised of any aggregates (skandha). They are known by six types of knowledge—excluding the knowledge of others' minds, the knowledge of suffering, the knowledge of origin, and the knowledge of the path—and are cognized by one consciousness. Latent dispositions (anuśaya) do not increase therein.

The phenomena subsumed under the noble truth of cessation alone are not subsumed under the elements, the bases, or the aggregates; they are known by a single knowledge, namely the knowledge of cessation; they are not cognized by consciousness, and the latent dispositions do not increase therein.

The phenomena subsumed under the Noble Truth of the Path are subsumed within the three realms, two bases, and five aggregates; they are known by seven knowledges—excluding the knowledges of suffering, origin, and cessation—and are cognized by one consciousness; the latent dispositions do not increase therein.

The phenomena subsumed under the Noble Truth of the Path are not subsumed under any element (dhātu), sense-field (āyatana), or aggregate (skandha). They are known by a single knowledge, namely the knowledge of the path (mārgajñāna); they are not cognized by consciousness, and latent dispositions (anuśaya) do not increase therein.

Dharmas not subsumed under the truths are comprised of one element, one base, and are not comprised of any aggregate; they are known by one knowledge, namely conventional knowledge, and cognized by one consciousness, and they are not the locus where latent dispositions increase.

Only those phenomena not subsumed under the Truths (satya) are not included within the elements (dhātu), the bases (āyatana), or the aggregates (skandha); they are not known by the knowledges (jñāna), not cognized by consciousness (vijñāna), and do not serve as the basis for the increase of underlying tendencies (anuśaya).

Phenomena abandoned through the vision of suffering (duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya) are included within the three realms, two bases, and four aggregates; they are known by eight knowledges—excluding the knowledge of cessation and the knowledge of the path—and are cognized by one consciousness; all underlying tendencies abandoned through the vision of suffering, as well as the universal underlying tendencies abandoned through the vision of origin (samudaya), increase with respect to them.

Only those phenomena abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya*) are not subsumed under the elements (*dhātu*), the bases (*āyatana*), or the aggregates (*skandha*); they are not known by knowledge (*jñāna*), nor cognized by consciousness (*vijñāna*); and the non-universal latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) abandoned through the vision of suffering increase therein.

The phenomena abandoned through the vision of the origin (*samudaya-darśana-prahātavya*) are subsumed within the three realms, two bases, and four aggregates; they are known by eight knowledges, excluding the knowledge of cessation and the knowledge of the path, and are cognized by one consciousness. All latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) abandoned through the vision of the origin, as well as the universal latent dispositions abandoned through the vision of suffering, increase in relation to them.

Only those phenomena abandoned through the vision of the origin (samudaya-darśana-prahātavya) are not subsumed under the elements (dhātu), the bases (āyatana), or the aggregates (skandha); they are not known by knowledge (jñāna) and are not cognized by consciousness (vijñāna). The non-universal latent dispositions (asāmānya-anuśaya) abandoned through the vision of the origin increase in association with them.

The phenomena abandoned through the vision of cessation (*nirodhadarśana-prahātavya*) are subsumed under three realms, two bases, and four aggregates; they are known by eight knowledges—excluding the knowledge of cessation and the knowledge of the path—and cognized by one consciousness. All universal (*sarvatraga*) and non-universal (*asarvatraga*) latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) abandoned through the vision of cessation increase in association with them.

Only those phenomena abandoned through the vision of cessation (nirodha-darśana-prahātavya) are not subsumed under the elements (dhātu), the bases (āyatana), or the aggregates (skandha); they are not known by knowledge (jñāna) and are not cognized by consciousness (vijñāna). All latent dispositions (anuśaya) to be abandoned through the vision of cessation increase in relation to them.

The dharmas abandoned by the path of seeing (*darśanamārga-prahātavya*) are subsumed within the three realms, two bases, and four aggregates; they are known by eight knowledges, excluding the knowledge of cessation and the knowledge of the path, and are cognized by one consciousness; all pervasive (*sarvatraga*) and universal (*anuvartaka*) latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) are increased in relation to them.

Only those phenomena abandoned by the path of seeing (darśana-mārga-prahātavya-dharma) are not subsumed under the elements (dhātu), the bases (āyatana), or the aggregates (skandha); they are not known by knowledge (jñāna) and are not cognized by consciousness (vijñāna). All latent dispositions (anuśaya) to be abandoned by the path of seeing increase in relation to them.

The factors to be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) are subsumed within the eighteen elements (*dhātu*), the twelve bases (*āyatana*), and the five aggregates (*skandha*). They are known by eight cognitions (*jñāna*), excluding the cognition of cessation (*nirodha-jñāna*) and the cognition of the path (*mārga-jñāna*), and are cognized by the six consciousnesses (*vijñāna*). All latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) to be abandoned by cultivation, as well as the universal (*sarvatraga*) latent dispositions, increase in association with them.

Only those phenomena abandoned through cultivation consist of fifteen elements (dhātus) and ten bases (āyatanas). They are not subsumed under the aggregates (skandhas), are not known by the [supramundane] knowledges, and are cognized by the five consciousnesses. All latent dispositions (anuśayas) to be abandoned through cultivation increase in association with them.

Dharmas not to be abandoned (*apraheya*) are subsumed under the three realms (*dhātu*), two bases (*āyatana*), and five aggregates (*skandha*). They are known by eight cognitions (*jñāna*), excluding the cognition of suffering (*duḥkha-jñāna*) and the cognition of origin (*samudaya-jñāna*); they are cognized by one consciousness (*vijñāna*), and latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) do not increase therein.

Only those phenomena that are not to be abandoned (aheya-dharma) are not subsumed under the elements (dhātu), the bases (āyatana), or the aggregates (skandha). They are known by two types of knowledge—namely, the knowledge of cessation (nirodha-jñāna) and the knowledge of the path (mārga-jñāna)—are not cognized by consciousness (vijñāna), and are not increased by latent dispositions (anuśaya).

The aggregate of form (rūpaskandha) is subsumed under eleven elements (dhātu), eleven bases (āyatana), and one aggregate; it is known by eight knowledges (jñāna), excluding the knowledge of others' minds and the knowledge of cessation; it is cognized by the six consciousnesses (vijñāna); and the pervasive latent dispositions (anuśaya) of the desire and form realms, as well as those to be abandoned through cultivation, increase therein.

The aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*) is subsumed under ten elements (*dhātu*), ten bases (*āyatana*), and one aggregate; it is not known by [supramundane] knowledge, is cognized by the five consciousnesses, and is not increased by latent dispositions (*anuśaya*).

The aggregate of feeling (*vedanāskandha*) is subsumed under one element, one base, and one aggregate; it is known by nine knowledges—excluding the knowledge of cessation—and is cognized by one consciousness; all latent dispositions increase therein.

Only the aggregate of feeling (vedanā-skandha) is comprised by one aggregate, neither by the elements (dhātu) nor the bases (āyatana); it is not known by knowledge (jñāna), not cognized by consciousness (vijñāna), and no latent dispositions (anuśaya) increase therein.
The same applies to the aggregates of perception (saṃjñā) and formations (saṃskāra).

The aggregate of consciousness (vijñāna-skandha) is subsumed under seven elements (dhātu), one base (āyatana), and one aggregate; it is known by nine knowledges (jñāna), excluding the knowledge of cessation (nirodha-jñāna);

it is cognized by one consciousness (vijñāna); and all latent proclivities (anuśaya) increase therein. The aggregate of consciousness alone is subsumed under seven elements, one base, and one aggregate; it is not known by any knowledge, nor cognized by any consciousness, and no latent proclivities increase therein.

The eye-base (cakṣur-āyatana) is subsumed under one element, one base, and one aggregate; it is known by seven cognitions—excluding the cognition of others' minds and the cognitions of cessation and the path—and is cognized by one consciousness. The latent dispositions (anuśaya) that are universal in the desire and form realms, as well as those to be abandoned through cultivation, increase in association with it.

Only the eye-base (cakṣur-āyatana) consists of one element, one base, and is not included within the aggregates; it is not known by knowledge, not cognized by consciousness, and in it latent dispositions do not increase.
The same applies to the bases of the ear, nose, tongue, and body.

The sense base of form (rūpāyatana) is subsumed under one element, one base, and one aggregate; it is known by seven cognitions—excluding the cognition of others' minds, the cognition of cessation, and the cognition of the path—and is cognized by two consciousnesses; the pervasive latent dispositions (anuśaya) of the desire and form realms, as well as those to be abandoned through cultivation, increase in relation to it.

Only the sphere of visible form (rūpāyatana) comprises one element (dhātu), one base (āyatana), and is not included within the aggregates (skandha). It is not known by any [supramundane] cognition, is cognized by a single consciousness, and is not the locus where latent dispositions (anuśaya) increase.
The same applies to the spheres of sound (śabdāyatana) and tangibles (spraṣṭavyāyatana).

The sphere of fragrance (*gandhāyatana*) is subsumed under one element, one base, and one aggregate; it is known by six types of knowledge—excluding the knowledge of types (*anvayajñāna*), the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*), the knowledge of cessation (*nirodhajñāna*), and the knowledge of the path (*mārgajñāna*)—and is cognized by two consciousnesses. The latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) that are universal in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) and those to be abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) increase in association with it.

The sphere of odor alone consists of one element, one base, and is not included within the aggregates; it is not known by [the mundane] knowledge, is cognized by one consciousness, and is not increased by latent dispositions.
The same applies to the sphere of taste.

The mind-base (*manāyatana*) is subsumed under seven elements (*dhātu*), one base, and one aggregate (*skandha*); it is known by nine knowledges, excluding the knowledge of cessation (*nirodhajñāna*); it is cognized by one consciousness; and all latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) increase therein.

The exclusive mind-base is subsumed under seven elements, one base, and one aggregate; it is not known by any knowledge, not cognized by any consciousness, and no latent dispositions increase therein.

The sphere of phenomena (*dharmāyatana*) is subsumed under one element, one sphere, and four aggregates; it is known by ten knowledges and cognized by one consciousness; all latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) increase therein.

The exclusive sphere of phenomena is subsumed under one element, one sphere, and three aggregates; it is known by one knowledge, namely the knowledge of cessation (*nirodhajñāna*); it is not cognized by consciousness, nor do latent dispositions increase therein.

The eye-element (cakṣurdhātu) is subsumed under one element, one base, and one aggregate; it is known by seven knowledges—excluding the knowledge of others' minds, the knowledge of cessation, and the knowledge of the path—and is cognized by one consciousness; the latent dispositions (anuśaya) that are universal in the desire and form realms, as well as those to be abandoned through cultivation, increase therein.

Only the eye-element (cakṣurdhātu) comprises one element, one base, and is not subsumed under any aggregate; it is not known by knowledge, not cognized by consciousness, and in it latent dispositions do not increase.
The same applies to the ear-, nose-, tongue-, and body-elements.

The form realm (rūpadhātu) is comprised of one element, one base, and one aggregate; it is known by seven knowledges—excluding the knowledge of others' minds, the knowledge of cessation, and the knowledge of the path—and is cognized by two consciousnesses; the pervasive latent dispositions (anuśaya) of the desire and form realms, as well as those to be abandoned through cultivation, increase therein.

Only the form realm (rūpadhātu) consists of one element (dhātu), one base (āyatana), and is not subsumed under any aggregate (skandha); it is not known by any cognition (jñāna), is cognized by one consciousness (vijñāna), and is not the locus where latent dispositions (anuśaya) increase.
The same applies to the sound element (śabdadhātu) and the tangible element (spraṣṭavyadhātu).

The fragrance element (*gandhadhātu*) is subsumed under one element, one base, and one aggregate; it is known by six types of knowledge—excluding the knowledge of categories (*anvayajñāna*), the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*), the knowledge of cessation (*nirodhajñāna*), and the knowledge of the path (*mārgajñāna*)—and is cognized by two consciousnesses. The latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) that are universal in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) and those to be abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanāheya*) increase in association with it.

Only the fragrance element (*gandhadhātu*)—one element, one base—is not subsumed under the aggregates; it is not known by [the six] cognitions, but is cognized by one consciousness; and latent dispositions do not increase therein.
The taste element (*rasadhātu*) is likewise.
The mind-element (*manodhātu*) is as [explained for] the mind-base (*manāyatana*).
The phenomena-element (*dharmadhātu*) is as [explained for] the phenomena-base (*dharmāyatana*).

The eye-consciousness-element (*cakṣurvijñānadhātu*) is subsumed under two elements, one base, and one aggregate; it is known by eight knowledges, excluding the knowledge of cessation and the knowledge of the path; it is cognized by one consciousness; and the pervasive latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) of the desire and form realms, as well as those to be abandoned through cultivation, increase therein.

Only the eye-consciousness element (cakṣurvijñānadhātu) is comprised of one element, but is not comprised of any base (āyatana) or aggregate (skandha); it is not known by knowledge (jñāna), not cognized by consciousness (vijñāna), and is not the locus for the increase of latent dispositions (anuśaya).
The same applies to the ear-, body-, and mind-consciousness elements.

The nose-consciousness element (ghrāṇavijñānadhātu) is subsumed under two elements, one base, and one aggregate; it is known by seven knowledges—excluding the knowledge of types (anvayajñāna), the knowledge of cessation (nirodhajñāna), and the knowledge of the path (mārgajñāna)—and is cognized by one consciousness. The pervasive (sarvatraga) and cultivation-abandoned (bhāvanā-heya) latent dispositions (anuśaya) of the desire realm increase [in association] with it.

Only the nose-consciousness element (ghrāṇavijñānadhātu) is comprised of one element, neither a base nor an aggregate; it is not known by cognition, not cognized by consciousness, and latent dispositions do not increase therein.
The tongue-consciousness element is likewise.

The consciousness element (manovijñānadhātu) is comprised of two elements, one base, and one aggregate; it is known by nine knowledges, excluding the knowledge of cessation (nirodhajñāna); it is cognized by one consciousness; and all latent dispositions (anuśaya) increase therein.

The mental consciousness element (*manovijñānadhātu*) alone is comprised of one element, neither a base (*āyatana*) nor an aggregate (*skandha*); it is not known by any cognition (*jñāna*), not cognized by any consciousness (*vijñāna*), and is not the locus for the increase of latent dispositions (*anuśaya*). The eye faculty (*cakṣurindriya*) is comprised of one element, one base, and one aggregate;

it is known by seven cognitions—excluding the cognition of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*), the cognition of cessation (*nirodhajñāna*), and the cognition of the path (*mārgajñāna*)—and is cognized by one consciousness; the universal latent dispositions of the desire and form realms (*kāma- and rūpadhātu-kleśa*) as well as those to be abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) increase therein.

The eye faculty consists of one element, one base, and is not included within the aggregates; it is not known by knowledge, not cognized by consciousness, and is not the locus where latent tendencies increase.
The same applies to the faculties of the ear, nose, tongue, and body.

The female faculty (*strī-indriya*) is subsumed under one element, one base, and one aggregate; it is known by six types of knowledge—excluding the knowledge of subsequent realization (*anvaya-jñāna*), the knowledge of others' minds (*paracitta-jñāna*), the knowledge of cessation (*nirodha-jñāna*), and the knowledge of the path (*mārga-jñāna*)—and is cognized by one consciousness; the pervasive (*sarvatraga*) and cultivation-abandoned (*bhāvanā-heya*) latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) of the desire realm increase in association with it.

Only the female faculty (strī-indriya) is not subsumed under the elements (dhātu), the bases (āyatana), or the aggregates (skandha); it is not known by the knowledges (jñāna), not cognized by consciousness (vijñāna), and in it latent dispositions (anuśaya) do not increase.
The male faculty (puruṣa-indriya) is likewise.

The life-faculty (jīvitendriya) is subsumed under one element, one base, and one aggregate; it is known by seven knowledges—excluding the knowledge of others' minds, the knowledge of cessation, and the knowledge of the path—and is cognized by one consciousness. The latent dispositions (anuśaya) that are universal throughout the three realms and those to be abandoned through cultivation increase in association with it.

Only the life-faculty (jīvitendriya) is not subsumed under the elements (dhātu), the bases (āyatana), or the aggregates (skandha); it is not known by knowledge (jñāna), not cognized by consciousness (vijñāna), and in it latent dispositions (anuśaya) do not increase.
The mind-faculty (manendriya) is as explained under the mind-base (mana-āyatana).

The faculty of pleasure (*sukhendriya*) is subsumed under one element, one base, and one aggregate; it is known by nine knowledges, excluding the knowledge of cessation (*nirodhajñāna*), and is cognized by one consciousness. It is associated with all latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), the universal [latent dispositions] of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), and those to be abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*).

The pleasure faculty (*sukhendriya*) alone is not subsumed under any element (*dhātu*), sense-field (*āyatana*), or aggregate (*skandha*); it is not known by any cognition (*jñāna*), not cognized by any consciousness (*vijñāna*), and is not increased by any underlying tendency (*anuśaya*).

The pain faculty (*duḥkhendriya*) is subsumed under one element, one sense-field, and one aggregate; it is known by seven cognitions—excluding the cognition of subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*), the cognition of cessation (*nirodhajñāna*), and the cognition of the path (*mārgajñāna*)—and is cognized by one consciousness. It is increased by the pervasive underlying tendencies of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) and those to be abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*).

The faculty of suffering (*duḥkhendriya*) alone is not subsumed under any element (*dhātu*), sense-field (*āyatana*), or aggregate (*skandha*); it is not known by any cognition (*jñāna*), nor cognized by any consciousness (*vijñāna*), and no latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) increase in relation to it.

The faculty of joy (*saumanasyendriya*) is subsumed under one element, one sense-field, and one aggregate. It is known by nine cognitions, excluding the cognition of cessation (*nirodhajñāna*), and is cognized by one consciousness. All latent dispositions of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) increase in relation to it; furthermore, all other latent dispositions of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) increase in relation to it, with the exception of doubt (*vicikitsā*) that takes the untainted as its object and the ignorance (*avidyā*) associated with that doubt.

The faculty of joy (*sukhendriya*) is not subsumed under any element (*dhātu*), sense-base (*āyatana*), or aggregate (*skandha*); it is not known by any cognition (*jñāna*), nor is it cognized by consciousness (*vijñāna*), and no latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) increase therein.

The faculty of grief (*daurmanasyendriya*) is subsumed under one element, one sense-base, and one aggregate; it is known by seven cognitions—excluding the cognition of similarity (*anvayajñāna*), the cognition of cessation (*nirodhajñāna*), and the cognition of the path (*mārgajñāna*)—and is cognized by one consciousness; all latent dispositions of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) increase therein.

Only the faculty of sorrow (*daurmanasyendriya*) is not subsumed under any element (*dhātu*), sense-field (*āyatana*), or aggregate (*skandha*); it is not known by any cognition (*jñāna*), not cognized by any consciousness (*vijñāna*), and no latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) increase therein.

The faculty of equanimity (*upekṣendriya*) is subsumed under one element, one sense-field, and one aggregate; it is known by nine cognitions, excluding the cognition of cessation (*nirodhajñāna*), and is cognized by one consciousness; all latent dispositions increase therein.

Only the faculty of equanimity (*upekṣendriya*) is not subsumed under any element (*dhātu*), base (*āyatana*), or aggregate (*skandha*); it is not known by any cognition (*jñāna*), not cognized by any consciousness (*vijñāna*), and no latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) increase therein.

The faculty of faith (*śraddhendriya*) is subsumed under one element, one base, and one aggregate; it is known by nine cognitions, excluding the cognition of cessation (*nirodhajñāna*); it is cognized by one consciousness; and the latent dispositions that are universal throughout the three realms as well as those to be abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) increase therein.

Only the faculty of faith (śraddhendriya) is not subsumed under the elements (dhātu), the bases (āyatana), or the aggregates (skandha); it is not known by knowledge (jñāna), not cognized by consciousness (vijñāna), and in it latent dispositions (anuśaya) do not increase.
The same applies to the faculties of energy (vīrya), mindfulness (smṛti), concentration (samādhi), and wisdom (prajñā).

The faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīndriya) is subsumed under three realms, two bases, and three aggregates; it is known by seven cognitions—excluding the cognitions of suffering, origin, and cessation—and is cognized by one consciousness; it is not increased by latent dispositions (anuśaya).

Only the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (ājñāsyāmīndriya) is not subsumed under the elements (dhātu), the bases (āyatana), or the aggregates (skandha); it is not known by any cognition (jñāna), not cognized by consciousness (vijñāna), and in it no latent dispositions (anuśaya) increase.
The same applies to the faculty of "having known" (ājñendriya) and the faculty of "one who has fully known" (ājñātāvīndriya).

The latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) to be abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya*) in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) are subsumed under one element (*dhātu*), one base (*āyatana*), and one aggregate (*skandha*). They are known by seven cognitions—excluding the cognition of subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*), the cognition of cessation (*nirodha-jñāna*), and the cognition of the path (*mārga-jñāna*)—and are cognized by one consciousness. All latent dispositions to be abandoned through the vision of suffering in the desire realm, as well as the universal (*sarvatraga*) latent dispositions to be abandoned through the vision of origin (*samudaya-darśana-prahātavya*), increase in association with them.

Only those latent dispositions (anuśaya) abandoned through the vision of suffering within the desire realm are not subsumed under the elements (dhātu), the bases (āyatana), or the aggregates (skandha); they are not known by knowledge (jñāna), not cognized by consciousness (vijñāna), and do not increase through the proliferation of latent dispositions.

The latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) to be abandoned by the vision of the origin (*samudaya-darśana-prahātavya*) in the desire realm are subsumed under one element, one base, and one aggregate; they are known by seven cognitions—excluding the cognition of subsequent knowledge, the cognition of cessation, and the cognition of the path—and are cognized by one consciousness. All such dispositions to be abandoned by the vision of the origin, as well as the universal (*sarvatraga*) latent dispositions to be abandoned by the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya*), increase in association with them.

The latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) to be abandoned through the vision of cessation (*nirodha-darśana-prahātavya*) in the desire realm are subsumed under one element (*dhātu*), one base (*āyatana*), and one aggregate (*skandha*). They are known by seven cognitions—excluding the cognition of subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*), the cognition of cessation (*nirodha-jñāna*), and the cognition of the path (*mārga-jñāna*)—and are cognized by one consciousness. With the exception of the unique ignorance (*āveṇika-avidyā*) to be abandoned through the vision of cessation in the desire realm, all other latent dispositions to be abandoned through the vision of cessation in the desire realm, as well as the universal (*sarvatraga*) latent dispositions, increase in association with them.

Only the latent dispositions (anuśaya) to be abandoned through the vision of the cessation [of suffering] in the desire realm are not subsumed under the elements (dhātu), the bases (āyatana), or the aggregates (skandha); they are not known by knowledge (jñāna), not cognized by consciousness (vijñāna), and do not increase as latent dispositions.

With the exception of the unique ignorance (*āveṇikī avidyā*) to be abandoned by the path of seeing in the desire realm, all other latent dispositions to be abandoned by the path of seeing in the desire realm, as well as the universal (*sarvatraga*) latent dispositions, increase in association with them.

Only those latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) abandoned by the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) within the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) are not subsumed under the elements (*dhātu*), the bases (*āyatana*), or the aggregates (*skandha*); they are not known by the knowledges (*jñāna*), not cognized by consciousness (*vijñāna*), and do not increase through the proliferation of latent dispositions.

The proclivities (*anuśaya*) to be abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) are subsumed within one element (*dhātu*), one base (*āyatana*), and one aggregate (*skandha*). They are cognized by one consciousness (*vijñāna*). All proclivities to be abandoned through cultivation in the desire realm, as well as the universal (*sarvatraga*) proclivities, increase (*anuśerate*) in relation to them.

The latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya*) in the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) are comprised within one element (*dhātu*), one base (*āyatana*), and one aggregate (*skandha*). They are known by seven cognitions, excluding the cognition of cessation (*nirodha-jñāna*) and the cognition of the path (*mārga-jñāna*), and are cognized by one consciousness. All [defilements] abandoned through the vision of suffering and all pervasive (*sarvatraga*) latent dispositions abandoned through the vision of origin (*samudaya-darśana-prahātavya*) increase in association with them.
